entries.name: Abhyanga (Ayurvedic oil massage)
entries.uses: In Ayurveda this is part of dinacharya, the daily routine. People rub warm sesame or herbal oil over the whole body before bathing, to calm vata (the airy, restless energy) and keep the skin and joints supple. Champi, an oil massage of the head, is done before sleep and is common in Indian families. Clinics also offer it with two therapists working in time.

lore.text: In Sanskrit sneha means both oil and love, so oiling the body is a kind of affection.

research.text: A few small studies on stress, and studies on oil massage of newborn babies.

safety.summary: Oil makes floors and bathtubs slippery. Some people react to the oils, and sesame oil can set off a sesame allergy.

entries.what: A massage where you rub warm oil into your own skin before a bath, from India.
entries.know: The English word shampoo comes from the Hindi chāmpo, "press, knead": it first meant a head massage.

entries.name: Aconite (monkshood, wolfsbane)
entries.latin: Aconitum napellus; A. carmichaelii (fu zi, Chinese)
preps: TCM: long-processed fu zi in decoctions; Ayurveda: purified vatsanabha
entries.uses: In Chinese medicine the heavily processed side root, fu zi, is traditionally used to "rescue collapsed yang" (to revive the body's warm, active force when it fails) and to warm cold, painful joints. In Ayurveda a purified root, vatsanabha, is used in tiny amounts. In Europe it was historically a poison for wolves, arrow tips and enemies.

history.text: Studies from Hong Kong found aconite the leading cause of serious herbal poisoning there, often from badly processed roots.

lore.text: Greek myth says it sprang from the foaming jaws of Cerberus when Heracles dragged the hound up from the underworld. It is Hecate's herb, and Medea was said to use it. In later werewolf stories wolfsbane keeps the beast away.

research.text: Aconitine causes fatal heart rhythms. Long boiling and processing lower it but do not remove it.

safety.summary: Deadly. Tingling and numbness of the mouth and limbs come first, then vomiting and a chaotic heartbeat that can kill within hours. Poisonings follow even from handling the root and from badly processed fu zi. Never prepare it at home. Poisoning is an emergency. History and lore only.
safety.pets: Poisonous to pets and livestock.

entries.what: A tall plant with hooded blue-purple flowers, among the most poisonous plants of Europe and Asia.

entries.name: Aconitum napellus (homeopathic)
entries.uses: In homeopathy, the first remedy reached for after sudden fear, panic or shock, and for fevers and colds that start suddenly after a cold, dry wind.

research.text: No good trials show a reliable effect beyond placebo.

safety.summary: The plant is one of the deadliest in Europe: its poison, aconitine, can pass through the skin and stop the heart. Never handle the plant. Avoided in pregnancy.

entries.what: Monkshood diluted into homeopathy's remedy for sudden fright and colds that come on fast.
entries.know: Its other name, wolfsbane, comes from its old use as a poison for wolves.

entries.name: Acupressure and shiatsu
entries.uses: People press the same points used in acupuncture. P6 (Neiguan), about three finger-widths above the inner wrist crease, is pressed for nausea, and travel-sickness wristbands press it with a small plastic stud. LI4 (Hegu), in the web between thumb and first finger, is pressed for headaches. Tui na and shiatsu work the points and channels in a full massage.

research.text: Several trials found P6 pressure and wristbands reduced nausea and vomiting after surgery compared with fake points, though the studies were of low quality. Results for morning sickness are mixed.

safety.summary: LI4 and SP6 (a hand-width above the inner ankle) are traditionally avoided in pregnancy, because they were thought to bring on labour. Pressing hard on bruises, broken skin, varicose veins or fresh injuries can hurt them.

entries.what: Firm finger pressure on acupuncture points instead of needles, including Japanese shiatsu and Chinese tui na massage.

entries.name: Acupuncture
parts: fine needles at points along meridians
entries.uses: In Chinese medicine, needles go into points along the meridians (the channels that carry qi, the body's life energy) to move qi and blood. Traditionally used for pain and a very wide range of other problems. Japan and Korea have their own styles; Japanese needles are often thinner and set through a guide tube.

history.text: First described in the Huangdi Neijing (the Yellow Emperor's Inner Classic), compiled around the 2nd to 1st century BCE. Interest in the West took off in 1971, after a New York Times reporter wrote about the acupuncture he was given in Beijing for pain after surgery.

lore.text: Qi flows through twelve main meridians, like rivers, and eight extra vessels that act like reservoirs. The standard map has 361 points on the meridians, each with a name, such as Hegu, "joining valley", in the web of the thumb.

research.text: Reviews found a modest effect on chronic pain (back, neck, knee arthritis), fewer tension headaches and migraines, and less vomiting after chemotherapy. Fake-needle comparisons are hard to design, and how much of the effect is placebo is still argued over.

safety.summary: Risks are low with trained hands and single-use sterile needles. Rare problems are a punctured lung from needles in the chest or upper back, infections and fainting. Bleeding disorders raise the risk of bleeding and bruising. Some points are traditionally avoided in pregnancy.

entries.what: Fine needles placed at set points on the body, from Chinese medicine and now used around the world.
entries.know: Song dynasty China cast bronze teaching figures marked with the points; for exams they were said to be waxed over and filled with water, which spurted out when a student hit a point.

sources.title: NCCIH, health topics A-Z (practices: acupuncture, massage, yoga, tai chi, meditation)

entries.name: African potato
entries.uses: Zulu and Sotho healers traditionally boil the corm (the swollen underground stem) for urinary and prostate troubles and as a general tonic. In South Africa in the AIDS years it was heavily promoted as an immune tonic.

history.text: In the early 2000s South Africa's health ministry promoted it, with garlic, beetroot and lemon, while delaying antiretroviral drugs. A 2008 Harvard study estimated that the delay cost more than 330,000 lives.

research.text: Plant sterols (beta-sitosterol) like those it contains eased urinary symptoms of an enlarged prostate in a Cochrane review, but the corm itself has barely been tested. It showed no benefit in HIV.

safety.summary: Lab studies show it can change the liver enzymes that clear many HIV medicines; a small human study found no change in one of them (efavirenz). Not used in pregnancy.

entries.what: A grassland plant with yellow star flowers and a dark tuber-like root, boiled as a tonic in southern Africa.

entries.name: African wormwood
entries.uses: One of the most used medicines in southern Africa. People drink the bitter tea for colds, coughs and fevers, breathe in its steam, push a rolled fresh leaf into the nostril for a blocked nose, and burn it to clear a sickroom.

research.text: Mostly lab studies. A 2019 trial claiming its tea beat malaria pills was retracted.

safety.summary: Contains thujone, which in large or long use can cause fits. Not used in pregnancy.

entries.what: A feathery grey, strongly scented wormwood that grows across southern and eastern Africa.
entries.know: Unlike its Chinese cousin sweet wormwood, African wormwood contains little or no artemisinin, the antimalarial compound.

entries.name: Agrimony
entries.uses: Traditionally drunk as a tea for loose bowels, gargled for a sore throat, and used to wash small cuts. It is astringent, meaning its tannins tighten and dry the tissue they touch. The EMA, the EU's medicines agency, accepts traditional use for mild diarrhoea, a sore mouth or throat, and small surface wounds.

history.text: Anglo-Saxon healers wrote it into their leechbooks (handwritten medical books) as a wound herb. Later it was one of the herbs in eau d'arquebusade, a wound water made for soldiers hurt by early firearms.

lore.text: Laid under the pillow, it was said to bring a sleep so deep the sleeper would not wake until it was taken away.

research.text: Rich in tannins, but almost untested in people. The EMA's listing rests on long use, not on trials.

safety.summary: Usually gentle as a tea. The tannins can upset a sensitive stomach, and drunk with meals they reduce how much iron you absorb.

entries.what: A tall wayside plant of the rose family with spikes of small yellow flowers, dried for an astringent tea.

entries.name: Ajwain
entries.uses: In India people chew a pinch with salt for wind and indigestion. In Tamil homes omam water, seeds boiled in water, was given for colic, including to babies. Seeds dropped in hot water make a steam for blocked noses.

research.text: Studied in cells and animals, mostly for thymol.

safety.summary: The oil (thymol) irritates skin and the gut. Babies are sensitive to it; WHO advice is breast milk or formula alone for the first six months, with no waters or teas.

entries.what: Tiny striped seeds tasting strongly of thyme, used in Indian breads, snacks and home remedies.

entries.name: Alfalfa
entries.uses: Traditionally taken as a nourishing spring tonic and during recovery from illness, much as farmers fed it to animals to build them up. In modern herbalism it is sold for cholesterol and general vitality.

history.text: Grown in Persia (Iran) and brought into Greece around 490 BCE as fodder for the horses of Persian armies. The word alfalfa came into Spanish from Arabic, and goes back to a Persian word for horse fodder. The popular gloss "father of all foods" is a modern story, not the word's real meaning.

research.text: Its saponins (soapy plant compounds) block some cholesterol absorption in animals. A few very small human studies in the 1980s saw cholesterol fall on alfalfa seed. Nothing larger has followed.

safety.summary: Seeds and sprouts contain L-canavanine, an amino acid linked to a lupus-like illness in monkeys and to flare-ups in people with lupus. Raw sprouts have caused Salmonella and E. coli outbreaks; pregnant people, small children, older people and anyone with a weak immune system are advised not to eat them raw. The leaf is high in vitamin K, which works against warfarin.

entries.what: The pea-family fodder crop also called lucerne, eaten as sprouts and sold as a dried-leaf supplement.
entries.know: Its Latin name, Medicago, comes from Media, the ancient Persian land the Greeks believed it came from.

sources.title: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database

entries.name: Alisma
preps: in Wu Ling San, Liu Wei Di Huang Wan
entries.uses: In Chinese medicine ze xie "drains damp" (heavy, stuck fluid) out through the urine. It is traditionally used for swelling, scanty urination and dizziness said to come from fluid pooling in the body.

research.text: Animal studies on urine output.

safety.summary: It acts as a diuretic, so it may add to water pills. The fresh plant irritates the skin and gut. High doses harmed the kidneys of lab animals.

entries.what: The bulb-like root of a water plantain, a marsh plant, used in Chinese medicine to drain fluid.

sources.title: Bensky, Clavey & Stöger, Chinese Herbal Medicine: Materia Medica, 3rd ed. (2004)

entries.name: Allium cepa
entries.uses: In homeopathy, given for hay fever and colds with a streaming, burning nose and mild, watery eyes, like the effect of peeling onions.

research.text: No good trials show a reliable effect beyond placebo.

safety.summary: At usual potencies there is no measurable onion.

entries.what: Red onion diluted into a homeopathic remedy for hay fever with a streaming nose.
entries.know: Cutting an onion releases a sulphur gas that stings the eyes into watering.

entries.name: Allspice
entries.uses: In Jamaica people drink allspice tea for colds and wind and soak in leaf baths for aching muscles. It is the key spice of jerk seasoning. The Maya are said to have used it in embalming.

lore.text: Burned or carried for money and luck.

research.text: Rich in eugenol, the same oil as clove; studied only in the lab.

safety.summary: Food amounts are fine.

entries.what: The dried berry of a Caribbean tree, tasting like cinnamon, clove and nutmeg at once.
entries.know: English cooks named it allspice in the 1600s because it seemed to taste of every spice together.

entries.name: Aloe vera
entries.uses: The clear inner gel is spread on burns, sunburn and dry skin. The bitter yellow latex, the sap just under the leaf skin, was traditionally taken as a purgative (a strong laxative that empties the bowel). In Ayurveda, where the plant is called kumari ("young girl"), it is used for the skin and the menstrual cycle.

history.text: Aloe appears in the Ebers Papyrus, an Egyptian medical scroll from about 1550 BCE. Arab traders carried it along their sea routes. Across the Caribbean a pot of it still sits by many kitchen doors.

lore.text: Hung over doorways in Mexico and the Middle East for luck and to keep harm out. In Egypt it was called the plant of immortality.

research.text: Studies of the gel on burns and wounds have mixed results. In 2002 the US stopped over-the-counter sale of aloe laxatives because no maker sent safety data. In a 2011 study by the US National Toxicology Program, whole-leaf extract caused gut tumours in rats.

safety.summary: The gel on skin is usually fine; try a small patch first. Latex and whole-leaf products taken by mouth can cause cramps, diarrhoea, low potassium and kidney damage, and liver injury has been reported.
safety.pets: Toxic to cats and dogs if eaten (ASPCA): vomiting, diarrhoea and lethargy.
safety.regulatory: Aloe latex laxatives were removed from US over-the-counter sale in 2002. Since 2021 the EU has restricted hydroxyanthracene derivatives, the laxative compounds in aloe latex, in foods.

entries.cat: The gel's for your sunburn, not my lunch. I checked. You didn't.
entries.what: A spiky succulent whose leaves hold a clear gel for the skin and a bitter yellow sap that purges.
entries.know: Aloe vera is not known anywhere in the wild. It probably came from the Arabian Peninsula and has been spread by people for thousands of years.

entries.name: Amadou (tinder fungus)
entries.uses: Traditionally pressed on cuts to stop bleeding (barbers and surgeons once kept amadou pads for this) and used as tinder to catch a spark and carry fire.

history.text: For tinder it was boiled, dried and beaten flat, sometimes soaked in saltpetre. In parts of Romania craftspeople still make hats and bags from the felted fungus, and fly fishers use it to dry their flies.

research.text: Hardly studied.

safety.summary: It is not sterile, so it can carry germs into a wound.

entries.what: A soft, felt-like layer cut from a hoof-shaped tree fungus, used to light fires and to stop bleeding.
entries.know: Ötzi the Iceman, who died in the Alps about 5,300 years ago, carried pieces of this fungus in his kit, along with birch polypore.

entries.name: Amalaki (amla)
entries.uses: It is one of the three fruits in triphala and the base of chyawanprash, a herbal jam. In Ayurveda it is a rasayana (a rejuvenating tonic). People eat it fresh or pickled, drink the juice, and rub amla oil into their hair. It is also traditionally used for the eyes and digestion.

lore.text: Ayurveda says it holds five of the six tastes, all but salty. It is cooling and balances all three doshas (the body's energies of air, fire and water), above all pitta, the hot, fiery one. The amla tree is worshipped on Amalaki Ekadashi, a spring fast day sacred to Vishnu.

research.text: The fruit is rich in vitamin C and tannins. Small trials have looked at cholesterol and blood sugar.

safety.summary: Generally gentle. It may lower blood sugar and slightly slow blood clotting.

entries.what: A sour, pale-green Indian gooseberry, eaten fresh or pickled and used as the base of many Ayurvedic tonics.

entries.name: American ginseng
entries.uses: Haudenosaunee (Iroquois), Meskwaki and other nations used the root as a tonic and as a love medicine. In Chinese medicine it is xi yang shen, a cooling tonic for qi (vital energy) and yin (the body's cool, moist side), given for exhaustion with heat and dryness.

history.text: A French Jesuit missionary found it near Montreal in 1716, with help from Mohawk people, after reading about Chinese ginseng. A trade to China followed. Daniel Boone dug and sold "sang". It is still a major export to Asia.

research.text: Small trials suggest it may lower blood sugar after meals. A patented extract was tested for colds with modest results. The evidence is limited.

safety.summary: May lower blood sugar. Some people sleep badly on it. In one trial it weakened the effect of warfarin, a blood thinner.
safety.regulatory: On CITES Appendix II. Wild harvest is licensed and seasonal under US state rules.
safety.ethics: Wild plants are badly depleted and poaching is common. Buy cultivated or certified woods-grown root.

entries.what: A forest root of eastern North America, prized in China as a cooling tonic and shipped there for 300 years.
entries.know: Wisconsin farms grow most of the cultivated ginseng in the United States.

entries.name: American skullcap
entries.uses: Cherokee people used it for women's complaints such as late periods. In the 1800s American herbalists made it their nerve tonic for tension, twitching and sleeplessness. The name mad-dog skullcap comes from an 18th-century claim that it was a remedy for rabies.

research.text: One small trial in healthy adults found a calmer mood.

safety.summary: Past cases of liver injury were mostly traced to products mixed or swapped with germander, a plant that harms the liver. Buy tested products. It can add to sedatives.

entries.what: A small blue-flowered mint of North American wetlands, taken as a tea or tincture for frayed nerves.
entries.know: Skullcap is named for the little helmet-shaped cup that holds each seed.

entries.name: Angelica
entries.uses: Traditionally taken as a warming bitter (a bitter-tasting herb used to rouse a slow stomach) for weak digestion, wind and poor appetite, and for chesty coughs. The root is one of the flavours of Chartreuse, Bénédictine and many gins.

history.text: One of the first herbs grown in gardens in the far north. Norse farmers grew and traded it in Norway and Iceland by Viking times. In plague-time Europe people chewed the root against contagion.

lore.text: Said to have been shown to a monk by an archangel in a time of plague, and to bloom on the feast of the archangel Michael. Worn to ward off witchcraft and evil spirits.

research.text: Its essential oil and furanocoumarins (plant compounds that make skin sensitive to light) have been studied in the lab. Angelica root is one of nine herbs in Iberogast, a German blend with several trials for indigestion. Angelica on its own has not been tested.

safety.summary: Furanocoumarins can make skin burn and blister in sunlight. Wild plants of the same carrot family include deadly hemlock and water hemlock, which look very alike. Never forage it without certain identification.

entries.what: A tall, sweet-smelling herb of the far north whose root and seeds flavour gin and herbal liqueurs.
entries.know: Candied green angelica stems were once a standard decoration on British cakes and trifles.

entries.name: Anise
entries.uses: A tea of the seeds is a traditional remedy for wind and for coughs with a cold; the EU's herbal committee lists both. Nursing mothers in the Mediterranean and Middle East drink it to make more milk.

history.text: Romans served mustaceum, a cake with anise and other seeds, at the end of feasts, and it is sometimes called an ancestor of wedding cake.

lore.text: Kept by the bed against nightmares, and hung up against the evil eye.

research.text: Little modern research.

safety.summary: In large amounts it has weak oestrogen-like effects. People allergic to celery, carrot or fennel may react.

entries.what: Small grey-green seeds with a sweet liquorice taste, the flavour behind ouzo, raki and pastis.
entries.know: Ouzo turns cloudy white when you add water, because anise oil falls out of the alcohol as tiny droplets.

entries.name: AOD-9604
entries.uses: Sold in clinics and online for fat loss and joint cartilage, by injection or by mouth.

history.text: Developed in Melbourne, Australia, in the 1990s. Its maker dropped it as an obesity drug after a large trial failed in 2007. It came up again in Australia's 2013 sports-doping inquiries.

research.text: Phase 2b trials with hundreds of people found no meaningful weight loss compared with placebo. The joint claims rest on animal work.

safety.summary: Long-term safety is unknown. Grey-market vials carry contamination and dosing risks.
safety.regulatory: As of November 2026: not approved as a medicine. FDA took it off Category 2 in September 2024 after the nomination was withdrawn, and its advisers reviewed it in December 2024; it is not on the list pharmacies may compound from. Prohibited by WADA (S2).

entries.what: A modified fragment of human growth hormone, sold for fat loss after it failed as a diet drug.

entries.name: Apis mellifica
entries.uses: In homeopathy, given for hot, pink, puffy swellings that sting and feel better for cold: insect stings, hives, swollen eyelids.

research.text: No good trials show a reliable effect beyond placebo.

safety.summary: At usual potencies the pills contain no measurable bee. Never for anaphylaxis: swelling of the lips, tongue or throat, or trouble breathing, is an emergency; use adrenaline and call emergency services.

entries.what: A homeopathic remedy made from the whole honeybee, matched to stinging, puffy swellings.

entries.name: Argan oil
entries.uses: Amazigh (Berber) women of south-west Morocco traditionally crack the nuts by hand and press the oil. Roasted kernels give a cooking oil, raw ones an oil for skin and hair. Amlou, a spread of argan oil, almonds and honey, is eaten for strength.

history.text: The argan forest became a UNESCO biosphere reserve in 1998, and UNESCO listed the know-how of argan as intangible heritage in 2014. Women's cooperatives now press much of the oil.

research.text: Mostly cosmetic studies, plus a few small diet studies.

safety.summary: Allergy is rare.
safety.ethics: Choose oil from women's cooperatives; the forests are under threat.

entries.what: A golden oil from the kernels of the argan tree of south-west Morocco, eaten and used on hair and skin.
entries.know: Goats really do climb argan trees, right up into the branches, to eat the fruit.

entries.name: Aristolochia (birthwort)
entries.latin: Aristolochia spp.; mislabelled as Stephania or Akebia (guang fang ji, guan mu tong)
entries.uses: Its Greek name means "best birth": in old Europe it was given to women in labour and to bring out the afterbirth. Chinese medicine used several species for swelling and joint pain. It is now banned in many countries.

history.text: In early-1990s Belgium a slimming clinic's pills had Aristolochia swapped in for a similar-named Chinese herb. Over 100 women got kidney failure, many needed dialysis or a transplant, and many later got cancers of the urinary tract. Balkan endemic nephropathy, a kidney disease of Danube villages, was traced to Aristolochia seeds mixed into wheat flour.

research.text: Aristolochic acid is a known human carcinogen (IARC Group 1) and a kidney poison.

safety.summary: It destroys the kidneys and causes cancer, even in small amounts, sometimes years later. There is no safe dose. Imported herbal products have been found to hide Aristolochia under other names.
safety.regulatory: Banned or recalled in the US (FDA import alert, 2001), the UK, Australia, Canada and many EU countries. China removed several Aristolochia herbs from its official pharmacopoeia in the 2000s.

entries.cat: The kidney-killer with a pretty name. Check the label, then check it again.
entries.what: A group of climbing plants with pipe-shaped flowers, once used in childbirth and now known to wreck the kidneys.
entries.know: Many Aristolochia flowers trap flies inside overnight, dust them with pollen and then let them go.

entries.name: Arjuna
entries.uses: In Ayurveda the bark is the classic heart herb. People boil it in milk (kshirapaka) or take it as a powder.

history.text: Arjuna is Sanskrit for "white" or "bright", for the smooth pale bark; the hero of the Mahabharata carries the same name. Later classical Ayurvedic texts name the bark for the heart.

research.text: Small Indian trials in angina and heart failure; the quality is limited.

safety.summary: It adds to the effect of heart, blood-pressure and blood-thinning drugs.

entries.what: A large riverside tree of India whose pale bark is boiled in milk as the classic Ayurvedic heart tonic.
entries.know: Its leaves feed the caterpillars of the tasar silk moth, whose golden wild silk is woven in eastern India.

sources.title: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India
Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database

entries.name: Arnica
entries.uses: Rubbed on unbroken skin for bruises, sprains and aching muscles. The EMA accepts traditional external use for bruises, sprains and local muscle pain.

history.text: A staple in Alpine and Carpathian mountain homes. A famous German poet is said to have drunk arnica tea for his heart in old age.

lore.text: In German folk custom, bunches were set at the corners of fields at Midsummer to guard the harvest from storms.

research.text: Some trials of arnica gel found small effects on bruising. One found it did about as well as ibuprofen gel for arthritis pain in the hands. Overall the results are mixed.

safety.summary: Only on unbroken skin. Swallowed, the plant is poisonous: it can cause vomiting and dangerous heart effects. On the skin it can cause an itchy allergic rash, especially in people allergic to daisies. Homeopathic arnica is a different thing, with its own entry.
safety.pets: Toxic to pets if eaten.
safety.regulatory: Wild arnica is protected in several European countries and listed in the EU Habitats Directive. Buy cultivated.
safety.ethics: Wild picking puts pressure on Alpine and Carpathian meadows. The Apuseni mountains of Romania supply much of Europe's wild-picked flowers.

entries.what: A yellow mountain daisy of the Alps and Carpathians, made into gels and ointments for bruises.

entries.name: Arnica montana 30C
entries.uses: In homeopathy, given for bruising, shock and soreness after falls, surgery, dental work and hard exercise; called "the first remedy after any injury". Many people keep a tube in the first-aid box.

lore.text: Its remedy picture (the set of signs a remedy is matched to): someone sore and bruised all over who insists they are fine and wants to be left alone, and finds the bed too hard.

research.text: Trials after surgery and exercise give mixed results; reviews found no reliable effect beyond placebo.

safety.summary: 30C pills contain no measurable arnica. Herbal arnica gels and creams are a different, real-dose product: for unbroken skin only, and never swallowed, since arnica taken by mouth is poisonous.

entries.what: Mountain arnica made into tiny sugar pills by homeopathic dilution, the best-known first-aid remedy for bruises.
entries.know: Picking wild arnica is restricted in much of Europe, as its mountain meadows shrink.

sources.title: Australian NHMRC, Information Paper: evidence on the effectiveness of homeopathy (2015)
Homoeopathic Pharmacopoeia of the United States

entries.name: Arsenicum album
entries.uses: In homeopathy, given for food poisoning with vomiting and diarrhoea, in a person who is restless, chilly, anxious and fussy about order, often worse after midnight. In January 2020 India's AYUSH ministry advised Arsenicum album 30C during COVID-19.

research.text: No good trials show a reliable effect beyond placebo.

safety.summary: Low potencies contain real arsenic and have caused poisoning. Diarrhoea and vomiting dry the body out fast, especially in babies and older people; fluids and salts come first.

entries.what: Arsenic, diluted into a homeopathic remedy for food poisoning and restless, chilly anxiety.

sources.title: Australian NHMRC, Information Paper: evidence on the effectiveness of homeopathy (2015)
Government of India, Ministry of AYUSH

entries.name: Artichoke leaf
entries.uses: Taken as a bitter after heavy, fatty meals and for sluggish bile, the digestive juice the liver makes. The EMA accepts traditional use for indigestion.

history.text: Greeks and Romans ate its wild cousin, the cardoon. The globe artichoke was bred from it in Italy by the 1400s. Bitter artichoke liqueurs later joined Italy's after-dinner digestivi.

lore.text: An Aegean story tells of Cynara, a mortal girl whom Zeus made a goddess. When she slipped home to see her family, he threw her back to earth as the first artichoke.

research.text: A few trials found leaf extract eased indigestion. Pooled trials show a modest fall in cholesterol, though a Cochrane review called that evidence limited.

safety.summary: It increases bile flow, so it is cautioned with blocked bile ducts or gallstones. People allergic to daisies may react.

entries.what: The bitter leaves of the globe artichoke plant, taken as an extract or tea after heavy meals.
entries.know: Cynar, the Italian artichoke liqueur launched in 1952, has an artichoke on its label.

sources.title: European Medicines Agency, Committee on Herbal Medicinal Products (HMPC) monographs

entries.name: Asafoetida
entries.uses: Cooks add it to bean and lentil dishes against wind. Ayurveda counts it among the strongest spices for calming vata (the airy, restless energy behind gas and cramps). In India a little paste is rubbed on a baby's belly for colic.

history.text: Persians and Romans cooked with it. In the 1918 flu, American families hung little bags of asafoetida around children's necks.

lore.text: In hoodoo and European folk magic it is burned to drive away demons and evil spirits: the stink chases them out.

research.text: Studied in cells and animals.

safety.summary: Not to be given to infants by mouth: it has caused methaemoglobinaemia, a blood disorder that starves the body of oxygen. Ground hing is usually cut with wheat flour, so it holds gluten.

entries.what: A dried, very smelly plant resin; a pinch fried in oil gives Indian dishes an onion-garlic taste.
entries.know: Romans used it as a cheaper stand-in for silphium, a prized seasoning that had gone extinct.

sources.title: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India
Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database

entries.name: Ashwagandha
preps: churna in warm milk with ghee and honey
entries.uses: In Ayurveda it is a chief rasayana (a rejuvenating tonic taken over months to build strength and slow ageing). People stir the root powder (churna) into warm milk with ghee and honey, for strength, stamina, sleep and calm, especially in old age or after an illness. It is also a vajikarana herb, one taken for sexual vigour.

history.text: It appears in the classical Sanskrit medical texts of about 2,000 years ago. Since the 2010s it has become one of the best-selling "adaptogen" supplements in Europe and North America, mostly as branded root extracts.

lore.text: The name means "smell of a horse". The fresh root smells horsey, and it is said to give the strength of a horse. Ayurveda calls it warming and bitter-astringent. It calms vata and kapha, two of the three doshas (the body's ruling energies): vata is airy and restless, kapha heavy and slow.

research.text: Many small trials have looked at stress, sleep and testosterone, and most report modest benefits. Reviews point out that the trials are short and small, and many tested a maker's own extract.

safety.summary: Rare but serious liver injury has been reported, sometimes weeks after starting. It can raise thyroid hormone levels and can add to the effect of sedatives. It may raise testosterone, so it is cautioned in hormone-sensitive prostate cancer. Large amounts may cause miscarriage, so it is avoided in pregnancy. It is in the nightshade family, so people who react to nightshades may react to it.
safety.regulatory: Denmark banned it in food supplements in 2023. In 2024 France's food-safety agency (ANSES) warned some groups, including pregnant women, against it, and EU food-safety chiefs asked for an EU-wide safety review. By late 2026 that review had not formally begun.

entries.cat: Smells like a horse, sold like gold dust. Your liver gets a vote too.
entries.what: A small Indian shrub in the tomato family whose root is dried and powdered, now one of the West's best-selling supplements.
entries.know: Its Latin species name, somnifera, means "sleep-bringing".

entries.name: Astragalus
entries.uses: In Chinese medicine huang qi builds qi (the body's moving life energy) and especially wei qi, the protective qi said to guard the skin against cold and wind. It is traditionally used for people who catch every cold, sweat easily, tire fast or swell with fluid. Families drop the flat slices into chicken soup through the winter and fish them out before eating.

history.text: Listed in the Shennong Bencao Jing, the oldest Chinese book of herbs, compiled around the 1st or 2nd century CE. It leads the Jade Windscreen formula (Yu Ping Feng San).

research.text: Mostly lab studies on the immune system. Small trials in China have looked at kidney disease, heart failure and the side effects of chemotherapy.

safety.summary: It may work against immunosuppressant drugs, so people with a transplant or autoimmune disease are cautioned. It may change lithium levels and blood sugar.
safety.pets: Some wild Astragalus species, the locoweeds of North America, poison horses, cattle and sheep. The medicinal root is a different species.

entries.what: The sliced yellow root of a Chinese milk vetch, often simmered in winter soups.
entries.know: Astragalus is one of the largest plant genera on Earth, with around 3,000 species.

entries.name: Atractylodes
entries.uses: In Chinese medicine bai zhu strengthens the "spleen", the digestive system that turns food into energy, and "dries damp", the heavy, sticky fluid a weak digestion is said to leave behind. It is traditionally used for tiredness, a poor appetite, loose stools and swelling, and it is one of the four herbs in the Four Gentlemen formula (Si Jun Zi Tang).

research.text: Lab studies and studies of formulas.

safety.summary: Thought to be gentle. Little has been studied on its interactions.

entries.what: A knobbly aromatic root of the daisy family, one of the core herbs for digestion in Chinese medicine.

sources.title: Bensky, Clavey & Stöger, Chinese Herbal Medicine: Materia Medica, 3rd ed. (2004)

entries.name: Autumn crocus (meadow saffron)
entries.uses: Historically used for gout and swollen joints, a use said to go back to ancient Egypt and taken up by Byzantine physicians in the 6th century. Colchicine made from it is still a medicine for gout and some kinds of heart inflammation.

lore.text: The name naked ladies comes from the flowers rising bare from the ground, long after the leaves have died back.

research.text: Colchicine is an established medicine for gout and pericarditis (inflammation of the sac around the heart), with a narrow safety margin.

safety.summary: Deadly. The leaves have been mistaken for wild garlic (ramsons) and the flowers for saffron crocus. Poisoning starts hours later with violent vomiting and diarrhoea like cholera, then organ failure, and is an emergency. History and lore only.
safety.pets: Toxic to pets.

entries.what: A pink crocus-like flower that blooms without leaves in autumn, the source of the gout drug colchicine.
entries.know: Plant breeders use colchicine to double a plant's chromosomes, which is the first step in breeding seedless watermelons.

entries.name: Ayahuasca
entries.uses: Shipibo-Konibo, Asháninka, Cofán, Tukano and many other Amazonian peoples drink it in ceremony, and so do the Brazilian churches Santo Daime and União do Vegetal. It is taken with a curandero or vegetalista (a healer taught by plants) for healing, vision and guidance, with a strict diet before and after, the dieta.

history.text: Western botanists recorded it in the 1850s. In 2006 the US Supreme Court protected the União do Vegetal's use, and Brazil regulates church use.

lore.text: The vine teaches. Icaros, the songs the healer sings, guide the ceremony, and the purge cleans.

research.text: Small studies have looked at depression and addiction. The chemistry is well understood: the vine holds harmine and harmaline, which let the DMT in the leaf act when swallowed.

safety.summary: The vine is an MAOI (it blocks the enzyme monoamine oxidase), so it is dangerous with antidepressants, stimulants and many other medicines and some foods, risking serotonin syndrome and blood pressure spikes. There is a risk of psychosis with a personal or family history of it. People have died at unregulated retreats.
safety.regulatory: DMT is a controlled substance in most countries; religious exemptions vary.

entries.what: A sacred Amazonian brew of a jungle vine and leaves, drunk in night ceremonies for healing and visions.

sources.title: Schultes & Hofmann, Plants of the Gods (1979/2001)
NIH National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health, Herbs at a Glance

entries.name: Badger fat
preps: rubbed on the chest and back
taken by spoon with milk and honey (traditional)
entries.uses: Traditionally rubbed on the chest and back for stubborn coughs, and taken by the spoonful with warm milk and honey in winter for weak lungs. Russian pharmacies sell it in jars and capsules.

research.text: Not studied.

safety.summary: Home-rendered fat from wild animals can carry germs and parasites.
safety.ethics: The animals are killed for it. Badgers are protected in many countries, including the UK.

entries.what: Rendered fat from badgers, an old Russian chest rub and winter tonic still sold in pharmacies.

sources.title: Łuczaj et al., Wild food and medicinal plants in Slavic and Eastern European ethnobotany (Journal of Ethnobiology and Ethnomedicine papers)

entries.name: Baikal skullcap
entries.uses: In Chinese medicine huang qin is used to clear "damp heat" (a pattern of fever, yellow phlegm, burning and heaviness) from the lungs, gut and liver: for fevers, coughs with yellow phlegm and hot, urgent diarrhoea. In Siberia, where it grows wild, it is said to be a folk remedy for nerves and blood pressure.

history.text: Recorded in the Shennong Bencao Jing, China's oldest herbal, put together about 2,000 years ago. It is one of the seven herbs in the Kampo (Japanese herbal medicine) formula sho-saiko-to.

research.text: Its main compound, baicalin, has been studied widely in cells and animals. Trials in people are few.

safety.summary: Liver injury has been reported, mostly with combination products. In Japan in the 1990s, sho-saiko-to taken together with interferon caused lung inflammation, and some people died; the two must never be combined. It may change ciclosporin levels and add to diabetes medicines.

entries.what: The bitter yellow root of a skullcap from Siberia and China, a staple of Chinese medicine.

sources.title: Bensky, Clavey & Stöger, Chinese Herbal Medicine: Materia Medica, 3rd ed. (2004)

entries.name: Banya (Russian bathhouse)
parts: wood-fired steam room, birch or oak brooms (venik), cold plunge or snow, herbal teas
preps: rounds of steam, beating with venik, cold plunge, rest with tea
entries.uses: In Russia, Ukraine and Belarus people go weekly to sweat out colds and tiredness, soften the skin and wash body and soul. The venik, a bundle of birch or oak twigs soaked in hot water, is swished and pressed over the body like a massage. Then comes a cold plunge or a roll in the snow, and tea. Babies were often born in the banya, the cleanest warm room on the farm.

history.text: Russian villages traditionally had a banya for each family or for a few households.

lore.text: The bannik, the bathhouse spirit, lives behind the stove. People leave him the last steam, a bit of soap and water, and don't bathe late at night, which is his time. At Svyatki (the winter holy days), girls told their fortunes in the banya.

research.text: Large Finnish studies found that men who took saunas often had fewer deaths from heart disease. These are observational studies, so they show a link, not cause and effect.

safety.summary: Heat and alcohol together have killed people. Not with unstable heart disease, low blood pressure or a fever. High heat is cautioned in pregnancy. Drink water between rounds.

entries.cat: Get beaten with branches in a hot shed, then roll in snow. Leave the bannik his steam, or he'll scald you.
entries.what: The Russian steam bath: a hot wooden room, a beating with leafy birch twigs, then a cold plunge.
entries.know: The Primary Chronicle (compiled around 1113) has the apostle Andrew marvel at people near Novgorod who steamed in wooden bathhouses, beat themselves with twigs and poured cold water over themselves.

sources.title: Laukkanen et al., Cardiovascular and other health benefits of sauna bathing (Mayo Clin Proc 2018)

entries.name: Baobab
entries.uses: Across Africa the fruit pulp is traditionally stirred into water or milk and drunk for fevers and diarrhoea and as a rich food. The leaves are dried and cooked in soups such as Hausa miyan kuka, and the bark is boiled for fevers. The tree itself is a village meeting place and a home for spirits.

lore.text: Many stories say the gods planted it upside down, its branches really roots, sometimes as punishment for its vanity. Spirits live in its hollow trunk and in its flowers, and some trees hold the graves of griots (praise singers).

research.text: Nutrient studies show the pulp is high in vitamin C and fibre. Little clinical work.

safety.summary: A normal food.
safety.regulatory: The dried fruit pulp was approved as a novel food in the EU in 2008 and accepted as safe (GRAS) in the US in 2009.
safety.ethics: A 2018 study found that 9 of the 13 oldest and 5 of the 6 biggest baobabs in Africa had died, wholly or partly, since 2005.

entries.what: A huge, fat-trunked African tree whose dry, chalky fruit pulp is eaten and drunk.
entries.know: Panke, a baobab in Zimbabwe, was about 2,500 years old when it died in 2011.

entries.name: Barley tea
entries.uses: Drunk iced all summer in Japan and Korea in place of water, to cool down in the heat and after meals.

research.text: Studied as food.

safety.summary: It contains gluten, so it is not for people with coeliac disease.

entries.what: A caffeine-free tea of roasted barley grains, drunk iced all summer in Japan and Korea.
entries.know: Many Korean restaurants pour boricha for free instead of water.

sources.title: Victor Mair & Erling Hoh, The True History of Tea (2009)

entries.name: Bay laurel
entries.uses: Cooks add a leaf to stews to make heavy food sit easier. Oil pressed from the berries goes into Aleppo soap, used for skin. In folk magic people write a wish on a bay leaf and burn it.

history.text: The priestess at Delphi, the Pythia, is said to have chewed or burned laurel leaves before she prophesied. Winners at the Pythian Games were crowned with laurel.

lore.text: Apollo's tree: the nymph Daphne became a laurel to escape him. Romans believed laurel kept lightning away. A bay leaf under the pillow brings dreams that show the future.

research.text: Little modern research.

safety.summary: Whole leaves stay stiff and sharp; take them out before eating. Several poisonous shrubs are also called laurel, including cherry laurel and mountain laurel; only sweet bay is the kitchen leaf.
safety.pets: Listed as toxic to cats, dogs and horses (vomiting and diarrhoea).

entries.what: The stiff, fragrant leaf of the Mediterranean laurel tree, dropped into soups and stews.

entries.name: Bee venom (apitherapy)
entries.uses: In apitherapy, practised in Korea, China and Eastern Europe, live bees are held to the skin to sting on purpose, for arthritis and pain. In Korea diluted venom is also injected into acupuncture points.

history.text: Ancient Greek, Egyptian and Chinese texts mention bee stings as medicine. Bee venom acupuncture is common in Korea today.

research.text: Small trials only. In 2018 a case was reported from Spain of a woman who died of anaphylaxis (a severe allergic reaction) during live bee acupuncture, after two years of sessions.

safety.summary: Anaphylaxis can kill, even in people who handled stings fine before. It is an emergency.

entries.what: The venom from bee stings, given through live stings or injections in a practice called apitherapy.

entries.name: Belladonna (homeopathic)
entries.uses: In homeopathy, its remedy picture (the signs it is matched to) is sudden, hot, red and throbbing: fevers that flare fast, a flushed face, wide pupils, pounding headaches, and dislike of light and jarring.

history.text: In 2016 and 2017 the FDA found uneven, sometimes high, amounts of belladonna in homeopathic teething tablets, after reports of seizures and infant deaths. The best-known brand was recalled across the US in April 2017.

research.text: No good trials show a reliable effect beyond placebo.

safety.summary: Low-potency products have contained toxic amounts of atropine-like alkaloids. Never for babies or teething.

entries.what: Deadly nightshade diluted into a homeopathic remedy for sudden, hot, throbbing fevers.
entries.know: Belladonna is Italian for "beautiful lady"; women once put the plant's juice in their eyes to widen the pupils.

entries.name: Benzoin
entries.uses: Burned as temple incense across Southeast Asia and India. In Europe compound benzoin tincture, called friar's balsam, is stirred into hot water and the steam breathed in for colds. It is also painted on skin under dressings.

history.text: Benzoic acid, now a common food preservative, was first made from this resin in the 16th century.

lore.text: In folk magic it is burned for purification and prosperity.

research.text: Hardly studied.

safety.summary: It can cause skin allergy; compound benzoin tincture is a known contact allergen.

entries.what: A sweet, vanilla-scented resin from Southeast Asian trees, burned as incense and used in steam inhalations.

sources.title: Tisserand & Young, Essential Oil Safety, 2nd ed. (2014)

entries.name: Berberis vulgaris (homeopathic)
entries.uses: In homeopathy, given for kidney and bladder pains that radiate outward (as with stones), bubbling sensations in the kidneys, and gout-type joint pain.

research.text: No good trials show a reliable effect beyond placebo.

safety.summary: Kidney stone pain with fever, vomiting or no urine is an emergency. Low potencies contain berberine.

entries.what: Barberry root bark diluted into a remedy for radiating kidney and bladder pains.

sources.title: Australian NHMRC, Information Paper: evidence on the effectiveness of homeopathy (2015)

entries.name: Bergamot oil
entries.uses: Used in aromatherapy to lift mood and ease tension. It flavours Earl Grey tea and is a classic note in eau de cologne.

history.text: The first eau de Cologne, made in Cologne from 1709, used bergamot from Italy.

research.text: A few small studies have looked at breathing it in for stress.

safety.summary: Strongly phototoxic: its bergapten makes oiled skin burn badly in sunlight, leaving dark marks. For skin, people use bergapten-free oil, labelled FCF (furocoumarin-free).
safety.pets: Citrus oils are listed as toxic to cats and dogs.

entries.what: A fresh citrus oil pressed from the peel of the bergamot orange; it is the flavour of Earl Grey tea.
entries.know: Most of the world's bergamot grows on a narrow strip of coast around Reggio Calabria, in the toe of Italy.

sources.title: Tisserand & Young, Essential Oil Safety, 2nd ed. (2014)

entries.name: Bergenia (Chigirian tea)
entries.uses: In the Altai and Siberia people collect the leaves that have spent the winter under snow and turned black, and brew them as a tonic tea called Chigirian or Mongolian tea. The root is boiled as an astringent (something that tightens tissue) for diarrhoea and sore gums.

research.text: Rich in arbutin, bergenin and tannins; studied only in the lab.

safety.summary: The tannins can be constipating. It contains arbutin, so long use is best avoided.

entries.what: A Siberian plant with big leathery leaves; the leaves that blacken under the snow are brewed into tea.

sources.title: Sokolov & Zamotaev, Handbook of Medicinal Plants (USSR, 1984/1990)

entries.name: Betel quid (paan)
parts: areca nut, betel leaf, slaked lime
entries.uses: Across South and Southeast Asia and the western Pacific, hundreds of millions of people chew the quid to stay alert, after meals for digestion, and to welcome guests. The leaf and nut are offered at weddings, to the gods and to the ancestors. In Vietnam trầu cau (betel and areca) is still exchanged at engagements.

lore.text: A Vietnamese story tells of two loving brothers and the elder brother's wife. When all three died of grief, they became the areca palm, the limestone rock beside it and the betel vine that climbs it, which is why the three are chewed together and turn red like blood.

research.text: IARC (the WHO's cancer agency) lists areca nut and betel quid, with or without tobacco, as causes of cancer in humans. Regions where heavy chewing is common have very high rates of mouth cancer.

safety.summary: Chewing causes mouth cancer and oral submucous fibrosis, a stiffening of the mouth that can stop it opening. It is addictive and stains the teeth red-black. Areca nut can bring on asthma attacks and upset heart rhythm. Avoid in pregnancy: it is linked to low birth weight.

entries.what: A chew of sliced areca nut and slaked lime wrapped in a betel leaf, used daily by millions across Asia.
entries.know: Stained teeth found in Duyong Cave in the Philippines show people were chewing betel about 4,600 years ago.

sources.title: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database

entries.name: Bhasma (Ayurvedic metal ashes)
parts: metals and minerals purified and incinerated
preps: ash taken with honey or ghee
entries.uses: In rasa shastra (Indian medical alchemy), metals and minerals go through long purification (shodhana) and repeated burning to become bhasma, a fine ash. It is taken with honey or ghee for strength, long life and serious illness.

history.text: Rasa shastra grew from about the 8th century CE. Tibetan "precious pills" (rinchen rilbu) contain purified mercury (tsothel).

lore.text: In the tradition, proper processing changes the metal's nature, so the finished ash is no longer raw metal but a medicine.

research.text: US studies found lead, mercury or arsenic in about 1 in 5 Ayurvedic products bought in Boston shops (JAMA 2004) and online (JAMA 2008). Lead poisoning cases linked to these products are still being reported.

safety.summary: There is a real risk of heavy-metal poisoning. Never for children or in pregnancy, and only from certified makers. Poisoning shows up in blood lead and mercury tests.

entries.what: Metals such as gold, iron and mercury, processed by Indian alchemy into a fine ash and taken in tiny amounts.
entries.know: A finished bhasma is tested by sprinkling it on water: it should be fine enough to float (varitara).

sources.title: Saper et al., Heavy metal content of Ayurvedic herbal medicine products, JAMA 2004
Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India

entries.name: Bhringraj
entries.uses: In Ayurveda it is the chief hair herb: bhringraj oil is massaged into the scalp for greying and thinning hair. The juice or powder is also taken for the liver.

lore.text: In Chinese medicine han lian cao nourishes liver and kidney yin (the cooling, moistening side of the body) and blackens the hair.

research.text: Animal studies on hair growth.

safety.summary: Gentle on the skin. Little is known about taking it by mouth.

entries.what: A small daisy-like weed of damp ground, made into the best-known Indian hair oil.

sources.title: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India
Bensky, Clavey & Stöger, Chinese Herbal Medicine: Materia Medica, 3rd ed. (2004)

entries.name: Bibhitaki
entries.uses: It is the third fruit of triphala. In Ayurveda it is used for kapha conditions of the chest and throat (kapha is the heavy, wet energy, linked to mucus) and for the bowels.

lore.text: In the Mahabharata tale of King Nala, the demon Kali (not the goddess) leaves Nala's body and hides in a bibhitaka tree. The tree is said to house him still, and some people avoid resting in its shade.

research.text: Little beyond triphala studies.

safety.summary: Gentle; it is a laxative.

entries.what: The fruit of a tall Indian forest tree, one of the three fruits in triphala.
entries.know: In the Rigveda's "Gambler's Hymn", about 3,000 years old, the dice are bibhitaka nuts.

sources.title: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India

entries.name: Bilberry
entries.uses: Dried berries are traditionally used for mild diarrhoea and as a rinse for a sore mouth; the EMA accepts both as traditional uses. The berries are also eaten for the eyes and for fragile veins.

history.text: Gathered by the pailful in the forests of the Baltic, Russia and Scandinavia. The leaf was a folk tea for sugar in the blood.

lore.text: A wartime story says British pilots ate bilberry jam to see better at night. The story became the berry's modern selling point.

research.text: Its anthocyanins (the purple pigments) have been studied. Eye trials are small and inconsistent, and controlled tests did not find better night vision.

safety.summary: The berries are food. The leaf taken for a long time was linked to poisoning in older animal work, and it can lower blood sugar.

entries.what: The small wild blueberry of northern European forests, eaten fresh and dried for tea.
entries.know: Unlike the cultivated blueberry, the bilberry is purple-blue all the way through and stains fingers and teeth.

entries.name: Birch (leaf, bud, sap, tar)
entries.uses: People in Russia and across Europe drink birch leaf tea to pass more water and flush the urinary tract. The EU's herbal committee (EMA) lists this as a traditional use. Folk healers also give the tea for rheumatism, meaning stiff, aching joints. In spring the fresh sap is tapped and drunk as a cleansing tonic, sometimes fermented into kvass. Birch tar goes into soap and ointment for skin and wounds. In the banya, the Russian steam bath, bathers beat themselves with a leafy birch broom called a venik.

history.text: A birch-tar ointment made by a Soviet surgeon in the 1920s became a standard wound dressing in Soviet hospitals. It is still sold in Russian pharmacies. The Novgorod birch-bark letters date from the 11th to the 15th centuries.

lore.text: The birch is Russia's tree of girls and of spring. At Semik and Trinity, early-summer festivals about seven weeks after Easter, girls tied ribbons on young birches and twisted their branches into wreaths. That same week the rusalki, water spirits of drowned maidens, were said to swing in its branches.

research.text: Few clinical studies of the leaf. Betulin, a compound from the bark, has been studied in the lab. A gel made from birch bark extract (Filsuvez) was approved in the EU in 2022 and the US in 2023 for wounds in epidermolysis bullosa, a rare blistering skin disease.

safety.summary: The leaf tea is mild. It is not for swelling caused by heart or kidney failure. EMA does not recommend it in pregnancy or breastfeeding, because there is not enough safety data. People with birch pollen allergy can react to it, and that allergy often crosses over to apples, hazelnuts and carrots. Tar can irritate skin.

entries.what: The white-barked tree of northern Europe, whose leaves, spring sap and smoky tar all go into folk remedies.
entries.know: Since 1951 archaeologists in Novgorod, Russia, have dug up more than a thousand letters scratched on birch bark, some from the 1000s.

entries.name: Bitter leaf
entries.uses: In Nigeria and across West Africa the leaves are washed by hand to tame their bitterness and cooked in soups such as Igbo ofe onugbu. The squeezed juice is traditionally drunk for fevers, worms and high blood sugar, and the stems are chewed to clean teeth. Wild chimpanzees chew the bitter pith when they are ill.

history.text: Studies of sick chimpanzees chewing it helped start zoopharmacognosy, the study of how animals use medicinal plants.

research.text: Mostly lab and animal studies, with a few very small human tests on blood sugar.

safety.summary: A normal food in usual amounts. It may lower blood sugar, so it can add to diabetes medicines.

entries.what: A West African shrub with very bitter leaves that are washed and cooked into soups.
entries.know: In 1987 in Tanzania's Mahale Mountains, researchers watched a sick chimpanzee chew bitter leaf pith and recover within a day.

sources.title: PROTA4U, Plant Resources of Tropical Africa

entries.name: Black cohosh
entries.uses: Cherokee, Iroquois and other nations used the root for women's complaints, for childbirth and for rheumatism. Today people take extracts for hot flushes and night sweats around menopause. The EU herbal committee (EMA) accepts this as a well-established use.

history.text: The root went into a famous American patent medicine for women sold from the 1870s. A German extract has been sold and studied since the 1950s.

research.text: Trials for hot flushes disagree with each other. A 2012 Cochrane review found too little good evidence to say whether it eases them.

safety.summary: Rare but serious liver injury has been reported. Stop at once if urine turns dark, skin or eyes turn yellow, or you feel unusually tired. It is cautioned with hormone-sensitive cancers such as some breast cancers.
safety.ethics: Most of it is dug from wild Appalachian forests. United Plant Savers lists it as at-risk.

entries.what: A tall woodland plant of eastern North America whose root is taken today mostly for menopause hot flushes.

entries.name: Black currant leaf
entries.uses: The leaf tea is traditionally drunk for joint pain and gout and to pass more water. EMA lists traditional uses for minor joint pain and for flushing the urinary tract. The berries are taken for colds. In Russia the leaves go into pickle jars and into the teapot.

research.text: Little clinical study.

safety.summary: Mild. Like other teas that make you pass more water, it is not for swelling caused by heart or kidney failure.

entries.what: The leaves of the black currant bush, the berry behind cassis, made into a tea for aching joints.
entries.know: The US banned growing black currants in the early 1900s because they spread a fungus that kills white pines; New York only lifted its ban in 2003.

sources.title: European Medicines Agency, Committee on Herbal Medicinal Products (HMPC) monographs
Sokolov & Zamotaev, Handbook of Medicinal Plants (USSR, 1984/1990)

entries.name: Black pepper
entries.uses: In Ayurveda and Siddha (the Tamil medical tradition) it is used to kindle agni, the digestive fire, and to clear phlegm. Pepper stirred into honey is a home cough remedy across India. In Tamil homes a bowl of peppery rasam broth is the classic food for a cold.

history.text: Its nickname was "black gold". Peppercorns were packed into the nostrils of the pharaoh Ramesses II when he was mummified in 1213 BCE. When the Goths besieged Rome in 408 CE, part of the ransom they demanded was 3,000 pounds of pepper.

lore.text: In hoodoo and other folk magic, black pepper is sprinkled to banish unwanted people and protect the home.

research.text: Piperine, pepper's hot compound, raised blood levels of several drugs (such as phenytoin and propranolol) in small human studies, and of turmeric's curcumin. That is why it is added to supplements.

safety.summary: Food amounts are fine. Piperine extracts can raise blood levels of many drugs.

entries.what: The dried berry of a tropical vine from south-west India, ground onto food all over the world.
entries.know: Pepper was once so precious that rent was paid in it; in English law a "peppercorn rent" still means a token rent.

sources.title: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database
Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India

entries.name: Black radish with honey
parts: root, hollowed and filled with honey
preps: radish syrup (honey drawn into the hollowed root overnight)
entries.uses: In Russia and Poland people cut a hollow in the top of the root, fill it with honey and leave it overnight. The sweet, sharp syrup that collects is given by the spoonful to children and grandparents for coughs. The juice is also drunk for the gallbladder.

history.text: One of the best-known Russian home remedies, still made in many families.

research.text: Not studied clinically.

safety.summary: Honey must never be given to babies under 1 year old (risk of infant botulism). Radish juice can irritate stomach ulcers and may set off pain in people with gallstones.

entries.what: A big black-skinned winter radish, hollowed out and filled with honey to make a homemade cough syrup.

entries.name: Black seed (nigella)
entries.uses: In Prophetic medicine (the healing customs drawn from the sayings of the Prophet Muhammad) many people take a spoonful of seeds every day. The seeds are taken with honey for coughs and asthma, and the oil is rubbed into skin and hair.

history.text: Nigella seeds were found among the grave goods in Tutankhamun's tomb.

lore.text: A hadith calls it healing for every disease except death. It is the seed of blessing, and a guard against the evil eye.

research.text: Small trials looked at asthma, blood pressure and hay fever, with some encouraging results.

safety.summary: It may lower blood pressure and blood sugar. The oil can cause a skin rash. A few case reports link large amounts of the oil or seed to kidney injury.

entries.what: Tiny black, onion-flavoured seeds sprinkled on naan and bread, and pressed into an oil.

entries.name: Black tea
entries.uses: Drunk everywhere from the Russian samovar to Turkish tulip-shaped glasses. Strong black tea is a folk remedy for diarrhoea, and cooled tea bags go on tired eyes and small burns.

history.text: From 1727 camel caravans carried Chinese tea to Russia through the border town of Kyakhta. In the 1830s the British began planting tea in Assam, India, from a local wild variety.

research.text: Large observational studies link tea drinking with less heart disease and stroke. Studies like these show links, not cause.

safety.summary: Caffeine. Tannins cut iron absorption. Drinking tea very hot, above about 65 °C, is linked to cancer of the oesophagus.

entries.what: Tea leaves left to oxidise until they turn dark, the everyday cup from Britain to Turkey to Russia.
entries.know: In Chinese, black tea is hong cha, "red tea", after the colour of the brew.

sources.title: NIH National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health, Herbs at a Glance
Victor Mair & Erling Hoh, The True History of Tea (2009)

entries.name: Bladderwrack
entries.uses: In Europe it was taken for a sluggish thyroid, because it is rich in iodine, and added to baths for rheumatism. Today it is sold for weight loss; the EMA accepts its traditional use alongside a low-calorie diet for overweight adults.

history.text: Iodine was first discovered in seaweed ash, in France in 1811. Burning kelp for soda and iodine was an island industry in Scotland and Ireland.

research.text: It really is a source of iodine. Trials do not back up the weight-loss claims.

safety.summary: Too much iodine can push the thyroid either way, too fast or too slow. It can contain arsenic and heavy metals from the sea. Not with thyroid medicines, amiodarone or an iodine allergy, and it may add to blood thinners.

entries.what: A brown seaweed of rocky Atlantic shores, with little air pockets that pop when squeezed.
entries.know: The air pockets lift the fronds toward the light when the tide comes in.

sources.title: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database
European Medicines Agency, Committee on Herbal Medicinal Products (HMPC) monographs

entries.name: Bloodroot
entries.uses: Algonquian and other eastern nations used the red root as a dye and face paint, and in small amounts for coughs. In the 1800s American "black salves" used it to burn off skin growths.

history.text: These escharotic salves (pastes that burn away flesh) are still sold online today as "black salve".

research.text: Its main alkaloid, sanguinarine, destroys healthy and diseased tissue alike. A toothpaste and mouthwash made with the extract were linked to pale pre-cancerous patches in the mouth (leukoplakia).

safety.summary: Black salves have eaten away noses, faces and healthy skin, and have delayed real cancer care. The FDA lists them among fake cancer products. The root is poisonous when swallowed.
safety.regulatory: The FDA has warned against black salve.
safety.ethics: United Plant Savers lists it as at-risk.

entries.what: A white spring wildflower whose root bleeds red sap, once a dye and now behind dangerous "black salves".
entries.know: Puccoon comes from an Algonquian word for plants that give dye.

entries.name: Blue cohosh
entries.uses: Cherokee, Ojibwe and other nations used the root around childbirth and for menstrual troubles. American midwives used it to bring on labour and ease it.

history.text: Listed in the US Pharmacopoeia from 1882 to 1905.

research.text: There are no proper trials. Case reports describe heart attack, stroke and heart failure in newborns whose mothers took it near the birth. Lab work found a nicotine-like alkaloid and compounds that narrow blood vessels.

safety.summary: Dangerous in pregnancy and labour: it has been linked to serious heart damage and stroke in newborns. The seeds are poisonous.
safety.ethics: United Plant Savers lists it as at-risk in the wild.

entries.what: A woodland plant of eastern North America with bright blue seeds, once used by midwives to start labour.
entries.know: Its blue "berries" are really bare seeds: the fruit wall splits early and leaves them naked on the stalk.

sources.title: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database

entries.name: Boneset
entries.uses: Many nations, and later settlers, used it as a hot, bitter tea to sweat out fevers and flu. The name is tied to "break-bone fever", a fever with aching bones.

history.text: One of the most used home remedies in 19th-century America, hung in dried bundles in farmhouse attics.

research.text: Very little clinical work.

safety.summary: It contains small amounts of pyrrolizidine alkaloids (plant chemicals that damage the liver), so it is used only for short spells. Large amounts cause vomiting.

entries.what: A white-flowered meadow plant of eastern North America, drunk as a hot bitter tea in fevers and flu.
entries.know: Its leaves wrap right round the stem, as if joined, which settlers read as a sign it could knit bones.

sources.title: Daniel Moerman, Native American Ethnobotany (1998) and the BRIT Native American Ethnobotany database
Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database

entries.name: Borage
entries.uses: Traditionally taken to "gladden the heart" and give courage, often as flowers floated in wine. The seed oil, rich in GLA (gamma-linolenic acid, a fatty acid), is sold for skin and joints.

history.text: A Roman natural history called it euphrosynum, the herb that brings gladness. Knights leaving for the Crusades are said to have been handed stirrup cups with borage flowers floating in them.

lore.text: An old line runs "I, borage, bring always courage." It was floated in wine before battle.

research.text: Small trials of the seed oil for rheumatoid arthritis found some benefit. For eczema, a Cochrane review found it did no better than placebo.

safety.summary: Leaves and flowers contain pyrrolizidine alkaloids (PAs), plant toxins that damage the liver. Only PA-free seed oil is used. The oil may make seizures more likely with some drugs and may add to bleeding risk.

entries.what: A hairy, cucumber-scented herb with star-shaped blue flowers, grown for its seed oil and for drinks.
entries.know: Borage flowers often open pink and turn blue as the sap in the petals changes.

entries.name: BPC-157
parts: synthetic 15-amino-acid fragment of a protein found in gastric juice
entries.uses: Sold and talked about in gyms, sports forums and longevity clinics, mostly for torn tendons, sore joints, muscle strains and gut trouble. People usually inject it under the skin near the sore spot. Capsules and nasal sprays are sold too, and it is often "stacked" (taken together) with TB-500.

history.text: Made by a research group in Zagreb, Croatia, in the early 1990s, from a fragment of a protein they found in human gastric juice. It moved from rat studies to bodybuilding forums in the 2010s, then to wellness clinics in the 2020s.

research.text: Hundreds of studies in rats and cells, most from the same Zagreb group, report faster repair of tendon, muscle and gut. In people there are only a few tiny pilot studies, each with a handful to a few dozen people, and no proper controlled trials. Nobody has measured long-term safety in humans. Researchers flag one theoretical worry: in animals it spurs new blood vessels to grow (angiogenesis), and tumours use new blood vessels too.

safety.summary: Long-term safety in people is unknown. Grey-market vials sold "for research use only" are often mislabelled, too weak or too strong, or contaminated with bacteria or endotoxin (bits of dead bacteria that cause fever and shock). Injecting carries a risk of abscess and infection. FDA reviewers also raised possible immune reactions and impurities. Because of the blood-vessel worry, people with cancer or a past cancer are warned off it.
safety.regulatory: As of November 2026: not approved as a medicine anywhere. FDA put it on its Category 2 list (compounding ingredients with significant safety risks) in 2023 and took it off in April 2026 after the nomination was withdrawn. In July 2026 FDA's Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee voted 8 to 6, with one abstention, to add it to the 503A bulks list (the ingredients pharmacies may compound from), against the advice of FDA's own reviewers. The vote does not bind FDA, and FDA has not added it. On 30 October 2026 HHS published a policy saying it will not act against licensed pharmacies that compound single-ingredient BPC-157 on prescription while rulemaking goes on. Sources disagree on whether that policy is a draft or already in force; comments closed 13 November 2026. "Research use only" vials sold online are still illegal for human use. Prohibited in sport by WADA (class S0, unapproved substances).

entries.cat: Rats loved it. You're not a rat. Mostly.
entries.what: A lab-made chain of 15 amino acids, sold online and in clinics as an injectable "recovery peptide".

entries.name: Brahmi (bacopa)
entries.uses: In Ayurveda it is a medhya rasayana, a tonic for the intellect, taken for memory, learning and calm. People take the powder or brahmi ghrita (the herb cooked in ghee), and massage brahmi oil into the scalp.

lore.text: Named for Brahman, the universal consciousness. It was given to Vedic students who learned long scriptures by heart. In north India "brahmi" also names gotu kola, so the two get mixed up.

research.text: Several 12-week trials, pooled in two reviews, found small improvements on memory tests.

safety.summary: It can upset the stomach and slow the heart rate. It may affect thyroid hormone.

entries.what: A small creeping wetland herb from India, taken as a memory tonic and massaged into the scalp as oil.
entries.know: It grows happily underwater and is sold in aquarium shops as water hyssop.

sources.title: NIH National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health, Herbs at a Glance
Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database
Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India

entries.name: Bremelanotide (PT-141)
entries.uses: Prescribed in the US since 2019 for low sexual desire in women before menopause, injected under the skin about 45 minutes before sex. Also sold off-label and grey-market, as PT-141 vials and nasal sprays, to men and women.

history.text: Developed from Melanotan II, and approved by FDA as Vyleesi in June 2019.

research.text: Trials found a modest rise in desire and less distress about it, compared with placebo. The number of satisfying sexual encounters did not clearly change.

safety.summary: Nausea is common (about 4 in 10 in trials). Flushing, headache and a short rise in blood pressure. Dark patches can appear on the face, gums or breasts, more with frequent use. It lowers blood levels of naltrexone taken by mouth.
safety.regulatory: As of November 2026: prescription only in the US; not approved in the EU or UK. Grey-market PT-141 is unapproved.

entries.what: A licensed injection, used before sex, for low sexual desire in women before menopause.
entries.know: It was found because volunteers testing the tanning drug Melanotan II reported unexpected arousal.

sources.title: US FDA, bulk drug substances for compounding (503A categories)

entries.name: Bryonia alba
entries.uses: In homeopathy, given for dry, painful coughs and pains made worse by the slightest movement. The patient wants to lie still, is very thirsty and irritable, and wants to be left alone.

research.text: No good trials show a reliable effect beyond placebo.

safety.summary: The fresh plant is a violent purgative poison, and its red berries are dangerous to children. Avoided in pregnancy.

entries.what: White bryony root diluted into a remedy for dry coughs and pains that are worse for any movement.

sources.title: Australian NHMRC, Information Paper: evidence on the effectiveness of homeopathy (2015)

entries.name: Buchu
entries.uses: The Khoi of the Western Cape traditionally ground the dried leaves with fat and rubbed them on the body as a perfume, and drank them for stomach and bladder complaints. Cape families still steep the leaves in brandy (boegoebrandewyn) and take it for colds, stomach aches and the kidneys.

history.text: Exported to Britain around 1790, it entered the British Pharmacopoeia in 1821 as a remedy for bladder infections (cystitis).

research.text: Very little clinical work. Lab studies have looked at its oils.

safety.summary: Some buchu, especially oval buchu (Agathosma crenulata, often mixed into the trade), contains a lot of pulegone, which can damage the liver. Too much can irritate the kidneys. Not used in pregnancy or with inflamed kidneys.

entries.what: A small aromatic shrub from South Africa's Western Cape whose leaves smell of blackcurrant and are brewed as tea.

sources.title: van Wyk, van Oudtshoorn & Gericke, Medicinal Plants of South Africa (2009)

entries.name: Bupleurum
preps: in formulas (Xiao Yao San, Xiao Chai Hu Tang)
entries.uses: In Chinese medicine chai hu frees "constrained liver qi": the liver is said to keep energy and mood flowing, and stress knots it up. It also works the "half-outside, half-inside" layer of the body, where an illness sits when chills and fever take turns. It is traditionally used for irritability, alternating chills and fever and tension before a period.

research.text: Its saponins (soapy plant compounds) have been studied in the lab. Formulas containing it have been tested in Asia.

safety.summary: Sho-saiko-to, a formula built on bupleurum, caused serious lung inflammation in Japan, especially with interferon. It can make people drowsy.

entries.what: The bitter root of a thin-leaved Asian plant, central to Chinese formulas for stress and lingering fevers.

sources.title: Bensky, Clavey & Stöger, Chinese Herbal Medicine: Materia Medica, 3rd ed. (2004)

entries.name: Burdock
entries.uses: The root is traditionally taken as a "blood cleanser" for skin complaints. Burdock root oil (repeinoe maslo) is a Russian and Polish folk hair oil. In Chinese medicine the seed, niu bang zi, is used for sore throats and for colds at their very start.

history.text: Eaten as a root vegetable, gobo, in Japan, where it is sliced thin and braised with carrot.

lore.text: In Ukraine the root was hung up against the evil eye.

research.text: Lab work on its antioxidants; very few human trials.

safety.summary: Shop-bought root has been mixed with deadly nightshade (belladonna) root, and people have been poisoned. It may lower blood sugar. People allergic to daisies may react.

entries.what: A big-leaved thistle relative whose long root is eaten in Japan and used as a cleansing herb in Europe.
entries.know: Burdock burrs stuck in a Swiss engineer's dog's fur in 1941 gave him the idea for Velcro.

entries.name: Butter tea (po cha)
entries.uses: Traditionally drunk many times a day on the Tibetan plateau for warmth and energy, and to keep lips from cracking in the high, dry cold. Brick tea is boiled for a long time, then churned with butter and salt in a tall wooden tube.

lore.text: It is offered to every guest, and the host tops up the cup after each sip for as long as you stay.

research.text: Studied mainly as food. Studies in Tibet have looked at the fluoride in the brick tea it is made from.

safety.summary: Lots of salt and saturated fat. The brick tea used is often high in fluoride, and heavy lifelong drinking has caused fluorosis of bones and teeth in Tibet.

entries.what: Strong tea churned with yak butter and salt, drunk all day on the Tibetan plateau.
entries.know: In Ladakh it is called gur gur cha, after the sound the churn makes.

sources.title: Victor Mair & Erling Hoh, The True History of Tea (2009)

entries.name: Cacao
entries.uses: Maya and Aztec (Mexica) nobles drank it bitter and frothy, often with chilli, and it was poured in ceremony as a sacred, heart-opening drink. Cacao butter is rubbed on skin as a balm. Today's "cacao ceremonies" draw on this.

history.text: Cacao beans were used as money in the Aztec empire. Pots from early Mexican sites hold cacao traces about 3,500 years old.

lore.text: Cacao was the gift of Quetzalcoatl, the feathered serpent. It is offered to the dead on Día de Muertos.

research.text: Trials of flavanol-rich cocoa (cocoa high in the plant compounds called flavanols) found a small drop in blood pressure.

safety.summary: It contains caffeine and theobromine, a related stimulant. It brings on migraines in some people.
safety.pets: Toxic to dogs and cats because of theobromine; dark chocolate and cacao powder are the worst.

entries.what: The bean of a rainforest tree, made into the sacred drink of the Maya and Aztecs and now into chocolate.
entries.know: The oldest traces of cacao use come from pottery in Ecuador's Amazon, about 5,300 years old.

Schultes & Hofmann, Plants of the Gods (1979/2001)

entries.name: Calcarea carbonica
parts: middle layer of oyster shell, triturated and diluted
entries.uses: In homeopathy, a constitutional remedy (chosen for a person's lifelong type) for chilly, steady, easily tired people who are slow and careful, sweat on the head in sleep and worry about the future.

research.text: No good trials show a reliable effect beyond placebo.

safety.summary: At usual potencies the pills contain no measurable shell.

entries.what: Calcium from oyster shell, diluted into a constitutional remedy for chilly, steady, easily tired people.
