entries.name: Calcium
entries.uses: Taken for bones, often with vitamin D, especially after menopause; chewed as antacid tablets for heartburn.

history.text: Chalk and crushed shell have been sold as antacids for centuries; "coral calcium" was a 2000s infomercial craze.

research.text: Calcium with vitamin D lowers fractures in older people in care homes; for others the effect is small. Some studies raised concern about supplements and heart attacks; results are mixed.

safety.summary: Constipation and bloating. High supplement doses raise kidney-stone risk. Calcium blocks absorption of iron, thyroid pills and several antibiotics: take them hours apart.

entries.what: The mineral bones and teeth are built from; it also fires every nerve and muscle, heartbeat included.

nutrient.low: Usually no signs for years, then weaker bones; very low blood calcium causes tingling and cramps.
nutrient.limit: US 2,500 mg a day (ages 19–50), 2,000 mg (51+); EU 2,500 mg a day.

entries.name: Calendula
entries.uses: Traditionally used in salves and washes for minor wounds, burns, nappy rash and sore skin, and as a mouth rinse. The EMA accepts traditional use for minor skin inflammation, small wounds and a sore mouth or throat.

history.text: Used on wounds in the American Civil War. Calendula tincture, diluted for gargling, is a staple of Russian pharmacies.

lore.text: Strewn on doorsteps against evil and woven into wedding garlands. A flower of the sun, it opens and closes with the light.

research.text: One trial found calendula cream lessened skin damage from radiation therapy for breast cancer; a later trial found no difference from a plain cream. Wound studies are small.

safety.summary: People allergic to daisies may react. It is a different plant from the French and African marigolds (Tagetes).

entries.what: The orange pot marigold, made into oils, salves and washes for sore skin.

entries.name: Camphor
entries.uses: In Hindu worship camphor is burned in aarti, the flame waved before the deity at the end of puja. It is rubbed on the chest for colds and on aching muscles. In Russia camphor alcohol (kamforny spirt) is rubbed on aching joints and used in warm ear compresses.

history.text: In the late 1800s Taiwan was the world's main source of natural camphor, and Japan made it a state monopoly there in 1899.

lore.text: In Hindu teaching the camphor flame burns away completely and leaves no ash, like the ego dissolving in the divine.

research.text: Licensed in low-strength rubs as a counterirritant, a substance that cools or warms the skin to take the mind off pain.

safety.summary: Swallowing small amounts has caused seizures and deaths in children. Never near a baby's nose, and never on broken skin. Not for people with epilepsy. Avoid in pregnancy.
safety.pets: Toxic to cats and dogs.
safety.regulatory: The US has limited camphor to 11% in over-the-counter products since the early 1980s, when 20% camphorated oil was taken off the market.

entries.what: A white, waxy crystal with a sharp smell, from the wood of the camphor laurel tree or made in factories.
entries.know: Most camphor sold today is synthetic, made from turpentine distilled from pine trees.

entries.name: Cantharis
entries.uses: In homeopathy, given for burning, cutting bladder pain and for scalds and burns that blister.

history.text: The raw beetle's poison, cantharidin, was a notorious and sometimes deadly "aphrodisiac".

research.text: No good trials show a reliable effect beyond placebo.

safety.summary: Raw cantharidin is poisonous. A bladder infection can spread to the kidneys; fever and back pain with it are serious.

entries.what: The Spanish fly beetle diluted into a remedy for burning bladder pain and blistering burns.
entries.know: Spanish fly is not a fly at all but a shiny green beetle.

sources.title: Australian NHMRC, Information Paper: evidence on the effectiveness of homeopathy (2015)

entries.name: Caraway
entries.uses: A traditional tea for wind and colic, listed by the EU's herbal committee. In Germany capsules of peppermint and caraway oil are sold for indigestion with no clear cause (functional dyspepsia).

lore.text: Caraway keeps lovers faithful and keeps things from being stolen. Pigeon keepers fed their birds caraway dough so they would come home.

research.text: Several trials found peppermint-and-caraway oil capsules eased functional dyspepsia better than placebo.

safety.summary: Food amounts are fine. The pure oil is strong and not for small children. Peppermint oil capsules can cause heartburn.

entries.what: Curved brown seeds with a sharp, warm taste, best known in rye bread and sauerkraut.

sources.title: European Medicines Agency, Committee on Herbal Medicinal Products (HMPC) monographs

entries.name: Cardamom
entries.uses: In India pods are chewed after meals for digestion and fresh breath. Ayurveda counts it as balancing all three doshas (the body's three energies) and adds it to milk and coffee to soften their heaviness and jitter. In Arabia it goes into gahwa, the coffee poured for guests.

history.text: Known as the "queen of spices". Scandinavia bakes it into buns, and a popular story says Vikings brought it home from Constantinople. The first written Nordic mention is in a 13th-century Danish cookbook, and it may have come through Moorish trade instead.

lore.text: A love spice, said to be brewed into love potions in tales of the Arabian Nights.

research.text: A few small trials, on things like blood pressure and digestion.

safety.summary: Food amounts are fine. Medicinal amounts may set off gallstone pain (theoretical).

entries.what: Small green pods full of fragrant black seeds, from a ginger-family plant of south India.
entries.know: Guatemala, where it was planted about a century ago, now grows more cardamom than any other country.

Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India

entries.name: Castor oil
entries.uses: Traditionally taken as a strong laxative, and warmed on a cloth as a castor oil pack over the liver, the belly and sore joints. In the Caribbean it is a "wash-out" and a hair oil. Midwives have used it to start labour, which is risky.

history.text: The Ebers Papyrus, an Egyptian medical scroll from about 1550 BCE, lists it as a laxative, and Egyptians burned it in their lamps.

research.text: Licensed as a laxative. Castor oil packs are unstudied. A review of its use to start labour found too little good evidence, and nausea was common.

safety.summary: The seeds contain ricin and can kill if chewed; the pressed oil has no ricin and is safe on the skin. As a laxative it causes cramps. It is dangerous in pregnancy: it can bring on strong contractions and distress the baby. Not for anyone with a blocked bowel.
safety.pets: The seeds can kill pets.

entries.what: A thick oil pressed from castor beans, best known as a strong laxative and for warm castor oil packs.
entries.know: The motor oil brand Castrol is named after castor oil, which early aircraft engines ran on.

entries.name: Cat's claw
entries.uses: Asháninka and other Peruvian peoples boil the inner bark for inflammation, wounds and stomach complaints. Abroad people take it for arthritis and immunity.

history.text: It became a Western supplement in the 1990s, after European lab work in the 1970s and 1980s.

research.text: Small trials in rheumatoid arthritis and osteoarthritis found modest effects. Most other work is in the lab.

safety.summary: It may lower blood pressure. It is avoided in autoimmune disease and after organ transplants because it may stir up the immune system.

entries.what: A woody Amazon vine with hooked thorns like a cat's claws, whose bark is boiled into tea.

sources.title: NIH National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health, Herbs at a Glance
Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database

entries.name: Catnip
entries.uses: Traditionally drunk as a mild calming tea by restless children and adults, and given for colic and feverish colds.

history.text: Brought to North America by European settlers. Several Indigenous nations, among them the Cherokee and the Iroquois, took it up for babies with colic.

lore.text: Grown near the house to call good spirits, and used in love charms.

research.text: Nepetalactone, its scented oil, repels mosquitoes in lab tests. There are no good human trials of the tea.

safety.summary: Mild. Large amounts may cause headache or vomiting.
safety.pets: Safe for cats in small amounts. Between half and two-thirds of cats respond to it; young kittens usually don't. The high lasts about 10 minutes.

entries.cat: Finally. Something in this book worth reading.
entries.what: A grey-green mint that sends many cats into a rolling, drooling fit, and makes a mild herb tea.
entries.know: Lions, leopards and jaguars react to catnip too.

entries.name: Cayenne and chili
entries.uses: Traditionally sprinkled in socks for cold feet, rubbed on aching joints and eaten to sweat out a cold. Today capsaicin creams and skin patches are sold for nerve pain and joint pain.

history.text: Chilies were domesticated in Mexico more than 6,000 years ago. Within a century of 1492 they were growing in India, Africa and Hungary.

lore.text: In New Mexico strings of dried chilies (ristras) hang by the door to protect the house. Chilies are burned against evil.

research.text: A high-strength capsaicin patch is a licensed medicine for nerve pain after shingles. Reviews of the weaker creams found a modest effect.

safety.summary: Burns the eyes and broken skin, so wash your hands after handling it. Large amounts upset the stomach.

entries.what: The hot red peppers of the Americas, dried and ground or eaten fresh; capsaicin gives the burn.
entries.know: Birds can't feel capsaicin's heat, so they eat chilies freely and spread the seeds.

entries.name: CBD oil (hemp extract)
parts: seed (hemp seed oil has no CBD)
entries.uses: Cannabis has old uses in Ayurveda, as bhang and vijaya, and in Chinese medicine, where the seed (huo ma ren) is given as a laxative. CBD extracts are sold and widely discussed today for anxiety, sleep and pain.

history.text: In 2018 the US approved Epidiolex, a purified CBD medicine, for two rare childhood epilepsies (Dravet and Lennox-Gastaut syndromes). A third condition, tuberous sclerosis complex, was added in 2020.

research.text: Strong trial evidence for those epilepsies. Evidence for anxiety, sleep and pain is limited and mixed.

safety.summary: Higher doses can raise liver enzymes. It interacts with many drugs, including blood thinners, epilepsy drugs and sedatives, because it slows the liver enzymes (CYP450) that clear them. Products are often mislabelled or contain THC, which can show up in drug tests. Avoid in pregnancy.
safety.pets: THC products are toxic to dogs.
safety.regulatory: Rules vary by country and US state. The EU and UK treat CBD foods as novel foods that need approval. The US FDA does not accept CBD in foods or dietary supplements. A US federal law from November 2025 narrows the legal meaning of hemp and caps total THC at 0.4 mg per container, which would take most full-spectrum CBD products off the shelves. Most of it was due on 12 November 2026 and was pushed back to 11 December 2026 (status as of November 2026).

entries.what: Oil drops made with cannabidiol (CBD), a compound from the hemp plant that does not make you high.

entries.name: Cedar (northern white and western red)
entries.uses: In the winter of 1535 to 1536 the St Lawrence Iroquoians of Stadacona gave Jacques Cartier's sick crew a tea from a tree they called annedda, probably white cedar, and the men recovered from scurvy. Cedar is used in sweat lodges and burned as a cleansing smoke. In Western herbal practice thuja ointment is put on warts.

history.text: The name arborvitae, "tree of life", is said to come from the Cartier story.

lore.text: One of the four sacred medicines. Cedar boughs line the floor of sweat lodges and are said to protect.

research.text: It contains thujone. There is little clinical work.

safety.summary: Thujone can cause seizures, so the oil and large amounts are dangerous. Internal use stays within the small amounts of tradition.

entries.what: Northern white cedar and western red cedar, evergreen trees used in ceremony, smoke and sweat lodges.

sources.title: Daniel Moerman, Native American Ethnobotany (1998) and the BRIT Native American Ethnobotany database

entries.name: Celery seed
entries.uses: In Western herbalism it is taken for gout and rheumatism, and to pass more water. In Ayurveda the seed, ajmoda, is used for joints and wind.

research.text: Studied mostly in animals, plus one small blood-pressure trial.

safety.summary: It can make skin burn more easily in sunlight. Celery allergy can be severe, and often goes with mugwort and spice allergy. Not for people with kidney inflammation.

entries.what: The tiny, strongly flavoured seeds of the celery plant, used in pickles and as an herbal remedy.

entries.name: Cerasee (bitter melon)
entries.uses: In Jamaica and across the Caribbean cerasee tea is the classic bitter "wash-out" and blood cleanser. Across Asia people cook and eat the fruit for blood sugar and to cool heat.

history.text: Okinawa's best-known home dish, goya champuru, is a stir-fry of bitter melon with tofu and egg.

research.text: Small trials found modest drops in blood sugar.

safety.summary: It can drop blood sugar dangerously alongside diabetes medicines. Children have gone into a coma from low blood sugar after drinking the tea. The seeds can set off a sudden anaemia (red blood cells breaking down) in people with G6PD deficiency, an inherited enzyme shortage.

entries.what: The bitter melon vine; in the Caribbean its leaves and stems make cerasee, a famously bitter bush tea.

sources.title: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database
NIH National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health, Herbs at a Glance

entries.name: Cerebrolysin
parts: mixture of peptides from pig brain
entries.uses: Prescribed in Russia, Eastern Europe, China and elsewhere after stroke and brain injury and for dementia, given by injection or drip. Sought abroad as a nootropic (a focus drug).

research.text: A Cochrane review updated in 2023 found it probably does not lower deaths after ischaemic stroke and may raise non-fatal serious side effects. Trials in dementia and brain injury are mixed.

safety.summary: Prescription injection. Seizures, agitation, dizziness and allergic reactions are reported. Cautioned in epilepsy and severe kidney failure.
safety.regulatory: As of November 2026: approved in about 50 countries (the maker's figure), not in the US or UK.

entries.what: An injected mix of small peptides from pig brain, prescribed in Eastern Europe and Asia after stroke.

sources.title: Cochrane Library systematic reviews

entries.name: Chaga
entries.uses: In Siberia and northern Russia people break chaga into chunks and drink it as a daily tea and a stomach remedy. Soviet pharmacies sold a chaga extract called befungin for gastritis (an inflamed stomach lining).

history.text: The Khanty of western Siberia drank chaga as tea and used it as tinder. It became famous abroad through Cancer Ward, a 1960s Soviet novel in which patients talk about a birch-fungus tea.

research.text: Only lab and animal studies so far. There are no proper human trials.

safety.summary: Chaga is very high in oxalate (a natural compound that can form kidney stones). Kidney failure has been reported in a woman who took chaga powder every day for months. It may also lower blood sugar and slow blood clotting.
safety.ethics: It grows slowly. Wild chaga is being over-harvested in Russia, Finland and Canada since it became a trend.

entries.what: A black, cracked, charcoal-like growth on birch trees, broken up and brewed into tea in the far north.
entries.know: Chaga is not a mushroom cap at all. It is a hard mass of fungus (a sclerotium), and the fungus only makes its spore-bearing body after the birch dies.

entries.name: Chamomile
entries.uses: Drunk as a bedtime tea for calm and sleep, given for colic, wind and upset stomachs, and used in washes for sore skin and eyes. The EMA accepts traditional use for mild stomach complaints and skin inflammation.

history.text: Said to have been dedicated to the sun in ancient Egypt. Manzanilla is the household tea of Mexico and Spain. In Russia people breathe romashka steam for colds.

lore.text: Sprinkled to draw money and luck, and added to baths to attract love. Called the plants' healer, it was said to make sickly plants near it grow strong.

research.text: Small trials for generalised anxiety found a modest effect. Sleep trials are mixed.

safety.summary: People allergic to daisies may react, rarely severely. It may add to the effect of sedatives, and there are case reports of bleeding with warfarin.

entries.cat: You want sleep, drink the flower tea. You want me to sleep, stop talking.
entries.what: A daisy-like flower dried for tea, probably the world's best-known bedtime herb.
entries.know: Its name comes from the Greek for "earth apple", after the flowers' apple-like smell.

entries.name: Chamomilla
entries.uses: In homeopathy, given for teething and for the furious, inconsolable child who wants to be carried, then pushes everything away; often one cheek red and the other pale.

research.text: No good trials show a reliable effect beyond placebo.

safety.summary: At usual potencies the pills contain no measurable chamomile. Teething products with belladonna are a separate danger (see Belladonna).

entries.what: Chamomile diluted into a homeopathic remedy for teething babies and furious, inconsolable moods.

entries.name: Chaparral
entries.uses: Tohono O'odham, Akimel O'odham (Pima) and other desert peoples used it for colds, rheumatism and skin sores. In Mexico it is gobernadora. Salves made from it are still common in the Southwest.

history.text: The smell of the desert after rain is mostly creosote bush. In 1992 the FDA warned the public about chaparral after reports of liver damage.

research.text: Its main compound, NDGA, has been studied in the lab. Taken by mouth, chaparral has caused serious liver injury.

safety.summary: Taken by mouth it has caused severe liver damage, some needing a liver transplant, and kidney damage.

entries.what: The creosote bush of the Southwest deserts, a sticky, strong-smelling shrub made into teas and salves.
entries.know: One ring of creosote bush clones in the Mojave Desert, called King Clone, is thought to be about 11,700 years old.

entries.name: Chaste tree (vitex)
entries.uses: Traditionally taken for the menstrual cycle, premenstrual breast pain and mood. The EMA accepts standard extracts as a well-established use for premenstrual syndrome (PMS).

history.text: Its name is said to come from monasteries, where the berries were thought to cool desire. At the Thesmophoria, an Athenian women's festival, women slept on beds of its branches.

lore.text: A herb of chastity and of the goddess Hera, who was said to have been born under one on the island of Samos.

research.text: Several trials found it eased PMS symptoms. Lab work suggests it acts on dopamine receptors in the brain and lowers prolactin, a hormone.

safety.summary: Can cause headache, nausea and skin rash. It is cautioned with hormone-sensitive conditions and during fertility treatment.

entries.what: A Mediterranean shrub whose peppery berries are taken for the menstrual cycle and premenstrual symptoms.

entries.name: Chickweed
entries.uses: Traditionally laid on fresh, or made into an ointment, to cool itchy, hot skin. It is also eaten as a spring green.

history.text: A cottage-garden weed in nearly every old European herbal, used for itch and inflammation. Its name comes from feeding it to chickens and cage birds.

research.text: Little studied.

safety.summary: Gentle. The plant can build up nitrate, which matters only in large amounts.

entries.what: A small, soft garden weed with tiny white star flowers, eaten as a green and laid on itchy skin.

sources.title: Maud Grieve, A Modern Herbal (1931)

entries.name: Chicory
entries.uses: In Unani and Persian medicine chicory (kasni) is traditionally used as a cooling herb for the liver and for fevers, as seeds, root or leaf juice. The roasted root is brewed as a coffee substitute or blend in France, Russia and New Orleans, and the bitter leaves are eaten in salads.

lore.text: Its flowers open and close at set hours, so it had a place on the 18th-century Swedish flower clock. In German legend a girl waiting by the roadside for her lover to come home was turned into chicory, still watching the road.

research.text: The root is rich in inulin, a fibre that feeds gut bacteria. EU regulators accept that chicory inulin keeps bowel movements regular. The traditional liver uses are not well studied.

safety.summary: Can cause allergy in people sensitive to daisies, ragweed and their relatives. It may increase bile flow, so it is used with caution with gallstones.

entries.what: A roadside plant with sky-blue flowers whose roasted root is brewed like coffee.
entries.know: The German name, Wegwarte, means "the one who waits by the road".

sources.title: National Formulary of Unani Medicine (India)

entries.name: Chinese yam
entries.uses: In Chinese medicine shan yao gently strengthens the spleen, lung and kidney. The "spleen" here is the digestive system that turns food into energy, and the "kidney" a system of vitality and ageing. It is traditionally eaten for tiredness, loose stools and frequent urination, and it is one of the six herbs in Liu Wei Di Huang Wan.

research.text: Studied as a food.

safety.summary: A common food. The raw slime can make the skin itch while peeling.

entries.what: A long, pale, slippery yam eaten as a vegetable in China, Japan and Korea, and used as a gentle tonic.
entries.know: In Japan nagaimo is grated raw into a frothy white paste called tororo and poured over rice.

sources.title: Bensky, Clavey & Stöger, Chinese Herbal Medicine: Materia Medica, 3rd ed. (2004)

entries.name: Choline
entries.uses: Taken in prenatal vitamins and sold as a "nootropic" for memory and focus.

history.text: The US named it an essential nutrient only in 1998.

research.text: Needed for the liver (established); small, mixed studies for memory supplements.

safety.summary: High doses cause a fishy body odour, sweating, low blood pressure and stomach upset. Gut bacteria turn choline into TMAO, a substance studied for heart risk.

entries.what: A nutrient your liver and brain use to build cell walls and the memory messenger acetylcholine; eggs are the classic source.

nutrient.low: Fatty liver and muscle damage in people fed diets without it.
nutrient.limit: US 3,500 mg a day; the EU set no upper limit.

entries.name: Chromium
entries.uses: Sold for blood sugar, weight loss and sugar cravings.

history.text: Brewer's yeast's "glucose tolerance factor" was linked to chromium in the 1950s–70s.

research.text: Trials for blood sugar and weight show small or no effects.

safety.summary: Kidney and liver damage case reports with high doses. Can add to diabetes medicines.

entries.what: A trace mineral marketed for blood sugar and cravings, best known as chromium picolinate.

nutrient.low: Rarely seen; first described in people fed only through a drip.
nutrient.limit: No upper limit set (US or EU).

entries.name: Chrysanthemum tea
entries.uses: In Chinese medicine ju hua is said to clear wind-heat (a pattern of fever, headache and red eyes) and to brighten the eyes. People traditionally drink it for red, tired eyes, headaches and summer heat, often with goji berries.

lore.text: The flower of autumn and long life. On the Double Ninth festival (the ninth day of the ninth month) people climb hills and drink chrysanthemum wine.

research.text: Little study in people.

safety.summary: People allergic to daisy-family plants may react.

entries.what: Dried yellow or white chrysanthemum flowers steeped into a light, floral tea in China and Korea.
entries.know: The emblem of Japan's emperor is a 16-petal chrysanthemum, and the monarchy is called the Chrysanthemum Throne.

sources.title: Bensky, Clavey & Stöger, Chinese Herbal Medicine: Materia Medica, 3rd ed. (2004)

entries.name: Chyawanprash
parts: amla base with 30–50 herbs, ghee, honey and sugar
preps: jam taken by the spoon, often in winter
entries.uses: Children and elders alike take it by the spoonful, often in winter, as a rasayana (rejuvenating tonic) for strength, the lungs and resistance to colds. It is amla cooked down with 30 to 50 herbs, ghee, honey and sugar.

history.text: It is named for the sage Chyavana, who, the story goes, was made young again by the Ashvins, the twin physicians of the gods.

research.text: Small studies, mostly on nutrition.

safety.summary: It is high in sugar, which matters with diabetes. Buy products tested for heavy metals.

entries.what: A dark, sticky Indian herbal jam made from amla fruit, taken by the spoonful.

sources.title: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India
Government of India, Ministry of AYUSH

entries.name: Cinchona (Peruvian bark)
entries.uses: Quechua healers in Peru are said to have used the bark for chills and shivering. From the 1630s Jesuits brought it to Europe as "Jesuits' bark" for malaria fevers. Quinine still gives tonic water and bitters their taste.

history.text: Quinine was isolated from the bark in 1820. The British in India took their daily quinine in tonic water, and added gin.

research.text: Quinine is an approved malaria medicine, now mostly a second choice. The FDA warns against using it for leg cramps.

safety.summary: Quinine can cause cinchonism (ringing ears, headache, nausea, blurred sight), dangerous heart rhythm changes and rare, serious blood reactions. Malaria itself is an emergency, never to be handled with bark or tonic water.

entries.what: An Andean tree whose bark gave the world quinine, the first malaria medicine, and tonic water its bite.
entries.know: A cinchona tree stands on Peru's coat of arms.

sources.title: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database

entries.name: Cinnamon (Ceylon and cassia)
entries.uses: Used in many places to warm a cold stomach and cold hands, for colds and for period cramps. Chinese medicine uses two parts of cassia: the twig, gui zhi, to bring on a light sweat at the start of a cold, and the bark, rou gui, to warm "kidney yang", the body's deep store of heat.

history.text: Ancient Egyptians used cassia in embalming, and cinnamon is one of the spices of the Song of Songs. The Greek historian Herodotus heard that giant birds built nests of cinnamon sticks, a tale that kept the real source secret.

lore.text: A spice of money, love and the Sun. It is burned as incense, or blown across the threshold on the first of the month, to draw in success.

research.text: Trials on blood sugar in type 2 diabetes have given mixed results.

safety.summary: Cassia holds far more coumarin than Ceylon cinnamon; large amounts of coumarin can damage the liver, and the EU limits it in food. The oil burns skin and the mouth.

entries.what: The rolled inner bark of two related trees: thin, sweet Ceylon cinnamon and thicker, hotter Chinese cassia.

entries.name: CJC-1295 and ipamorelin
entries.uses: Sold and discussed in anti-ageing clinics and gyms, usually as a pair injected at bedtime, for muscle, fat loss, sleep and recovery.

history.text: CJC-1295 came from a Canadian company in the 2000s; its trial was halted in 2006 after a participant died, and the drug's part in the death was never established. Ipamorelin was made in Denmark in the late 1990s and tested for gut recovery after surgery, but never approved.

research.text: Short studies show both raise growth hormone and IGF-1 (a growth factor the liver makes in response). There are no long-term trials of what that means for health, and none of the two together.

safety.summary: Water retention, tingling or numb hands, flushing, headache and raised blood sugar. Raised IGF-1 over the long term is a theoretical cancer-growth risk. Grey-market vials carry contamination and dosing risks.
safety.regulatory: As of November 2026: neither is approved. FDA took CJC-1295 and ipamorelin off its Category 2 list in September 2024 after the nominations were withdrawn, and its advisers reviewed CJC-1295 in December 2024; neither is on the list pharmacies may compound from. Sources conflict on ipamorelin: FDA's own page (April 2026) still shows it in the Category 2 table for outsourcing pharmacies (503B) as well as under nominations withdrawn, while HHS said in February 2026 that most restricted peptides would move to the gentler Category 1. Neither is in the October 2026 HHS compounding policy. Prohibited by WADA (S2).

entries.what: Two lab-made peptides injected together to make the body release more of its own growth hormone.

entries.name: Clary sage
entries.uses: Used in aromatherapy, in massage oil or a diffuser, for period cramps and calm. Its seeds swell into a jelly in water and were once put in the eye to wash out specks, which gave it the name clear eye. German wine merchants added it to wine to make it taste like muscatel.

research.text: Small massage studies on period pain, using oil blends.

safety.summary: Folk warnings say it brings heavy drowsiness when mixed with alcohol. It is traditionally avoided in pregnancy.

entries.what: A tall sage with lilac flower spikes whose musky oil is used in aromatherapy for period cramps.

sources.title: Tisserand & Young, Essential Oil Safety, 2nd ed. (2014)

entries.name: Clay (bentonite, kaolin, rhassoul)
entries.uses: Clay masks and poultices are traditionally used for skin, swellings and bruises. In parts of Africa and the American South, eating certain clays (geophagy) is a tradition, especially in pregnancy. Kaolin was long sold as a medicine for diarrhoea.

history.text: Mesopotamian clay tablets list medicinal clays. Rhassoul, from Morocco's Atlas Mountains, is the soap of the hammam; its name comes from an Arabic word for washing.

research.text: Kaolin was a standard diarrhoea medicine for decades but has mostly been replaced. Tests of clays sold for eating found lead and arsenic in many samples.

safety.summary: Eating clay can cause lead and arsenic poisoning and blockages in the gut. The UK Food Standards Agency has warned pregnant women against calabash chalk because of lead, and the US FDA warned in 2016 about lead in a bentonite clay sold to be eaten.

entries.what: Fine natural earths such as bentonite, kaolin and Moroccan rhassoul, used as face masks and, in some cultures, eaten.

sources.title: US FDA, dietary supplement warnings and safety information
Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database

entries.name: Cleavers
entries.uses: Traditionally taken in spring as a "lymphatic" tonic, meant to move fluid through the lymph glands, and as a diuretic (something that makes you pass more urine). People use it for swollen glands, puffiness and skin.

history.text: Greek shepherds used a tangle of it as a sieve to strain hairs out of milk.

research.text: Little studied.

safety.summary: Gentle. It is diuretic, so take care with diuretic drugs and kidney disease.

entries.what: A sticky, clinging hedgerow weed that children throw onto each other's backs, made into a spring tonic.
entries.know: Cleavers is in the same plant family as coffee, and its roasted seeds were brewed as a coffee substitute.

sources.title: Maud Grieve, A Modern Herbal (1931)
Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database

entries.name: Clove
preps: whole bud held on a tooth
entries.uses: Traditionally a bud is held against an aching tooth, or diluted oil is dabbed on the gum. Cloves are also chewed for bad breath and used for wind. Dentists still use eugenol, clove's main oil, in some temporary fillings.

history.text: In Han-dynasty China (about 200 BCE onward) courtiers held cloves in their mouths to sweeten their breath before speaking to the emperor. In the 1600s the Dutch cut and burned clove trees on the outer Moluccan islands so that only their own plantations on Ambon could supply the world.

lore.text: Worn for protection. An orange studded with cloves, the pomander, was carried for luck and against plague.

research.text: Small dental trials compared clove gel with benzocaine, a standard numbing gel, and found similar numbing.

safety.summary: The oil is caustic undiluted. Swallowed, it has caused liver failure and seizures in children. It may raise bleeding risk.
safety.pets: Clove oil is toxic to cats.

entries.what: The dried, nail-shaped flower bud of a tree from the Moluccas, strong enough to numb a tooth.

sources.title: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database
Tisserand & Young, Essential Oil Safety, 2nd ed. (2014)

entries.name: Coca leaf
entries.uses: People in the Andes have chewed the leaf for thousands of years, with a pinch of lime or plant ash (acullico, chaccheo), for strength and against hunger and the cold of the heights. Mate de coca, coca tea, is served to visitors for altitude sickness. Leaves are read for divination and offered to Pachamama, Mother Earth.

history.text: Coca leaves found in house floors in northern Peru are about 8,000 years old. Cocaine was isolated from the leaf in 1860. Bolivia left the UN drug convention in 2012 and rejoined in 2013 with an exception for chewing.

lore.text: Mama Coca is the sacred mother. Three perfect leaves, the k'intu, are offered to the mountains.

research.text: The leaf holds small amounts of cocaine, released slowly when chewed or brewed. The leaf is not the same as the purified drug.

safety.summary: Leaf tea and chewing make drug tests positive. Its stimulant effects are cautioned with heart conditions.
safety.regulatory: Legal for traditional use in Peru and Bolivia and in parts of Colombia and Argentina, and illegal almost everywhere else (Schedule I of the 1961 UN Single Convention). In 2025 the WHO's drug committee reviewed the leaf and advised keeping it in Schedule I; the UN Commission on Narcotic Drugs upheld this in April 2026.

entries.what: The leaf of an Andean shrub, chewed or brewed as tea for thousands of years; cocaine is made from it.

entries.name: Coconut oil
entries.uses: Traditionally used across the tropics on hair, skin and babies, and in Pacific massage (Hawaiian lomilomi, Samoan fofō). In Kerala it is the everyday cooking oil and is used for oil pulling. In Tahiti tiare flowers are steeped in it to make monoi.

history.text: In the Pacific the coconut palm is the tree of life, giving food, drink, rope, roofing and medicine.

research.text: Lauric acid, its main fat, has been studied in the lab. Eaten, it raises LDL ("bad") cholesterol more than vegetable oils do.

safety.summary: It is mostly saturated fat when eaten in quantity.

entries.what: The white fat pressed from coconut flesh, used across the tropics on hair and skin, in massage and in cooking.
entries.know: A coconut can float across the sea for months and still sprout when it washes ashore.

sources.title: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database

entries.name: Coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10)
entries.uses: Taken by people on statins for muscle aches, and sold for energy, heart health and migraines.

history.text: Discovered in 1957; Japan approved it for heart failure in the 1970s.

research.text: Trials for statin muscle pain are mixed; small studies for migraine prevention and heart failure show some benefit.

safety.summary: Usually well tolerated; mild stomach upset and insomnia. It can weaken warfarin's effect and add to blood-pressure drugs.

entries.what: A substance your cells make to turn food into energy; levels drop with age and with statin drugs.

nutrient.low: No clear deficiency signs outside rare genetic disorders.
nutrient.limit: No upper limit set (US or EU).

sources.title: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements, vitamin and mineral fact sheets (health professional versions)
NIH National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health, Herbs at a Glance

entries.name: Coffea cruda
entries.uses: In homeopathy, given for sleeplessness from a racing, overactive or overjoyed mind: the coffee state, met by its own remedy, as the law of similars teaches.

research.text: No good trials show a reliable effect beyond placebo.

safety.summary: At usual potencies there is no measurable coffee or caffeine.

entries.what: Unroasted coffee beans diluted into a remedy for a mind too excited to sleep.

sources.title: Australian NHMRC, Information Paper: evidence on the effectiveness of homeopathy (2015)

entries.name: Coffee
entries.uses: In Ethiopia's buna ceremony the beans are roasted, ground and brewed in front of the guests and served in three rounds. Sufis in Yemen drank it in the 1400s to stay awake for night prayers. Today it is the world's favourite stimulant, and the grounds are read for fortunes (tasseography).

history.text: Legend says an Ethiopian goatherd saw his goats dancing after they ate coffee cherries. From the 1500s to the 1700s the Yemeni port of Mocha shipped most of the world's coffee.

lore.text: In Turkish coffee reading (kahve falı) the cup is turned upside down on its saucer to cool, and the shapes left by the grounds tell the future.

research.text: Large observational studies link moderate drinking with lower risks of liver disease, type 2 diabetes and Parkinson's disease. These studies show links, not proof.

safety.summary: Caffeine can cause anxiety, poor sleep and palpitations, and stopping suddenly brings withdrawal headaches. It raises levels of clozapine and theophylline and can shift lithium levels. Boiled and unfiltered coffee raises LDL cholesterol. High caffeine in pregnancy is linked with miscarriage and low birth weight, so it is usually kept low.

entries.what: The roasted seed of a red cherry from an African shrub, the world's favourite caffeine drink.
entries.know: Turkish coffee culture was added to UNESCO's list of intangible heritage in 2013.

sources.title: NIH National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health, Herbs at a Glance
Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database

entries.name: Cold water and winter swimming
entries.uses: In Russia and Ukraine the best-known custom is the Epiphany plunge on 19 January, through a hole cut in the ice in the shape of a cross. Winter swimmers are nicknamed "walruses" (morzhi). Children were doused with cold water to "harden" them (zakalivanie). Athletes now sit in ice baths after training.

history.text: Soviet kindergartens and sports clubs promoted cold hardening. From the 1930s a Soviet folk healer taught a system of cold dousing and barefoot walks in the snow that gained a huge following.

research.text: Small studies on mood and inflammation. In trials, regular ice baths after weight training reduced muscle gains.

safety.summary: Cold shock (the gasp and racing heart of the first minute) can cause drowning and heart attacks. Never go in alone or after alcohol. Not with heart disease, high blood pressure or Raynaud's. Hypothermia sets in fast, and the body keeps cooling for a while after you get out.

entries.cat: Jumping through a hole in the ice on a holy day. Bold. Bring a friend with a rope.
entries.what: Dipping or swimming in icy water, from Russian winter swimming to the modern ice bath.

sources.title: Łuczaj et al., Wild food and medicinal plants in Slavic and Eastern European ethnobotany (Journal of Ethnobiology and Ethnomedicine papers)

entries.name: Collagen peptides
entries.uses: Sold as a food supplement and stirred into coffee or smoothies for skin, hair, nails and joints. Bone broths and aspics are traditional foods for strength and recovery in many kitchens, from Russian kholodets to Chinese pig-trotter soups.

research.text: Many trials report small gains in skin moisture and elasticity and less joint pain, but most were paid for by makers. A 2025 review of 23 trials found the skin effects vanished in the high-quality and independently funded studies; a 2026 review still found effects on moisture and elasticity, though not on wrinkles.

safety.summary: A food. Products come from fish, cattle, pigs or chicken, so people with those allergies check the source.

entries.what: Collagen protein broken into small pieces and sold as a powder for drinks, or eaten as bone broth.
entries.know: Kholodets, the Russian meat jelly, sets on its own from the collagen in long-boiled trotters and bones.

sources.title: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database
https://nutraingredients.com/Article/2025/08/26/industry-reacts-to-meta-analysis-concluding-collagen-supplements-show-no-proven-benefit-for-skin-aging

entries.name: Colloidal silver
entries.uses: Sold and promoted as a "natural antibiotic" drink. Hospitals use silver dressings on wounds. In India, edible silver leaf (vark) decorates sweets, and Ayurvedic mineral medicine turns silver into a fine ash (rajata bhasma).

history.text: Silver vessels were used to keep water fresh. Silver nitrate drops were once put into newborns' eyes against infection.

research.text: Silver dressings have some evidence for wounds. Drinking silver has no proven benefit.

safety.summary: Swallowed over time, it can turn the skin permanently blue-grey (argyria). It lowers the absorption of some antibiotics and of thyroid medicine.
safety.regulatory: In 1999 the US FDA ruled that over-the-counter colloidal silver products are not recognised as safe and effective.

entries.what: Tiny silver particles in water, sold as a drink or spray and promoted as a natural antibiotic.

sources.title: NIH National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health, Herbs at a Glance
US FDA, dietary supplement warnings and safety information

entries.name: Coltsfoot
entries.uses: Traditionally used for coughs; its Latin name, Tussilago, means "cough dispeller". The leaf was smoked for asthma in old Europe. In Chinese medicine the flower bud, kuan dong hua, is used for cough.

history.text: The leaf was painted on the signs of French apothecaries. The Russian name comes from the leaf itself: the soft, downy underside feels warm like a mother, the smooth top feels cold like a stepmother.

research.text: It contains pyrrolizidine alkaloids (PAs), plant toxins that damage the liver. There are no good modern trials for cough.

safety.summary: Its PAs can cause veno-occlusive disease, where the small veins of the liver block up. In a 1988 Swiss case a newborn died of it after the mother drank a pharmacy herbal tea, sold as containing coltsfoot, every day of her pregnancy. In another case a toddler fell ill after the family picked a look-alike, Alpendost, thinking it was coltsfoot. Only certified PA-free varieties are used, briefly, if at all.
safety.regulatory: Germany and Austria restrict PAs in herbal medicines, and EU legal limits on PAs in herbal teas have applied since 2022.

entries.what: An early spring flower whose hoof-shaped leaves were once Europe's standard cough herb.
entries.know: Its yellow flowers come up in early spring, weeks before any leaves appear.

entries.name: Comfrey
entries.uses: Traditionally put on the skin over sprains, bruises, sore joints and broken bones, hence the name knitbone. The EMA accepts traditional external use for bruises and sprains.

history.text: Its Latin name, Symphytum, comes from Greek for "to grow together". The English name goes back to a Latin word for knitting or healing together.

lore.text: Carried for safe travel, and tucked into luggage so it won't go astray.

research.text: Several trials of root ointments found benefit for ankle sprains, back pain and sore knees.

safety.summary: Only on unbroken skin, for short spells. Swallowed, its pyrrolizidine alkaloids have caused fatal liver disease.
safety.pets: Toxic to animals if eaten.
safety.regulatory: In 2001 the US FDA told makers to take oral comfrey products off the market. The UK, Canada and Australia also ban or restrict oral use.

entries.what: A big, hairy-leaved herb with drooping bell flowers, called knitbone and made into ointments for sprains.

entries.name: Copal
entries.latin: Protium copal, Bursera spp., Hymenaea (South America)
entries.uses: Burned on charcoal in Maya and Aztec rites, in curanderismo limpias (spiritual cleansings where smoke or herbs are passed over the body), and on Día de Muertos altars to guide the dead home. It is sold as white, gold and black copal, from different trees and ways of collecting.

lore.text: Called the blood of trees and the food of the gods. In the Popol Vuh, the K'iche' Maya book of creation, the first people burned copal as they waited for the first sunrise.

research.text: Hardly studied.

safety.summary: The smoke irritates the lungs when burned indoors.
safety.ethics: Buy community-harvested copal.

entries.what: A fragrant tree resin from Mexico and Central America, burned in Maya and Aztec rites and still on altars today.

sources.title: research/HEALING-CODEX.md in this repo (fuller prose on many of these items)
Schultes & Hofmann, Plants of the Gods (1979/2001)

entries.name: Copper
entries.uses: Taken in multivitamins; copper bracelets are worn for arthritis in folk tradition.

history.text: Copper bracelets for rheumatism go back centuries in European folk medicine.

research.text: A UK trial found copper bracelets made no difference to arthritis pain.

safety.summary: Too much damages the liver; people with Wilson's disease (a genetic copper-storage disorder) must avoid extra copper. High zinc drains copper.

entries.what: A trace mineral used to make red blood cells, connective tissue and skin pigment.

nutrient.low: Anaemia and nerve damage (unsteady walking, numbness), often caused by years of high-dose zinc.
nutrient.limit: US 10 mg a day; EU 5 mg a day.

sources.title: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements, vitamin and mineral fact sheets (health professional versions)
National Academies (IOM), Dietary Reference Intakes: tolerable upper intake levels
EFSA, overview of tolerable upper intake levels (2024 update)

entries.name: Coptis
entries.uses: In Chinese medicine it clears "fire" and "damp heat". Fire means signs of strong heat such as redness, thirst and agitation; damp heat is heat stuck with sticky, heavy fluid. So it is traditionally used for hot, urgent diarrhoea, mouth sores, irritability and red skin eruptions.

research.text: Berberine, its yellow alkaloid, has been tested in many small trials, mostly in China, for blood sugar and cholesterol, with modest results. Coptis itself has been studied far less.

safety.summary: Berberine interacts with many drugs and can raise ciclosporin levels. It must not be given to newborns: it can push up bilirubin and worsen newborn jaundice. It can upset the stomach.

entries.what: A small, bright yellow root, one of the bitterest herbs in Chinese medicine.

sources.title: Bensky, Clavey & Stöger, Chinese Herbal Medicine: Materia Medica, 3rd ed. (2004)
Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database

entries.name: Cordyceps
aka: dong chong xia cao (Chinese, "winter worm summer grass")
entries.uses: In Chinese and Tibetan medicine it is said to tonify (strengthen) the lungs and kidneys. People take it for a lingering cough, tiredness, low sex drive and getting back on their feet after illness, often stewed in soup with duck or chicken.

history.text: Tibetan medical writing from the 15th century describes it. In 1993 Chinese women runners broke world records, and their coach credited a tonic of cordyceps and turtle blood; later reports pointed to doping. The best wild pieces can sell for more than their weight in gold.

lore.text: A worm in winter, a grass in summer. The fungus infects a ghost moth caterpillar underground, fills its body and sends up a thin stalk in spring.

research.text: A few small trials, mostly from China, looked at exercise and kidney function, with mixed results. Most products sold today are cultivated C. militaris or lab-grown mycelium, not the wild fungus.

safety.summary: Lead has been found in some products, and Chinese regulators warned about high arsenic in wild cordyceps in 2016. It may affect blood sugar, clotting and drugs that dampen the immune system.
safety.ethics: The wild harvest in Tibet and Nepal is shrinking and has led to fights over picking grounds. Cultivated C. militaris avoids this.

entries.what: A fungus that sprouts from a buried caterpillar in the Tibetan highlands, prized as a costly tonic.
entries.know: In parts of Tibet and Nepal, picking cordyceps each spring brings in a large share of a family's cash for the whole year.

sources.title: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database
Bensky, Clavey & Stöger, Chinese Herbal Medicine: Materia Medica, 3rd ed. (2004)
Men-Tsee-Khang (Tibetan Medical & Astro-Science Institute), Dharamsala

entries.name: Coriander (cilantro)
entries.uses: In Ayurveda the seed is a cooling digestive, and seed water is drunk for burning when passing urine. The fresh leaf is a garnish in kitchens from Mexico to Thailand.

history.text: Coriander seeds were found in Tutankhamun's tomb. It is one of the oldest spices still in use.

lore.text: A love herb in the Arabian Nights. In Chinese folk belief the seeds were said to bring long life, even immortality.

research.text: Very few human studies. Online claims that the leaf pulls heavy metals out of the body are not backed by trials.

safety.summary: Food amounts are fine. Some people are allergic. To some people the leaf tastes of soap, which is linked to a common gene variant for smell.

entries.what: One plant, two flavours: the fresh green leaf (cilantro) and the round, citrusy dried seed.

sources.title: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database
Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India

entries.name: Corn silk
entries.uses: Traditionally used around the world as a mild diuretic and a soother of the bladder, for swelling, cystitis and stones. In Mexico it is brewed as tea, in China it is simmered as yu mi xu, and Russian pharmacies sell it dried in boxes.

research.text: Animal studies on urine output, and very few in people.

safety.summary: It makes the body pass more water and potassium, and low potassium has been reported with long use. It is not for people with kidney failure, and it may clash with diuretics and blood-pressure drugs. Skin rashes and allergy have been reported.

entries.what: The fine golden threads at the tip of an ear of corn, dried for tea in many countries.

sources.title: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database
Bensky, Clavey & Stöger, Chinese Herbal Medicine: Materia Medica, 3rd ed. (2004)

entries.name: Cornflower
entries.uses: In Slavic folk medicine the flowers were made into a cool eyewash for tired eyes and a mild diuretic tea.

history.text: The cornflower became the emblem of Prussia. In Russia it grew among the rye, and village girls wove it into summer wreaths.

lore.text: A Russian legend tells of Vasily, a young man lured into the rye by a rusalka (a water spirit) and turned into the blue flower, vasilyok.

research.text: Little studied.

safety.summary: Gentle. People allergic to daisies may react. Any eyewash has to be sterile.

entries.what: A bright blue cornfield flower, used in Slavic folk medicine as an eyewash and a mild tea.
entries.know: Its blue is so distinctive that "cornflower blue" became the name of a colour, and of the most prized sapphires.

sources.title: Sokolov & Zamotaev, Handbook of Medicinal Plants (USSR, 1984/1990)
Maud Grieve, A Modern Herbal (1931)

entries.name: Couch grass
entries.uses: Traditionally drunk as a tea to flush the urinary tract and soothe the bladder. The EMA accepts its traditional use to increase urine flow in minor urinary complaints.

history.text: The folk name dog grass comes from dogs chewing it, said to be how they make themselves sick. In France it is chiendent, "dog's tooth", a tisane for the kidneys.

research.text: Little clinical study.

safety.summary: The method relies on drinking plenty of water. It is not for people who must limit fluids, as in heart or kidney failure.

entries.what: A creeping, hard-to-kill grass whose underground stems are boiled into a tea for the bladder.

sources.title: European Medicines Agency, Committee on Herbal Medicinal Products (HMPC) monographs
Sokolov & Zamotaev, Handbook of Medicinal Plants (USSR, 1984/1990)

entries.name: Cranberry
entries.uses: Wampanoag, Lenape and other Algonquian peoples ate the berries and pounded them into pemmican (dried meat, fat and berries). They also dyed with them and put them on wounds as poultices. Today people drink the juice or take capsules to avoid repeat bladder infections. In Russia klyukva mors, a sweet berry drink, is given in fevers.

history.text: The name comes from "craneberry": settlers thought the flower looked like a crane's head. American sailors are said to have carried cranberries against scurvy.

research.text: A 2023 Cochrane review found cranberry products cut repeat urinary infections in women who get them often, in children, and in people having some medical procedures. They have not been shown to clear an infection already under way.

safety.summary: The juice is often high in sugar. A few case reports suggest it may strengthen the effect of warfarin. Concentrated tablets can add oxalate to urine, which matters for people who form kidney stones.

entries.what: A tart red berry of North American bogs, drunk as juice by people who get repeat bladder infections.
entries.know: Cranberries don't grow underwater. Bogs are flooded only at harvest, so the berries float up and can be skimmed off.

sources.title: NIH National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health, Herbs at a Glance
Cochrane Library systematic reviews
Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database

entries.name: Cumin
entries.uses: Used for wind, bloating and digestion. In Indian homes people sip jeera water (seeds boiled in water). Ayurveda's "CCF tea" brews cumin, coriander and fennel seeds together.

history.text: Cumin seeds about 4,000 years old have been found in Syria, and ancient Egyptians cooked with it. Romans kept ground cumin on the table the way we keep pepper.

lore.text: In European folk magic it keeps lovers faithful, and chickens from wandering off.

research.text: A few small trials looked at irritable bowel and weight loss.

safety.summary: Food amounts are fine. "Black cumin" is a different plant (nigella, see black seed).

entries.what: Small ridged seeds with a warm, earthy smell, central to Indian, Mexican and Middle Eastern cooking.

sources.title: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database
Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India

entries.name: Cupping
entries.uses: Done in Chinese medicine, in Islamic medicine (where wet cupping is called hijama) and in Slavic homes. A flame heats the air inside a glass cup, the cup goes on the skin, and the cooling air pulls the skin up. In Russia and Poland grandmothers put glass banki on the back for bronchitis and colds. In hijama, small cuts are made first so a little blood is drawn into the cup.

history.text: Ancient Greek, Arabic and Chinese texts describe cupping, and the Egyptian Ebers Papyrus (about 1550 BCE) is often said to mention it. Round purple marks on US swimmers at the 2016 Rio Olympics brought a new wave of interest.

lore.text: A hadith recommends hijama on the 17th, 19th and 21st days of the Islamic lunar month.

research.text: Small trials suggest it may ease neck and back pain, but the studies are small and of low quality.

safety.summary: Leaves round bruises that fade over days to weeks. Fire cupping can burn the skin, hair and clothes. Wet cupping can spread infection and blood-borne disease without sterile, single-use tools. Not on broken skin. Bleeding disorders and blood thinners raise the risk of bleeding.

entries.what: Cups held on the skin by suction, leaving round marks; known in China, the Middle East and Eastern Europe.

sources.title: Cao et al., Clinical research evidence of cupping therapy in China: a systematic literature review (BMC CAM 2010) and later Cochrane reviews

entries.name: Daikenchuto (Da Jian Zhong Tang)
parts: Japanese pepper (sansho), dried ginger, ginseng, malt sugar
entries.uses: In Kampo (Japan's own form of Chinese herbal medicine) it is traditionally used to warm "the middle", the belly, when it feels cold, bloated and cramping. Japanese surgeons widely give it after abdominal operations to get the bowels moving again.

research.text: Many trials in Japan and the US after bowel and stomach surgery. Some reviews found bowels woke up sooner. A 2020 Cochrane review judged the evidence very weak and unclear.

safety.summary: Usually mild. Japanese labels list rare liver problems and rare lung inflammation (interstitial pneumonia); a dry cough, breathlessness or fever means stop.

entries.what: A spicy Kampo formula of Japanese pepper, ginger, ginseng and malt sugar for a cold, cramping belly.

sources.title: Japan Ministry of Health, Kampo formulas approved for national health insurance (148 formulas)
Cochrane Library systematic reviews

entries.name: Damiana
entries.uses: In Mexico people drink it as a love tonic and for nerves. The Maya are said to have used it. A damiana liqueur is sold in a bottle shaped like a woman, said to be a goddess.

history.text: It reached the US in the 1870s, sold as a "sexual tonic", and was in the US National Formulary from 1888 to 1947.

research.text: Lab and animal studies only.

safety.summary: It may lower blood sugar. Convulsions were reported in one person who took a very large amount of extract.

entries.what: A small fragrant Mexican shrub drunk as a tea or liqueur, long known as a love tonic.

sources.title: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database

entries.name: Dan shen
entries.uses: In Chinese medicine it is the chief herb to "invigorate the blood", that is, to get stuck blood moving. Stagnant blood is said to cause fixed, stabbing pain. So dan shen is traditionally used for chest pain, period pain and lumps.

research.text: Compound Danshen Dripping Pills, a Chinese product, have been tested for angina in China and in US trials, with mixed results.

safety.summary: It strongly raises the effect of warfarin, and dangerous bleeding has been reported. It adds to antiplatelet drugs. It can throw off blood tests for digoxin.

entries.what: The brick-red root of a Chinese sage, used in Chinese medicine for the heart and circulation.
entries.know: Dan means cinnabar red, for the colour of the root.

sources.title: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database
Bensky, Clavey & Stöger, Chinese Herbal Medicine: Materia Medica, 3rd ed. (2004)

entries.name: Dandelion
entries.uses: The leaf is traditionally used as a diuretic and the root as a bitter for the liver, bile and appetite. The EMA accepts traditional use of the leaf to flush the urinary tract and of the root for digestion. In Chinese medicine pu gong ying "clears heat and toxins" (in its terms, cools inflammation and infection) and is used for swellings of the breast and skin.

history.text: Arabic medical writers described it in the 10th and 11th centuries. The French name, pissenlit ("wet the bed"), records the leaf's reputation.

lore.text: Blow the seed clock to tell the time or send a wish. Its yellow flower is the sun, its white head the moon, and its scattering seeds the stars.

research.text: A small pilot study in 17 people found the leaf made them pass urine more often. The leaf is rich in potassium.

safety.summary: People allergic to daisies may react. Avoid it with blocked bile ducts. Take care with lithium and diuretics. Its high potassium matters for anyone who must limit potassium.

entries.what: The common yellow weed with a puffball seed head, used as a bitter root and a diuretic leaf.
entries.know: Each dandelion "flower" is really a cluster of 100 or more tiny florets, and each floret makes one seed.

entries.name: Dang shen
entries.uses: In Chinese medicine it is a gentler, cheaper qi tonic than ginseng. Qi is the body's moving life energy. It is traditionally used for tiredness, a poor appetite and weak lungs, and the soft sweet roots are cooked whole in family soups.

research.text: Very little clinical work.

safety.summary: Thought to be gentle. Little has been studied, so its interactions are not known.

entries.what: A sweet root of the bellflower family, the everyday stand-in for ginseng in Chinese kitchens.

sources.title: Bensky, Clavey & Stöger, Chinese Herbal Medicine: Materia Medica, 3rd ed. (2004)

entries.name: Dashamoola
parts: ten roots (bilva, agnimantha, shyonaka, patala, gambhari, brihati, kantakari, shalaparni, prishniparni, gokshura)
entries.uses: In Ayurveda it is used for vata conditions (vata is the airy, dry, moving energy, linked to pain and stiffness): aches, joint and back pain, and coughs. It is also given to new mothers after birth, often as Dashamoolarishta, a fermented tonic.

research.text: Little clinical work.

safety.summary: The arishta (fermented) forms contain alcohol.

entries.what: A classic Ayurvedic blend of ten roots, boiled into a tea or fermented into a tonic wine.
entries.know: The ten roots split into five tree roots and five small herb roots, and each group of five is a formula of its own.

sources.title: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India

entries.name: Dates (ajwa)
entries.uses: In Prophetic medicine a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim says that whoever eats seven ajwa dates in the morning will not be harmed that day by poison or magic. Following the Prophet's practice, Muslims traditionally break the Ramadan fast with a date. Women across the Middle East eat dates in late pregnancy and labour, as Mary did in the Qur'an.

research.text: Several small trials found eating dates in the last weeks of pregnancy was linked to a riper cervix and less need to start or speed labour with drugs.

safety.summary: Very sweet, which matters with diabetes.

entries.what: Soft, dark dates of a prized variety grown in Medina, eaten in Prophetic medicine.
entries.know: The Qur'an tells that Mary, in labour under a palm tree, was told to shake its trunk so fresh dates would fall to her (19:23 to 26).

sources.title: Ibn Qayyim al-Jawziyya, Medicine of the Prophet (al-Tibb al-Nabawi, 14th c.)
https://sunnah.com/bukhari:5445
https://quran.com/19/23-26

entries.name: Datura (thorn apple)
preps: historic: asthma cigarettes, offerings to Shiva, vision ceremonies
entries.uses: Historically the leaves were smoked in asthma cigarettes in Europe and America. In India the flowers and spiny fruit are offered to Shiva. Indigenous peoples of Mexico and southern California used datura (toloache) in vision and initiation ceremonies, led by elders with great caution.

history.text: "Jimsonweed" comes from Jamestown, Virginia, where soldiers ate it boiled as greens in 1676 and acted mad for 11 days.

lore.text: Datura is Shiva's flower, offered to him on Maha Shivaratri, his great night. Among some California peoples toloache opened the way to visions and a spirit helper at a young person's initiation.

research.text: It contains scopolamine and atropine.

safety.summary: Deadly. Poisoning brings delirium that can last for days, high temperature, a racing heart, seizures and death, and is an emergency. Teenagers are taken to hospital every year after trying it. Angel's trumpet (Brugmansia) is just as dangerous. History and lore only.
safety.pets: Toxic to pets.

entries.what: A rank weed with huge white trumpet flowers and spiny seed pods, poisonous in every part.

sources.title: Schultes & Hofmann, Plants of the Gods (1979/2001)
research/HEALING-CODEX.md in this repo (fuller prose on many of these items)

entries.name: Deadly nightshade (belladonna)
entries.uses: Italian Renaissance women are said to have dripped the juice into their eyes to widen the pupils, which gave the plant the name bella donna, "beautiful lady". Historically it went into old pain plasters and the legendary flying ointments of witches. The medicine atropine comes from it.

history.text: Atropine was isolated from the plant in the 1830s. It is on the WHO list of essential medicines, used to speed a slow heart, widen the pupils for eye exams and counter nerve-agent and pesticide poisoning.

lore.text: The name Atropa comes from Atropos, the Fate who cuts the thread of life. Folk belief says the devil tends the plant all year and leaves it alone only on Walpurgis Night (30 April).

research.text: Its alkaloids atropine and scopolamine (hyoscine) are established medicines.

safety.summary: Deadly. Every part is poisonous. A few berries can kill a child, and the sweet black berries look like cherries or bilberries. Poisoning brings a dry mouth, hot flushed skin, huge pupils, a racing heart, delirium and seizures, and is an emergency. History and lore only.
safety.pets: Toxic to pets and horses.

entries.what: A tall European nightshade with glossy black berries, one of the most poisonous plants in the world.
entries.know: Atropine from this plant is carried by soldiers in auto-injectors as an antidote to nerve gas.

sources.title: research/HEALING-CODEX.md in this repo (fuller prose on many of these items)

entries.name: Decoction
preps: simmered in water, often reduced by half or a quarter, strained
entries.uses: The traditional way to draw out hard parts: roots, bark and seeds are simmered for anything from 20 minutes to hours. It is the standard form of Chinese formulas (tang, "soup") and of Ayurvedic kashayas.

history.text: Chinese prescriptions spell out when each herb goes in. Minerals and shells go first so they boil longest; aromatic herbs go in last so their oils don't boil away.

research.text: In many clinics in China, Taiwan and Japan, dried granule extracts have replaced home decoctions.

safety.summary: Strength changes with simmering time. Label it and keep it in the fridge.

entries.what: A brew made by simmering tough roots, barks or seeds in water for a long time.
entries.know: Japan's national health insurance covers 148 Kampo formulas, most of them given as ready-made granules rather than home brews.

sources.title: Bensky, Clavey & Stöger, Chinese Herbal Medicine: Materia Medica, 3rd ed. (2004)

entries.name: Devil's claw
entries.uses: San and Khoi peoples of the Kalahari traditionally dig the side tubers, slice and dry them, and drink them as a bitter brew for pain, fever and poor digestion. In Europe the extract is taken for stiff joints and back pain. The EU herbal committee (EMA) lists it as a traditional remedy for mild joint pain and for indigestion and poor appetite.

history.text: In the early 1900s a German farmer in colonial Namibia saw a local healer use it and sent it home to Europe. German labs began studying it in the 1950s.

research.text: Several trials, mostly small and German, found extracts eased low back pain and arthritis pain a little more than a dummy pill. A Cochrane review of herbs for back pain rated the evidence as low to moderate in quality.

safety.summary: Often upsets the stomach and raises stomach acid, so it is avoided with stomach ulcers. It may increase bile flow, so it is avoided with gallstones. Lab and animal work suggest it can change heart rate, blood pressure and blood sugar, so it may add to heart, blood-pressure and diabetes medicines. A bleeding case has been reported with warfarin. Not used in pregnancy.
safety.ethics: Most of it is still dug from the wild by San and other rural harvesters in Namibia and Botswana, who are often paid little. Fair-trade and permit schemes exist; look for them.

entries.what: A Kalahari desert plant whose bitter root tubers are dried and taken for aching joints.
entries.know: The name comes from the fruit, a woody pod covered in hooked arms that snag on the feet of passing animals.

entries.name: Digestive bitters
parts: gentian, wormwood, angelica, orange peel, aloe and others
preps: drops on the tongue before meals
entries.uses: Traditionally taken before or after meals to wake up digestion. In central Europe Swedish bitters were rubbed on bruises and drunk for nearly every complaint.

history.text: The Swedish bitters recipe became famous through an Austrian herbalist's 1980 book. Italian amari began in monasteries and old pharmacies.

research.text: A bitter taste sets off digestive reflexes such as saliva and stomach juices, but clinical trials are few.

safety.summary: Most contain alcohol. The aloe in Swedish bitters is a laxative.

entries.what: Bitter herbal drops or liqueurs taken around meals, like Italian amaro and Swedish bitters.
entries.know: Angostura bitters is named after the town of Angostura in Venezuela, now Ciudad Bolívar, where it was first made in 1824.

sources.title: Maud Grieve, A Modern Herbal (1931)
European Medicines Agency, Committee on Herbal Medicinal Products (HMPC) monographs

entries.name: Dill
entries.uses: Traditionally dill water, the first gripe water, was spooned to babies with colic and wind. The fresh leaf goes into almost every Slavic dish.

history.text: Dill water was a staple of English pharmacies, and the first branded gripe water (1851) was based on it. A popular story links the name to Old Norse dilla, "to lull"; the real origin is unknown.

lore.text: Hung over cradles and doors to keep witches away, and used in love charms.

research.text: Little modern research.

safety.summary: Food amounts are fine.

entries.what: A feathery green herb with seeds, used fresh on fish and potatoes and in pickles.

sources.title: Maud Grieve, A Modern Herbal (1931)

entries.name: Dong quai
preps: in formulas (Si Wu Tang, Dang Gui Shao Yao San)
entries.uses: In Chinese medicine it is the chief herb to nourish and move the blood. Here "blood" means both the fluid and the nourishing power it carries. It is traditionally used for the monthly cycle, period pain and a pale, tired look. In southern China it is stewed in soups for new mothers in the month after birth.

lore.text: The name dang gui is often read as "ought to return": the herb that brings a wife back to her husband, or the blood back to its proper course.

research.text: One trial in menopausal women found it did no better than a dummy pill for hot flushes when taken alone. Few other good trials exist.

safety.summary: It strongly raises the effect of warfarin, and serious bleeding has been reported. It contains coumarins and can make the skin burn more easily in sun. The essential oil contains safrole, a known carcinogen in animals.

entries.what: A fragrant root of the celery family, the best-known women's herb in Chinese medicine.

entries.name: Dragon's blood (Socotra and Dracaena)
aka: dam al-akhawain (Arabic, "blood of the two brothers")
entries.uses: On Socotra and in Chinese medicine (xue jie) it is put on wounds to stop bleeding. In magic it is burned for power and protection and mixed into ink. It was also used to colour varnish, and it is often said to be in the varnish of old Italian violins.

lore.text: A Roman naturalist wrote that it was the blood of a dragon killed in a fight with an elephant. In Socotran legend it is the blood of two brothers who fought to the death.

research.text: Hardly studied in people.

safety.summary: There is little safety data.
safety.ethics: The IUCN lists Socotra's dragon tree as Vulnerable. Cyclones, goats eating the seedlings and a drying climate threaten it.

entries.what: A deep red resin from Socotra's umbrella-shaped dragon trees and from Asian rattan palms.

sources.title: IUCN Red List of Threatened Species

entries.name: Ear candling
preps: lit at one end, other end in the ear
entries.uses: Practised and sold for earwax, sinus pressure and relaxation. One person lies on their side while another holds a burning cone upright in their ear for about 10 to 15 minutes.

research.text: Lab tests found no suction and no earwax removed. The residue left in the cone is candle wax, and candle wax and ash have been found in ears afterwards.

safety.summary: Burns to the face, hair and ear canal, burst eardrums, and candle wax blocking the ear.
safety.regulatory: The US FDA warns against ear candles, has seized them and stops them at import.

entries.what: A hollow, wax-coated cloth cone lit at one end while the other end sits in the ear.
entries.know: The Hopi tribe has said ear candling was never a Hopi practice and asked sellers to stop using its name.

sources.title: US FDA, dietary supplement warnings and safety information

entries.name: Echinacea
entries.latin: Echinacea purpurea, E. angustifolia, E. pallida
entries.uses: Lakota, Cheyenne, Comanche and other Plains nations used the root for snakebite, wounds, toothache and sore throats; a piece of root was chewed and held on a sore tooth. Today people mostly take it at the first sign of a cold. The EMA accepts the pressed juice of E. purpurea as a well-established use for short-term colds.

history.text: In the 1870s and 1880s a Nebraska patent-medicine seller sold it as a "blood purifier". In 1939 a German firm began selling a pressed juice of E. purpurea, and it became a household cold remedy in Germany.

research.text: A 2014 Cochrane review found some products may slightly lower the chance of catching a cold. Effects on how long a cold lasts were small or unclear. Products differ a lot by species and plant part.

safety.summary: People allergic to the daisy family can react to it, and anaphylaxis (a severe whole-body allergic reaction) is rare but recorded. EU labels advise against it in autoimmune disease and against long courses. In the UK it is not given to children under 12. It may change how the body clears some drugs handled by the liver enzyme CYP3A4.
safety.ethics: Wild E. angustifolia has been over-dug, and United Plant Savers lists echinacea as at-risk. Cultivated E. purpurea is the kinder buy.

entries.what: A purple daisy of the American prairies, now one of the world's best-known cold remedies.

entries.name: Elder (elderberry and elderflower)
entries.uses: Elderflower tea is traditionally drunk hot to sweat out a feverish cold; the EMA accepts this for the first signs of a cold. Cooked elderberry syrup is traditionally taken for colds and flu.

history.text: Long called "the medicine chest of the country people". Elderberry syrup was a staple of European pharmacies.

lore.text: In Denmark the Elder Mother (Hyldemoer) lives in the tree. Ask her permission before cutting it, or bad luck follows. Never burn elder wood, and never make a cradle from it.

research.text: Small trials of berry extract found colds and flu ended a little sooner. The studies are few and small.

safety.summary: Raw berries, leaves, bark and unripe fruit contain compounds that release cyanide and cause vomiting, so the berries are always cooked. Dwarf elder (S. ebulus) is toxic.
safety.pets: Leaves, stems and raw berries are toxic to pets.

entries.cat: Ask the Elder Mother before you cut. She's like me: she remembers.
entries.what: A hedgerow tree whose creamy flowers make cordial and whose black berries, always cooked, make syrup.

entries.name: Elecampane
entries.uses: Traditionally taken for deep, wet coughs and weak digestion. In Russia devyasil was said to hold nine strengths against nine illnesses.

history.text: Its Latin name, helenium, ties it to Helen of Troy: it was said to have sprung from her tears, or to have been in her hand when Paris carried her off. Romans ate the candied root after feasts.

lore.text: In Anglo-Saxon charms it was an elf herb, used against elf-shot, sudden pains blamed on elves' invisible arrows.

research.text: Alantolactone, a compound from the root, has been studied in the lab. There is little clinical work.

safety.summary: People allergic to daisies may react. Large amounts cause vomiting.

entries.what: A towering yellow daisy whose fragrant root is boiled into syrups for deep coughs.
entries.know: Inulin, a starchy sugar now added to many foods, was first found in this root in 1804 and named after it.

sources.title: Maud Grieve, A Modern Herbal (1931)

entries.name: Eleuthero (Siberian ginseng)
entries.uses: In the USSR it was given to factory workers, sailors and athletes for stamina, and is said to have gone to the Chernobyl clean-up crews. In Chinese medicine ci wu jia is used to strengthen the spleen and kidney, which in that system are the organs that make energy and hold the body's reserves. EMA lists a traditional use for fatigue and weakness.

history.text: A Soviet pharmacologist coined the word adaptogen in 1947, for a substance thought to raise general resistance to stress. From the late 1950s his student led large studies of eleuthero in Vladivostok, and it became a liquid extract sold in Soviet pharmacies.

research.text: Trials on fatigue and immunity are mixed, and many older Soviet studies are hard to judge.

safety.summary: It can cause insomnia and raise blood pressure. It can make blood tests for digoxin (a heart drug) read high. It may change blood sugar and add to sedatives. Avoid in pregnancy.

entries.what: A thorny shrub of the Russian Far East whose root was the Soviet Union's favourite tonic; a cousin of ginseng, not ginseng itself.
