entries.name: Emu bush and gumby gumby
entries.uses: Many Aboriginal peoples traditionally burn emu bush leaves in smoking ceremonies for healing, for newborns and their mothers, and in mourning, and use the leaves in washes. In Queensland gumby gumby leaf tea is drunk as a bush remedy for colds and many other ills.

lore.text: Smoking ceremonies cleanse people and places of bad spirits and welcome visitors to Country (the land a People belongs to and cares for).

research.text: Lab studies of the leaves' activity against microbes.

safety.summary: There is little safety data for either plant. Avoid in pregnancy.
safety.ethics: A ceremony belongs to the Peoples and Country it comes from.

entries.what: Two Australian shrubs: emu bush, burned in Aboriginal smoking ceremonies, and gumby gumby, brewed as a bush tea.

sources.title: Royal Botanic Gardens Kew, Plants of the World Online and State of the World's Plants

entries.name: Epazote
entries.uses: Across Latin America people cook it with black beans against wind, and drink small amounts of the leaf tea against worms. In the Andes it is called paico.

history.text: Oil of chenopodium, distilled from the plant, was a standard worm medicine until the 1940s, when safer drugs replaced it.

research.text: The oil's main compound, ascaridole, kills worms and is also poisonous to people.

safety.summary: The oil is deadly even in small amounts. The leaf is used only in cooking amounts. It is not given to children.

entries.what: A strong-smelling Latin American herb cooked with black beans, and once the source of a worm medicine.
entries.know: Its Nahuatl name, epazotl, is usually translated as "skunk sweat".

sources.title: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database
James A. Duke, Handbook of Medicinal Herbs (2nd ed., 2002) and Dr. Duke's Phytochemical and Ethnobotanical Databases

entries.name: Ephedra (ma huang)
aka: Mormon tea (related N. American species, low alkaloid)
entries.uses: In Chinese medicine ma huang "opens the lungs" and brings on a sweat for chills and wheezing at the start of a cold. It is given only for a few days and always inside formulas such as Ma Huang Tang and Kakkonto. In the American West, settlers and Native peoples brewed a related low-alkaloid shrub as Mormon tea.

history.text: A Japanese chemist isolated ephedrine from ma huang in 1885. Pseudoephedrine, a close relative from the same plant, became a common decongestant.

research.text: Ephedra weight-loss and sports supplements were linked to strokes, heart attacks and deaths. Ephedrine itself is a licensed drug.

safety.summary: It raises heart rate and blood pressure. Strokes, heart attacks and sudden deaths were reported with supplements, sometimes in young, healthy people. It is risky with heart disease, high blood pressure, anxiety, glaucoma or an overactive thyroid.
safety.pets: Ephedra and ephedrine products are poisonous to dogs and cats: a racing heart, tremors and fits.
safety.regulatory: Supplements containing ephedra alkaloids have been banned in the US since 2004 (FDA). Ephedrine is on the WADA list, banned in competition.

entries.what: A leafless green shrub from the steppes whose stems contain ephedrine, a strong stimulant.

entries.name: Epitalon
parts: synthetic tetrapeptide modelled on a pineal gland extract
entries.uses: Sold as a longevity "bioregulator", usually in short courses of injections, said to lengthen telomeres (the protective caps on the ends of chromosomes) and to reset sleep rhythms. Part of a Soviet and Russian tradition of short "bioregulator" peptides, each matched to one organ.

history.text: Grew out of 1980s work in Leningrad (now St Petersburg) on epithalamin, an extract of the pineal gland, a small gland in the brain that makes melatonin. The short synthetic version came later from the same research centre.

research.text: Mostly Russian studies in animals and cells, plus small human studies of the pineal extract, nearly all from one research centre. Not independently repeated.

safety.summary: Safety is unknown, and grey-market quality varies.
safety.regulatory: As of November 2026: not approved in the US or EU. FDA took it off Category 2 in April 2026. Its advisory committee voted 7 to 4 in July 2026 to allow it in compounding (not binding), and the October 2026 HHS enforcement policy covers injectable epitalon in intermittent courses, on prescription. Falls under WADA's ban on unapproved substances (S0).

entries.what: A lab-made four-amino-acid peptide sold as an anti-ageing "bioregulator", from Russian pineal-gland research.

entries.name: Eucalyptus oil
entries.uses: Aboriginal peoples traditionally used the leaves for fevers and wounds, and burned them in smoking ceremonies. The oil is breathed in steam and rubbed on the chest for colds, a traditional use EMA lists. In Russia it is splashed on the hot stones of the banya, the steam bath.

history.text: Commercial distilling began in Victoria in 1852.

research.text: Cineole (also called eucalyptol), the oil's main compound, is sold as licensed capsules in Germany, with trial support for bronchitis and sinusitis.

safety.summary: A few millilitres swallowed can poison a child (seizures, coma). Never on or near the face of babies and young children. EU rules say medicines made from it must not be used in children under 2, because it can make the voice box spasm shut. Not for people with epilepsy.
safety.pets: Toxic to cats and dogs.

entries.what: The cool, sharp oil from eucalyptus leaves, breathed in steam and rubbed on the chest for colds.
entries.know: The first eucalyptus oil was distilled in Sydney in 1788, the year the First Fleet landed, and sent back to England.

entries.name: Eucommia
entries.uses: In Chinese medicine du zhong strengthens the "kidney", a system said to rule the bones and lower back as well as vitality. It is traditionally used for a weak, aching lower back and knees. In Japan the leaves are brewed as tochu-cha, a roasted tea drunk for blood pressure.

research.text: A few small trials on blood pressure.

safety.summary: It may add to blood-pressure and diabetes drugs.

entries.what: The bark of a Chinese tree, the only living member of its plant family, used for the back and knees.
entries.know: Snap a eucommia leaf or bark in two and fine threads of natural rubber stretch between the halves.

sources.title: Bensky, Clavey & Stöger, Chinese Herbal Medicine: Materia Medica, 3rd ed. (2004)
Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database

entries.name: Evening primrose oil
entries.uses: Indigenous North Americans traditionally put the plant on bruises and ate the root. The seed oil, rich in GLA (gamma-linolenic acid, an omega-6 fat), is sold for eczema, breast pain and PMS.

history.text: In 2002 the UK withdrew the licences of evening primrose oil medicines for eczema and breast pain, for lack of evidence.

research.text: A Cochrane review (2013) found no benefit for eczema. There is little evidence for PMS.

safety.summary: Older reports linked it with seizures in people taking phenothiazines (a group of antipsychotic drugs). It may slightly raise bleeding risk with blood thinners. Avoid in pregnancy.

entries.what: Oil from the seeds of a yellow wildflower that opens in the evening, sold in capsules.
entries.know: The flowers open at dusk fast enough to watch, ready for the night moths that visit them.

Cochrane Library systematic reviews
Daniel Moerman, Native American Ethnobotany (1998) and the BRIT Native American Ethnobotany database

entries.name: Eyebright
entries.uses: Traditionally used in compresses for tired, sore eyes, and drunk as a tea for hay fever and catarrh (a blocked, runny nose).

history.text: Its Latin name comes from Euphrosyne, one of the three Graces, whose name means gladness. In the poem Paradise Lost (1667) the archangel Michael clears Adam's sight with eyebright and rue.

research.text: One small uncontrolled study of eyebright eye drops. There is no good evidence beyond that.

safety.summary: Home-made eye preparations carry a real risk of infection. Anything put near the eye has to be sterile.

entries.what: A tiny meadow plant with white, purple-veined flowers marked like an eye, used for tired eyes.
entries.know: Eyebright is a half-parasite: its roots tap into the roots of nearby grasses for food.

entries.name: Fasting traditions
parts: abstaining from food (and sometimes water) for set times
preps: plant-only fasts (Orthodox: about 180 days a year)
entries.uses: Practised as spiritual discipline in nearly every religion. Muslims fast from dawn to dusk in Ramadan, Orthodox Christians keep plant-only fasts on about 180 days a year, and Jews fast a full day on Yom Kippur. Ayurveda uses light fasting (langhana) to rekindle agni, the digestive fire. Intermittent fasting is popular for weight and metabolism.

research.text: In trials, intermittent fasting led to about the same weight loss as ordinary calorie cutting.

safety.summary: Cautioned with type 1 diabetes and with insulin or sulfonylurea pills, since blood sugar can fall dangerously low. With blood pressure drugs, pressure can drop too far during a fast. Cautioned in pregnancy, with eating disorders and in children. Dry fasts in hot weather cause dehydration. Eating normally too soon after a very long fast can be dangerous (refeeding syndrome).

entries.what: Going without food, or some foods, for set times; a practice found in nearly every religion.
entries.know: The Qur'an excuses the sick and travellers from the Ramadan fast, and Islamic law also excuses pregnant and nursing women.

sources.title: NCCIH, health topics A-Z (practices: acupuncture, massage, yoga, tai chi, meditation)

entries.name: Fennel
entries.uses: Used for wind and babies' colic (it goes into gripe water and Russian "dill water", which is really fennel). In India sugared seeds called mukhwas are chewed after meals. People also drink it for coughs and to make more breast milk. The EU's herbal committee lists it as a traditional remedy for bloating and mild period cramps.

history.text: In Greek myth Prometheus stole fire from the gods hidden in the hollow stalk of giant fennel, a tall cousin. Roman gladiators are said to have eaten it for strength.

lore.text: Hung over doors on Midsummer Eve against evil, and stuffed into keyholes to keep ghosts out.

research.text: A few small trials on infant colic and period pain found some benefit.

safety.summary: Food amounts are fine. The EU herbal committee advises against fennel as a medicine for children under 4, because of estragole, a compound in the oil. It has weak oestrogen-like effects. Some breastfed babies became ill when mothers drank large amounts of mixed herbal teas with fennel.

entries.what: A feathery plant with a sweet aniseed taste; the seeds, bulb and oil are all used.
entries.know: The Battle of Marathon was named for a fennel field: marathon is the Greek word for fennel.

entries.name: Fenugreek
entries.uses: Traditionally used to bring in breast milk, to raise the appetite and for blood sugar. Ground seed is made into a warm poultice for the skin. The EU's herbal committee lists it as a traditional remedy for loss of appetite.

history.text: Ancient Egyptians used it in embalming and in childbirth, and seeds were found in Tutankhamun's tomb. In Yemen and Ethiopia it is everyday food, whipped into hilbeh paste or ground into spice blends.

research.text: Small trials found it lowered blood sugar a little. The evidence for more breast milk is weak.

safety.summary: It can make sweat and urine smell of maple syrup, in mothers and in breastfed babies. It can lower blood sugar. People allergic to peanuts or chickpeas may react to it. In pregnancy more than food amounts may be unsafe: it can stimulate the womb, and animal studies linked it to birth defects.

entries.what: Hard, bitter, yellow seeds of a clover-like plant, smelling of maple syrup; the leaves are eaten too.
entries.know: Fenugreek's smell compound, sotolon, is so like maple that the seed is used to flavour imitation maple syrup.

entries.name: Feverfew
entries.uses: Traditionally taken to ward off migraine attacks, often as a few fresh leaves chewed each day. The EMA accepts traditional use for warding off migraine.

history.text: Named in Greek medicine for women's complaints. The English name comes from the Latin febrifugia, "fever dispeller".

lore.text: Planted around houses to purify the air and keep disease away.

research.text: Migraine trials are mixed. A Cochrane review found a small, uncertain benefit.

safety.summary: Fresh leaves can cause mouth ulcers. Stopping suddenly may bring rebound headaches and aching joints. People allergic to daisies may react. It may add to bleeding risk with blood thinners.
safety.pets: Toxic to cats, dogs and horses (ASPCA): vomiting, diarrhoea and bleeding.

entries.what: A small, sharp-smelling daisy whose fresh leaves are chewed to ward off migraines.

entries.name: Finnish sauna
parts: heated room, water on stones, vihta/vasta whisk, cold water or lake
entries.uses: In Finland the sauna is close to sacred: it was used for washing, healing, giving birth and laying out the dead. An old saying calls it "the poor man's pharmacy". People sit in the heat, swat themselves with a birch whisk (vihta or vasta), then cool off in a lake, the snow or a cold shower.

history.text: Sauna culture in Finland joined UNESCO's intangible heritage list in 2020. The smoke sauna (savusauna), heated without a chimney, is the oldest kind.

lore.text: Behave in the sauna as you would in church. The saunatonttu, a small sauna elf, guards it and can burn it down if it is treated badly.

research.text: Large Finnish studies found frequent sauna use linked with fewer deaths from heart disease and from all causes. These are observational, so they show a link, not proof.

safety.summary: Heat and alcohol together are dangerous. Not with unstable heart disease. Dehydration and fainting are the common risks. High heat is cautioned in pregnancy.

entries.what: The Finnish hot room, where water thrown on hot stones makes a burst of steam (löyly).
entries.know: Finland has about three million saunas for 5.5 million people.

sources.title: Laukkanen et al., Cardiovascular and other health benefits of sauna bathing (Mayo Clin Proc 2018)

entries.name: Fire cider
parts: apple cider vinegar, horseradish, garlic, onion, ginger, chili, honey (recipes vary)
preps: vinegar infusion for weeks, then honey
entries.uses: A folk vinegar tonic, traditionally taken by the spoonful in winter for colds and blocked sinuses.

history.text: Popularised by a New England herbalist in the 1970s. When a company registered the name as a trademark in 2012, herbalists fought it, and in 2019 a US federal court ruled that "fire cider" is a generic name anyone may use.

research.text: Not studied.

safety.summary: The acid can wear away tooth enamel and burn the throat, and it can make reflux worse.

entries.what: A fiery cider-vinegar tonic of horseradish, garlic, onion, ginger and chili, sweetened with honey.

entries.name: Flower essences
parts: flowers floated in spring water in sunlight, then preserved in brandy
preps: drops under the tongue or in water
entries.uses: Used and taught as subtle remedies for emotional states: one flower for fear, another for despair or impatience, and a five-flower "rescue" blend for shock.

history.text: A London homeopath created 38 remedies in the 1930s, each matched to a mood. Many systems followed, from California to the Australian bush and the Himalayas.

lore.text: The water is said to hold the flower's imprint, like sunlight caught in a glass.

research.text: Reviews of the trials, mostly for anxiety, found no effect beyond placebo. Practitioners report otherwise.

safety.summary: Very dilute, but it contains brandy (alcohol).

entries.what: Drops made by floating flowers in sunlit spring water, kept in brandy, and taken for moods.
entries.know: The essence is traditionally made by the sun method: flowers float in a glass bowl of spring water in full sun for about three hours.

sources.title: NHS (UK), Homeopathy overview

entries.name: Fly agaric
preps: vodka tincture rubbed on joints (Russian folk)
entries.uses: Traditionally eaten dried by the Koryak, Chukchi, Evenk and other Siberian peoples: by shamans to journey to the spirit world, and by others at feasts. In Russian folk medicine it is steeped in vodka and rubbed on aching joints. Today it is sold in gummies for sleep.

history.text: Its name comes from the old European habit of crumbling it into milk to stun flies. Travellers described the Siberian practice from the 17th and 18th centuries. It is the red-and-white mushroom of fairy tales and Christmas cards.

lore.text: Reindeer seek it out. Some trace Santa's flying reindeer and red-and-white suit to Siberian shamans. Some also identify it with soma, the sacred drink of the Rig Veda.

research.text: Its main active compounds are ibotenic acid, which acts on glutamate receptors, and muscimol, which acts on GABA receptors (the brain's main calming signal). Drying turns much of the ibotenic acid into muscimol. No human trials have tested any traditional use.

safety.summary: Poisonous. Eating it can cause confusion, delirium, muscle twitching, seizures and coma. Unregulated gummies sold as Amanita have put people in hospital, and some contained other substances not on the label. It can be confused with other Amanitas, some of them deadly, such as the death cap. A rain-washed fly agaric can lose its white spots and is easier to mistake.
safety.pets: Toxic to dogs and cats, which can be poisoned by eating it in gardens and woods.
safety.regulatory: As of November 2026: in December 2024 the US FDA said Amanita muscaria and its compounds (muscimol, ibotenic acid, muscarine) are not authorised in food. It is not a federally controlled drug in the US. Louisiana bans it except as an ornamental plant, and the Netherlands has banned it since December 2008.

entries.cat: Pretty red cap, Siberian shamans, Christmas cards. Also delirium. Stay on the card.
entries.what: The red mushroom with white spots from fairy tales. It is poisonous and alters the mind.
entries.know: Eighteenth-century travellers in Siberia wrote that people drank the urine of someone who had eaten fly agaric, because its effects passed through the body.

entries.name: Folate (vitamin B9)
entries.uses: Taken in prenatal vitamins before and during early pregnancy, and added to flour by law in about 70 countries.

history.text: The US made flour fortification mandatory in 1998; spina bifida and similar birth defects fell by about a quarter to a third.

research.text: Folic acid before conception and in early pregnancy lowers neural tube defects (spina bifida, anencephaly): one of the clearest results in nutrition.

safety.summary: High folic acid can hide a B12 deficiency, letting nerve damage go on unnoticed. Some epilepsy and cancer drugs (methotrexate) work against folate.

entries.what: A B vitamin needed to copy DNA and make new cells, which is why it matters so much just before and in early pregnancy.
entries.know: Its name comes from the Latin "folium", leaf: it was first pulled out of spinach.

nutrient.low: Tiredness, breathlessness and pale skin from large red blood cells (anaemia); a sore tongue.
nutrient.limit: Synthetic folic acid: US 1,000 mcg a day; EU 1,000 mcg a day (food folate has no limit).

entries.name: Forest bathing (shinrin-yoku)
preps: two hours slow in woodland, phones off
entries.uses: Slow time among trees, walking, sitting and noticing, practised for calm. Japan's forestry agency named it shinrin-yoku in 1982. Japan now certifies forest therapy bases, and South Korea runs national healing forests.

lore.text: In Shinto, kami (spirits) dwell in great trees, which are marked with a straw rope (shimenawa). Many cultures keep sacred groves.

research.text: Small studies found lower stress-hormone (cortisol) levels, pulse and blood pressure after time in a forest.

safety.summary: Ticks can carry Lyme disease. People do get lost.

entries.what: Spending slow, quiet time in a forest using all the senses, a practice named in Japan.
entries.know: Friluftsliv, Norway's "open-air life", first appeared as a word in an 1859 Norwegian poem.

sources.title: NCCIH, health topics A-Z (practices: acupuncture, massage, yoga, tai chi, meditation)

entries.name: Four Thieves Vinegar
parts: vinegar with rosemary, sage, thyme, lavender, rue, wormwood, garlic, cloves (recipes vary)
entries.uses: Traditionally used as a protective wash and a vinegar against contagion. In folk magic it is used to drive enemies away.

history.text: The legend says four thieves robbed plague victims unharmed thanks to this vinegar, and traded the recipe for their lives. Tellers place it in Toulouse in the 1620s or in Marseille in 1720.

lore.text: In hoodoo (African American folk magic), a few drops sprinkled where an enemy walks make them leave.

research.text: Vinegar and some of the herbs kill microbes in the lab.

safety.summary: Versions with rue and wormwood are not for drinking.

entries.what: A herbal vinegar from a French plague legend, used as a protective wash and in folk magic.

entries.name: Foxglove
entries.uses: Historically used in English folk medicine for dropsy (swelling from trapped fluid, often from heart failure). An 18th-century English physician wrote that he first heard of it through an old woman's secret family recipe in Shropshire, and in 1785 he published ten years of cases. The heart drugs digitoxin and digoxin come from foxgloves.

lore.text: The flowers are fairies' gloves. Fairies are said to have given them to foxes to muffle their steps on raids, and picking one offends the fairies.

research.text: Digoxin is an established heart drug with a narrow gap between a useful dose and a poisonous one.

safety.summary: Deadly. Every part is poisonous and can throw the heart into fatal rhythms, with nausea, vomiting and yellow-green vision. Before it flowers, the leaf rosette is easily mistaken for comfrey or borage, and people have died after making tea from the wrong leaves. Poisoning is an emergency. History and lore only.
safety.pets: Toxic to pets.

entries.what: A tall cottage-garden flower with purple bell-shaped blooms, the original source of the heart drug digitalis.

entries.name: Frankincense
entries.latin: Boswellia sacra, B. carterii, B. serrata (shallaki)
entries.uses: Burned in temples, churches, mosques and homes for prayer and to cleanse a space. In Ayurveda, Indian frankincense (shallaki) is used for the joints. In Oman people chew luban and drink water it has soaked in overnight, for digestion and fresh breath.

history.text: Camel caravans carried it along the incense road from southern Arabia to the Mediterranean. Ancient Egyptians burned it in temples and called incense senetjer, "to make divine". In the Gospel of Matthew it is one of the three gifts of the Magi.

lore.text: Ruled by the Sun and Fire. Its smoke is said to carry prayers to heaven.

research.text: Small trials of Boswellia extracts for knee osteoarthritis found modest relief of pain and stiffness.

safety.summary: Extracts can upset the stomach. The essential oil can cause skin allergy once it oxidises (goes stale). The smoke irritates the lungs.
safety.pets: Incense smoke harms cats and birds, which have sensitive lungs.
safety.ethics: Frankincense trees are declining fast. A 2019 study in Nature Sustainability warned that production from Boswellia papyrifera in Ethiopia and its neighbours could halve within 20 years, because old trees are dying and few young ones survive.

entries.what: A pale golden tree resin from Arabia, the Horn of Africa and India, burned as incense for thousands of years.
entries.know: It is gathered by cutting the bark. The milky sap that oozes out dries into hard "tears" in a couple of weeks.

entries.name: Galangal
aka: kalgan (Russian, old name; today usually tormentil)
entries.uses: In Thai, Chinese and medieval European medicine it is used for a cold, upset stomach and nausea. A famous 12th-century German abbess praised it for pain around the heart.

lore.text: In hoodoo the root is called "Little John to Chew": people chew it and spit the juice on the courtroom floor for luck in a case.

research.text: Studied in cells and animals.

safety.summary: Food amounts are fine.

entries.what: A pale, peppery ginger-like root that flavours Thai soups and curries.

entries.name: Garlic
entries.uses: Traditionally eaten against colds, coughs and infections, for worms, and for the heart and blood. In the Soviet Union during the Second World War it was nicknamed "Russian penicillin".

history.text: A Greek historian wrote that the builders of the Great Pyramid were fed garlic, onions and radishes. Greek athletes are said to have eaten it before the games. In medieval plague years it went into protective vinegars such as Four Thieves.

lore.text: Hung against vampires, the evil eye and witches across the Slavic and Mediterranean worlds. Yogic, Jain and some Buddhist traditions avoid it as too stirring for the mind.

research.text: Trials of supplements found a modest drop in blood pressure and small effects on cholesterol. The evidence that it wards off colds is weak.

safety.summary: It raises bleeding risk with blood thinners and before surgery. Garlic kept in oil at room temperature can grow botulism. Raw garlic left on the skin can burn it.
safety.pets: Toxic to cats and dogs: it damages their red blood cells.

entries.cat: Vampires hate it, I hate it, and the vet says it wrecks my blood. Three for three.
entries.what: The pungent kitchen bulb, used as food and medicine on every inhabited continent for thousands of years.
entries.know: Garlic only gets its sharp smell when a clove is cut or crushed: an enzyme then turns a scentless compound into allicin.

entries.name: Gelsemium sempervirens
entries.uses: In homeopathy, given for stage fright and dread before an exam or a performance (weak, trembling, heavy eyelids) and for slow, heavy flu with chills and no thirst.

research.text: No good trials show a reliable effect beyond placebo.

safety.summary: The plant is deadly; its alkaloid gelsemine stops breathing. Low potencies are risky. Avoided in pregnancy.

entries.what: Yellow jessamine diluted into homeopathy's remedy for stage fright and heavy, droopy flu.
entries.know: Yellow (Carolina) jessamine is the state flower of South Carolina.

entries.name: Gentian
entries.uses: Traditionally taken as the classic bitter before meals, to wake up appetite and digestion. The EMA accepts traditional use for loss of appetite and indigestion.

history.text: Named after Gentius, a king of Illyria in the Balkans in the 2nd century BCE. It goes into Angostura and other bitters, Alpine Enzian schnapps and the French aperitif Suze.

research.text: The gut has bitter-taste receptors, and open studies report easier digestion, but controlled trials are few.

safety.summary: Avoid it with stomach ulcers or reflux. Before it flowers, wild yellow gentian looks like deadly white hellebore (Veratrum album), and people have been poisoned by mixing them up.
safety.ethics: Protected in much of Europe. Buy cultivated.

entries.what: A tall yellow Alpine plant whose very bitter root flavours aperitifs and herbal bitters.
entries.know: Amarogentin, the bitter in the root, can still be tasted diluted about one part in 58 million.

entries.name: GHK-Cu (copper peptide)
parts: naturally occurring tripeptide bound to copper
entries.uses: Sold widely in skincare serums and creams for wrinkles, firmness and skin repair. Some clinics also inject it for skin and hair, and it is sold online in "research" vials.

history.text: First isolated from human blood plasma in 1973. Its level in the blood is reported to fall with age, which made it a cosmetics ingredient.

research.text: Small cosmetic studies of creams and serums report smoother, firmer skin, often run by the makers. Injected use has not been tested in good trials.

safety.summary: On the skin it is widely used and usually tolerated, though some people get irritation. Injected forms have unknown safety, and FDA reviewers raised the risk of immune reactions. Grey-market vials carry contamination and dosing risks.
safety.regulatory: As of November 2026: cosmetic creams and serums are legal. Injectable GHK-Cu is not approved. FDA's own page (April 2026) lists the injectable form under nominations withdrawn; one law-firm summary says instead that FDA removed it from Category 1, so sources disagree on its history. An FDA advisory committee is due to review it before the end of February 2027. It is not covered by the October 2026 HHS compounding policy.

entries.what: A tiny three-amino-acid peptide that carries copper, found in human blood and sold in anti-ageing skin serums.
entries.know: GHK-Cu dissolved in water is a deep blue, from its copper.

entries.name: Ginger
entries.uses: Used almost everywhere for nausea, travel sickness, colds, chills, wind and period pain. In Ayurveda dry ginger is called vishwabheshaj, "the universal medicine". Chinese medicine counts fresh and dry as two remedies: fresh ginger "releases the exterior" (brings on a sweat at the start of a cold), dry ginger "warms the middle" (the stomach and spleen).

history.text: Romans bought it from Indian and Arab traders. Nuremberg had its own gingerbread bakers' guild by 1643. The Analects record that Confucius always kept ginger at his meals.

lore.text: Planted by the door or carried in a pocket for protection and success. In parts of the Pacific and Southeast Asia, healers chew ginger and spit it out to drive away spirits.

research.text: Several trials and reviews found ginger eased nausea in pregnancy. Results for motion sickness and period pain are smaller and less consistent.

safety.summary: Large amounts can cause heartburn. It may slightly raise bleeding risk with blood thinners.

entries.cat: Sick on the boat? Ginger. Sick of you? No herb for that.
entries.what: The knobbly, hot root sold fresh in every market, used in cooking, teas and ginger beer.
entries.know: Cultivated ginger has never been found growing wild; it exists only because people kept planting it.

entries.name: Ginkgo
entries.uses: In modern European herbal medicine the leaf extract is taken for memory and circulation in old age. In Chinese medicine the cooked nut, bai guo, is traditionally used for cough and wheezing.

history.text: A "living fossil": its line goes back about 200 million years, and it survived in the wild only in a few corners of China.

lore.text: Planted at temples in China and Japan as a tree of long life and hope.

research.text: The large GEM trial, in about 3,000 adults over 75, found it did not lower the rate of dementia. A Cochrane review found no meaningful benefit for leg pain on walking caused by narrowed arteries (claudication). The EMA accepts a standard extract for mild age-related decline in memory and thinking.

safety.summary: It raises bleeding risk with blood thinners. Raw seeds are poisonous (ginkgotoxin causes seizures), and seizures have been reported with leaf extract. In a US government study, a leaf extract caused liver and thyroid tumours in rats and mice.

entries.what: An ancient tree with fan-shaped leaves, whose leaf extract is sold for memory and circulation.
entries.know: Several ginkgo trees within about two kilometres of the 1945 Hiroshima blast survived it and still grow there.

entries.name: Ginseng (Asian, Korean red)
entries.uses: In Chinese and Korean medicine it is the great tonic for yuan qi, the "original" life energy a person is born with. People take it for exhaustion, a weak voice and pulse, slow recovery and old age. In Korea a whole small root is cooked inside a chicken for samgyetang, eaten on the hottest days of summer. The EU lists it as a traditional herbal medicine for tiredness and weakness.

history.text: Wild roots once sold for more than their weight in gold. Korean red ginseng, steamed and dried until it turns amber, was a state monopoly from about 1899 until 1996. The word "adaptogen" was coined by a Soviet scientist in 1947, and Soviet labs then tested ginseng and its cousin eleuthero under that label.

lore.text: The forked root looks like a little person, hence "man root". In Manchuria hunters tied a red thread to a plant the moment they found it, so the root could not slip away underground before they dug it.

research.text: Trials on tiredness, memory and blood sugar disagree with each other. A Cochrane review found some low-quality support for erectile problems.

safety.summary: It can cause sleeplessness, jitters and swings in blood pressure. A 1979 report described a "ginseng abuse syndrome" in people taking large amounts with caffeine. It may lower blood sugar and can weaken warfarin. Mania has been reported with MAOI antidepressants.
safety.regulatory: Wild Panax ginseng from Russia is listed in CITES Appendix II, so its trade needs permits.
safety.ethics: Wild Asian ginseng is now very rare. Almost everything on sale is farmed, and farmed is the root to buy.

entries.what: A forked root from the forests of Korea and northeast China, the most famous tonic in East Asian medicine.
entries.know: The genus name Panax comes from the same Greek word as panacea, "all-healing".

entries.name: Goji (wolfberry)
entries.uses: In Chinese medicine the berries nourish the yin of the liver and kidney. Yin is the cool, moist, nourishing side of the body, and the "liver" is said to open into the eyes. So goji is traditionally eaten for long life and blurred or tired vision. People drop a handful into tea, porridge or soup.

lore.text: A well-known legend tells of a village where everyone lived past a hundred. Their well sat under goji vines, and the berries fell into the water.

research.text: Small trials have looked at the eye pigment that protects the retina, and at general wellbeing.

safety.summary: Several people on warfarin had bleeding after drinking goji tea or juice. It belongs to the nightshade family, so people allergic to tomatoes or peppers should take note. It may add to diabetes and blood-pressure drugs.

entries.what: Small red berries from a Chinese shrub, eaten dried like raisins and sold worldwide as a superfood.
entries.know: In Britain the same shrub is called the Duke of Argyll's tea tree, after an 18th-century label mix-up.

entries.name: Gokshura (tribulus)
entries.uses: In Ayurveda it is used for urine flow, stones and male vitality, often in the tablet Gokshuradi guggulu. In Bulgaria the extract became a sports and libido supplement.

history.text: Bulgarian athletes took tribulus extracts in the 1970s and 1980s, and a Bulgarian brand made it famous abroad.

research.text: Trials found it does not raise testosterone. A few small studies have looked at libido.

safety.summary: Rare kidney and liver injury has been reported with heavy use. It may lower blood sugar.
safety.pets: Toxic to sheep: it makes their skin burn in sunlight (photosensitisation).

entries.what: A low spreading weed with spiny seed pods, used in Ayurveda for the urinary tract and sold as a sports supplement.
entries.know: Its spiky burrs puncture bicycle tyres, which is why Americans call it puncture vine.

entries.name: Gol gav zaban (Persian borage tea)
preps: infusion, often with lemon (turns pink) and valerian
entries.uses: Traditionally drunk in Iran as a calming tea for worry, low spirits and poor sleep, often with a squeeze of lemon and sometimes a pinch of valerian root.

research.text: A few small Iranian trials found less anxiety and better mood than placebo.

safety.summary: Contains pyrrolizidine alkaloids, which can damage the liver over time. Kept to occasional use, never long-term, in pregnancy or with liver disease.

entries.what: Dried violet flowers of an Iranian borage, brewed as a calming tea that turns pink with lemon.
entries.know: The name means "ox-tongue flower", after the plant's rough leaves.

entries.name: Goldenrod
entries.uses: Traditionally drunk to flush the urinary tract and for minor bladder complaints; the EMA accepts this as traditional use. In North America it was taken for colds and catarrh.

history.text: Its Latin name, Solidago, means "to make whole". In 16th-century London dried goldenrod was imported and sold dear as a wound herb, until it was found growing wild near the city and the price collapsed.

lore.text: Used as a divining rod to find hidden water and treasure.

research.text: Small open studies; little controlled work.

safety.summary: Not for swelling caused by heart or kidney failure. People allergic to daisies may react.

entries.what: A late-summer plant with plumes of small yellow flowers, drunk as a tea to flush the bladder.
entries.know: Goldenrod gets blamed for hay fever, but its heavy pollen is carried by insects. Ragweed, which flowers at the same time, is the real culprit.

entries.name: Goldenseal
entries.uses: Cherokee and Iroquois people used the root as a wash for sore eyes and skin, as a bitter tonic for the stomach and for mouth sores. Today it is often sold mixed with echinacea for colds.

history.text: It was dug in huge amounts for the American drug trade in the late 1800s, which began its decline in the wild. Tests show it does not mask drugs in urine tests.

research.text: Berberine, the yellow alkaloid in the root, has been widely studied, but goldenseal itself has few human trials. It strongly blocks CYP3A4 and CYP2D6, liver enzymes that clear many medicines.

safety.summary: It raises the blood levels of many medicines, and in one study it lowered metformin levels. Not for newborns: berberine can make newborn jaundice worse. It is cautioned with high blood pressure.
safety.regulatory: Listed on CITES Appendix II since 1997, so international trade needs permits.
safety.ethics: The IUCN Red List rates it Vulnerable (2017) because of wild digging and lost forest. Buy only farm-grown root.

entries.what: A small forest plant of eastern North America with a bright yellow root, taken as a bitter.
entries.know: The belief that goldenseal hides drugs in a urine test is traced to a 1900 American novel in which it masks a poison.

entries.name: Gotu kola
preps: fresh salad (Sri Lankan gotu kola sambol)
entries.uses: Across South and Southeast Asia people eat it raw or drink the juice for long life and memory, and put it on wounds and skin. In Sri Lanka it is chopped fine into a fresh salad (gotu kola sambol). In Ayurveda it is mandukaparni.

history.text: A Sri Lankan saying holds that two leaves a day keep old age away.

lore.text: Elephants, long-lived and wise, are said to graze on it.

research.text: Trials have looked at extracts for swollen, aching leg veins (venous insufficiency) and for scars. Studies on memory are small.

safety.summary: Rare liver injury has been reported. It can make skin sensitive to sunlight and cause drowsiness.

entries.what: A small round-leaved creeping plant of Asian wetlands, eaten as a salad green and used in skin creams.
entries.know: Korean skincare calls it "tiger grass", from an old story that wounded tigers roll in it; the "cica" in creams comes from its Latin name.

sources.title: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database

entries.name: Grains of paradise
entries.uses: In West Africa the seeds are traditionally chewed in healing and ritual, and cooked as a warming spice for the stomach. At Yoruba naming ceremonies the baby is given a taste of atare, whose many seeds stand for many children and a fruitful life.

history.text: Liberia's coast was once called the Grain Coast after it. Medieval European cooks and brewers used it in place of costly black pepper, and later British law forbade brewers from using it in beer.

research.text: Mostly lab and animal studies on metabolism. One small study in young Japanese women found an extract raised energy burning in brown fat.

safety.summary: A normal food spice.

entries.what: Small peppery seeds of a West African ginger relative, used like black pepper with a hint of citrus.
entries.know: The name is often said to be a medieval sales pitch, hinting that the seeds came from the Garden of Eden.

sources.title: PROTA4U, Plant Resources of Tropical Africa

entries.name: Grapefruit
entries.latin: Citrus x paradisi (also Seville orange C. aurantium and pomelo C. maxima)
entries.uses: Eaten and drunk as a breakfast fruit. Mid-20th-century "grapefruit diets" promoted it for weight loss. Grapefruit seed extract is sold as a natural antimicrobial.

history.text: It arose on Barbados as a chance cross of pomelo and sweet orange. A 1750 natural history of the island first described it, as the "forbidden fruit".

research.text: Compounds in the juice called furanocoumarins switch off CYP3A4, a gut enzyme that breaks down many medicines, for a day or more. Blood levels of those medicines then rise. Researchers found this by accident in 1989, using grapefruit juice to hide the taste of alcohol in a drug study. Tests of seed extracts found synthetic preservatives that had been added.

safety.summary: The best-known food-drug interaction. One glass can raise levels of some statins (simvastatin, atorvastatin), blood-pressure drugs such as felodipine, ciclosporin, some heart-rhythm drugs, sedatives and dozens more, sometimes to dangerous levels. Seville orange and pomelo do the same. Check every prescription label for a grapefruit warning.
contra: taking any medicine with a grapefruit warning

entries.cat: Breakfast fruit with a grudge. Read the little sticker on your pills.
entries.what: A big, sour-sweet citrus fruit eaten for breakfast, famous for clashing with many medicines.
entries.know: It is called grapefruit because the fruits hang in clusters like grapes.

sources.title: MedlinePlus Herbs and Supplements (US National Library of Medicine)
US FDA, dietary supplement warnings and safety information

entries.name: Greater celandine
entries.uses: In Slavic folk medicine the orange sap is dabbed on warts, and the herb was once taken for liver and gallbladder complaints.

history.text: Its Russian name, chistotel, means "clean body". It was the classic wart remedy of the Russian countryside.

lore.text: Named for the swallow (chelidon in Greek). It was said to bloom when the swallows arrive, and mother swallows were said to bathe their chicks' eyes in its sap.

research.text: One small trial in the 1990s tested an extract for stomach cramps. Many case reports link oral products to acute hepatitis (liver inflammation), and in 2011 the EMA judged the risks of oral use greater than any benefit.

safety.summary: Swallowed, it has caused serious liver injury, including liver failure. The sap irritates skin and eyes.
safety.regulatory: Germany restricted oral products in 2008 and other countries followed. The EMA's 2011 assessment found the risk of oral use outweighed the benefit.

entries.what: A yellow-flowered poppy relative with bright orange sap, famous in Russia as a wart remedy.

entries.name: Green tea
entries.uses: Traditionally drunk in China, Japan and Korea for a clear head, digestion and long life. In Chinese medicine it counts as cooling and is drunk to "clear heat".

history.text: Chinese legend says tea leaves blew into a legendary emperor's pot of boiling water in 2737 BCE. Japanese Buddhist monks brought tea home from China from the 800s and drank it to stay awake in meditation.

research.text: Big Japanese population studies linked drinking green tea with less heart disease. In trials, extracts gave only small weight loss.

safety.summary: The drink is safe for most people. Concentrated extract pills (EGCG) have caused acute liver failure. Tea has caffeine and cuts iron absorption from food. It lowers blood levels of the beta-blocker nadolol, and EGCG can block the cancer drug bortezomib.
safety.regulatory: Since 2022 the EU has capped EGCG in green tea supplements and put them under review because of liver injury reports.

entries.what: Tea leaves heated soon after picking so they stay green, drunk across East Asia for well over a thousand years.
entries.know: Green, black, oolong and white tea all come from the same plant. Only the processing differs.

entries.name: Ground ivy
entries.uses: Traditionally drunk for catarrh and for blocked sinuses and ears. Before hops, brewers used it to clear and bitter beer.

history.text: Saxon brewers bittered and cleared their ale with it. In London it was sold in the streets as "gill tea".

lore.text: A wreath of it worn on Walpurgis night (30 April, the witches' night of German lore) let you see who was a witch.

research.text: Very little studied.

safety.summary: Mild in people.
safety.pets: Toxic to horses.

entries.what: A low, creeping mint with violet flowers, once used to clear and flavour ale before hops.

entries.name: Grounding (earthing)
parts: bare skin on earth, grass, sand or water
entries.uses: Walking barefoot on dew and earth is a Slavic folk custom; on Ivan Kupala morning (midsummer) the dew is said to heal. Modern grounding mats, plugged into the earth pin of a wall socket, are sold for sleep and inflammation.

lore.text: Mother Earth, Mat Syra Zemlya ("moist mother earth"), heals what touches her.

research.text: A few small, low-quality studies.

safety.summary: Bare feet risk cuts and infections. Grounding mats can be dangerous if the socket's wiring is faulty.

entries.what: Walking barefoot on earth or grass, or sleeping on a mat wired to the ground, to connect with the earth.

entries.name: Gua sha
parts: smooth tool (horn, jade, coin, spoon) with oil
preps: firm strokes until red marks (sha) rise
entries.uses: In China, Vietnam and Indonesia people scrape the back, neck or chest to "release the wind" during colds, fever, heatstroke and muscle pain. In Vietnam and Indonesia a coin with oil or balm is the usual tool. A gentler face version with jade or stone tools has become a skincare trend.

history.text: Western hospitals have mistaken the stripes from coin rubbing on Vietnamese children for signs of abuse, and medical journals have written about it as a cultural practice to recognise.

research.text: A few small trials on neck pain found short-term relief.

safety.summary: Leaves bruise-like marks that fade in a few days. Not on broken skin. Bleeding disorders and blood thinners raise the risk of heavy bruising.

entries.what: Scraping oiled skin with a smooth tool until red dots appear; practised in China, Vietnam and Indonesia.
entries.know: Gua means "to scrape" in Chinese, and sha is the name for the red, sand-like dots that rise on the skin.

sources.title: NCCIH, health topics A-Z (practices: acupuncture, massage, yoga, tai chi, meditation)

entries.name: Guarana
preps: roasted seed paste grated into water (traditional)
entries.uses: The Sateré-Mawé people traditionally roast the seeds, shape the paste into hard sticks, and grate them into water to drink for energy and against hunger on long journeys. It is now in Brazilian sodas and energy drinks.

lore.text: In a Sateré-Mawé legend a beloved child was killed, and from his eyes, planted in the earth, grew the guarana plant, whose seed looks like an eye.

research.text: The seeds hold more caffeine than coffee beans, often two to three times as much. Small trials have looked at alertness and memory.

safety.summary: Guarana in "natural" energy products can hide a lot of caffeine. It can cause palpitations, jitters and poor sleep. Avoid with heart rhythm problems and in pregnancy.

entries.what: A climbing Amazon plant whose red fruits split open to show a black seed in white flesh, like an eye.
entries.know: Guaraná Antarctica, Brazil's best-known guarana soda, has been sold since 1921.

sources.title: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database

entries.name: Guayusa
entries.uses: Kichwa families in Ecuador's Amazon traditionally brew big pots of it before dawn and drink it together while they share and interpret the night's dreams. Hunters drink it to stay alert at night.

history.text: Guayusa leaves were found in a healer's bundle about 1,500 years old, in a tomb in the Bolivian highlands far from where it grows.

research.text: It contains caffeine and theobromine (the stimulant in chocolate). There is little other study.

safety.summary: Caffeine.

entries.what: A caffeine-rich holly leaf from the Ecuadorian Amazon, brewed by Kichwa families before dawn.
entries.know: Guayusa is a holly, a close cousin of yerba mate and yaupon.

sources.title: James A. Duke, Handbook of Medicinal Herbs (2nd ed., 2002) and Dr. Duke's Phytochemical and Ethnobotanical Databases

entries.name: Guduchi (giloy)
entries.uses: In Ayurveda people boil the stem into a decoction, drink the juice, or take satva (a starch washed out of the crushed stem) for recurring fevers, low immunity and hot, painful joints. India's AYUSH ministry (its ministry for traditional medicine) promoted it heavily during COVID-19.

lore.text: One of its names is amrita, "the immortal". It is said to have sprung up where drops of amrita, the nectar of the gods, fell to earth.

research.text: Lab studies on the immune system; a few small human trials.

safety.summary: In 2021 liver specialists in Mumbai reported six people with liver injury after taking giloy, some with signs of autoimmune hepatitis. The AYUSH ministry disputed the link, but more Indian case reports followed. It may lower blood sugar.

entries.what: A climbing vine with heart-shaped leaves, common across India; its stem is boiled into a bitter drink.
entries.know: The vine often climbs neem trees, and guduchi grown on neem (neem giloy) is the most prized.

entries.name: Guelder rose (kalina)
entries.uses: In Russia and Ukraine the berries are traditionally mashed with honey or sugar and taken for colds, coughs and high blood pressure. In Western herbalism the bark, sold as cramp bark, is used for period pain and muscle cramps.

lore.text: Kalyna is a national symbol of Ukraine. It stands for a girl's beauty, for love and for the homeland, and its red berries fill wedding wreaths, embroidery and songs. The best known is "Chervona kalyna", a marching song of the Ukrainian Sich Riflemen from 1914.

research.text: Little clinical study.

safety.summary: Raw berries eaten in quantity can cause vomiting and diarrhoea. Traditionally they are picked after the first frost and cooked. Use caution in pregnancy.

entries.what: A shrub with bright red, bitter berries, used for colds in Russia and a national symbol of Ukraine.
entries.know: In 2022 Pink Floyd built a song, Hey Hey Rise Up, around the Ukrainian song about the red kalyna in the meadow.

entries.name: Guggul
entries.uses: In Ayurveda the raw resin is first purified (shodhana, usually by boiling it in herbal decoctions). It then goes into many tablets, such as Yogaraj guggulu for the joints and Kaishore guggulu for the skin, and others taken for weight and fat. It is also burned as temple incense.

history.text: In the 1980s India approved a guggul extract (gugulipid) for high cholesterol, based on Indian trials.

research.text: A US trial published in JAMA in 2003 found guggul did not lower cholesterol, and LDL ("bad" cholesterol) rose a little. Some people got rashes.

safety.summary: It can cause rash and stomach upset. It affects thyroid hormone and how the liver breaks down drugs, and it has lowered blood levels of the heart drugs propranolol and diltiazem.
safety.regulatory: Listed as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List.
safety.ethics: Heavy tapping is killing wild trees in Gujarat and Rajasthan. Buy cultivated resin.

entries.what: A sticky, fragrant gum resin tapped from a thorny desert shrub of western India, used in tablets and as incense.

entries.name: Gymnema (gurmar)
entries.uses: In Ayurveda and Siddha it is used for madhumeha ("honey urine", the classical name for diabetes) and for sugar cravings. People chew the leaf, and sweet things then taste of nothing for up to an hour.

history.text: Its gymnemic acids sit on the tongue's sweet receptors and block them.

research.text: Small trials suggest lower blood sugar; the quality is limited.

safety.summary: It can add to diabetes medicines and cause low blood sugar (a hypo). Rare liver injury has been reported.

entries.what: A woody climbing vine of India whose leaves, when chewed, briefly stop you tasting sweetness.
entries.know: Its sweet-blocking trick was first described in English in a report from India in 1847.

entries.name: Hammam
parts: steam rooms, black soap, kessa glove, rhassoul clay
entries.uses: Visited weekly across the Islamic world for cleanliness, healing and company. Brides go before the wedding and mothers after childbirth. In Morocco bathers soften the skin with black soap, scrub it with a rough kessa glove and wash the hair with rhassoul clay.

history.text: The hammam grew out of the Roman and Byzantine baths. Ottoman Istanbul built great domed hammams, such as the Çemberlitaş bath of 1584, which is still open.

research.text: Little specific study.

safety.summary: The usual heat cautions apply: heart disease, low blood pressure and pregnancy. Hard scrubbing can irritate or break the skin.

entries.what: The steam bath of the Middle East and North Africa: heat, a hard scrub, a wash, then rest.

sources.title: Ibn Sina (Avicenna), The Canon of Medicine (al-Qanun fi al-Tibb, 1025)

entries.name: Haritaki
entries.uses: In Ayurveda people take the powder as a gentle bowel tonic and as a rasayana (a rejuvenating tonic). In Tibetan medicine it is arura, the "king of medicines", and the Medicine Buddha is painted holding the fruit in his right hand.

lore.text: One story says it grew from a drop of amrita, the nectar of immortality, that fell while the god Indra was drinking. It balances all three doshas and above all vata, the airy, dry energy that Ayurveda links to constipation.

research.text: Small trials, mostly of triphala.

safety.summary: It is a laxative, so it is avoided with dehydration or diarrhoea, and in pregnancy.

entries.what: The wrinkled dried fruit of an Indian tree, the most prized of the three fruits in triphala.

sources.title: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India
Men-Tsee-Khang (Tibetan Medical & Astro-Science Institute), Dharamsala

entries.name: Harmal (Syrian rue)
entries.uses: Burned on charcoal across Iran, Turkey, Central Asia, the Caucasus and North Africa to protect against the evil eye, at weddings, births, exams and in new homes. In Uzbekistan dried bundles are burned and hung in houses and cars. In the past it was also swallowed for worms and pain.

lore.text: The seeds crackle and pop on the coals as a short prayer or rhyme is said against the envious eye, and each burst is the evil eye breaking. The smoke is circled around the person or room.

research.text: Its alkaloids, harmine and harmaline, block the enzyme MAO, which breaks down serotonin and other brain chemicals.

safety.summary: Swallowed, it poisons: vomiting, hallucinations, tremor and a slow heart. It has been used to end pregnancies. It clashes dangerously with antidepressants, stimulants and foods rich in tyramine (aged cheese, salami, soy sauce). Burning it is the traditional use.
safety.pets: Poisonous to grazing animals, which usually avoid it.

entries.what: A desert plant whose small seeds are burned on hot coals against the evil eye.
entries.know: On the eve of the Persian new year and at weddings, families wave the smoking esfand around the heads of loved ones.

sources.title: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database
Schultes & Hofmann, Plants of the Gods (1979/2001)

entries.name: Hawthorn
entries.latin: Crataegus monogyna, C. laevigata; C. pinnatifida (Chinese shan zha)
entries.uses: In Europe the flowering tops and leaves are traditionally taken as tea or tincture for an ageing heart, nervous palpitations and mildly high blood pressure. The EMA lists traditional use for nervous heart complaints, such as a fluttering heart from mild anxiety, once serious causes are ruled out. In Chinese medicine the dried fruit of a related species (shan zha) is eaten or brewed after heavy, meaty meals.

history.text: Hawthorn tincture sits on the shelf of almost every Russian pharmacy. Its career as a heart herb in Western Europe took off in the late 1800s.

lore.text: Hawthorn is the fairy tree. In Ireland and Britain a lone hawthorn in a field must never be cut, or the fairies who live in it take revenge. May blossom brought indoors was said to bring a death in the house. Christian legend says the crown of thorns was woven from it.

research.text: Several small trials in mild heart failure found people felt better and could exercise a little longer. The large SPICE trial (2008, about 2,700 patients) found no clear drop in heart events or deaths.

safety.summary: Hawthorn adds to the effect of heart and blood-pressure drugs, including digoxin, beta-blockers, nitrates and Viagra-type drugs. Side effects are usually mild: dizziness, nausea and an upset stomach. Avoid in pregnancy.

entries.cat: Don't cut the lone thorn tree. The ones who live in it are less forgiving than me.
entries.what: A thorny hedge tree of the rose family whose flowers, leaves and red berries are made into heart remedies.
entries.know: In 1999 a new road in County Clare, Ireland, was rerouted so that a fairy hawthorn at Latoon would not be cut down.

entries.name: He shou wu (fo-ti)
entries.uses: In Chinese medicine the prepared root, cooked in black-bean juice, nourishes the liver and kidney "essence" (jing, the inborn reserve said to set growth and ageing). It is traditionally taken to darken grey hair and for a long life. The raw root is used as a laxative.

lore.text: The legend of Mr He: old, grey and childless, he dug up the root of a vine whose stems twined together at night. He ate it, his hair turned black and he fathered children. The herb's name means "Mr He's black hair".

research.text: Research has mostly gathered case reports of liver injury, some severe, from both raw and prepared root.

safety.summary: It is one of the leading causes of herb-related liver injury in China and abroad. Jaundice (yellow skin or eyes), dark urine or sudden tiredness mean stop at once. The raw root is a laxative.
safety.regulatory: Liver-injury warnings have been issued in the UK (2006), Australia and China.

entries.what: The root of a Chinese climbing knotweed, famous as a herb for keeping hair black.

entries.name: Heartsease
entries.uses: In European folk medicine the flowering plant is made into a tea or a wash for cradle cap, eczema and itchy skin, and drunk for coughs. The EMA lists traditional use for mild seborrhoeic skin trouble (greasy, flaky patches such as cradle cap).

history.text: In A Midsummer Night's Dream (about 1595) it is "love-in-idleness", the flower Puck uses for his love potion.

lore.text: A love charm. Its juice dropped on a sleeper's eyelids makes them fall for the first creature they see on waking.

research.text: Barely studied in people.

safety.summary: Generally gentle. It contains small amounts of salicylates (aspirin-like compounds), so people allergic to aspirin may react.

entries.what: A small wild pansy with purple, yellow and white flower faces, brewed as a tea and a skin wash.
entries.know: The name pansy comes from the French pensée, "thought".

entries.name: Helichrysum (immortelle)
entries.uses: The oil of H. italicum is used in aromatherapy on bruises, scars and skin. In Slavic folk medicine a tea of sandy everlasting (H. arenarium) is drunk for the gallbladder and liver, and EMA lists a traditional use for indigestion.

lore.text: The everlasting flower of immortality, woven into dried wreaths for the dead.

research.text: Little clinical study.

safety.summary: People allergic to daisy-family plants can react. Not for people with gallstones or a blocked bile duct. Avoid in pregnancy.

entries.what: Immortelle, a yellow daisy-family flower that keeps its colour when dried; its oil goes on bruises and scars.
entries.know: The Mediterranean species is called curry plant because its leaves smell of curry, though it is not part of curry powder.

entries.name: Hemlock
entries.latin: Conium maculatum; water hemlock Cicuta virosa / C. maculata
entries.uses: Historically the poison the Athenian state gave to the condemned, Socrates among them in 399 BCE. Old herbals used tiny amounts on the skin for pain and swellings. Water hemlock is a different plant of wet ground, and even deadlier.

lore.text: In English lore hemlock is a witches' plant, and the purple blotches on its stem are said to be the mark of Cain.

research.text: Hemlock's coniine paralyses the muscles, the breathing muscles last. Water hemlock's cicutoxin causes violent seizures.

safety.summary: Among the deadliest plants of the northern hemisphere. Hemlock and water hemlock look like wild carrot, parsley, parsnip, angelica and osha, and foragers have died from the mix-up. Never eat any white-flowered plant of the carrot family without expert certainty. Poisoning is an emergency. History and lore only.
safety.pets: Deadly to livestock and pets.

entries.what: A tall white-flowered weed of the carrot family with purple-spotted stems, the poison that killed Socrates.
entries.know: Plato's account of Socrates' death describes a numbness creeping up from his feet towards his heart.

entries.name: Henbane
entries.uses: Historically the seeds were burned and the smoke breathed in for toothache, and seers at ancient oracles are said to have used the smoke too. German brewers added it to beer, and it went into witches' ointments.

history.text: A pouch of henbane seeds was buried with a woman at Fyrkat, a Viking-age fort in Denmark. The 1516 Bavarian beer purity law, which allowed only barley, hops and water, is said to have been partly aimed at henbane beer.

lore.text: The dead in Hades were said to wear crowns of henbane as they wandered by the river Styx. In Slavic villages it is said to have been burned or dipped in water as rain magic in times of drought.

research.text: It contains scopolamine and hyoscyamine, which are used as medicines in purified form.

safety.summary: Deadly. Every part is poisonous. Poisoning brings delirium, hallucinations that feel real, a racing heart, high temperature, coma and death, and is an emergency. History and lore only.
safety.pets: Poisonous to pets and livestock.

entries.what: A sticky, foul-smelling nightshade with purple-veined cream flowers, famous in Europe as a poison and witches' herb.
entries.know: In Russian, "beleny obyelsya" ("he's eaten too much henbane") means someone is acting crazy.

entries.name: Henna
preps: paste on skin, hair and nails
entries.uses: Traditionally painted on hands and feet for weddings and festivals across North Africa, the Middle East and South Asia. The paste is also spread on the feet and scalp to cool them in the heat, used to colour grey hair and nails, and put on fungal skin. In Prophetic medicine, hadith recommend henna for dyeing grey hair, and one tells of henna on aching legs.

history.text: Henna has been found on the hair and nails of Egyptian mummies.

lore.text: The henna night (laylat al-henna) before a wedding brings the bride baraka (blessing) and protection, and in Morocco and elsewhere the patterns guard against the evil eye and jinn.

research.text: Its dye, lawsone, has been studied in the lab. Little clinical work.

safety.summary: "Black henna" is usually mixed with PPD hair dye and can cause severe skin reactions, blistering and scars. Even natural henna can break down red blood cells (haemolysis) in babies and children with G6PD deficiency, an inherited enzyme shortage, and this can be serious.
safety.regulatory: In the US the FDA has approved henna only as a hair dye, not for direct use on skin.

entries.what: A shrub whose dried, powdered leaves make a red-brown paste for painting skin and dyeing hair.

entries.name: Hibiscus (roselle, sorrel)
entries.uses: Drunk cold across Egypt, West Africa, the Caribbean and Mexico as a cooling, sour drink in the heat, and traditionally for fevers and high blood pressure.

history.text: In Egypt karkade is served to toast weddings and to break the fast in Ramadan. In Jamaica and Trinidad sorrel brewed with ginger is the Christmas drink.

research.text: Several small trials and their reviews found a modest drop in blood pressure.

safety.summary: It may add to blood-pressure drugs. In one study it lowered levels of the malaria drug chloroquine, and it may interact with the water pill hydrochlorothiazide. A paracetamol interaction is only theoretical. Avoid in pregnancy.

entries.what: The tart, deep-red flower cups of a tropical hibiscus, brewed hot or iced into a sour red drink.
entries.know: The red part is not the petals but the calyx, the fleshy cup that holds the flower.

entries.name: Hochuekkito (Bu Zhong Yi Qi Tang)
aka: Tonify the Middle and Augment the Qi
parts: astragalus, ginseng, atractylodes, dong quai, bupleurum, cimicifuga, tangerine peel, licorice, jujube, ginger
entries.uses: In Kampo and Chinese medicine it is the classic formula for exhaustion, a poor appetite and "sinking qi", the sense that energy is draining downward. It is traditionally given after a long illness or an operation.

history.text: From the Treatise on the Spleen and Stomach (1249), a book of the 13th-century "earth school", which put digestion at the centre of health.

research.text: Small Japanese trials on tiredness and on COPD (long-term lung disease).

safety.summary: Its licorice can raise blood pressure and drop potassium with long use.

entries.what: A ten-herb Kampo and Chinese formula for deep tiredness after illness or surgery.

entries.name: Holy basil (tulsi)
entries.uses: In Indian homes people drink tulsi tea or take a few fresh leaves every day, and take the juice with honey for coughs, colds and fevers. It is also drunk for a calm mind. After worship, a tulsi leaf is often given with the holy water.

history.text: Many Hindu homes keep a tulsi plant on a raised pillar altar (tulsi vrindavan) in the courtyard. It is watered and walked around in prayer each morning.

lore.text: Tulsi is the goddess Vrinda, devoted to Vishnu and to Krishna. A leaf is placed in the mouth of the dying, with Ganges water. Prayer beads (malas) are carved from tulsi wood, especially by devotees of Krishna.

research.text: Small trials have looked at stress and blood sugar. Reviews call the evidence early.

safety.summary: It may slow blood clotting and lower blood sugar. Animal studies found effects on fertility, and it is traditionally avoided when trying to conceive.

entries.what: A sacred basil grown in pots and courtyard shrines across India, drunk as tea and offered in worship.
entries.know: Each year in the month of Kartik (October to November), many Hindu families hold Tulsi Vivah, a full wedding between the tulsi plant and Vishnu.

entries.name: Homeopathy
parts: remedies from plants, minerals and animal sources, serially diluted and shaken (succussed)
entries.uses: A system of medicine begun in Germany in 1796 and now practised worldwide. It is state-recognised in India, with its own colleges and hospitals, and Switzerland's basic health insurance has covered it since 2017. A homeopath takes a long interview about body, mind, sleep, food and moods, then chooses one remedy whose "picture" fits the whole person. Remedies are small sugar pills (pillules) or drops, dissolved under the tongue.

history.text: It began with a German physician's experiment in 1790: he took cinchona bark (the source of quinine) while healthy and felt symptoms like malaria's. He concluded that what causes symptoms in the healthy can relieve the same symptoms in the sick, and published the idea in 1796. Homeopathic hospitals opened across Europe and the Americas in the 1800s. India today has more than 300,000 registered practitioners. France stopped paying for remedies through national insurance in 2021.

lore.text: Three principles. The law of similars: let like be treated by like (similia similibus curentur). The minimum dose: a remedy is diluted step by step and shaken hard at every step (succussion), and this potentisation is held to make it stronger, not weaker. The single remedy, chosen for the whole person, body, mind and temperament (constitutional prescribing). New remedies are learned through provings, where healthy volunteers take a substance and write down every symptom it brings. Practitioners speak of a vital force that illness unsettles, and of water and sugar carrying the remedy's imprint.

research.text: Beyond 12C (diluted 1:100 twelve times) it is unlikely that a single molecule of the starting substance remains. Australia's national review (2015) and a UK parliamentary committee (2010) found no condition with reliable evidence of an effect beyond placebo. Practitioners point to patient satisfaction, long clinical experience and their own trials.

safety.summary: At high potencies the pills are sugar or lactose with no measurable starting substance. The real risks: putting off effective care for serious illness; low potencies (1X to 6X) of poisonous plants and metals can still contain enough to harm; and "homeopathic vaccines" (nosodes, remedies made from disease material) do not protect the way vaccines do.
safety.regulatory: NHS England stopped funding it in 2017. The FDA regulates remedies as drugs and, under its 2022 guidance, focuses on higher-risk products. The EU registers remedies through a simplified route that needs no proof of efficacy. India regulates it through the Ministry of AYUSH.

entries.what: A system of medicine from Germany that matches very diluted, shaken remedies to a person's whole set of symptoms.
entries.know: The Homoeopathic Pharmacopoeia of the United States was written into US federal drug law in 1938.

entries.name: Honey
aka: mānuka honey (from the Māori name of the tree)
entries.uses: People in nearly every culture use honey for coughs, sore throats, wounds and burns. In Prophetic medicine (healing based on the sayings of the Prophet Muhammad) it is "healing for people" (Qur'an 16:69). Hospitals use medical-grade honey dressings, often made from New Zealand mānuka honey.

history.text: Ancient Egyptian medical papyri list honey in hundreds of remedies, including wound dressings. In Russia villagers kept bees in hollow trees and log hives for centuries.

lore.text: Food of the gods. In Norse myth the mead of poetry, brewed with honey, turned whoever drank it into a poet. Slavic wedding customs give the couple honey for a sweet married life.

research.text: A Cochrane review found honey may ease children's night coughs a little more than no treatment. Another found burns dressed with honey closed faster than with some standard dressings.

safety.summary: Never give honey to babies under 1 year old: it can carry botulism spores. It is still sugar. "Mad honey" made from rhododendron nectar, in Turkey's Black Sea region and in Nepal, is poisonous and can cause dangerously low blood pressure and a slow heartbeat.

entries.what: The sweet syrup bees make from flower nectar, put on coughs and wounds in almost every culture.
entries.know: Pots of honey thousands of years old have been found in ancient Egyptian tombs, still recognisable as honey.

entries.name: Honeybush
entries.uses: Traditionally drunk in the Eastern and Western Cape for coughs. It is now sold worldwide as a caffeine-free tea.

research.text: Lab studies only.

safety.summary: Gentle. Little is known about very large amounts.

entries.what: A caffeine-free South African tea from a shrub whose yellow flowers smell of honey.

entries.name: Honeysuckle flower
aka: jin yin hua (Chinese, "gold and silver flower")
entries.uses: In Chinese medicine jin yin hua "clears heat". Paired with forsythia it makes Yin Qiao San, the classic formula for a cold that starts with sore throat and fever. It is also used for hot sores and boils. The name "gold and silver flower" comes from the blooms, which open white and turn yellow.

research.text: Lab work on viruses, and trials in China of formulas that contain it.

safety.summary: The flowers are thought to be gentle. The berries of some honeysuckle species are mildly poisonous.

entries.what: The unopened flower buds of Japanese honeysuckle, a classic Chinese herb for colds with sore throat.
entries.know: Japanese honeysuckle escaped from American gardens in the 1800s and is now an invasive weed across the eastern US.

entries.name: Hoodia
entries.uses: San hunters traditionally peel and chew the fleshy stem to stave off hunger and thirst on long hunts in the Kalahari. In the 2000s it was marketed worldwide as a weight-loss supplement.

research.text: A 2011 trial of a purified extract found no drop in food intake or weight, and it raised blood pressure, heart rate and some liver markers.

safety.summary: Many products held little or no real hoodia. In the trial it raised heart rate, blood pressure and bilirubin (a liver marker). Not used in pregnancy.
safety.regulatory: All hoodia species have been on CITES Appendix II since 2004, so trade needs permits.
safety.ethics: The 2003 benefit-sharing deal between the San and the CSIR was one of the first in the world for Indigenous knowledge.

entries.what: A spiny Kalahari succulent chewed by San hunters, later sold worldwide as a diet pill.
entries.know: South Africa's CSIR patented hoodia's appetite compound in the 1990s before asking the San, which led to a landmark deal.

entries.name: Hops
entries.uses: In Europe hops are traditionally drunk as tea or tincture for restlessness and poor sleep, often mixed with valerian, and stuffed into pillows to sleep on. The EMA lists traditional use for mild stress and to aid sleep.

history.text: Hop pickers were said to grow sleepy in the fields. Hops show up in brewing records from the 9th century (a French abbey's rules of 822 mention them) and slowly pushed out gruit, the older herb mix for beer, and ground ivy. In England hopped beer won out in the 1400s and 1500s.

lore.text: In Slavic wedding songs the hop is the merry bridegroom; in Russian khmel means both hops and tipsiness. Newlyweds were showered with hops and grain for a fertile, happy home.

research.text: Hop and valerian mixes showed small effects on sleep in a few trials. Hops contain 8-prenylnaringenin (8-PN), one of the strongest plant oestrogens known.

safety.summary: Hops can make you drowsy and add to sedatives and alcohol. Their plant oestrogens are a concern with hormone-sensitive cancers and hormone treatments. Old herbals warned against hops for people who are depressed. Avoid in pregnancy.
safety.pets: Very toxic to dogs. Eating hops, including spent hops from home brewing, can set off malignant hyperthermia, a runaway fever that is an emergency. Greyhounds and Labrador retrievers seem most at risk.

entries.what: The papery green cones of a climbing vine, best known for flavouring beer and as a bedtime herb.
entries.know: Hops are a close cousin of cannabis. Both belong to the same small plant family, Cannabaceae.

entries.name: Horse chestnut
entries.uses: Standardised seed extract is taken as tablets or rubbed on as a gel for heavy, aching legs and varicose veins. The EMA lists well-established use (backed by trials) for chronic venous insufficiency, where weak leg veins let blood pool and ankles swell.

history.text: The tree is native to the mountains of the Balkans. Seeds reached Vienna from Constantinople in 1576, and from there it spread to parks across Western Europe.

lore.text: In Britain a conker carried in the pocket was said to keep off piles and rheumatism.

research.text: A Cochrane review (2012) of short trials found standardised extract eased leg pain, swelling and itching. One trial found it did about as well as compression stockings.

safety.summary: Raw seeds, leaves, bark and flowers are poisonous. They contain aesculin and large amounts of aescin, and can cause vomiting, muscle twitching and paralysis. Conkers look a little like sweet chestnuts, and mixing them up is a known cause of poisoning. Only standardised extracts with the aesculin removed are used. Take care with kidney or liver disease, blood thinners and diabetes medicines. Avoid in pregnancy.
safety.pets: Toxic to dogs, cats and horses. Dogs that swallow conkers can get vomiting, diarrhoea and blocked guts.

entries.what: A big shade tree with spiky green husks and shiny brown nuts (conkers); a seed extract is sold for leg veins.
entries.know: In 1917 British schoolchildren collected conkers for the war effort; factories used them to make acetone for explosives.

entries.name: Horseradish
entries.uses: People sniff or eat freshly grated root to clear blocked sinuses at the start of a cold. Grated root wrapped in cloth is laid on aching muscles. In Germany tablets of horseradish with nasturtium are sold for bladder infections.

history.text: Many Ashkenazi Jewish families use it as the bitter herb (maror) on the Passover plate. It sits on the Slavic Easter table beside the ham.

research.text: A German trial of horseradish with nasturtium found fewer repeat bladder infections than placebo.

safety.summary: Burns the skin and eyes. Large amounts can irritate stomach ulcers and may affect the thyroid.

entries.what: A long white root that is grated into a sharp, nose-clearing sauce.
entries.know: Most "wasabi" served outside Japan is horseradish coloured green.

entries.name: Horsetail
entries.uses: Traditionally brewed as a tea to flush the urinary tract. The EMA lists that as traditional use, along with washes for small surface wounds. Because it is rich in silica, people also drink it for hair, nails and bones.

history.text: Its relatives grew as tall as trees in the coal swamps about 300 million years ago. The rough stems were used to scour pots and pewter, hence "scouring rush" and "shavegrass".

research.text: One small trial in 36 healthy men (2014) found it made them pass more urine, about as much as a mild water pill (hydrochlorothiazide).

safety.summary: Contains thiaminase, an enzyme that breaks down vitamin B1, and may lower potassium. It is not for swelling caused by heart or kidney disease, or for people short of vitamin B1, such as heavy drinkers. It may raise lithium levels, and low potassium makes digoxin more dangerous. Marsh horsetail (E. palustre) looks similar and is toxic. Avoid in pregnancy.
safety.pets: Toxic to horses. Hay with a lot of horsetail drains their vitamin B1 and can make them weak and staggering.

entries.what: A jointed green plant like a little bottlebrush, from one of the oldest plant groups on Earth.
entries.know: The gritty feel of the stems comes from silica, the same mineral as sand and glass.

entries.name: Hypericum (homeopathic)
entries.uses: In homeopathy, given for injuries to nerve-rich parts: crushed fingers and toes, falls on the tailbone, nerve pain after dental work.

research.text: No good trials show a reliable effect beyond placebo.

safety.summary: The pills contain no measurable herb at usual potencies. The herb itself has dangerous drug interactions (see St John's wort).

entries.what: St John's wort diluted into a homeopathic remedy for injuries to nerve-rich parts.
