entries.name: Hyssop
entries.uses: Traditionally drunk as tea or syrup for coughs and colds. In many traditions it is also a herb of ritual purification, used to sprinkle holy water and cleanse homes.

history.text: Psalm 51 says "purge me with hyssop". The biblical plant (ezov in Hebrew) was most likely za'atar (Origanum syriacum), not today's hyssop. Hyssop is a classic flavouring of absinthe.

lore.text: Hung in doorways against the evil eye. A cleansing herb for temples, homes and the body.

research.text: Little clinical study.

safety.summary: The essential oil contains pinocamphone, which can cause seizures. Never take the oil by mouth, and avoid hyssop in epilepsy. Avoid in pregnancy.

entries.what: A bushy mint-family herb with blue flower spikes, used for coughs and for ritual cleansing.
entries.know: Hyssop is one of the herbs steeped into absinthe at the end to give it its green colour.

Tisserand & Young, Essential Oil Safety, 2nd ed. (2014)

entries.name: Iboga
entries.uses: The sacrament of the Bwiti religion of Gabon, Cameroon and Equatorial Guinea. In initiation the grated root bark is eaten in large amounts through a night of music and dance, under the care of the community, so the initiate can meet the ancestors. Smaller amounts are taken in later ceremonies and for alertness. Its main alkaloid, ibogaine, is given for opioid addiction in clinics outside the US, often without a licence.

lore.text: Iboga opens the way to the ancestors and shows initiates the truth about their own lives. The first great initiation makes a person a banzi, one who has seen.

research.text: Small observational studies of ibogaine for opioid addiction report fewer withdrawal symptoms and less use. Deaths from heart rhythm problems have been documented.

safety.summary: Ibogaine can cause dangerous heart rhythm problems (QT prolongation), and dozens of deaths have been reported, many at clinics. The risk rises with heart disease and with almost any other drug, opioids included. Not used in pregnancy.
safety.regulatory: Ibogaine is a Schedule I controlled substance in the US and is controlled in several other countries. Gabon declared iboga a national heritage plant in 2000. In 2025 Texas funded ibogaine trials.
safety.ethics: Wild iboga is being over-harvested for export, and Gabon works to keep benefits with the communities that hold the tradition.

entries.what: A Central African forest shrub whose root bark is the sacred, visionary sacrament of the Bwiti religion.

sources.title: Schultes & Hofmann, Plants of the Gods (1979/2001)

entries.name: Ignatia amara
entries.uses: In homeopathy, the remedy of acute grief, shock and disappointment: sighing, a lump in the throat, moods that swing from tears to laughter.

research.text: No good trials show a reliable effect beyond placebo.

safety.summary: The raw seed contains strychnine and is poisonous. Grief that does not lift, or thoughts of ending your life, deserve support from the people around you or a crisis line.

entries.what: The St Ignatius bean diluted into homeopathy's remedy for fresh grief and shock.
entries.know: Jesuit missionaries in the Philippines named the bean after the founder of their order and sent it to Europe around 1700.

entries.name: Infused (macerated) oil
parts: flowers, leaves, roots in carrier oil
preps: Ayurvedic taila paka (oil cooked with decoction and paste)
entries.uses: Traditionally made by steeping flowers such as St John's wort, calendula or arnica in olive oil in the sun. Ayurveda cooks herbs into sesame oil for massage; well-known tailas (medicated oils) include Mahanarayan and Ksheerabala.

research.text: Depends on the herb.

safety.summary: Garlic or fresh herbs in oil can grow botulism. Keep it cold and use it quickly.

entries.what: Flowers, leaves or roots steeped in oil, used on the skin or for massage.
entries.know: St John's wort flowers turn olive oil blood red after a few weeks in the sun.

entries.name: Infusion (tisane)
preps: hot water poured over and covered
entries.uses: The most common way herbs are traditionally taken. Soft parts are steeped in just-boiled water under a lid, which stops the scented oils escaping with the steam. Mucilage herbs (slimy, soothing plants such as marshmallow root) are soaked in cold water overnight instead. In Ayurveda a hot infusion is called phant.

history.text: Herbal infusions appear in Egyptian medical papyri, and they have never left the kitchen since.

research.text: Water draws out different compounds from alcohol or capsules, so a trial of one form says little about another.

safety.summary: Strength varies from cup to cup. "Natural" teas can still interact with medicines.

entries.what: A herb tea made by pouring just-boiled water over leaves or flowers and letting them steep.
entries.know: The word tisane comes from the Greek ptisane, a drink of barley water.

entries.name: Iodine
entries.uses: Added to salt in about 120 countries; potassium iodide tablets are handed out near nuclear plants to protect the thyroid after an accident.

history.text: Goitre was so common in Alpine valleys and around the US Great Lakes ("the goitre belt") that iodised salt (Switzerland 1922, US 1924) changed whole regions.

research.text: Iodised salt is one of the most effective public health measures known for preventing goitre and iodine-related intellectual disability.

safety.summary: Too much iodine can trigger both overactive and underactive thyroid, especially in people with thyroid disease. Kelp tablets vary wildly in strength.

entries.what: The trace element your thyroid gland uses to make its hormones; most people get it from iodised salt.

nutrient.low: A swollen neck (goitre), tiredness, weight gain, feeling cold; in pregnancy, harm to the baby's brain.
nutrient.limit: US 1,100 mcg a day; EU 600 mcg a day.

entries.name: Iron
entries.uses: Taken for low iron, very commonly by people with heavy periods and in pregnancy; Victorian "iron tonics" were wine laced with iron salts.

history.text: In the US, iron pills were once the leading cause of fatal poisoning in children under six. Warning labels (1997) and single-dose blister packs for strong pills cut those deaths sharply.

research.text: Supplements reliably fix iron-deficiency anaemia. Taking them every other day may be absorbed as well as daily, with fewer stomach problems (small studies).

safety.summary: Iron pills are deadly to small children: a handful can kill. Keep them locked away. Constipation, black stools and nausea are common. People with iron overload (haemochromatosis) must not take it. Tea, coffee, calcium and antacids block absorption; iron blocks thyroid pills and some antibiotics.

entries.cat: Lock the iron pills up. Toddlers think they're sweets and I'm not babysitting.
entries.what: The mineral at the heart of haemoglobin, which carries oxygen in your blood.
entries.know: Plant iron is absorbed better with vitamin C and worse with tea, coffee or calcium in the same meal.

nutrient.low: Tiredness, pale skin, breathlessness on stairs, cold hands, brittle or spoon-shaped nails, craving ice.
nutrient.limit: US 45 mg a day; EU 40 mg a day (a "safe level" set in 2024, because the data were too thin for a formal limit).

entries.name: Isatis root
entries.uses: In Chinese medicine ban lan gen "clears heat and toxins", the hot, red, swollen side of an illness. Sachets of sweet instant granules are stirred into hot water at the first sore throat. They are probably China's best-known household remedy for flu season.

history.text: In Europe the same plant, woad, was the main blue dye until indigo arrived from India in the 1500s and 1600s. Roman writers said the Britons painted themselves blue, and woad is often thought to be the dye.

research.text: Lab studies on viruses. Very few human trials.

safety.summary: It can upset the stomach. Allergic reactions have been reported.

entries.what: The root of woad, the old European blue-dye plant, sold in China as an instant drink for sore throats.
entries.know: During the 2003 SARS outbreak Chinese shoppers emptied pharmacy shelves of ban lan gen granules.

sources.title: Bensky, Clavey & Stöger, Chinese Herbal Medicine: Materia Medica, 3rd ed. (2004)

entries.name: Ivan-chai (fireweed)
entries.uses: In Russia the leaves are rolled, left to ferment and dried like black tea, then drunk as an everyday tea. It was the country's home-grown tea before Chinese tea became cheap. Folk use gives it for digestion, calm sleep and men's urinary troubles. In Central Europe fireweed and small-flowered willowherb (E. parviflorum) are used for the urinary symptoms of an enlarged prostate, and EMA lists this as a traditional use. The young shoots are eaten as spring greens.

history.text: Russian tradition says Koporye tea, named after a village near St Petersburg, was shipped to England in the 1700s and 1800s. Since the 2010s it has come back as a craft tea.

lore.text: It is the first plant to spring up on burned ground, which is where the name fireweed comes from.

research.text: Lab studies have looked at its anti-inflammatory compounds, such as oenothein B. One Italian trial (2021) gave 128 men with enlarged prostates a fireweed extract or a dummy pill for six months. The extract group had fewer night-time trips to the toilet and less urine left in the bladder.

safety.summary: Mild. It has no caffeine.

entries.what: Fireweed, a tall pink wildflower whose leaves Russians ferment into a drink much like black tea.
entries.know: Fireweed spread over London's bomb sites so fast after the Blitz that Londoners called it bombweed.

entries.name: Ivy leaf
entries.uses: Standardised ivy leaf extract is sold in European pharmacies as a syrup for chesty, productive coughs. The EMA lists it as well-established use for loosening mucus so it can be coughed up.

history.text: Ivy crowned Dionysus, the Greek god of wine, and later the poets. Ivy-leaf syrups are among Germany's best-selling cough medicines.

lore.text: In English midwinter custom holly is the male plant and ivy the female. Ivy growing on a house was said to protect it.

research.text: A few placebo-controlled trials found coughs eased somewhat faster. Reviews call most of the trials small and of mixed quality.

safety.summary: Fresh leaves and berries are poisonous, and the sap can blister skin; only pharmacy extracts are taken by mouth. Not for children under 2, as it can make their breathing worse. It can upset the stomach. Avoid in pregnancy.
safety.pets: Toxic to dogs, cats and horses (ASPCA).

entries.what: Leaves of common climbing ivy, made into pharmacy cough syrups in Germany and across Europe.
entries.know: Old taverns hung a bush of ivy outside to show they sold wine, which gave the English proverb "good wine needs no bush".

sources.title: European Medicines Agency, Committee on Herbal Medicinal Products (HMPC) monographs
Cochrane Library systematic reviews

entries.name: Jamaican dogwood
entries.uses: Caribbean fishers threw crushed bark and leaves into the water to stun fish. Western herbalists later used a tincture of the root bark for nerve pain and sleeplessness.

research.text: There is little clinical work. The bark holds rotenone-type compounds, the same family as other fish poisons.

safety.summary: It is toxic in excess and can slow breathing; the gap between a dose and a poisoning is narrow.

entries.what: A Caribbean tree whose bark was thrown into water to stun fish, later used in tinctures for pain.

entries.name: Jasmine
entries.uses: Traditionally worn in garlands and in the hair, layered with green tea in China to scent it, and used in perfume and aromatherapy for mood. In India flowers are bound on the breasts to dry up the milk when a baby is weaned.

lore.text: Perfumers call jasmine the king of flowers, with rose as the queen. It opens at dusk and belongs to the moon and to love.

research.text: A few small studies of its scent. An Indian trial (1988) found jasmine flowers on the breasts reduced milk about as well as bromocriptine, a drug then used for this.

safety.summary: Absolutes, the concentrated extracts used in perfume, can carry traces of the solvent used to make them, and can cause skin allergy.

entries.what: Small white star-shaped flowers with a heavy, sweet scent, made into perfume, garlands and jasmine tea.
entries.know: Jasminum sambac is the national flower of both the Philippines (sampaguita) and Indonesia (melati putih).

sources.title: Tisserand & Young, Essential Oil Safety, 2nd ed. (2014)

entries.name: Jatamansi (spikenard)
entries.uses: In Ayurveda and Unani it is taken for sleep, anxiety and a restless mind, and added to hair oils. Its oil was the precious nard of ancient perfume.

history.text: Mary of Bethany anointed Jesus' feet with costly nard (John 12). Nard was carried from the Himalaya to Rome, where it was one of the dearest perfumes.

research.text: Animal studies on sedation.

safety.summary: It causes drowsiness and adds to sedatives.
safety.regulatory: Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List; CITES Appendix II.
safety.ethics: Wild-dug to scarcity. Buy cultivated, or use valerian.

entries.what: The hairy, fragrant root of a Himalayan relative of valerian, the spikenard of ancient perfume.
entries.know: In John's gospel the jar of nard is valued at 300 denarii, about a year's pay for a labourer.

sources.title: IUCN Red List of Threatened Species
CITES appendices (international trade in endangered species)
Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India

entries.name: Jujube
preps: dried fruit in soups and teas
entries.uses: In Chinese medicine the red date gently builds qi (the body's life energy) and calms the spirit. A few dates go into many formulas to protect the stomach from harsher herbs. In Unani, the Greek-Arabic medicine of South Asia and the Middle East, unab is used for coughs and to "purify the blood".

history.text: Grown in China for at least 4,000 years. Dates appear at weddings because zao, "date", sounds like "early" in the wish zao sheng gui zi, "may you soon have a noble son".

research.text: Mostly studied as food, with a few small human studies.

safety.summary: A common food.

entries.what: A chewy red date from a thorny tree, eaten as a snack and added to many Chinese formulas.
entries.know: At a Korean pyebaek wedding rite the couple's parents toss jujubes, and the bride catches them in her skirt for future children.

sources.title: Bensky, Clavey & Stöger, Chinese Herbal Medicine: Materia Medica, 3rd ed. (2004)

entries.name: Juniper
entries.uses: Traditionally taken as a tea for indigestion and wind and to flush the urinary tract (both EMA traditional uses), rubbed on aching joints, and burned to cleanse rooms and sickrooms. In the Russian banya, juniper branches are steeped in the water thrown on the stones.

history.text: Juniper berries were found in Tutankhamun's tomb (about 1323 BCE). Older herbals say French hospitals burned juniper with rosemary to clean the air of sickrooms. Gin takes its name and flavour from it.

lore.text: At Scottish Hogmanay, homes were "sained" (blessed) with juniper smoke. In Slavic and Baltic lands juniper hung over doorways kept witches out.

research.text: Little clinical work.

safety.summary: Long or heavy use can irritate the kidneys; avoid with kidney disease or inflammation. Savin (J. sabina), a related juniper, is poisonous and was once used to cause abortions. Juniper may add to diuretics and diabetes medicines and raise lithium levels. Avoid in pregnancy.

entries.what: A prickly evergreen shrub whose blue-black berries flavour gin and are burned as cleansing smoke.
entries.know: Gin is named after juniper: the Dutch jenever comes from the Latin juniperus.

sources.title: European Medicines Agency, Committee on Herbal Medicinal Products (HMPC) monographs
Maud Grieve, A Modern Herbal (1931)
research/HEALING-CODEX.md in this repo (fuller prose on many of these items)

entries.name: Kakadu plum
entries.uses: Aboriginal peoples of the Kimberley and Arnhem Land traditionally eat the fruit fresh as bush food in the dry season, and use the bark in washes for skin sores. Today it is also sold as a powder and used in cosmetics.

research.text: Lab tests have measured some of the highest vitamin C levels recorded in any fruit. There is little human research.

safety.summary: Eaten as a food.
safety.ethics: Aboriginal-owned enterprises harvest and sell it, and the knowledge of native foods belongs to the Peoples who hold it. Patents filed on the fruit by a foreign cosmetics company drew biopiracy complaints and were dropped.

entries.what: A small green bush fruit from northern Australia that holds more vitamin C than almost any other fruit.

sources.title: Royal Botanic Gardens Kew, Plants of the World Online and State of the World's Plants

entries.name: Kakkonto (Ge Gen Tang)
parts: kudzu, ephedra, cinnamon, peony, licorice, ginger, jujube
entries.uses: In Kampo, Japan's own form of Chinese herbal medicine, it is taken at the very first chills of a cold, when the neck and shoulders go stiff and there is no sweat yet. It is sold over the counter in most Japanese pharmacies. It is also one of the 148 Kampo formulas covered by Japan's national health insurance.

history.text: From the Shang Han Lun, a Chinese classic on fevers written around 200 CE.

research.text: A 2014 Japanese trial in about 400 adults with early colds found kakkonto no better than an ordinary over-the-counter cold medicine at stopping the cold from getting worse.

safety.summary: It contains ephedra and licorice. Ephedra raises heart rate and blood pressure; licorice can raise blood pressure and drop potassium. It is risky with heart disease or high blood pressure.

entries.what: Japan's best-known Kampo cold formula, made around kudzu root and taken at the first chill.
entries.know: An old Japanese comic story mocks a healer who prescribes kakkonto for every complaint, even for the patient's friend waiting outside.

sources.title: Japan Ministry of Health, Kampo formulas approved for national health insurance (148 formulas)
Bensky, Clavey & Stöger, Chinese Herbal Medicine: Materia Medica, 3rd ed. (2004)

entries.name: Kalmegh (andrographis)
entries.uses: Across South and Southeast Asia people boil it or take tablets for fevers, colds and the liver. Thailand lists it as a national herbal medicine for colds, and in Scandinavia it is sold for colds as Kan Jang. In Siddha medicine (the old healing system of Tamil South India) it is the main herb in Nilavembu kudineer.

history.text: It is said to have been used against the 1918 to 1919 flu pandemic in India. The Tamil Nadu government handed out Nilavembu kudineer during dengue outbreaks.

research.text: Trials and a 2017 review found colds were somewhat shorter and milder, but most of the trials were of low quality.

safety.summary: Very bitter. It can cause allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis (a sudden severe allergy, which is an emergency); Australia's medicines regulator has warned about this. It may lower blood pressure.

entries.what: A very bitter green herb of South and Southeast Asia, taken for colds and fevers.

sources.title: NIH National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health, Herbs at a Glance
Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database
https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0181780

entries.name: Kambo (frog secretion)
parts: dried secretion of the giant monkey frog
entries.uses: Used by the Matsés, Katukina and other Panoan peoples of the Amazon to bring hunting luck and drive out panema (bad luck and laziness). The secretion is scraped from the frog, dried on a stick and dabbed onto small burns on the skin, which brings fast, violent vomiting. It is now sold at Western retreats as a "detox".

research.text: The secretion holds peptides (small proteins) with strong effects on the heart, blood vessels and gut. Only studied in the lab.

safety.summary: Deaths have been reported at retreats. Effects include vomiting, collapse, liver injury and psychosis. The large amounts of water drunk beforehand have caused dangerously low blood sodium. Not with heart disease or alongside any medication.
safety.regulatory: Brazil's health agency banned advertising it as a medicine in the mid-2000s. In 2021 Australia put it in Schedule 10 of the Poisons Standard, which bans its sale, supply and use.

entries.what: The waxy secretion of an Amazonian tree frog, dabbed onto small burns on the skin to bring on purging.

sources.title: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database
https://www.tga.gov.au/scheduling-decision-final/notice-final-decisions-amend-or-not-amend-current-poisons-standard

entries.name: Kanna
entries.uses: Khoi and San peoples traditionally crush the plant, let it ferment for a few days in a sealed bag, dry it, then chew it or take it as snuff to lift the mood, ease hunger and thirst on long walks, and bring people together.

history.text: Dutch settlers at the Cape wrote about trading for it in 1662, and a 1685 expedition drew the plant.

research.text: A few small trials of a standardised extract found less anxiety and less fear response in the brain's amygdala on scans. Its main compound, mesembrine, acts on serotonin.

safety.summary: Acts on serotonin, so it is not mixed with antidepressants or other serotonin drugs. Not used in pregnancy.
safety.ethics: Commercial kanna extract comes with a benefit-sharing agreement with the South African San Council.

entries.what: A South African succulent that is crushed, fermented and chewed to lift mood.
entries.know: Its Afrikaans name, kougoed, simply means something to chew.

sources.title: van Wyk, van Oudtshoorn & Gericke, Medicinal Plants of South Africa (2009)

entries.name: Kapikacchu (velvet bean)
entries.uses: In Ayurveda the seed is a vajikarana (a herb for sexual vigour), taken in milk for male vitality. It is also used for kampavata, the classical name for shaking disorders.

research.text: The seed contains natural L-DOPA, the main Parkinson's drug. A few small trials in Parkinson's found it acted much like standard L-DOPA.

safety.summary: Because of its L-DOPA it interacts with Parkinson's drugs and MAOI antidepressants, and it can cause psychosis or low blood pressure. The pod hairs cause intense itching.

entries.what: A climbing bean of India with velvety, itchy pods; the seeds are powdered as a tonic.
entries.know: The fine hairs on its pods were once sold as itching powder for pranks.

sources.title: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database
Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India

entries.name: Kava
entries.uses: Across Fiji, Tonga, Samoa, Vanuatu and Hawaii people pound or grind the root, knead it in cold water and strain it through cloth into a shared wooden bowl. It is drunk to welcome guests, seal agreements, honour chiefs and mark weddings and funerals, and in the evening simply to unwind together. Traditionally it is also used for worry, sleeplessness and aches. In the West it is sold as capsules and extracts for stress.

history.text: Pacific islanders have grown kava for about 3,000 years, and it was probably first bred in northern Vanuatu. In the 1990s Europe sold kava extracts as anxiety medicines. After reports of liver injury, Germany, Switzerland, France, the UK and other countries banned or restricted them in 2002. A German court overturned the German ban in 2014. In 2016 the WHO and FAO reviewed the traditional water drink and judged it low risk when made from noble varieties and drunk in moderation.

lore.text: In a Tongan story a poor couple on the island of ʻEueiki had nothing to feed their king in a famine, so they offered their daughter. Kava grew from her grave, with sugarcane beside it. A rat nibbled the kava and staggered, then ate the sugarcane and steadied, and so people learned to drink the one and eat something sweet after.

research.text: A 2003 Cochrane review of about a dozen short trials found anxiety scores fell more with kava extract than with placebo. A larger 16-week trial published in 2020, in people with generalised anxiety, found no difference from placebo. Liver injury has been linked mostly to extracts made with solvents or from poorer "tudei" (two-day) varieties.

safety.summary: Kava can injure the liver. This is rare and mostly linked to extracts, but cases after the traditional drink are known too. Never mix it with alcohol or sedatives, and do not drive after drinking it. Heavy daily drinking causes dry, scaly skin (kava dermopathy), which fades when the drinking stops. It can weaken the effect of levodopa, the Parkinson's medicine. Avoid in pregnancy.
safety.regulatory: Checked November 2026. UK: kava food has been banned since 2002, and so have unlicensed kava medicines. Germany: a court overturned the 2002 ban in 2014. Australia: allowed as food since December 2021, with import permits; new import rules took effect on 13 October 2026. A Codex standard for kava drinks was adopted in 2020. US: sold as a supplement; the FDA warned of liver risk in 2002.

entries.cat: Ceremony drink, numb lips, deep calm. Mix it with booze and your liver files for divorce.
entries.what: A pepper-family root pounded and mixed with water into a muddy, calming drink shared in Pacific island ceremonies.
entries.know: In Fiji a visitor's welcome, the sevusevu, begins with a gift of dried kava root to the village chief.

entries.name: Kawakawa
entries.uses: In rongoā Māori (traditional Māori healing) the leaves are traditionally brewed into a tonic tea, made into balms for skin and sore muscles, and chewed for toothache. Leaves with insect holes are thought to be the strongest. Wreaths of kawakawa are worn at tangihanga (funerals).

lore.text: Kawakawa stands for life and death together. Leaves are picked from the sunny side of the plant, often after a karakia (a prayer or chant), and given back to the earth with respect.

research.text: Only lab studies so far.

safety.summary: Kawakawa is related to kava but holds little of kava's active compounds. It does contain myristicin, the strong compound also found in nutmeg. There is little safety data. Avoid in pregnancy.
safety.ethics: Rongoā is a taonga (treasure) of Māori. Harvest follows tikanga (customary protocol): ask first, take only what is needed, and give thanks.

entries.what: A native New Zealand shrub of the pepper family with heart-shaped leaves, used in Māori healing for teas and balms.
entries.know: The holes in the favoured leaves are eaten by the caterpillar of the kawakawa looper moth, found only in New Zealand.

sources.title: Te Ara, Encyclopedia of New Zealand: Rongoā (Māori medicine)

entries.name: Kefir, ryazhenka and soured milks
parts: fermented milk with kefir grains or cultures
entries.uses: Traditionally drunk every day for digestion and strength. In Russia people with tuberculosis, or getting over a long illness, went to steppe sanatoria for koumiss stays (koumissolechenie): weeks of drinking fermented mare's milk. In Bulgaria yogurt (kiselo mlyako) is linked with long life.

history.text: In 1907 a biologist born near Kharkiv, who won a Nobel prize the next year, argued that Bulgarian peasants lived long thanks to the bacteria in their yogurt. The idea launched probiotics.

research.text: Live yogurt cultures make lactose easier to digest, a claim EU food regulators (EFSA) accepted in 2010. For other effects the evidence depends on the bacterial strain and is mixed.

safety.summary: These are foods. People with weak immune systems, and pregnant women, should avoid unpasteurised products because of listeria. Kefir and koumiss hold a little alcohol.

entries.what: Kefir and the other soured milks of Russia and the Balkans, drunk daily as food and as a mild tonic.
entries.know: The yogurt bacterium Lactobacillus bulgaricus is named after Bulgaria; a Bulgarian medical student found it in Geneva in 1905.

sources.title: Łuczaj et al., Wild food and medicinal plants in Slavic and Eastern European ethnobotany (Journal of Ethnobiology and Ethnomedicine papers)
Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database
https://www.efsa.europa.eu/en/efsajournal/pub/1763

entries.name: Khamira (Unani heart tonics)
parts: borage-like gaozaban, pearl (marwareed), saffron, silk cocoon, sugar
entries.uses: In Unani medicine (the Greek-Arabic system practised in India and Pakistan) these are mufarrih, "exhilarants": tonics for the heart and brain, taken for palpitations, low spirits and weakness. Khamira marwareed is made with pearl, khamira gaozaban with the herb gaozaban.

history.text: Unani pharmacy follows the Canon of Medicine (1025). Hakims (Unani physicians) in India and Pakistan still make them.

research.text: Little clinical work.

safety.summary: Some contain pearl or gold, and all are heavy in sugar. Buy from regulated makers.

entries.what: Sweet, soft Unani confections made with herbs, pearl or silk, taken as heart and brain tonics.
entries.know: Gaozaban, the main herb, is Persian for "cow's tongue", after its rough leaves.

sources.title: National Formulary of Unani Medicine (India)
Ibn Sina (Avicenna), The Canon of Medicine (al-Qanun fi al-Tibb, 1025)

entries.name: Khat
entries.uses: In Yemen, Ethiopia, Somalia, Djibouti and Kenya people traditionally chew the fresh leaves in long afternoon gatherings, holding a wad in the cheek. It is chewed for sociability, to stay awake at work, and in some Sufi communities to stay alert through night prayers and religious study.

research.text: Its main compound, cathinone, is an amphetamine-like stimulant. Heavy use has been linked to mouth cancer, heart attacks and psychosis.

safety.summary: Can lead to dependence, sleeplessness, high blood pressure and a fast heart. Liver injury and psychosis have been reported. Use in pregnancy is linked to low birth weight. Not used with heart disease or a history of psychosis.
safety.regulatory: Legal in Yemen, Ethiopia, Djibouti, Kenya and Somalia. Banned in the UK since 2014 and the Netherlands since 2013. In the US its active compounds are controlled substances.

entries.what: A shrub of East Africa and Yemen whose fresh leaves are chewed for a mild stimulant buzz.

sources.title: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database

entries.name: Kinkeliba
aka: "tisane de longue vie" (French, "tea of long life")
entries.uses: Across Senegal and the Sahel people drink the leaf tea at breakfast, often with bread, and in Ramadan to break the fast at sundown. It is traditionally taken for the liver, fevers and digestion, and to pass water.

research.text: Mostly lab and animal studies, including on blood sugar.

safety.summary: Little safety data.

entries.what: A West African bush whose leaves make a mild, slightly bitter breakfast tea in Senegal.

sources.title: PROTA4U, Plant Resources of Tropical Africa

entries.name: Kola nut
entries.uses: Traditionally chewed for energy and to hold off hunger on long journeys. It is offered to guests, broken and shared to open gatherings and seal agreements, and given at weddings. In Yoruba and Igbo practice the lobes of the many-lobed kola (Cola acuminata) are cast in obi divination. In Jamaica it is grated into water as bissy.

lore.text: An Igbo saying goes "he who brings kola brings life". In obi divination the split lobes are thrown, and how many land face up or face down answers the question put to the orisha or ancestors.

research.text: Contains caffeine and theobromine, the same stimulants as coffee and cocoa. Little other study.

safety.summary: The caffeine can cause sleeplessness, a racing heart and jitters, especially with other stimulants. Heavy chewing stains teeth and has been linked to mouth sores.
safety.pets: Caffeine is poisonous to dogs and cats.

entries.what: The bitter, caffeine-rich seed of a West African rainforest tree, chewed and shared as a sign of welcome.
entries.know: Kola extract gave cola drinks their name and some of their first caffeine in the 1880s.

sources.title: PROTA4U, Plant Resources of Tropical Africa
ASPCA Animal Poison Control, toxic and non-toxic plants

entries.name: Kombucha
parts: sweet tea fermented with a symbiotic culture of bacteria and yeast
entries.uses: Traditionally kept in jars on Russian windowsills and drunk as a homemade fermented tonic. It is now sold worldwide and promoted for gut health.

history.text: Russian and German writers described the "tea fungus" in the early 1900s. Western sales boomed from the 2000s.

research.text: Very few human studies. A pilot trial (2023) in 12 adults with type 2 diabetes found lower fasting blood sugar after four weeks of drinking it.

safety.summary: Home brews have caused acidosis, a dangerous build-up of acid in the blood; in 1995 a US woman died. Brewing in glazed ceramic jars has caused lead poisoning. Batches can grow mould or harmful germs, and they contain a little alcohol. Avoid in pregnancy and with weakened immunity.

entries.what: Sweet tea fermented by a rubbery disc of bacteria and yeast into a fizzy, tangy drink.
entries.know: In Japan the word kombucha means something else: a tea made from kelp seaweed.

sources.title: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37588049/

entries.name: KPV and LL-37
entries.uses: Sold in peptide clinics: KPV by mouth or on the skin for gut and skin inflammation, LL-37 by injection for infections and "immunity".

research.text: Lab and animal work only; neither has had proper human trials in the forms sold.

safety.summary: Unknown in people. LL-37 is a natural part of the skin's defences, but too much of it is linked to rosacea and psoriasis in skin research. Grey-market quality varies.
safety.regulatory: As of November 2026: neither is approved. KPV was taken off Category 2 in April 2026; the FDA advisory committee voted 8 to 6 for it in July 2026, and the October 2026 HHS policy covers KPV by mouth or on the skin (not injected). LL-37: FDA's April 2026 page lists it under nominations withdrawn, but some later summaries still call it restricted, so sources disagree; it is due for advisory review before the end of February 2027 and is not covered by the HHS policy.

entries.what: Two small immune peptides, one for inflammation and one against germs, sold by peptide clinics.
entries.know: KPV is only three amino acids long (lysine, proline, valine), the tail end of a hormone that darkens skin.

entries.name: Kratom
entries.uses: In southern Thailand and Malaysia farm workers and rubber tappers traditionally chew the fresh leaves or brew them as tea to keep going through hard work in the heat, and use them for pain, coughs and diarrhoea. In villages it is also offered to guests. In the West it is sold as powders, capsules and shots, and people take it for pain and to come off opioids.

history.text: Thailand banned kratom in 1943, reportedly because it cut into the state's opium income, and made the leaf legal again in 2021.

research.text: Its main compounds, mitragynine and 7-hydroxymitragynine (7-OH), act on the same brain receptors as opioids. Surveys and a few small studies describe the effects people report, and dependence and withdrawal are well documented. There are no large trials, and the FDA has approved no medical use.

safety.summary: People become dependent and go through withdrawal. Reported harms include liver injury, seizures, a racing heart and deaths, most of them with other drugs in the mix. Concentrated 7-OH products sold in shops are far stronger than the leaf. Mixing it with opioids, sedatives or alcohol is especially dangerous. Avoid in pregnancy: babies have been born in withdrawal.
safety.regulatory: Checked November 2026. US: no federal ban on the leaf, and many states ban or regulate it. In August 2026 the DEA temporarily put mitragynine pseudoindoxyl and two related compounds in Schedule I. In October 2026 it gave notice that 7-OH and mitragynine pseudoindoxyl above a set strength will follow (an earlier July 2026 plan was withdrawn); that order was not yet in force. Thailand took kratom off its narcotics list in 2021 and licenses it under a 2022 act. Banned in Australia, controlled in Malaysia, and illegal to sell in the UK.

entries.what: The leaf of a Southeast Asian tree in the coffee family, chewed or brewed for energy and now sold worldwide.

entries.name: Kudzu
entries.uses: In Chinese and Japanese medicine ge gen "releases the exterior", the skin and muscles where a cold first strikes. It is the lead herb of Kakkonto, taken for a cold with a stiff neck and shoulders. The flower and root are traditionally used for hangovers, and in Japan kuzu starch is cooked into a clear, soothing gruel.

research.text: Small trials found that a kudzu extract cut how much heavy drinkers drank.

safety.summary: It contains plant oestrogens. It may affect blood sugar and clotting, and it may raise methotrexate levels.

entries.what: A fast-climbing Asian vine whose starchy root is a Chinese and Japanese medicine and a cooking starch.
entries.know: The US government paid farmers to plant kudzu against erosion in the 1930s and 40s. It is now called "the vine that ate the South".

sources.title: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database
Bensky, Clavey & Stöger, Chinese Herbal Medicine: Materia Medica, 3rd ed. (2004)

entries.name: Kukui (candlenut)
entries.uses: In Hawaii the oil is traditionally rubbed on babies' skin and on fishers' skin against sun and salt. The sap from the green nut is dabbed on mouth sores and thrush in babies. People burned strings of nuts as candles, and ground roasted nuts with salt into ʻinamona, a relish.

lore.text: Kukui stands for light, hope and learning. Lei of polished black nuts were worn by aliʻi (chiefs) and are still given as gifts.

research.text: Mostly cosmetic studies of the oil.

safety.summary: Raw nuts are poisonous and act as a violent laxative, with vomiting and cramps. Only roasted nuts are eaten, and only a little. The oil on skin is mild.

entries.what: Hawaii's state tree, whose oily nuts were once strung on a stick and burned as candles.
entries.know: In Indonesia and Malaysia the nut, called kemiri, is ground into curry pastes, and it is always cooked first.

sources.title: Kamakau, Ka Poʻe Kahiko and the Hawaiian lāʻau lapaʻau literature; Bishop Museum ethnobotany

entries.name: Kutki
aka: hu huang lian (Chinese, a close relative)
entries.uses: In Ayurveda the intensely bitter rhizome (underground stem) is used for the liver and for fevers, as a powder or a decoction.

research.text: Lab and animal studies on liver protection.

safety.summary: It acts as a strong laxative in larger amounts.
safety.regulatory: On CITES Appendix II since 1997, so international trade needs permits. Rated endangered in several Indian Himalayan states.
safety.ethics: Wild stocks are heavily dug. Buy cultivated only.

entries.what: A small plant of the high Himalaya with a very bitter root, dug wild for Ayurvedic and Tibetan medicine.

sources.title: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India
CITES appendices (international trade in endangered species)

entries.name: Kvass
parts: fermented rye bread, sugar, sometimes mint, raisins or beets
entries.uses: Traditionally drunk as an everyday summer refreshment, after the banya (Russian steam bath) and for hangovers. In Ukraine beet kvass is drunk as a tonic for the blood and liver, and is also the sour base for borscht.

history.text: In Soviet cities kvass was sold by the mug from yellow tanker barrels on street corners.

research.text: Kvass is a fermented food, and few studies have looked at its microbes.

safety.summary: Kvass holds a little alcohol, usually under 1.5%. Home ferments can spoil.

entries.what: A fizzy, sour-sweet drink fermented from rye bread, the everyday summer drink of Russia and Ukraine.
entries.know: Kvass is in the Primary Chronicle: in 996 CE Prince Vladimir of Kyiv had it carted round in barrels for the poor and sick.

sources.title: Łuczaj et al., Wild food and medicinal plants in Slavic and Eastern European ethnobotany (Journal of Ethnobiology and Ethnomedicine papers)

entries.name: Labrador tea (marsh rosemary)
entries.uses: In Siberia a weak tea of the leaves is traditionally taken for coughs, and the dried plant is strewn to keep off moths and fleas. In North America the related R. groenlandicum is drunk as a mild everyday tea by Cree, Dene and Inuit peoples.

lore.text: Its heady smell over the bog was said to cloud the mind. The Russian name, bagulnik, is often traced to an old word for poisoning or making dizzy.

research.text: Little clinical study. The leaf oil contains ledol and other compounds that are toxic to the nervous system.

safety.summary: R. tomentosum is poisonous in anything beyond tiny amounts: it can cause dizziness, vomiting and collapse. Honey made from its flowers is also toxic. Avoid in pregnancy.
safety.pets: Plants of the rhododendron group are poisonous to grazing animals, dogs and cats.

entries.what: A low bog shrub with leathery, rust-furred leaves and a heavy scent; a mild tea in North America, a moth repellent in Siberia.

sources.title: Sokolov & Zamotaev, Handbook of Medicinal Plants (USSR, 1984/1990)
Daniel Moerman, Native American Ethnobotany (1998) and the BRIT Native American Ethnobotany database

entries.name: Lady's mantle
entries.uses: In European and Slavic folk medicine it is traditionally drunk as a tea for heavy periods, as a women's tonic and for diarrhoea. ESCOP, a European herbal research group, lists it for mild diarrhoea.

history.text: Its English name refers to the Virgin Mary's cloak, which the scalloped leaf was thought to resemble.

lore.text: Alchemists gathered the drops from its leaves as the purest water for the Great Work, hence the Latin Alchemilla, "little alchemist".

research.text: Little study in people.

safety.summary: Gentle. Its tannins can upset a sensitive stomach. Avoid in pregnancy, as there is too little safety data.

entries.what: A low garden herb with soft, scalloped leaves that hold glittering drops of water.
entries.know: The "dew" on its leaves is mostly the plant's own water, pushed out through the leaf edges at night.

sources.title: ESCOP monographs, European Scientific Cooperative on Phytotherapy
Maud Grieve, A Modern Herbal (1931)

entries.name: Lavender (herb)
aka: ustukhuddus (Unani, mainly French lavender L. stoechas)
entries.uses: Traditionally drunk as a calming tea, sewn into sleep sachets and added to baths. The EMA lists traditional use for mild stress and to aid sleep.

history.text: Its name is often traced to the Latin lavare, "to wash". Legend says the glove-makers of Grasse in France, who scented their leather with it, escaped the plague.

lore.text: A herb of protection, love and peace. Thrown on Midsummer fires and laid in linen chests.

research.text: Silexan, a lavender oil capsule, beat placebo for anxiety in several trials. The flower tea itself has barely been studied. See the Lavender oil card.

safety.summary: Mild. It may add to sedatives. Some people get a skin allergy from it.
safety.pets: Toxic to cats and dogs in quantity (ASPCA). Cats are especially sensitive to the essential oil.

entries.what: A purple-flowered Mediterranean shrub with a clean, strong scent, dried for tea, baths and linen sachets.
entries.know: Many of the famous purple fields of Provence are lavandin, a hybrid grown because it gives more oil.

sources.title: European Medicines Agency, Committee on Herbal Medicinal Products (HMPC) monographs

entries.name: Lavender oil
entries.uses: Used in aromatherapy for calm and sleep, in a diffuser, a bath or a massage oil, or as a few drops on the pillow. Diluted, it is dabbed on small burns, bites and spots. In Germany a licensed lavender oil capsule (Silexan, sold as Lasea) is sold in pharmacies for anxious restlessness.

history.text: The same chemist told how he burned his hand in a lab explosion around 1910 and plunged it into lavender oil. The story helped launch modern aromatherapy.

research.text: Trials of Silexan capsules found it eased generalised anxiety more than a placebo. Studies of breathing in the scent are small.

safety.summary: Old, oxidised oil can cause skin allergy. Case reports linked repeated use of lavender products in young boys to breast growth (prepubertal gynaecomastia), which went away when the products were stopped; the link is debated. The oil is not for swallowing, apart from licensed capsules, which can add to the effect of sedatives.
safety.pets: Toxic to cats. Diffusers can harm cats and birds.

entries.what: The oil distilled from lavender flowers, the best-known calming scent in aromatherapy.
entries.know: The word aromatherapy was coined by a French perfume chemist in a 1937 book.

sources.title: Tisserand & Young, Essential Oil Safety, 2nd ed. (2014)
NIH National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health, Herbs at a Glance

entries.name: Leech therapy (hirudotherapy)
entries.uses: Used in Russian, Ayurvedic (jalaukavacharana, "leech application") and Unani medicine for congested veins, varicose veins and sore joints. In modern surgery, leeches drain pooled blood from reattached fingers and skin flaps.

history.text: Leeching is described in ancient Indian, Greek and Arabic medicine. In 2004 the US FDA cleared medicinal leeches as a medical device.

research.text: An accepted tool in reconstructive surgery. Small trials in knee arthritis.

safety.summary: Infection with Aeromonas, a germ from the leech's gut (hospitals give antibiotics for this), and long bleeding after the bite. Only medical-grade leeches, each used once.
safety.regulatory: Cleared by the US FDA as a medical device in 2004. The medicinal leech (Hirudo medicinalis) has been on CITES Appendix II since 1987, so trade across borders needs permits.

entries.what: Putting live medicinal leeches on the skin to draw blood, an old practice still used in surgery.
entries.know: In the 1830s France was importing tens of millions of leeches a year.

entries.name: Lemon balm
entries.uses: Traditionally drunk as tea to "make the heart merry", calm the nerves and settle a nervous stomach. The EMA lists traditional use for mild stress, sleep and mild stomach upsets such as bloating and wind. In Germany creams made from it are sold for cold sores.

history.text: Medieval Persian physicians wrote that it gladdens the heart. In 1611 Carmelite nuns in Paris began distilling eau de mélisse, "Carmelite water".

lore.text: Melissa is Greek for honeybee. Beekeepers rubbed it inside empty hives to make a new swarm stay.

research.text: Small trials suggest a calmer mood, and cold sores that clear a little faster with the cream.

safety.summary: Mild. It can make you drowsy. Lab studies show it can block thyroid-stimulating signals, so take care with an underactive thyroid or thyroid medicine.

entries.what: A lemon-scented mint-family herb, loved by bees, drunk as a calming tea.
entries.know: A lemon balm spirit called Klosterfrau Melissengeist has been made and sold in Germany since 1826.

sources.title: European Medicines Agency, Committee on Herbal Medicinal Products (HMPC) monographs

entries.name: Lemon myrtle
entries.uses: Aboriginal peoples of the Queensland rainforests are said to have used the leaves in cooking and healing. Today it is drunk as a bush-food tea, baked into biscuits and sauces, and its oil goes into soaps.

research.text: Lab studies show the oil and its citral kill some bacteria and fungi.

safety.summary: The leaf as a tea or spice is a food. The oil irritates skin.

entries.what: An Australian rainforest tree whose leaves smell strongly of lemon, used for tea and cooking.
entries.know: Its leaf oil is about 90 percent citral, more than lemongrass, so it smells more lemony than lemons do.

sources.title: Royal Botanic Gardens Kew, Plants of the World Online and State of the World's Plants

entries.name: Lemon verbena
entries.uses: Traditionally drunk after meals and at night in Peru, Chile, Argentina and Spain for digestion and calm.

history.text: The Spanish brought it from South America to Europe in the 1600s.

research.text: A few small studies.

safety.summary: Gentle. Large amounts are said to irritate the kidneys.

entries.what: A South American shrub with strongly lemon-scented leaves, brewed as an after-dinner tea.
entries.know: Its names Aloysia and hierba Luisa honour María Luisa of Parma, an 18th-century queen of Spain.

sources.title: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database

entries.name: Lemongrass and citronella
entries.uses: In Jamaica it is "fever grass", brewed as a bush tea for colds and fevers. In Brazil capim-santo tea is drunk for calm, and in Thailand the stalks go into soups and curries. Citronella oil is rubbed on or burned in candles to keep mosquitoes away.

research.text: Citronella keeps mosquitoes off for only a short time. A 1986 Brazilian trial of the traditional tea in volunteers found no calming or sleep effect.

safety.summary: The oil irritates skin and can cause skin allergy. The tea is mild.
safety.pets: The plant and the oil are toxic to cats and dogs.

entries.what: A tall lemon-scented grass used in Thai cooking and Caribbean bush tea; its cousin citronella gives the bug-repellent oil.

sources.title: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database
Tisserand & Young, Essential Oil Safety, 2nd ed. (2014)
ASPCA Animal Poison Control, toxic and non-toxic plants

entries.name: Licorice
entries.uses: Traditionally used for coughs, sore throats and an irritated stomach lining. In Chinese medicine gan cao goes into most formulas to "harmonise" them, softening and blending the other herbs. In Ayurveda yashtimadhu is used as a soothing rasayana (a rejuvenating tonic).

history.text: Licorice root was found in Tutankhamun's tomb. An ancient Greek writer said Scythian soldiers could go 11 or 12 days without water by chewing it with mare's-milk cheese. In Egypt erq sous, licorice water, is still sold on the street, above all during Ramadan.

lore.text: The great harmoniser of Chinese herbs, nicknamed guo lao, "the state elder", who keeps all the others in balance.

research.text: DGL (licorice with the glycyrrhizin taken out) was studied for stomach ulcers with mixed results. Glycyrrhizin's effects on hormones, potassium and blood pressure are well documented.

safety.summary: Real licorice (with glycyrrhizin) raises blood pressure, drains potassium and makes the body hold water. Heavy candy eating has caused heart rhythm problems and deaths; in 2020 a US man died after eating a bag and a half of black licorice a day for weeks. DGL avoids most of this. Avoid in pregnancy: heavy licorice eating has been linked with preterm birth.

entries.cat: Sweet as you think you are, and twice as bad for your blood pressure.
entries.what: The sweet root of a pea-family plant, used in medicine across Asia and Europe, and in black candy.
entries.know: Glycyrrhizin, the root's sweet compound, is 30 to 50 times sweeter than sugar.

entries.name: Lily of the valley
preps: historic Russian heart drops (Zelenin drops, with valerian and belladonna)
entries.uses: Historically used like foxglove for heart failure. It is still an ingredient of Zelenin drops, an old remedy sold in Russian pharmacies.

lore.text: In France people give sprigs of muguet on 1 May for luck, a custom said to go back to a king's gift in 1561. Christian legend says the flowers grew from Mary's tears at the cross. A Russian legend says they grew from the tears of the sea princess Volkhova for the singer Sadko.

research.text: Its heart glycosides, chiefly convallatoxin, act like those of foxglove.

safety.summary: Poisonous. Every part, even the water from a vase of the flowers, can disturb the heart rhythm. The leaves have been mistaken for wild garlic (ramsons) and eaten. Poisoning is an emergency. History and lore only.
safety.pets: Toxic to cats and dogs.

entries.what: A small spring woodland flower with sweet-scented white bells, poisonous in every part.

entries.name: Limpia (spiritual cleansing)
parts: egg, herbs (rue, basil, rosemary, pirul), copal smoke, holy water, prayer
preps: a curandera sweeps the body with herbs or an egg, then reads the egg in water
entries.uses: Performed by curanderas and curanderos (folk healers) in Mexico, Central America and the Andes for susto (soul fright), mal de ojo (the evil eye), envy and mal aire (bad air). The healer sweeps the body with a bundle of herbs or rolls an egg over it, with prayer and copal smoke, then cracks the egg into a glass of water to read it.

history.text: It blends Indigenous and Catholic practice and is common in Mexican markets today.

lore.text: The egg draws in what is bad. The shapes of the yolk and the bubbles in the water show what was taken out.

research.text: Not studied.

safety.summary: A child with a high fever is an emergency. Rue rubbed on the skin can blister it in sunlight. Copal and candle smoke in a small closed room irritates the lungs.

entries.what: A spiritual cleansing where a healer sweeps the body with herbs or an egg, from Mexico and Latin America.
entries.know: Mexico City's Mercado de Sonora, the "witches' market", sells limpia herbs, eggs and candles, and curanderos give cleansings right at the stalls.

entries.name: Linden (lime blossom)
entries.uses: In Russia, Poland and France people drink the tea hot to sweat out a feverish cold. It is also given to restless children and adults at bedtime. EMA lists traditional uses for colds and for mild stress. Linden honey is taken for sore throats.

history.text: In France the tea is tilleul, the classic after-dinner tisane. Russian peasants wove their bast shoes (lapti) from strips of linden inner bark.

lore.text: For the Slavs the linden was a sacred tree. Villagers met and settled disputes under the big village linden, and the tree was tied to love and to a goddess. It is still a national symbol of the Czechs, Slovaks and Slovenes.

research.text: Very little clinical study.

safety.summary: Mild. Some old references warn that stale flowers or very frequent use could harm the heart; this has never been confirmed.

entries.what: The flowers of the lime or linden tree, dried for a honey-scented tea drunk hot for colds and at bedtime.
entries.know: The Polish word for July, lipiec, comes from lipa, the linden, because the trees flower then.

sources.title: European Medicines Agency, Committee on Herbal Medicinal Products (HMPC) monographs

entries.name: Lingonberry (cowberry)
entries.uses: In Russia and Scandinavia the leaf tea is traditionally drunk to pass more water, and for bladder infections (cystitis), swelling and gout. Russian pharmacies sell the dried leaf in boxes. The berries are a winter food, full of vitamin C.

history.text: Russians kept lingonberries through the winter in barrels of water (mochenaya brusnika). In Sweden the jam is served with meatballs.

research.text: The leaf contains arbutin, the same compound as uva ursi (bearberry). A Finnish trial (2001) found that women who drank cranberry-lingonberry juice had fewer repeat bladder infections over six months.

safety.summary: The leaf is for short spells only: arbutin turns into hydroquinone in the body, which may be harmful with long use. Not for people with kidney disease. Avoid the leaf in pregnancy; the berries are food.

entries.what: A small, tart red berry of northern forests; the leaves are made into tea and the berries into jam.
entries.know: Lingonberries keep for months without cooking because they contain benzoic acid, a natural preservative.

entries.name: Lion's mane
entries.uses: In China and Japan people cook it as a delicacy, and Chinese medicine uses it for the stomach. Today it is sold as a nootropic (a supplement taken for memory and focus) and for the nerves.

lore.text: Its Japanese name honours the yamabushi, mountain ascetics whose robes carry fluffy pom-poms that look like the mushroom.

research.text: In lab studies it made nerve cells produce more nerve growth factor. A few small human trials, including one in Japan with older adults with mild memory loss, found better test scores while people took it. The gain faded after they stopped.

safety.summary: An ordinary food mushroom. People with a mushroom allergy can react, and a few cases of rash and breathing trouble have been reported.

entries.what: A white, shaggy mushroom that looks like a small frozen waterfall, eaten as food and sold as a supplement.

sources.title: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database
Paul Stamets, Mycelium Running (2005)

entries.name: Liu Wei Di Huang Wan (Six-Ingredient Rehmannia Pill)
parts: rehmannia, cornus, Chinese yam, alisma, poria, moutan
entries.uses: In Chinese medicine it is the classic pill to nourish kidney yin. The "kidney" is a whole system said to govern growth, bones, hearing and ageing, not just the organ. Yin is its cool, moist, nourishing side. So the pill is traditionally used for a sore lower back and knees, night sweats, ringing ears and dryness in ageing.

history.text: A Song-dynasty children's physician adapted it from an older Han-dynasty formula (Shen Qi Wan, around 200 CE) by leaving out the two warming herbs. It became the base of many variants.

research.text: Lab studies and small trials in Asia.

safety.summary: It can loosen the stools. Pills have been found with heavy metals or hidden drugs, so makers that test their products matter.

entries.what: A six-herb Chinese pill, the classic formula for the "kidney" in its cooling, nourishing (yin) side.

sources.title: Bensky, Clavey & Stöger, Chinese Herbal Medicine: Materia Medica, 3rd ed. (2004)

entries.name: Lobelia
entries.uses: Cherokee, Iroquois, Penobscot and other nations used it as medicine, and it was smoked for asthma and in ceremony. In the 1800s it was the centre of an American medical movement that used vomiting as its main way of healing.

history.text: Its alkaloid lobeline was sold in quit-smoking aids until the FDA banned it from them in 1993 for lack of proof.

research.text: Lobeline acts on the body much like nicotine. Studies are in the lab and in animals.

safety.summary: The gap between a dose and a poisoning is narrow. Too much brings vomiting, a racing heart and collapse, and deaths have been recorded.

entries.what: A small blue-flowered wild plant of eastern North America, called Indian tobacco, with a nicotine-like alkaloid.

sources.title: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database
Daniel Moerman, Native American Ethnobotany (1998) and the BRIT Native American Ethnobotany database

entries.name: Lomilomi
parts: hands, forearms, coconut or kukui oil, prayer (pule)
preps: long flowing strokes, often with chant
entries.uses: Done within Hawaiian families and by trained healers (kahuna), with prayer (pule), to restore flow and harmony (pono). Coconut or kukui-nut oil is used. Related traditions are fofō in Samoa and romiromi in Aotearoa (New Zealand).

lore.text: Hoʻoponopono, a family gathering to set things right through prayer and talk, often went alongside it.

research.text: Little study.

safety.summary: Gentle.

entries.what: Hawaiian massage with long, flowing strokes of the hands and forearms, often given with prayer.

sources.title: Kamakau, Ka Poʻe Kahiko and the Hawaiian lāʻau lapaʻau literature; Bishop Museum ethnobotany
Te Ara, Encyclopedia of New Zealand: Rongoā (Māori medicine)

entries.name: Long pepper
entries.uses: In Ayurveda it is a rasayana (a rejuvenating tonic) for the lungs. The powder is mixed with honey for coughs and wheeze, and it is one of the three spices in trikatu, taken to kindle digestion. In the old regimen pippali vardhamana, the number of fruits taken rises day by day and then falls back.

history.text: Long pepper reached ancient Greece before black pepper did. Roman price lists put it at more than three times the price of black.

research.text: Studied mostly in cells and animals.

safety.summary: Ayurveda counts it as very heating, so it is kept away from people with heartburn or a hot temperament. It carries the same piperine drug interactions as black pepper.

entries.what: A pepper that grows as small, dark catkin-like spikes, hotter and sweeter than black pepper.

sources.title: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India

entries.name: Lovage
entries.uses: Traditionally drunk as a root tea to flush the urinary tract (an EMA traditional use) and to ease wind. In Slavic custom it is a love herb.

history.text: A Frankish royal decree of about 800 (the Capitulare de villis) ordered it grown on the emperor's estates.

lore.text: Ukrainian and Polish girls washed their hair in lovage water so they would be loved, and tucked sprigs into wedding wreaths and bouquets.

research.text: Little study.

safety.summary: The plant contains furanocoumarins, which can make skin burn in sunlight. Not for inflamed kidneys or kidney disease. Avoid in pregnancy.

entries.what: A tall, celery-like herb whose leaves taste of stock cubes, used in soups and Slavic love charms.
entries.know: Germans call it Maggikraut because it tastes like Maggi seasoning, though Maggi contains no lovage.

sources.title: European Medicines Agency, Committee on Herbal Medicinal Products (HMPC) monographs
Sokolov & Zamotaev, Handbook of Medicinal Plants (USSR, 1984/1990)

entries.name: Lycopodium clavatum
parts: club moss spores, triturated and diluted
entries.uses: In homeopathy, given for bloating and wind that are worst in the late afternoon (classically 4 to 8 pm), and for people who fear failure but act confident.

history.text: Club moss spores burn in a bright flash and were once flash powder for photographers and fire effects in stage magic.

research.text: No good trials show a reliable effect beyond placebo.

safety.summary: At usual potencies the pills contain no measurable spores.

entries.what: Club moss spores, ground and diluted into a homeopathic remedy for bloating and hidden self-doubt.

sources.title: Australian NHMRC, Information Paper: evidence on the effectiveness of homeopathy (2015)

entries.name: Maca
entries.uses: High in the Peruvian Andes people eat it as a staple food for strength and fertility, and feed it to their livestock for the same reason.

history.text: It is grown above 4,000 m on the plateau around Lake Junín. Inca warriors are said to have eaten it before battle.

research.text: Small trials on sex drive and semen quality found some effects.

safety.summary: It is food-like. As a cabbage-family plant, very large amounts may affect how the thyroid uses iodine. It is cautioned with hormone-sensitive conditions.

entries.what: A turnip-like root grown on the high Andes plateau of Peru, eaten as food and sold as a powder.
entries.know: Most maca roots are sun-dried for months, then boiled or roasted; fresh ones are rarely eaten.

sources.title: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database
NIH National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health, Herbs at a Glance

entries.name: Magnesium
entries.uses: Taken at night for sleep, cramps and calm; magnesium citrate and oxide are sold as laxatives; Epsom salt baths for sore muscles.

history.text: Epsom salt is named after a bitter spring in Epsom, England, where, the story goes, cattle refused to drink in the 1600s.

research.text: Some evidence for migraine prevention and constipation; small, mixed studies for sleep and leg cramps.

safety.summary: Diarrhoea is common, especially with oxide and citrate. People with kidney disease can't clear it: build-up causes weakness, low blood pressure and heart rhythm problems. It blocks absorption of some antibiotics and bone drugs.

entries.what: A mineral in over 300 body reactions, from muscle relaxing to heartbeat; nuts, seeds and greens are full of it.

nutrient.low: Muscle twitches and cramps, tiredness, poor appetite; in severe cases, irregular heartbeat.
nutrient.limit: From supplements (not food): US 350 mg a day; EU 250 mg a day.

entries.name: Maitake
entries.uses: Eaten in Japan as a prized wild mushroom, and sold as a supplement for immunity and blood sugar.

research.text: Only small trials, including early studies in people with cancer and with diabetes. The results are not conclusive.

safety.summary: It may lower blood sugar and blood pressure. One case of a stronger warfarin effect (a raised INR, the blood clotting test) has been reported.

entries.what: A big, frilly cluster of grey-brown caps that grows at the foot of oak trees, eaten as food.
entries.know: Maitake means "dancing mushroom" in Japanese, said to be because people danced for joy when they found one.

sources.title: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database
National Cancer Institute PDQ: medicinal mushrooms, mistletoe and other complementary topics

entries.name: Mandrake
entries.uses: Historically used to put people to sleep for surgery, on "sleeping sponges" soaked in mandrake, opium and henbane and held under the nose. It was a love and fertility charm: in Genesis 30 Rachel trades with Leah for her mandrakes. Medieval herbals drew the root as a tiny human with leaves sprouting from its head.

lore.text: The root is said to shriek when pulled from the earth and to kill anyone who hears it, so a dog was tied to it to do the pulling. Some said it grew beneath the gallows. In German lands alraun dolls carved from the root were dressed, fed and kept for luck and wealth.

research.text: It contains tropane alkaloids (scopolamine and hyoscyamine), the same family as belladonna's.

safety.summary: Deadly. Every part is poisonous. Poisoning brings blurred vision, delirium, a racing heart and coma, and is an emergency. History and lore only.

entries.cat: Pull it and it screams. Eat it and you scream. Admire it on the card.
entries.what: A low Mediterranean plant with a forked root shaped like a little person, the most famous magic root of Europe.

entries.name: Manganese
entries.uses: Included in multivitamins and joint supplements.

history.text: Miners and welders who breathed manganese dust developed a Parkinson-like illness ("manganism").

research.text: No good evidence that extra manganese helps bones or joints in people who eat normally.

safety.summary: Some high-dose joint products exceed the limit. Breathed in, it damages the brain; that happens at work, not from food. People with liver disease clear it poorly.

entries.what: A trace mineral used in bone-building and antioxidant enzymes; tea, nuts and whole grains supply most of it.

nutrient.low: Almost never seen in people.
nutrient.limit: US 11 mg a day; EU set no upper limit (a "safe level" of 8 mg a day, from 2023).

entries.name: Manjistha
entries.uses: In Ayurveda it is the chief "blood purifier", taken for acne and other skin trouble and mixed into face packs. It is also used to "move and cool the blood" around periods.

history.text: Its root was a main red dye for Indian cotton and silk.

research.text: Lab studies only.

safety.summary: It turns urine red. There is little safety data.

entries.what: The red root of Indian madder, a climbing plant used in Ayurveda for the skin and once to dye cloth red.

sources.title: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India
Bensky, Clavey & Stöger, Chinese Herbal Medicine: Materia Medica, 3rd ed. (2004)

entries.name: Mantra and chanting
entries.uses: Taught across Hindu, Buddhist, Sufi and Christian traditions as prayer and healing. Hindus count japa on a mala of 108 beads, and Sufis repeat the names of God in dhikr. In Tibetan practice the Medicine Buddha mantra is chanted over the sick. In Slavic villages, whispered charms (zagovory) were said over an illness.

research.text: Small studies on calm and on breathing rhythm.

safety.summary: No physical risks are known.

entries.what: Repeating sacred words or sounds, aloud or silently, as prayer or meditation.
entries.know: A 2001 study in the BMJ found that saying the rosary in Latin and chanting a yoga mantra both slowed breathing to about six breaths a minute.

sources.title: NCCIH, health topics A-Z (practices: acupuncture, massage, yoga, tai chi, meditation)

entries.name: Maral root (leuzea)
entries.uses: In the Altai the root is traditionally taken for strength and for recovering after illness. It is named after the maral, a Siberian red deer said to dig it up in the rutting season. Soviet sports medicine gave it to athletes for strength.

research.text: The root is rich in ecdysterone, a steroid-like compound that insects use as a moulting hormone. The human evidence is small Soviet and Eastern European studies.

safety.summary: It may raise blood pressure and cause insomnia. Avoid in pregnancy.

entries.what: A thistle-like plant of the Altai mountains whose root was a Soviet sports tonic.
entries.know: The World Anti-Doping Agency added ecdysterone, the best-known compound in maral root, to its monitoring list in 2020.

entries.name: Marshmallow
entries.uses: Traditionally soaked in cold water and drunk to soothe dry coughs, sore throats and an irritated stomach or bladder. The EMA lists traditional use for dry cough, throat irritation and mild stomach discomfort. Althea syrup is a classic Russian children's cough syrup.

history.text: The name comes from the Greek althaino, "to heal". French confectioners of the 1800s whipped the root sap with sugar and egg white into pâte de guimauve, the first marshmallow sweets.

lore.text: In ancient Greece mallows were said to be planted on graves, because the dead fed on them.

research.text: The root's mucilage (a slippery gel) coats the throat. Clinical trials are few.

safety.summary: The mucilage may slow the absorption of medicines taken at the same time, so keep them an hour apart. It may lower blood sugar.

entries.what: A pale pink mallow of wet meadows whose slimy root sap was the original marshmallow sweet.

sources.title: European Medicines Agency, Committee on Herbal Medicinal Products (HMPC) monographs
Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database

entries.name: Masala chai
parts: black tea, milk, sugar, ginger, cardamom, cinnamon, clove, black pepper
entries.uses: Boiled up every day in Indian homes and at street stalls. With extra ginger, pepper and tulsi (holy basil), people drink it for colds, and it comes close to a kadha, a spiced herbal decoction.

history.text: Spiced herbal milks are old in India. Black-tea chai spread in the 1900s after the British-run Indian Tea Association campaigned to sell tea inside India; street sellers stretched the tea with milk, sugar and spices.

research.text: Studied as food, not as medicine.

safety.summary: Sugar and caffeine.

entries.what: Indian milk tea boiled with ginger, cardamom and other spices, sold on almost every street corner.
entries.know: Chai simply means tea, so "chai tea" means "tea tea".

sources.title: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India

entries.name: Mastic
entries.uses: Chewed since ancient times for the stomach and fresh breath. The European Medicines Agency recognises its traditional use for mild indigestion, and on the skin for minor inflammation and small wounds.

history.text: It comes only from the villages of southern Chios and has had EU protected origin status since 1997. Women of the Ottoman sultan's harem are said to have chewed it to sweeten their breath.

research.text: Small trials looked at H. pylori (the stomach bacterium behind many ulcers) and indigestion, with some positive results.

safety.summary: It can cause allergy, especially in people allergic to pistachio, cashew or mango, which are in the same family.

entries.what: Small clear resin "tears" from a shrub that grows only on the Greek island of Chios, chewed like gum.
entries.know: Mastic resin oozes from cuts in the bark and is left to drip and harden on the ground, which villagers sweep clean and dust with white clay first.

sources.title: European Medicines Agency, Committee on Herbal Medicinal Products (HMPC) monographs
Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database

entries.name: Matcha
entries.uses: Whisked and drunk in the Japanese tea ceremony (chanoyu, "the Way of Tea") as a practice of attention. Zen monks drank it for alert calm through long meditation.

history.text: A Zen monk brought powdered tea from China to Japan in 1191. The tea ceremony grew around wabi-sabi, the beauty of simple, worn and imperfect things.

lore.text: Ichi-go ichi-e, "one time, one meeting": every gathering happens only once, so give it your whole attention.

research.text: Small studies on L-theanine, an amino acid in tea, taken with caffeine for alert calm.

safety.summary: More caffeine per cup than steeped green tea, because you drink the whole leaf. For the same reason, any lead or other contaminants in the leaf are swallowed too.

entries.what: Green tea grown in shade and stone-ground to a fine powder, then whisked into hot water.
entries.know: Matcha bushes are shaded for about three weeks before picking, which makes the leaves greener and sweeter.

sources.title: Okakura Kakuzō, The Book of Tea (1906)
Victor Mair & Erling Hoh, The True History of Tea (2009)

entries.name: Māmaki
entries.uses: Hawaiians traditionally drink māmaki as a daily tonic tea and give it to children and new mothers. Today it is grown commercially on Hawaiʻi Island (the Big Island) and sold as loose tea.

research.text: Lab studies of its antioxidants. Little human research.

safety.summary: Drunk widely as a tea with no known problems, though there is little formal safety data. Unlike its nettle cousins it has no stinging hairs.

entries.what: A small native Hawaiian shrub of the nettle family whose dried leaves make a mild everyday tea.
entries.know: Māmaki is the main food plant of the Kamehameha butterfly's caterpillar, and that butterfly is Hawaii's state insect.

sources.title: Kamakau, Ka Poʻe Kahiko and the Hawaiian lāʻau lapaʻau literature; Bishop Museum ethnobotany

entries.name: Mānuka
entries.uses: In rongoā Māori (traditional Māori healing) the leaves and bark are traditionally steamed or boiled and drunk for colds, fevers and urinary complaints, and the sap and ash were put on burns. Today sterile, medical-grade mānuka honey is sold as a wound dressing.

history.text: Early European visitors and settlers brewed the leaves as a stand-in for tea. Medical-grade mānuka honey dressings were approved in several countries from the 2000s.

research.text: Lab work links mānuka honey's strong action against bacteria to a compound called methylglyoxal. A 2015 Cochrane review found honey dressings may let partial-thickness burns close faster than some standard dressings; for other wounds the evidence was unclear.

safety.summary: Never give honey to babies under one year old, because of the risk of botulism. Much honey sold as mānuka has turned out to be mislabelled. Wound dressings use sterile medical-grade honey, not table honey. Mānuka oil can irritate skin.
safety.regulatory: New Zealand defines genuine mānuka honey by four chemical markers and one DNA marker, and the tests have been required for exports since February 2018.

entries.what: A tough flowering shrub of New Zealand and southeast Australia, best known for the honey bees make from it.
entries.know: Captain Cook's crew brewed its leaves into tea in 1773, which is where the name "tea tree" comes from.

sources.title: Te Ara, Encyclopedia of New Zealand: Rongoā (Māori medicine)
Cochrane Library systematic reviews

entries.name: Meadowsweet
entries.uses: Traditionally drunk as a tea for acid stomach and heartburn, feverish colds and aching joints. The EMA lists traditional use for colds and minor joint pain.

history.text: In 1839 a German chemist isolated salicylic acid from its flower buds. When aspirin was named in 1899, the "spir" came from Spiraea, meadowsweet's old Latin name.

lore.text: Old herbals say it was one of the three herbs most sacred to the Druids, with vervain and water mint. It was strewn on church floors at weddings, hence "bridewort". In the Welsh Mabinogion, Blodeuwedd is a woman conjured from the flowers of oak, broom and meadowsweet.

research.text: It contains salicylates (aspirin-like compounds). There is little clinical work.

safety.summary: Avoid with aspirin allergy or aspirin-triggered asthma. Not for children with a viral illness or fever, because aspirin-like compounds are linked to Reye's syndrome, a rare brain and liver illness. It may add to blood thinners and NSAID painkillers. Avoid in pregnancy.

entries.what: A creamy, almond-scented wildflower of damp meadows, the plant that gave aspirin its name.
entries.know: Queen Elizabeth I is said to have liked meadowsweet strewn on her floors more than any other herb.

sources.title: European Medicines Agency, Committee on Herbal Medicinal Products (HMPC) monographs
Maud Grieve, A Modern Herbal (1931)
Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database

entries.name: Meditation
entries.uses: Taught by Hindu, Buddhist, Daoist, Jain, Sufi and Christian traditions as a path to insight and freedom. Styles include zazen (Zen sitting), vipassana (insight), metta (loving-kindness) and mantra. Secular mindfulness courses teach it for stress.

research.text: Reviews of mindfulness courses found moderate benefits for anxiety, depression and stress.

safety.summary: Long, intense retreats sometimes bring up distressing experiences. People living with trauma or psychosis go gently, with an experienced teacher.

entries.what: Training the attention by sitting quietly with the breath, a word or an image; found in many religions.
entries.know: The word Zen comes, through the Chinese chan, from the Sanskrit dhyana, meaning meditation.

sources.title: NCCIH, health topics A-Z (practices: acupuncture, massage, yoga, tai chi, meditation)

entries.name: Melanotan II
entries.uses: Sold illegally online and through social media for tanning without sun, and sometimes for libido.

history.text: Developed at the University of Arizona in the 1980s as a way to tan without ultraviolet light. Its relatives became approved medicines: afamelanotide for a rare light sensitivity (erythropoietic protoporphyria) and bremelanotide for low sexual desire.

research.text: Small human studies in the 1990s showed it darkens skin and causes erections. It was never approved. Case reports describe new and changing moles, melanoma, kidney injury and painful long-lasting erections.

safety.summary: Moles can darken, multiply and change, and melanoma has been reported in users. Nausea, flushing and loss of appetite are common. Kidney damage and priapism (an erection lasting hours, which is an emergency) are reported. Doses vary wildly: Australian tests of identical spray bottles found between 22 and 54 mg in each.
contra: history of melanoma or many moles
safety.regulatory: As of November 2026: not approved anywhere. Illegal to sell for human use in the UK, EU, US and Australia; Australia's regulator seized sprays and a seller paid fines of over A$100,000 in May 2026. FDA's April 2026 page lists it under nominations withdrawn, while legal summaries say it stays restricted; an FDA advisory committee is due to review it before the end of February 2027. TikTok blocks its main hashtags.

entries.what: An unlicensed injection or nasal spray that darkens the skin without sun, nicknamed the "Barbie drug".
