entries.name: Milk thistle
entries.uses: Traditionally the main liver herb of Western herbalism, taken for liver and gallbladder complaints and after heavy drinking. The EMA lists traditional use for indigestion and a full feeling, and for liver complaints.

history.text: Silibinin, a compound from the seed, is given by drip in some European hospitals for death cap mushroom poisoning.

lore.text: Christian legend says the white veins on its leaves are drops of the Virgin Mary's milk. Old herbals said it kept snakes away.

research.text: Trials in liver disease are mixed. A Cochrane review (2007) found no clear effect on deaths in alcohol-related or hepatitis B and C liver disease.

safety.summary: Usually well tolerated. It can cause allergy in people sensitive to daisy-family plants, loosen stools and lower blood sugar. It may affect drugs broken down by the liver enzyme CYP2C9.

entries.what: A tall purple thistle with white-veined leaves; its seeds are the best-known liver herb.

Cochrane Library systematic reviews
European Medicines Agency, Committee on Herbal Medicinal Products (HMPC) monographs
Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database

entries.name: Mineral waters and spa cures
entries.uses: People traditionally "take the waters" for joints, digestion and skin at spas from Bath and Baden to Karlovy Vary, Truskavets in Ukraine (whose Naftusya water is drunk for the kidneys) and the onsen (hot-spring baths) of Japan.

history.text: The Romans built baths at hot springs across their empire. In Soviet times trade unions sent millions of workers each year to kurorts (spa resorts).

research.text: European trials of spa therapy found modest relief for some kinds of arthritis and back pain, but most studies are small and hard to blind.

safety.summary: Hot baths put strain on the heart. Some waters are high in sodium or in laxative salts.

entries.what: Drinking and bathing in natural mineral and hot-spring waters at spa towns, often for weeks at a time.

sources.title: Cochrane Library systematic reviews

entries.name: Mistletoe (European)
entries.uses: In European folk medicine the leafy twigs were traditionally drunk as tea for high blood pressure and nervous complaints. In Germany, Switzerland and Austria injectable extracts are widely given alongside standard cancer care, mostly within anthroposophic medicine (a spiritual school of medicine founded in 1920s Switzerland).

history.text: A Roman writer of the 1st century CE described Druids cutting mistletoe from a sacred oak with a golden sickle and sacrificing two white bulls. In Norse myth the god Baldur is killed by a dart of mistletoe.

lore.text: Kissing under it at midwinter. Hung over doors against lightning and witches. Enemies who met beneath it in the forest were said to lay down their arms for the day.

research.text: Trials of the injected extracts in cancer are mixed. A careful Swedish trial in advanced pancreatic cancer (MISTRAL, 2024, 290 patients) found no gain in survival or quality of life, unlike an earlier open-label trial. Nothing supports the tea. The US National Cancer Institute's PDQ summary covers the trials.

safety.summary: Berries and leaves are poisonous if eaten, especially for children: vomiting, a slow heart and a drop in blood pressure. The injections are prescription medicines and often cause fever and skin reactions at the site. Mistletoe adds to blood-pressure and heart drugs. Avoid in pregnancy.
safety.pets: Toxic to pets (ASPCA).
safety.regulatory: Injectable mistletoe extracts are licensed medicines in Germany and Switzerland. In the US no mistletoe product is approved as a drug.

entries.cat: Kiss under it all you like. Eat it and I get the sofa.
entries.what: A half-parasitic evergreen with white berries that grows on tree branches; poisonous to eat.
entries.know: Birds plant it. The sticky seeds cling to their beaks or pass through them, and end up wiped or dropped onto branches.

entries.name: Miswak
entries.uses: People traditionally chew the end of a twig until it frays into bristles, then brush teeth and gums with it, cutting a fresh end each day. In Islam it is a sunnah, a practice of the Prophet: a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim says he would have ordered it before every prayer had it not been a burden. A 1987 WHO consensus report encouraged chewing sticks for oral hygiene.

research.text: Several trials found it removed plaque about as well as a toothbrush, some better. Most were small.

safety.summary: Safe for most people. Brushing too hard can wear the gums.

entries.what: A chewing-stick toothbrush cut from the arak tree, used across the Muslim world.
entries.know: Hadith tell that in the Prophet's last hours, Aisha softened a miswak with her teeth and he used it.

sources.title: Ibn Qayyim al-Jawziyya, Medicine of the Prophet (al-Tibb al-Nabawi, 14th c.)
WHO monographs on selected medicinal plants (vols 1-4)
https://sunnah.com/bukhari:887

entries.name: MK-677 (ibutamoren)
parts: oral growth-hormone secretagogue (not strictly a peptide; sold alongside them)
entries.uses: Sold online as a "research chemical" and taken by mouth for muscle, sleep and recovery.

research.text: Taken daily, it raises growth hormone and IGF-1 for months. A trial in older adults after hip fracture was stopped early after more cases of heart failure on the drug.

safety.summary: Big appetite, water retention, raised blood sugar and insulin resistance, and a heart-failure signal in older people. The quality of online products is unknown.
safety.regulatory: As of November 2026: not approved anywhere. Still on FDA's Category 2 safety-risk list (as ibutamoren mesylate) for both kinds of compounding pharmacy, per FDA's April 2026 page. Prohibited by WADA (S2).

entries.what: A drug taken by mouth that makes the body release growth hormone, sold alongside peptides though it isn't one.
entries.know: The "MK" is the code prefix of the drug company that made it in the 1990s.

sources.title: World Anti-Doping Agency Prohibited List (S0 non-approved substances; S2 peptide hormones)
https://www.fda.gov/drugs/human-drug-compounding/certain-bulk-drug-substances-use-compounding-may-present-significant-safety-risks

entries.name: Molybdenum
entries.uses: Included in multivitamins.

history.text: The only known natural deficiency cases come from rare genetic disorders and long-term drip feeding.

research.text: No evidence extra molybdenum does anything for people who eat normally.

safety.summary: Very high intakes may raise uric acid (gout) and lower copper.

entries.what: A trace mineral a few enzymes need to break down sulfites and purines; legumes are rich in it.

nutrient.low: Almost never seen in people who eat normally.
nutrient.limit: US 2,000 mcg a day; EU 600 mcg a day.

sources.title: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements, vitamin and mineral fact sheets (health professional versions)
National Academies (IOM), Dietary Reference Intakes: tolerable upper intake levels
EFSA, overview of tolerable upper intake levels (2024 update)

entries.name: Moringa
entries.uses: In India, Africa and the Philippines people cook the leaves as a green and the pods in curries. New mothers eat the leaves for milk and strength.

history.text: Ancient Egyptians used ben oil, pressed from moringa seeds, in perfume. Today aid groups plant the tree against malnutrition.

research.text: The leaves are rich in nutrients. Small studies have looked at blood sugar and breast milk.

safety.summary: The root and bark are toxic, and have been used to cause abortion. The leaves are eaten as food.

entries.what: A fast-growing tropical tree with feathery leaves and long "drumstick" pods, eaten as a vegetable in India and Africa.
entries.know: Crushed moringa seeds make mud sink out of river water, and village women in Sudan have long cleared drinking water this way.

sources.title: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database
PROTA4U, Plant Resources of Tropical Africa

entries.name: Moroccan mint tea
parts: Chinese gunpowder green tea, spearmint, sugar; wormwood (sheba) in winter
preps: poured from height into glasses, three times
entries.uses: Served to every guest across Morocco, Algeria and the Sahara, traditionally after meals to settle the stomach. It is poured from high above the glass to raise a foam, and a guest is offered three glasses.

history.text: The usual story is that British merchants, shut out of Baltic ports during the Crimean War (1850s), sold their Chinese green tea in Moroccan ports instead.

lore.text: A Maghrebi saying: "The first glass is gentle as life, the second strong as love, the third bitter as death."

research.text: Studied as food, not as medicine.

safety.summary: Sugar and caffeine. Keep the winter versions with wormwood (sheba) occasional, as wormwood contains thujone, which is toxic in large amounts.

entries.what: Green tea brewed with fresh spearmint and plenty of sugar, poured from a height across North Africa.
entries.know: People in the Maghreb jokingly call it "Berber whisky".

sources.title: James A. Duke, Handbook of Medicinal Herbs (2nd ed., 2002) and Dr. Duke's Phytochemical and Ethnobotanical Databases

entries.name: Motherwort
entries.uses: Traditionally taken for a nervous, racing heart and anxiety; the EMA lists traditional use for mild stress and nervous heart complaints. In Russia pustyrnik tincture and tablets are an everyday pharmacy sedative. In Chinese medicine yi mu cao, a related species, is a women's herb for the menstrual cycle and the weeks after birth.

history.text: Leonurus cardiaca means roughly "lion's tail, for the heart". Russian pharmacies sell it next to valerian.

research.text: Small Russian and Chinese studies on anxiety and blood pressure.

safety.summary: It stimulates the womb, so avoid in pregnancy. It may add to sedatives, heart drugs and blood thinners.

entries.what: A tall, square-stemmed mint-family herb with prickly flower whorls, long taken for a racing heart.

sources.title: European Medicines Agency, Committee on Herbal Medicinal Products (HMPC) monographs
Bensky, Clavey & Stöger, Chinese Herbal Medicine: Materia Medica, 3rd ed. (2004)
Sokolov & Zamotaev, Handbook of Medicinal Plants (USSR, 1984/1990)

entries.name: Mountain tea (ironwort)
entries.latin: Sideritis scardica, S. raeseri, S. syriaca
entries.uses: Traditionally drunk across the Balkan mountains for colds, coughs and upset stomachs. EMA lists traditional uses for a cough with a cold and for mild indigestion.

lore.text: The name Sideritis comes from sideros, Greek for iron. The plant was said to heal wounds made by iron weapons.

research.text: A few small studies in older adults have looked at memory and attention.

safety.summary: Mild.
safety.regulatory: Sideritis scardica is listed as critically endangered in Bulgaria's Red Book, and picking it from the wild is banned there, for personal use too (ministry orders of 2025 and 2026). Most mountain tea on sale is cultivated.

entries.what: Greek and Balkan mountain tea: the dried flowering stems of a woolly, sage-like herb.

sources.title: European Medicines Agency, Committee on Herbal Medicinal Products (HMPC) monographs
https://www.moew.government.bg/en/the-collection-of-herbs-for-commercial-purposes-from-24-species-of-medicinal-plants-from-their-natural-habitats-is-prohibited

entries.name: Moxibustion
entries.uses: Fluffy dried mugwort (moxa) is burned on or above acupuncture points to warm the channels. Traditionally used for "cold" and weak conditions, aching joints and period pain. Moxa held near the point at the outer corner of the little toenail (BL67) is used late in pregnancy to turn babies lying bottom-first (breech).

history.text: Moxa appears in the earliest Chinese medical texts. The English word comes from the Japanese mogusa, mugwort.

research.text: A Cochrane review found moxibustion may lower the number of babies still breech at birth, but the evidence is of low quality.

safety.summary: Burns, blisters and scars; some direct Japanese methods leave small scars on purpose. The smoke irritates the lungs and can set off asthma. Smouldering moxa is a fire risk.

entries.what: Burning dried mugwort on or near points of the body to warm them, from Chinese, Japanese and Korean medicine.
entries.know: The 1689 Japanese travel diary Narrow Road to the Deep North opens with the poet burning moxa on the point below his knee before setting off on foot.

sources.title: Cochrane Library systematic reviews

entries.name: Mugwort
entries.uses: Traditionally taken as a bitter for digestion and to bring on and warm the menstrual cycle. In Chinese and Japanese medicine the dried leaf fluff is burned as moxa, held over points on the skin. In many places it is a dream herb, slept on in pillows.

history.text: The Anglo-Saxon Nine Herbs Charm (10th century) calls it the oldest of herbs. Roman soldiers are said to have put it in their sandals against tiredness. In Korea and Japan young leaves go into green rice cakes and soups.

lore.text: On St John's Eve (Midsummer) people wore mugwort belts and threw them into the fire to burn away bad luck. Dream pillows for vivid and prophetic dreams. Washes for scrying mirrors.

research.text: Little clinical work. Trials of moxa for turning breech babies are small and of low quality.

safety.summary: It stimulates the womb, so avoid in pregnancy. Its pollen is a major hay fever trigger, and people allergic to daisy-family plants may react. It contains some thujone, which is toxic in large amounts.

entries.what: A common silvery-leaved roadside herb used for digestion, periods, dream pillows and moxa.
entries.know: In Korea's founding myth a bear became a woman by living in a cave on mugwort and garlic, and gave birth to Dangun, the first king.

sources.title: Bensky, Clavey & Stöger, Chinese Herbal Medicine: Materia Medica, 3rd ed. (2004)
Maud Grieve, A Modern Herbal (1931)

entries.name: Mullein
entries.uses: Traditionally drunk as a leaf or flower tea for coughs and chest complaints; the EMA lists traditional use of the flowers for coughs with colds. Flowers steeped in oil were a folk ear remedy.

history.text: The dried stalks were dipped in tallow and burned as torches, which gave the name "hag's taper".

lore.text: Some old writers said the moly that protected Odysseus from Circe's magic was mullein. A herb of protection and of light in the dark.

research.text: Little clinical work.

safety.summary: Strain the tea through fine cloth, because the tiny leaf hairs irritate the throat. Never put anything into an ear with a burst eardrum or discharge. The seeds are toxic and were used as a fish poison.

entries.what: A tall roadside plant with soft, woolly leaves and a spike of yellow flowers.
entries.know: Mullein seeds can wait for decades in the soil. In a Michigan experiment begun in 1879, seeds of moth mullein, a close cousin, still sprouted in 2000.

entries.name: Muña
entries.uses: Traditionally drunk in the Andes for wind, indigestion and the breathlessness of high altitude. Farmers layer the branches with stored potatoes to keep insects away.

research.text: Lab studies of its essential oil, which kills some insects and microbes.

safety.summary: Its oil contains pulegone, a liver toxin also found in pennyroyal. Avoid in pregnancy.

entries.what: A minty Andean shrub brewed as tea in Peru and Bolivia, and packed in with stored potatoes.

sources.title: James A. Duke, Handbook of Medicinal Herbs (2nd ed., 2002) and Dr. Duke's Phytochemical and Ethnobotanical Databases

entries.name: Mustard
entries.latin: Brassica nigra, Sinapis alba, B. juncea
entries.uses: For coughs and colds, people lay a mustard plaster on the chest or back for a few minutes until the skin goes red. At the first chill, feet go into a hot bath with mustard powder. In India babies and adults are massaged with warm mustard oil.

history.text: Ancient Greek writers recommended mustard for scorpion stings. Pharmacies sold mustard plasters through the 20th century, and Soviet homes kept a packet of gorchichniki in every medicine cabinet.

lore.text: In the Gospels, faith as small as a mustard seed can move mountains, and the kingdom of heaven grows from a mustard seed into a tree where birds nest.

research.text: Little modern research.

safety.summary: Plasters burn and blister if left on too long; not for children or sensitive skin. Mustard is a common food allergy and must be labelled in EU foods. In the US pressed mustard oil is sold for external use only because of its erucic acid.

entries.what: Tiny seeds of cabbage-family plants that turn fiery when crushed and wetted; the base of table mustard.

sources.title: Maud Grieve, A Modern Herbal (1931)
Sokolov & Zamotaev, Handbook of Medicinal Plants (USSR, 1984/1990)

entries.name: Myrrh
entries.uses: In Europe myrrh tincture is dabbed on mouth ulcers and sore gums, a traditional use recognised by the European Medicines Agency. In Chinese medicine mo yao is said to move the blood (get stuck blood flowing) and ease pain.

history.text: Ancient Egyptians used it in embalming and in kyphi, a temple incense of many ingredients.

lore.text: In Greek myth Myrrha was turned into a tree, her tears became the resin, and Adonis was born from its trunk. In Christian tradition the Magi's bitter myrrh foretold Christ's death and burial.

research.text: A few small studies in the mouth and gums.

safety.summary: Traditionally said to stimulate the womb, so it is avoided in pregnancy. It may lower blood sugar, and a stronger warfarin effect has been reported.

entries.what: A reddish-brown, bitter tree resin from Arabia and Somalia, used in incense and in remedies for the mouth.

sources.title: European Medicines Agency, Committee on Herbal Medicinal Products (HMPC) monographs
Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database

entries.name: Natrum muriaticum
entries.uses: In homeopathy, its remedy picture (the type it is matched to) is the reserved person who keeps old grief inside and dislikes being consoled, with cold sores, hammering headaches from the sun and a craving for salt. Also sold as tissue salt No. 9.

research.text: No good trials show a reliable effect beyond placebo.

safety.summary: At usual potencies there is no measurable salt in the pills.

entries.what: Table salt diluted into a homeopathic remedy for held-in grief, cold sores and headaches from the sun.

sources.title: Australian NHMRC, Information Paper: evidence on the effectiveness of homeopathy (2015)

entries.name: Neem
entries.uses: In India people chew neem twigs (datun) to clean their teeth, put leaf paste on rashes and sores, and add the leaves to bathwater. Dried leaves go into grain stores and between folded clothes against insects. Neem oil is rubbed into skin and hair, including against lice. In Ayurveda it is a bitter "blood cleanser" for the skin.

history.text: Long called the "village pharmacy" of India. Azadirachtin, a compound from the seeds, is now one of the main plant-based insecticides in farming.

lore.text: At Ugadi, the south Indian new year, people eat neem flowers with jaggery: the bitter and the sweet of the year ahead. On Gudi Padwa in Maharashtra a neem sprig is tied to the gudi flag raised outside homes. Neem is the tree of Shitala, goddess of poxes and fevers, and neem leaves are hung in a sickroom for her.

research.text: Small trials of neem dental gels; lab studies on germs.

safety.summary: Neem oil swallowed has caused severe poisoning and deaths in babies and small children, so it is never given to children by mouth. Neem is a traditional contraceptive, so it is avoided when trying to conceive and in pregnancy.
safety.pets: Concentrated neem oil irritates pets.

entries.what: A fast-growing Indian shade tree with bitter leaves; its twigs are chewed as toothbrushes and its seed oil repels insects.
entries.know: In 2000 Europe's patent office revoked a patent on a neem-oil fungicide after Indian campaigners showed farmers had used neem that way for centuries.

sources.title: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database
Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India

entries.name: Neroli and orange blossom
preps: orange flower water in sweets and coffee (white coffee, Lebanon)
entries.uses: In the Levant and North Africa orange blossom water is traditionally added to pastries, sweets and coffee. Stirred into hot water as "white coffee", it is drunk to settle the stomach and calm down before bed. Neroli oil is used in aromatherapy for anxiety.

history.text: The name is said to come from a princess of Nerola, a town near Rome, who scented her gloves and bath with it in the late 1600s.

lore.text: Brides wore orange blossom crowns for purity and fertility, a fashion that spread through Europe after a royal wedding in 1840.

research.text: A few small studies.

safety.summary: Neroli oil is not phototoxic, but oil pressed from bitter orange peel is. Bitter orange peel extract (synephrine) in weight-loss pills raises heart rate and blood pressure, more so with other stimulants.

entries.what: The oil and the scented water made from the white flowers of the bitter orange tree.
entries.know: Lebanese "white coffee" has no coffee in it: it is hot water with a splash of orange blossom water.

sources.title: Tisserand & Young, Essential Oil Safety, 2nd ed. (2014)
NIH National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health, Herbs at a Glance

entries.name: Neti and nasya
preps: salt water poured through one nostril and out the other
entries.uses: In yoga, jala neti is a cleansing practice: salt water goes in one nostril and out the other. In Ayurveda, nasya oils such as anu taila are dropped into the nose in the morning, traditionally for the head, the sinuses and a clear mind.

research.text: Reviews found salt-water rinsing eased symptoms of long-term sinusitis and hay fever, though many of the trials were small.

safety.summary: Use only sterile, distilled, or boiled-and-cooled water. Tap water in the nose has caused fatal brain infections with the amoeba Naegleria fowleri. Wash and dry the pot after each use.

entries.what: Rinsing the nose with salt water from a small pot (neti), or putting oil drops in the nose (nasya).

sources.title: Cochrane Library systematic reviews
US FDA, dietary supplement warnings and safety information

entries.name: Nettle
entries.uses: The leaf is traditionally drunk as a nourishing spring tonic, to flush the urinary tract and for aching joints, all EMA traditional uses. The root is taken for the urinary trouble of an enlarged prostate. In Slavic lands nettle shchi (soup) is spring food, and sore joints were whipped with fresh nettles ("urtication").

history.text: Legend says Roman soldiers in Britain rubbed themselves with nettles to keep warm. Nettle fibre was spun and woven into cloth for centuries. In Ukraine young nettles go into green borscht.

lore.text: In Andersen's tale The Wild Swans a sister knits nettle shirts in silence to free her eleven brothers, who have been turned into swans. Nettle guards against lightning and evil.

research.text: Root extract has modest trial support for prostate urinary symptoms. For joint pain the leaf has only a few small studies.

safety.summary: Nettle makes you pass more water, so take care with water pills, lithium and blood-pressure drugs. It is rich in vitamin K, which can weaken warfarin. It may lower blood sugar. The fresh plant stings; cook or dry it before eating.
contra: oedema from heart or kidney failure

entries.what: The stinging weed of every hedge and garden, eaten as spring greens and drunk as tea.
entries.know: In World War I Germany made army cloth from nettle fibre when cotton ran short.

entries.name: Nilavembu kudineer
parts: nine herbs including andrographis, vetiver, ginger, black pepper, sandalwood
entries.uses: In Tamil Siddha medicine the herbs are boiled and the drink taken for fevers. The Tamil Nadu government handed it out free during dengue and chikungunya outbreaks.

research.text: Lab work and small observational studies.

safety.summary: Dengue warning signs (bleeding, severe belly pain, vomiting that will not stop) are an emergency.

entries.what: A bitter nine-herb fever drink from Siddha, the old healing system of Tamil South India.

sources.title: Government of India, Ministry of AYUSH

entries.name: Noni
entries.uses: Across Polynesia healers lay crushed or warmed leaves on wounds, swellings and sore joints, and use the fruit for many kinds of illness. It was one of the "canoe plants" that voyagers carried from island to island. Since the 1990s the fermented juice has been sold around the world as a wellness drink.

research.text: Mostly lab and animal studies. A few small human trials, for example in smokers, have looked at the juice and blood fats. There are no large trials.

safety.summary: Several cases of liver injury have been reported after drinking noni juice. The juice is very high in potassium, which is dangerous with kidney disease or with drugs that raise potassium. One case report linked it to warfarin no longer working properly. Avoid in pregnancy.

entries.what: A lumpy, pale fruit from a small Pacific and Southeast Asian tree, known for its strong cheesy smell.
entries.know: In 2003 the European Union approved noni juice as a "novel food", one of the first foods passed under those rules.

entries.name: Nopal (prickly pear)
entries.uses: In Mexico people eat the pads (nopalitos) for blood sugar and digestion, and split pads open as poultices on burns and wounds. The fruit (tuna) is eaten after a night of drinking.

history.text: Mexica (Aztec) legend says Tenochtitlan was founded where an eagle stood on a nopal cactus. The scene is on Mexico's flag.

research.text: Small trials found lower blood sugar after meals. One small trial of a fruit extract found milder hangovers.

safety.summary: As food it is safe for most people. It may add to diabetes medicines. The fine hair-like spines (glochids) lodge in skin.

entries.what: The flat green pads of the prickly pear cactus, cooked as a vegetable all over Mexico.
entries.know: Cochineal insects that live on nopal pads are crushed to make carmine, a red dye still used in food and lipstick.

entries.name: Notoginseng
entries.uses: In Chinese medicine san qi is prized because it both stops bleeding and gets stuck blood moving again. It is traditionally used for cuts, bruises and sports injuries, sprinkled on wounds or swallowed as powder. It is the main ingredient of Yunnan Baiyao, which Viet Cong soldiers are said to have carried in the Vietnam War.

lore.text: "Three-seven" is said to come from the plant's three stems of seven leaflets, or from the three to seven years it grows before harvest.

research.text: Small studies on bleeding and circulation.

safety.summary: It interacts with warfarin and antiplatelet drugs. It is avoided in pregnancy.

entries.what: A small knobbly root, a cousin of ginseng, best known as the main ingredient in Yunnan Baiyao powder.
entries.know: The full recipe of Yunnan Baiyao is classed as a Chinese state secret.

entries.name: Nutmeg and mace
entries.uses: In Ayurveda a pinch grated into warm milk at bedtime is used for sleep and for loose stools. Many cuisines add it to rich dishes to settle digestion.

history.text: Nutmeg grew only on the tiny Banda Islands of Indonesia. In 1621 the Dutch killed or enslaved most of the islanders to control it. At the 1667 Treaty of Breda the Dutch kept the nutmeg island of Run, and the English kept Manhattan.

lore.text: Carried in the pocket as a charm for luck, and to keep off rheumatism and boils.

research.text: Myristicin, one of its oils, acts on the mind in large amounts and is toxic.

safety.summary: About 5 grams (one to two teaspoons) or more can cause poisoning: hallucinations, a racing heart, nausea and days of feeling ill. Teenagers have ended up in hospital after trying it as a drug. Keep to food pinches.
safety.pets: Toxic to dogs and cats.

entries.what: Two spices from one tropical fruit: nutmeg is the seed, mace the red lace wrapped around it.
entries.know: Connecticut is "the Nutmeg State", after a story that its peddlers sold carved wooden nutmegs to the unwary.

entries.name: Nux vomica
parts: seeds of the strychnine tree, diluted
entries.uses: In homeopathy, its remedy picture (the type it is matched to) is the irritable, driven, overworked person, chilly and impatient. It is given for hangovers, overeating, heartburn and constipation with urging. In Ayurveda the seed, kuchala, is used in tiny amounts after shodhana (a long purification by soaking and boiling); Chinese medicine also uses the processed seed, ma qian zi.

research.text: No good trials show a reliable effect beyond placebo.

safety.summary: The raw seed contains strychnine and can kill. Low potencies and badly purified Ayurvedic preparations have caused poisoning. Avoided in pregnancy.

entries.what: The homeopathic form of the poison nut, the seed of the strychnine tree, famous as the hangover remedy.
entries.know: Strychnine from these seeds was sold as rat poison and, in tiny doses, as a 19th-century "tonic".

entries.name: Oats (milky oat and oat straw)
entries.uses: Traditionally the milky green tops are made into a tincture for frayed nerves and exhaustion, and oat straw tea and oat baths are used for itchy skin. The EMA lists traditional use of the green oat plant for mild stress and to aid sleep. Oatmeal is eaten for the heart.

history.text: Colloidal oatmeal (oats ground very fine) is an approved skin protectant in the US. In Russia oat kvass and oat decoction were folk drinks for weakness.

research.text: Beta-glucan, the soluble fibre in oats, lowers LDL cholesterol; this is an authorised health claim in the US and EU. The nerve-calming uses have hardly been studied.

safety.summary: Gentle. Oats are often mixed with wheat in fields and mills, and a few people with coeliac disease also react to oat protein (avenin).

entries.what: The everyday cereal plant; herbalists also use the green "milky" seeds and the straw.
entries.know: In 1997 oats won the first food-specific health claim the US FDA ever allowed, for their soluble fibre and cholesterol.

entries.name: Oil pulling
preps: swished in the mouth for minutes, spat out (not swallowed)
entries.uses: In Ayurveda done each morning for the teeth, gums, breath and jaw. The old texts describe two kinds: gandusha, holding the mouth full of oil without moving it, and kavala, swishing a smaller amount around. Sesame oil is the classic choice; coconut oil is popular now.

research.text: Small trials found modest drops in plaque and gum inflammation. Nobody has tested it as a replacement for brushing.

safety.summary: Spit it in the bin, as oil clogs drains. Don't swallow it: oil breathed into the lungs can cause lipoid pneumonia, a serious lung inflammation. Young children can choke on it or inhale it.

entries.what: Swishing a spoonful of oil around the mouth for a few minutes, then spitting it out; from Ayurveda.

sources.title: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India

entries.name: Oleander
entries.uses: Historically used in tiny amounts on the skin in Ayurveda, where it is called karavira, and in Arab medicine for skin complaints. In 2020 an oleander extract (oleandrin) was promoted online for COVID-19 with no evidence behind it.

research.text: Its heart poison, oleandrin, acts much like foxglove's. Yellow oleander, a different plant, is a leading cause of self-poisoning in Sri Lanka and southern India.

safety.summary: Deadly. Every part is poisonous, fresh or dried. Burning the cuttings is warned against, because the smoke is thought to be poisonous too, and honey from its flowers is said to be. Poisoning brings vomiting, a slow or chaotic heartbeat and death, and is an emergency. History and lore only.
safety.pets: Deadly to pets and livestock.

entries.what: A tough evergreen shrub with pink, white or red flowers, planted in warm countries and poisonous in every part.

sources.title: ASPCA Animal Poison Control, toxic and non-toxic plants
US FDA, dietary supplement warnings and safety information

entries.name: Olive leaf
entries.uses: Around the Mediterranean the leaf is traditionally brewed for fevers and high blood pressure. The EMA lists traditional use of the leaf to pass more water in mild fluid retention. The oil is food, medicine and holy anointing oil.

history.text: Wreaths of wild olive crowned winners at the ancient Olympic Games. The oil was the base of Greek and Roman medicine. It is holy oil in Judaism, Christianity and Islam; the Qur'an (24:35) calls the olive "a blessed tree".

lore.text: Athena's gift that won her the city of Athens. The dove brought Noah an olive leaf after the flood. A sign of peace.

research.text: Small trials found leaf extract lowered blood pressure a little. Extra-virgin olive oil was part of the Mediterranean diet tested in PREDIMED, a large Spanish trial that found fewer heart attacks, strokes and heart deaths combined.

safety.summary: It may add to blood-pressure and diabetes drugs. As a water-passing herb it is not for people who must limit fluids, such as those with severe heart or kidney disease.

entries.what: Leaves of the olive tree, brewed as tea or sold as an extract; the same tree gives olive oil.
entries.know: Some olive trees still bearing fruit, such as one at Vouves on Crete, are thought to be over 2,000 years old.

sources.title: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database

entries.name: Omega-3 fats (fish oil)
entries.uses: Taken by millions for the heart, joints, brain and eyes; a spoon of cod liver oil was a northern European childhood ritual.

history.text: Studies of Greenland Inuit in the 1970s, eating seal and whale with few heart attacks, set off the fish-oil boom.

research.text: Fish oil lowers triglycerides (established). Big trials (VITAL, ASCEND) found ordinary doses didn't prevent heart attacks in most people; a high-dose prescription form cut heart events in one trial. Mixed for mood and joints.

safety.summary: High doses slightly raise the risk of an irregular heartbeat (atrial fibrillation) and may add to blood thinners. Fishy burps; cod liver oil also carries vitamin A.

entries.what: Long-chain fats (EPA and DHA) found in oily fish, part of every cell wall in your brain and eyes.

nutrient.low: No clear signs; diets with no fish are low in EPA and DHA.
nutrient.limit: No formal upper limit (US or EU). EPA plus DHA from supplements: the FDA and EFSA both found up to 5 g a day raised no safety concerns.

sources.title: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements, vitamin and mineral fact sheets (health professional versions)

entries.name: Opium poppy
entries.uses: Historically used for pain, sleep, coughs and diarrhoea in almost every old pharmacopoeia (official book of medicines), from Egypt and Greece to Persia, India and China. The seeds are a common food on bread and in cakes. Morphine and codeine, made from the sap, are standard medicines.

history.text: Poppy seeds turn up at Neolithic sites in Europe from around 5500 BCE. A long-repeated story says Sumerian tablets called it hul gil, the "joy plant", though scholars dispute that reading. Britain fought China in the Opium Wars (1839 to 1842 and 1856 to 1860) to keep the opium trade open. Morphine was first isolated in Germany around 1804.

lore.text: In Greek myth Hypnos (Sleep) and Morpheus (god of dreams) are crowned with poppies, and Demeter is said to have eaten them to forget her grief for Persephone. The red poppy worn for the war dead is a cousin, the field poppy.

research.text: Morphine and codeine are on the WHO list of essential medicines.

safety.summary: Deadly. Poppy tea and drinks made from unwashed seeds have caused fatal overdoses, because the morphine content swings wildly from batch to batch. Opium and its drugs are addictive, and an overdose stops breathing; it is an emergency. Eating poppy seed cakes can cause a positive drug test.
safety.regulatory: Opium, morphine and heroin are controlled worldwide under the 1961 UN Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs. The seeds are sold as food. Growing the plant is legal in some countries and licensed or banned in others.

entries.what: The poppy whose dried milky sap is opium, the source of morphine, codeine and heroin.
entries.know: The word "opium" comes from the ancient Greek opion, "poppy juice".

sources.title: WHO monographs on selected medicinal plants (vols 1-4)
Schultes & Hofmann, Plants of the Gods (1979/2001)

entries.name: Oregano oil
entries.latin: Origanum vulgare, O. onites (oil of oregano)
entries.uses: In Greek and Slavic homes the herb is traditionally brewed as a tea for coughs and colds. The oil is sold and discussed in modern natural health as a strong "natural antibiotic". People take it for colds and gut infections, and dab it, diluted, on fungal nails and skin.

history.text: Ancient Greeks gave oregano for poisonings and convulsions. The name is often read as "joy of the mountain", from oros (mountain) and ganos (joy). Oil of oregano became a big seller in North America in the 1990s.

lore.text: Aphrodite was said to have grown it. Greek and Roman couples wore crowns of oregano at weddings, and it was planted on graves so the dead would rest happily.

research.text: Its main compounds, carvacrol and thymol, kill bacteria and fungi in the lab. Human trials are very few and small: one uncontrolled study in 2000 gave capsules to 14 adults with gut parasites.

safety.summary: A strong irritant to skin and to mucous membranes, the moist lining of the mouth, nose and gut. Always diluted, never neat in the mouth or on skin. Swallowed oil can burn the throat and upset the stomach. It may lower blood sugar and slow iron absorption. People allergic to mint-family plants can react. It is no substitute for antibiotics when they are needed. Not for children; avoid in pregnancy.
safety.pets: Toxic to cats, which cannot break down its phenols, and listed as toxic to dogs.

entries.cat: Burns like your ex and clears the room like you. Dilute it.
entries.what: A fiery oil distilled from wild oregano leaves, sold today as a "natural antibiotic".

entries.name: Oscillococcinum
aka: Anas barbariae hepatis et cordis extractum 200CK
parts: Muscovy duck liver and heart, diluted 200 times at 1:100
entries.uses: In homeopathy, a tube of pellets is taken at the first signs of flu. One of the best-selling remedies in France, sold in many countries.

history.text: During the 1917 flu epidemic a French army physician reported seeing "oscillating" microbes in the blood of the sick, and later said he found them in duck liver. He coined the name in 1925. It is made at 200K: diluted 1:100 two hundred times by the Korsakov method, where one vial is emptied and refilled at each step.

research.text: A Cochrane review (2015) found no evidence that it stops flu, and too little good evidence to say whether it shortens it.

safety.summary: The pellets are sugar and lactose. Not a substitute for antiviral drugs in people at high risk from flu (babies, older people, pregnancy, long-term illness).

entries.what: A best-selling French flu remedy made from duck liver and heart, diluted far beyond any molecule.

sources.title: Cochrane Library systematic reviews
Australian NHMRC, Information Paper: evidence on the effectiveness of homeopathy (2015)

entries.name: Osha
entries.uses: Across the Rocky Mountains and the Southwest, Native and Hispano healers chew the root or make a tincture for coughs, colds and sore throats. It is also burned, and carried for protection.

history.text: Apache and Diné (Navajo) people use it in ceremony.

lore.text: Rattlesnakes are said to keep away from anyone carrying it. It is the bear's medicine, found and shown by the bear.

research.text: Lab studies only.

safety.summary: It looks very like poison hemlock and water hemlock, both deadly, so wild-dug root is easily mixed up with them.
safety.ethics: Nobody has yet grown it reliably on farms, and wild stands are shrinking. United Plant Savers lists it as at-risk.

entries.what: A wild mountain root of the Rockies, spicy and celery-scented, chewed for coughs and burned for protection.
entries.know: Bears have been seen chewing osha root and rubbing the paste into their fur.

sources.title: United Plant Savers, Species At-Risk list
Daniel Moerman, Native American Ethnobotany (1998) and the BRIT Native American Ethnobotany database

entries.name: Padma 28 (Tibetan formula)
parts: about 20 herbs including iceland moss, neem, myrobalan, cardamom, red sandalwood, costus, calcium sulphate
entries.uses: A classical formula of Sowa Rigpa, Tibetan medicine ("the science of healing"). It has been made in Switzerland since 1969 and is sold there for poor circulation in the legs and for inflammation.

history.text: It reached Europe through a Buryat family of Tibetan-medicine physicians who practised in St Petersburg. Switzerland registered it as a medicine in 1977.

research.text: Small trials in people whose legs cramp when they walk (intermittent claudication) found they could walk further.

safety.summary: Usually mild; stomach upset has been reported.

entries.what: A Tibetan herbal tablet made in Switzerland, sold for circulation in the legs.
entries.know: Padma is the Sanskrit word for lotus.

entries.name: Palo santo
entries.uses: In Peru and Ecuador people burn the sticks to clear a space of bad energy and to keep mosquitoes away, and curanderos (traditional healers) use it in ceremonies.

lore.text: Only wood from trees that died naturally and lay on the ground for years is said to carry the scent and the spirit.

research.text: Hardly studied.

safety.summary: The smoke irritates the lungs.
safety.pets: Smoke harms cats and birds.
safety.ethics: The IUCN rates Bursera graveolens as Least Concern, though Peru listed it as endangered in 2006 before removing it in 2014. A different tree also sold as palo santo, Bulnesia sarmientoi of the Gran Chaco, is CITES-listed. Buy wood from naturally fallen trees, ideally from community projects.

entries.what: A fragrant wood from the dry forests of Ecuador and Peru, burned as sticks to cleanse a room.
entries.know: Palo santo is a cousin of frankincense and myrrh: all three come from the same plant family, Burseraceae.

IUCN Red List of Threatened Species

entries.name: Panchakarma
parts: oiling, sweating, then vomiting (vamana), purging (virechana), enemas (basti), nasal medicine (nasya), bloodletting (raktamokshana)
preps: residential programme over days to weeks
entries.uses: In Ayurveda this is the classical cleanse of the doshas (the three body energies: vata, pitta and kapha). First come days of preparation: drinking ghee or oil, oil massage and sweating. Then come the five actions: vomiting (vamana), purging (virechana), enemas (basti), medicine through the nose (nasya) and, in some schools, bloodletting (raktamokshana). It is traditionally done at the change of seasons.

research.text: Mostly small studies, many without a comparison group.

safety.summary: Purging and vomiting can cause dehydration and a dangerous salt imbalance. Cautioned for frail people, in pregnancy, with heart disease and with eating disorders. Drinking large amounts of ghee is a heavy load of fat. Tests of Ayurvedic medicines bought in the US found lead, mercury or arsenic in about one in five.

entries.what: Ayurveda's deep cleanse: days of oiling and sweating, then purging, usually done in a residential clinic.

entries.name: Parsley
entries.uses: In Europe people drink parsley leaf or root tea to pass more water when they feel puffy, and to flush the urinary tract. The EU's medicines agency (EMA) accepts this as a traditional use. People also chew a sprig after a meal to freshen the breath.

history.text: In ancient Greece, winners at the Isthmian and Nemean games wore crowns of selinon, a word that covered both parsley and wild celery. The same plant was laid on graves, and "to need parsley" meant to be close to death.

lore.text: An old English saying goes that parsley "goes to the devil nine times" before it comes up, because the seed is so slow to sprout. Some said only a wicked person, or a pregnant woman, could grow it well.

research.text: In rats it made them pass more urine. There is very little work in people.

safety.summary: Kitchen amounts are fine. The seed and its oil contain apiol, which is poisonous in medicinal doses. It was once taken to end pregnancies, and women died from it. Not for anyone with inflamed kidneys. Parsley is rich in vitamin K, so big changes in how much you eat can upset warfarin. It may also add to diuretics and lithium.

entries.what: The bright green kitchen herb. Its leaf and root are also brewed as a tea in European folk medicine.

sources.title: European Medicines Agency, Committee on Herbal Medicinal Products (HMPC) monographs

entries.name: Passionflower
entries.uses: Cherokee and Houma peoples used the plant as medicine, and across Latin America people drink it as a calming tea for nerves and sleep. The EMA accepts it as a traditional use for mild stress and to aid sleep.

history.text: In the early 1600s Spanish missionaries read the flower as the Passion of Christ. The frilly corona was the crown of thorns, the five stamens the five wounds, the three styles the nails.

research.text: Small trials, some in people waiting for surgery, found modest drops in anxiety.

safety.summary: It can make you drowsy and may add to the effect of sedatives and alcohol.

entries.what: A climbing vine with a strange, frilled purple flower, drunk as a calming tea before bed.
entries.know: The name maypop is said to come from the hollow fruits popping when someone steps on them.

sources.title: NIH National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health, Herbs at a Glance

entries.name: Patchouli
entries.uses: In Chinese medicine huo xiang is used to "transform damp", which in that system means clearing a heavy, sticky state behind nausea and sluggish digestion. It is given for summer stomach upsets with nausea and diarrhoea, and leads the formula Huo Xiang Zheng Qi San.

history.text: In the 1800s traders packed Indian shawls with dried patchouli leaves to keep moths away, and Europeans came to expect the smell on a real Kashmir shawl. It became the signature scent of the 1960s counterculture.

lore.text: In hoodoo, the African American folk magic tradition, patchouli draws money and earthy love.

research.text: Lab studies only.

safety.summary: Mild. Use caution in pregnancy.

entries.what: A bushy mint-family herb whose leaves give a dark, earthy oil, used in Chinese medicine and in perfume.

sources.title: Bensky, Clavey & Stöger, Chinese Herbal Medicine: Materia Medica, 3rd ed. (2004)

entries.name: Pau d'arco
entries.uses: In Brazil, Paraguay and Argentina people boil the inner bark for fevers, infections and skin complaints. Abroad it is sold for candida (yeast) infections.

history.text: The hard wood was used for bows: pau d'arco is Portuguese for "bow stick".

research.text: Lapachol, from the wood, was tested as a cancer drug by the US National Cancer Institute in the 1970s. It was dropped because the doses needed caused bleeding.

safety.summary: Lapachol can cause bleeding and nausea. Many products are made from cheap sawmill wood instead of inner bark, and tests have found little or no lapachol in some.
safety.regulatory: The ipê trees (Handroanthus) were added to CITES Appendix II in 2022, in force for timber from November 2024.

entries.what: The inner bark of the South American ipê tree, boiled into a bitter tea called lapacho or taheebo.
entries.know: Ipê wood is so dense that it sinks in water.

entries.name: Pelargonium (umckaloabo)
entries.uses: Zulu, Xhosa and Sotho healers traditionally boil the root for coughs, chest complaints and stomach upsets. A German extract of it is one of Europe's best-selling herbal cold remedies, and the EMA lists it as a traditional remedy for the common cold.

history.text: In 1897 an Englishman with tuberculosis travelled to southern Africa, was given the root by a Basotho healer, and later said it had restored him. Back in Britain he sold it as a consumption (tuberculosis) remedy.

research.text: A Cochrane review found it may ease the symptoms of acute bronchitis in adults and children, and possibly sinusitis and colds, but the trials were of low quality and mostly from one maker.

safety.summary: Rare cases of liver injury have been reported. It contains coumarins, so in theory it may add to the effect of blood thinners. Stomach upset and allergic rashes happen now and then. Not used in pregnancy or with liver disease.
safety.ethics: In 2010 the people of Masithandane near Alice, in the Eastern Cape, won a challenge at the European Patent Office against a company's patents on the root. It became a landmark biopiracy case.

entries.what: A small South African geranium whose red root is made into a cough and cold syrup.
entries.know: Its plant source stayed a mystery for decades after it went on sale in Britain; botanists only pinned it down to this species in the 1970s.

entries.name: Pennyroyal
entries.uses: In the past it was strewn on floors and hung up to drive away fleas; its Latin name, pulegium, comes from pulex, flea. For centuries women also took it to bring on a period or end a pregnancy, at great risk.

history.text: Named in Roman and medieval herbals. In America it was a folk abortion remedy into the 20th century.

research.text: Its main compound, pulegone, damages the liver. Deaths are documented.

safety.summary: The essential oil can kill in small amounts through liver failure. Deaths are recorded in adults, and in babies given the tea. Never take it by mouth, and never use it on pets.
safety.pets: The oil, used as a flea treatment, has killed dogs and cats.

entries.what: A small creeping mint with a sharp smell, once used against fleas. The oil is deadly.

sources.title: NIH LiverTox: herbal and dietary supplements
Tisserand & Young, Essential Oil Safety, 2nd ed. (2014)
Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database

entries.name: Peppermint
entries.uses: Across Europe people drink peppermint tea after dinner for wind, cramps and queasiness, and breathe in the steam with a cold. Coated oil capsules, which open in the gut instead of the stomach, are taken for irritable bowel; the EMA lists this as a well-established use. Some rub the diluted oil on the temples for a tension headache.

history.text: Dried mint is said to have been found in Egyptian tombs from around 1000 BCE. Greeks and Romans wore crowns of mint at feasts. Peppermint was first described as its own plant in an English plant list of 1696.

lore.text: In Greek myth Minthe was a nymph loved by Hades, and Persephone turned her into the plant. Mint was strewn on floors and rubbed on tables to welcome guests.

research.text: Many trials and reviews found the coated oil capsules eased irritable bowel symptoms more than a dummy pill. A few small trials of the oil rubbed on the forehead for tension headache had good results.

safety.summary: It can make reflux and heartburn worse. Never put the oil on or near the face of a baby or young child: the menthol can make the throat spasm shut. Antacids and acid reducers can make the capsules dissolve too early. The oil may raise ciclosporin levels.
interactions: antacids and acid reducers (capsules dissolve early)
safety.pets: The oil is toxic to cats. The garden mint plant is listed as toxic to cats, dogs and horses.

entries.what: A cooling, sharp-tasting mint, drunk as a tea after meals and used as an oil.
entries.know: Peppermint is a natural cross of water mint and spearmint. It rarely sets good seed, so it is grown from runners.

sources.title: NIH National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health, Herbs at a Glance
European Medicines Agency, Committee on Herbal Medicinal Products (HMPC) monographs

ASPCA Animal Poison Control, toxic and non-toxic plants
research/HEALING-CODEX.md in this repo (fuller prose on many of these items)

entries.name: Peyote
preps: eaten or drunk as tea in ceremony
entries.uses: Peyote is the sacrament of the Native American Church and of the Wixárika (Huichol) people. It is taken in all-night prayer meetings and on pilgrimage, for healing and guidance. It is also put on wounds and sore places as a poultice.

history.text: Peyote buttons from a Texas cave have been dated to about 5,700 years ago. A 1994 US law, the American Indian Religious Freedom Act Amendments, protects ceremonial use by members of federally recognised tribes.

lore.text: Hikuri is a deer, a brother, and the pilgrim's teacher at Wirikuta, the sacred desert of the Wixárika.

research.text: Few studies of mescaline, its main active compound. One study of Navajo members of the Native American Church found no harm to memory or thinking.

safety.summary: Vomiting is common. It raises heart rate and blood pressure. There is a risk of psychosis.
safety.regulatory: A controlled substance in the US and Mexico except for protected religious use. The IUCN Red List rates wild peyote Vulnerable.
safety.ethics: Over-harvest and land loss threaten it, and United Plant Savers lists it as critical. Native leaders have asked non-Natives not to buy it or "decriminalise" it in ways that drain wild stocks.

entries.what: A small spineless cactus of Texas and Mexico, the sacrament of the Native American Church and of Wixárika pilgrims.
entries.know: Peyote grows so slowly that a plant can take ten years or more to reach the size of a harvested button.

sources.title: Schultes & Hofmann, Plants of the Gods (1979/2001)
IUCN Red List of Threatened Species
United Plant Savers, Species At-Risk list

entries.name: Pine and spruce resin
entries.uses: In Finland, Russia and among northern Indigenous peoples, people cook the resin with fat into a salve for wounds and chew it as gum. A spruce resin salve from Finnish Lapland is now sold as a certified medical product for wounds.

research.text: A few small Finnish trials found the resin salve closed pressure sores and wounds as well as or faster than standard dressings.

safety.summary: Resin (colophony) is a common cause of skin allergy.

entries.what: The sticky sap that oozes from wounds in pine and spruce bark, made into salves and chewing gum.
entries.know: Spruce gum was sold as chewing gum in the United States in the 1800s, before chicle gum took over.

sources.title: Łuczaj et al., Wild food and medicinal plants in Slavic and Eastern European ethnobotany (Journal of Ethnobiology and Ethnomedicine papers)
Daniel Moerman, Native American Ethnobotany (1998) and the BRIT Native American Ethnobotany database

entries.name: Pine buds and needles
entries.uses: In Russia pine buds are traditionally boiled into a cough decoction or syrup, and pharmacies sell them in boxes. In winter people steeped the needles in water against scurvy, the disease of too little vitamin C. Pine baths and the steam of the banya (Russian steam bath) are used for aches.

history.text: Soviet pharmacopoeias listed pine buds as an expectorant, a remedy to loosen phlegm. Siberian peoples drank needle infusions through the long winters.

research.text: Little clinical study.

safety.summary: Large amounts are not for people with kidney inflammation. Avoid in pregnancy.
safety.pets: Ponderosa pine needles can make pregnant cattle abort.

entries.what: The resinous spring buds and needles of Scots pine, boiled into cough syrup or steeped as a vitamin C drink.
entries.know: During the Siege of Leningrad (1941 to 1944) the city made pine-needle drinks on a large scale to keep people from getting scurvy.

sources.title: Sokolov & Zamotaev, Handbook of Medicinal Plants (USSR, 1984/1990)

entries.name: Plantago seed and psyllium
entries.latin: Plantago asiatica (che qian zi); P. ovata (psyllium)
entries.uses: Psyllium husk (isabgol) is stirred into water or yoghurt in India, a traditional Unani and Ayurvedic remedy for both constipation and loose stools. In Chinese medicine the seed of Asian plantain, che qian zi, is used to bring on urination and to clear "damp heat", heat stuck with sticky fluid in the bladder or gut.

research.text: Psyllium is an established bulk laxative. It lowers LDL cholesterol, and since 1998 the US FDA allows a heart-health claim for it.

safety.summary: Always take it with plenty of water: dry husk can swell in the throat or bowel and cause choking or a blockage. Keep other medicines at least an hour apart from it, because it slows their absorption. People who handle the powder at work can develop allergy and asthma.

entries.what: Tiny seeds and seed husks of plantain plants that swell into a gel in water; psyllium is the best known.

sources.title: NIH National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health, Herbs at a Glance
European Medicines Agency, Committee on Herbal Medicinal Products (HMPC) monographs
Bensky, Clavey & Stöger, Chinese Herbal Medicine: Materia Medica, 3rd ed. (2004)

entries.name: Plantain (ribwort and broadleaf)
entries.uses: Across Europe people chew a fresh leaf and press it on stings, bites and small cuts. Ribwort syrup is a common cough syrup; the EMA accepts its traditional use for a dry cough and an irritated mouth or throat.

history.text: It is one of the plants in the Anglo-Saxon Nine Herbs Charm, where waybread (plantain) is called "mother of herbs". Some Native American peoples called broadleaf plantain "white man's footprint", because it sprang up wherever European settlers went.

lore.text: In Russia children press a podorozhnik leaf on every scraped knee. It is the herb of the roadside and of travellers.

research.text: Its slippery mucilage and a compound called aucubin have been studied in the lab. There are almost no good trials in people.

safety.summary: Gentle. In 1997 some US supplements sold as plantain turned out to contain woolly foxglove (Digitalis lanata), a heart poison, after a mix-up at an importer; one young woman's heart went into complete block. It is not the cooking banana also called plantain.

entries.cat: The leaf from the path. Chew it, slap it on, stop whining.
entries.what: A low, tough weed with ribbed leaves that grows on paths, lawns and roadsides all over the world.

sources.title: European Medicines Agency, Committee on Herbal Medicinal Products (HMPC) monographs
Maud Grieve, A Modern Herbal (1931)
Daniel Moerman, Native American Ethnobotany (1998) and the BRIT Native American Ethnobotany database

entries.name: Pomegranate
entries.uses: In Persian, Unani and Ayurvedic medicine the dried rind is traditionally boiled for diarrhoea and worms and gargled for sore gums, while the juice is drunk for the heart and blood.

history.text: The root bark was a tapeworm medicine in Europe into the 20th century.

lore.text: In Greek myth Persephone ate pomegranate seeds in the underworld (one in the oldest hymn, six in later tellings) and must return there each year. Its many seeds stand for fertility. In Iran it is eaten on Yalda night, the longest night of the year.

research.text: Small trials suggest the juice may lower blood pressure a little.

safety.summary: The juice may interact with warfarin; case reports exist. It may affect some statins and other drugs the way grapefruit does, but much more weakly. The root and stem bark are toxic.

entries.what: A leathery red fruit packed with juicy seeds, used as food and medicine from Persia to India.
entries.know: The Qur'an names the pomegranate among the fruits of paradise (55:68).

sources.title: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database
https://quran.com/55/68

entries.name: Poria
entries.uses: In Chinese medicine fu ling is said to drain damp gently (clear a heavy, waterlogged state) and calm the shen (the spirit). It goes into a great many formulas for swelling, weak digestion and restless sleep.

history.text: Fu ling cakes, thin white wafers with a sweet filling, are a Beijing snack linked to the Qing court. In North America the same fungus was called tuckahoe or "Indian bread" and was dug up and eaten.

research.text: Lab and animal studies only.

safety.summary: Considered gentle in Chinese medicine. There is little modern safety data.

entries.what: A pale, coconut-sized fungal lump that grows on pine roots underground, a staple of Chinese medicine.

sources.title: Bensky, Clavey & Stöger, Chinese Herbal Medicine: Materia Medica, 3rd ed. (2004)

entries.name: Potassium
preps: small tablets (99 mg in the US)
entries.uses: Eaten more, or used as salt substitute, by people watching their blood pressure; over-the-counter pills in the US are capped at 99 mg.

history.text: The 99 mg cap on US pills followed reports of gut damage from concentrated potassium tablets.

research.text: Diets rich in potassium lower blood pressure (moderate evidence); salt substitutes cut strokes and deaths in a large Chinese village trial.

safety.summary: High potassium is dangerous and can stop the heart. Kidney disease, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, potassium-sparing diuretics and some heart drugs all raise levels: salt substitutes and supplements can tip people over.

entries.what: The mineral that sets your heartbeat and balances salt; bananas are famous for it, but beans and potatoes hold more.

nutrient.low: Weakness, cramps, constipation, fluttering heartbeat; often from vomiting, diarrhoea or water pills.
nutrient.limit: No upper limit set (US or EU). US supplement pills hold no more than 99 mg each.

sources.title: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements, vitamin and mineral fact sheets (health professional versions)
National Academies (IOM), Dietary Reference Intakes: tolerable upper intake levels

entries.name: Poultice and compress
parts: fresh or dried herbs, clays, grains
preps: cloth soaked in hot or cold tea (compress)
entries.uses: Used in some form nearly everywhere: chewed plantain leaf on a sting, cabbage leaves on swollen breasts or joints in Russia, hot ginger compresses in Japan, clay packs on bruises. In Ayurveda a herbal paste spread on the skin is called lepa.

research.text: Chilled cabbage leaves have been studied for swollen, overfull breasts in nursing mothers. They eased pain a little, but a Cochrane review called the evidence weak.

safety.summary: Hot packs can burn. Mustard and garlic poultices can blister the skin.

entries.what: Mashed herbs laid straight on the skin, or a cloth soaked in hot or cold herb tea (a compress).
entries.know: In Japan a hot ginger compress, shoga shippu, is laid on the belly or lower back.

sources.title: Maud Grieve, A Modern Herbal (1931)
Daniel Moerman, Native American Ethnobotany (1998) and the BRIT Native American Ethnobotany database
Cochrane Library systematic reviews

entries.name: Pranayama and breathwork
preps: slow breathing, breath holds, rapid breathing, humming (bhramari)
entries.uses: In yoga, pranayama guides prana (life breath) and steadies the mind. Common forms are alternate-nostril breathing (nadi shodhana), quick forceful out-breaths (kapalabhati) and humming like a bee (bhramari). Modern breathwork uses slow breathing for calm and fast cycles for energy or altered states. Tibetan tummo breathing is one of its roots.

research.text: Reviews found slow breathing (about six breaths a minute) lowers stress and blood pressure a little. In a small lab study, fast breathing with breath holds raised adrenaline levels.

safety.summary: Never do breath holds or fast breathing in or near water, in the bath or while driving: people have blacked out and drowned. Fast breathing can bring on seizures in people with epilepsy. Cautioned with heart disease and in pregnancy.

entries.what: Ways of controlling the breath, from slow, calm breathing to fast cycles, rooted in yoga.
entries.know: In 1982 Harvard researchers in India measured monks practising tummo, "inner fire", warming their fingers and toes by up to 8.3°C.

sources.title: Zaccaro et al., How breath-control can change your life: a systematic review (Front Hum Neurosci 2018)
NCCIH, health topics A-Z (practices: acupuncture, massage, yoga, tai chi, meditation)

entries.name: Propolis
entries.uses: In Russia and Eastern Europe people use propolis tincture as a throat spray and gargle, and dab it on mouth ulcers and small wounds.

history.text: Ancient Egyptians used it in embalming.

research.text: Small trials on cold sores and mouth ulcers reported some benefit.

safety.summary: Allergy is common, especially in people allergic to bee products or poplar buds, and it often causes skin rashes. It can set off asthma.

entries.what: A sticky resin bees gather from tree buds and use to seal gaps in the hive.
entries.know: The name is Greek for "before the city", because bees build it at the hive entrance like a city wall.

sources.title: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database
NIH National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health, Herbs at a Glance

entries.name: Psilocybin mushrooms
entries.latin: Psilocybe cubensis, P. mexicana and others
entries.uses: Mazatec curanderas (traditional healers) in Oaxaca, Mexico, eat them in all-night healing ceremonies called veladas. Today they are given in clinical trials and, in a few places, in licensed supervised sessions.

history.text: Mushroom-shaped stone carvings from Guatemala go back to about 1000 BCE. A 1957 Life magazine article about a Mazatec velada drew outsiders to the town of Huautla de Jiménez. Swiss chemists isolated psilocybin in 1958, and a 1971 UN treaty put it under the strictest control.

lore.text: The Mazatec call the mushrooms niños santos, the holy children. They are said to speak through the curandera, who sings and prays through the night to find the cause of an illness.

research.text: Many trials have tested psilocybin with therapy for hard-to-treat depression. Two large late-stage trials of a synthetic psilocybin, reported in 2025 and 2026, found more improvement than placebo or a very low dose. These trials are hard to keep blind, because people can usually tell what they took. Smaller trials have looked at alcohol use, smoking and distress in serious illness.

safety.summary: It can trigger psychosis in people with a personal or family history of psychotic illness or bipolar disorder. People can act dangerously while intoxicated, and a bad trip can be terrifying. Taken with lithium it has been linked to seizures, and it interacts with antidepressants and tramadol. It raises heart rate and blood pressure for a few hours. Foragers have been poisoned after mistaking deadly Galerina mushrooms for psilocybin species.
safety.pets: Dogs that eat them can become agitated, wobbly and overheated.
safety.regulatory: As of November 2026, psilocybin is a controlled drug in most countries and Schedule I under US federal law. Oregon (since 2023) and Colorado (since 2025) license supervised adult sessions, and New Mexico passed a medical psilocybin law in 2025 with a program due by the end of 2027. Australia has let authorised psychiatrists prescribe it for hard-to-treat depression since July 2023, and Czechia allowed medical use in specialised clinics from January 2026. In the US a company completed its application for FDA approval of a psilocybin medicine for treatment-resistant depression in November 2026; no decision yet.

entries.what: Small brown mushrooms with a mind-altering compound, eaten in Mazatec healing ceremonies and now in supervised therapy.
entries.know: Many psilocybin mushrooms turn blue where they are bruised or handled.
