entries.name: Pu-erh
entries.uses: Traditionally drunk after rich meals in Yunnan, in Hong Kong dim sum houses and in Tibet. Pressed bricks were carried by mule and horse caravans along the Tea Horse Road into Tibet and traded for horses.

research.text: Small studies on blood fats.

safety.summary: Caffeine. Mould can grow on badly stored cakes. Brick teas made from old, coarse leaves can be high in fluoride, and heavy daily drinking in Tibet has been linked to fluorosis of bones and teeth.

entries.what: A fermented, aged tea from Yunnan in China, often pressed into cakes and bricks.
entries.know: Ripe (shou) pu-erh comes from a fast wet-piling method worked out in Kunming in 1973. Before that, pu-erh darkened slowly over years.

sources.title: Victor Mair & Erling Hoh, The True History of Tea (2009)

entries.name: Pulsatilla
entries.uses: In homeopathy, its remedy picture (the type it is matched to) is the gentle, weepy person who wants comfort and company and feels better in fresh air. Symptoms shift and change, the catarrh (thick mucus) is yellow-green, thirst is low, and cycles are irregular.

research.text: No good trials show a reliable effect beyond placebo.

safety.summary: The fresh plant is toxic and its sap blisters skin; the pills contain none at usual potencies.

entries.what: The pasque flower made into a homeopathic remedy for gentle, changeable people and thick catarrh.
entries.know: "Pasque" means Easter: the flower opens around Easter time.

sources.title: Australian NHMRC, Information Paper: evidence on the effectiveness of homeopathy (2015)

entries.name: Punarnava
entries.uses: In Ayurveda it is used for swelling and water retention (shotha), for the kidneys and urine flow, and for the liver. People boil the root or the whole plant, or take Punarnavadi mandura, tablets made with purified iron oxide.

lore.text: The name means "new again": the plant dies back in the dry season and sprouts fresh with the rains. It is said to renew the body the same way.

research.text: Animal studies on the kidneys and urine flow; little human work.

safety.summary: It acts as a diuretic. It is cautioned when swelling comes from kidney or heart failure, and it can shift potassium levels.

entries.what: A sprawling weed with tiny pink flowers, common on Indian roadsides, whose root is boiled for swelling.

sources.title: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India
James A. Duke, Handbook of Medicinal Herbs (2nd ed., 2002) and Dr. Duke's Phytochemical and Ethnobotanical Databases

entries.name: Pygeum (African cherry)
entries.uses: In Cameroon, Kenya and other parts of East and Central Africa the bark is traditionally boiled for urinary complaints and fevers. In Europe and the US its extract is sold for the urinary symptoms of an enlarged prostate.

research.text: A 2002 Cochrane review of small, short trials found modest improvement in urinary symptoms and flow. The trials were old and the products varied.

safety.summary: Stomach upset now and then. Not used in pregnancy.
safety.regulatory: Listed on CITES Appendix II since 1995, so exports need permits. The EU stopped imports from Cameroon in 2007 until sustainable quotas were set.
safety.ethics: Stripping bark for export killed many trees in Cameroon, Madagascar and elsewhere. Look for certified sustainable harvest.

entries.what: A tall African mountain-forest tree whose bark is stripped and sold in prostate supplements.

sources.title: Cochrane Library systematic reviews
CITES appendices (international trade in endangered species)
PROTA4U, Plant Resources of Tropical Africa

entries.name: Qigong and tai chi
entries.uses: In China people practise in parks at dawn to build qi (life energy), balance and long life. Qigong sets like the Eight Brocades are short movements repeated with the breath. Tai chi began as a martial art, and its slow forms are still fighting moves done gently.

history.text: A painted silk chart of daoyin exercises (stretching and breathing moves) was found in a tomb at Mawangdui, sealed in 168 BCE.

lore.text: Practitioners gather the qi of heaven and earth into the dantian, the "elixir field" just below the navel.

research.text: Good evidence that tai chi improves balance and lowers the rate of falls in older people. Smaller studies found less knee arthritis pain and a small drop in blood pressure.

safety.summary: Very low risk. People with joint problems use higher, gentler stances.

entries.what: Slow, flowing exercise with steady breathing from China, together with tai chi, its martial-arts cousin.
entries.know: Tai chi (taijiquan) was added to UNESCO's list of intangible cultural heritage in 2020.

sources.title: NCCIH, health topics A-Z (practices: acupuncture, massage, yoga, tai chi, meditation)
Cochrane Library systematic reviews

entries.name: Rakia and vodka compresses
parts: grape or plum brandy, vodka, sometimes with vinegar or herbs
preps: cloth soaked and wrapped on the throat or joints
entries.uses: In Serbia, Bulgaria and Russia a cloth soaked in rakia (fruit brandy) or vodka, sometimes with vinegar or herbs, is traditionally wrapped on a sore throat or aching joint and covered with a wool scarf to keep it warm. Feverish skin is also rubbed down with it.

history.text: A family remedy from Belgrade to Vladivostok, passed down by grandmothers rather than written in books.

research.text: Not studied.

safety.summary: Alcohol rubbed on children can poison them through the skin and the fumes they breathe, and can drop their blood sugar dangerously. Never use it on babies or children.

entries.what: A cloth soaked in fruit brandy or vodka and wrapped round the throat or a sore joint, a Balkan and Russian home remedy.

sources.title: Łuczaj et al., Wild food and medicinal plants in Slavic and Eastern European ethnobotany (Journal of Ethnobiology and Ethnomedicine papers)

entries.name: Raspberry leaf
entries.uses: In Britain and North America many women drink the leaf tea in the last weeks of pregnancy to "tone the womb" for labour. Others drink it for period cramps, sore throats and loose bowels; the EMA accepts traditional use in adults for mild period cramps, a mildly sore mouth or throat, and mild diarrhoea. In Russia hot tea with dried raspberries or raspberry jam is the classic way to sweat out a fever.

history.text: A midwives' herb in Britain and North America for centuries.

research.text: One trial of 192 women found the tablets did not shorten the first stage of labour. The second stage was about ten minutes shorter, a small difference. Its safety in pregnancy has not been properly tested.

safety.summary: Where it is taken in pregnancy, tradition keeps it to the last weeks, never early. Its safety in pregnancy has not been established, and the EMA does not recommend it in pregnancy or breastfeeding for lack of data.

entries.what: The leaf of the garden raspberry, dried for a mild tea, famous as a late-pregnancy brew.
entries.know: A raspberry is not a true berry. Each one is a cluster of tiny fruits, each with its own seed.

sources.title: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database
European Medicines Agency, Committee on Herbal Medicinal Products (HMPC) monographs

entries.name: Red clover
entries.uses: In European and North American folk practice the flower tea was drunk as a "blood cleanser" for skin troubles and for coughs. Today extracts rich in isoflavones (plant compounds that act a little like oestrogen) are sold for hot flushes.

history.text: It went into 19th-century American "alterative" tonics, mixtures sold to slowly clean the blood.

lore.text: Its three leaves stand for the Trinity. A four-leaved clover brings luck, and in old belief lets you see fairies.

research.text: Most trials of the isoflavone extracts found little or no effect on hot flushes.

safety.summary: It acts weakly like oestrogen, so it is a poor match with hormone-sensitive cancers, tamoxifen, hormone therapy and the contraceptive pill. It contains coumarins, which in theory could thin the blood a little, so take care with warfarin.

entries.what: A pink-purple meadow clover whose flower heads are dried for tea and made into extracts.
entries.know: Red clover is the state flower of Vermont.

sources.title: NIH National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health, Herbs at a Glance
Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database

entries.name: Reflexology
preps: thumb walking on reflex maps of the body on the feet
entries.uses: Practised on the belief that a map of the whole body lies on the feet, hands and ears. The practitioner "walks" a thumb over each zone. People go for relaxation, and Chinese foot spas offer it everywhere.

history.text: A tomb painting at Saqqara in Egypt (about 2330 BCE) shows hands and feet being worked on; some read it as massage, others as a manicure. Modern zone therapy began in the US in the 1910s, and the foot maps used today were drawn in the 1930s.

research.text: People find it relaxing, but reviews found no reliable effect on any specific illness.

safety.summary: Gentle. Injured or infected feet are left alone.

entries.what: Pressing points on the feet or hands that are believed to link to organs and other parts of the body.

sources.title: NCCIH, health topics A-Z (practices: acupuncture, massage, yoga, tai chi, meditation)

entries.name: Rehmannia
preps: in Liu Wei Di Huang Wan
entries.uses: In Chinese medicine the black, prepared root (shu di huang) deeply nourishes kidney yin and the blood. The "kidney" here is a whole system of vitality, growth and ageing, not just the organ. Yin is the cool, moist side of the body. The raw root (sheng di huang) is used instead to cool "heat" in the blood, signs such as fever, rashes or bleeding. It is the base of the classic kidney-yin pill.

research.text: Lab studies only.

safety.summary: It can cause loose stools and bloating. It may lower blood sugar.

entries.what: A sticky root from northern China, used raw or steamed until black, a key "nourishing" herb.
entries.know: Prepared rehmannia is traditionally steamed and sun-dried nine times, until it turns jet black and sweet.

sources.title: Bensky, Clavey & Stöger, Chinese Herbal Medicine: Materia Medica, 3rd ed. (2004)

entries.name: Reiki and energy healing
parts: hands on or above the body
entries.uses: Practised to channel universal life energy through the hands, for relaxation and healing. Laying on of hands is found in many religions.

history.text: Reiki began in Japan in the 1920s and reached the West through Hawaii from the late 1930s. Some hospitals now offer it.

lore.text: Rei means spirit or universal; ki is life energy. Teachers pass sacred symbols to students in an attunement.

research.text: Reviews found no reliable effect beyond placebo, though people often report deep relaxation.

safety.summary: Gentle, with no physical risk.

entries.what: A Japanese practice of laying the hands on or just above the body to pass on life energy.
entries.know: Reiki's founder is said to have received it in 1922 after 21 days of fasting and meditation on Mount Kurama, north of Kyoto.

sources.title: NCCIH, health topics A-Z (practices: acupuncture, massage, yoga, tai chi, meditation)

entries.name: Reishi
entries.latin: Ganoderma lingzhi (G. lucidum in older texts)
entries.uses: In Chinese medicine lingzhi is a top-rank tonic for calming the shen (the spirit, said to live in the heart). People take it as a bitter tea or powder for sleep, worry, weak immunity and a long life.

history.text: The oldest Chinese herbal, the Shennong Bencao Jing, puts lingzhi in its highest class, safe to take for years. It is painted on imperial robes, carved on temple roofs and held by Taoist immortals in Chinese art.

lore.text: It is said to grow where immortals walk. Finding one was taken as a sign that the emperor ruled with virtue.

research.text: Most work is in cells and animals. A Cochrane review found too little evidence to use it as a cancer treatment on its own. Some small trials that added it to chemotherapy reported better immune markers and quality of life.

safety.summary: Rare cases of liver injury have been reported, mostly with reishi powder. It may increase bleeding and lower blood pressure and blood sugar.

entries.cat: The mushroom of immortality. You've got ninety years, tops. Make them less boring.
entries.what: A hard, shiny, reddish shelf mushroom from Asian forests, taken as bitter tea or powder for long life.
entries.know: The curled head of the ruyi, a Chinese ceremonial sceptre, is often carved in the shape of a lingzhi.

Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database
NIH LiverTox: herbal and dietary supplements
Christopher Hobbs, Medicinal Mushrooms (1995)
Cochrane Library systematic reviews

entries.name: Retatrutide
parts: investigational GIP, GLP-1 and glucagon receptor agonist
entries.uses: An investigational weight-loss drug from Eli Lilly, not yet approved anywhere. It is sold illegally online, in some shops and through social media as a "research chemical", often labelled "reta" or "GLP-3".

history.text: A phase 2 trial published in 2023 reported about 24% average weight loss at 48 weeks. Phase 3 trials (called TRIUMPH) reported results from December 2025 to July 2026, and the maker says it plans to file for US approval in the first quarter of 2027.

research.text: In phase 3 trials people lost about 21 to 23% of body weight on average at 80 weeks, and more in one knee-pain trial. These are the maker's headline results; no regulator has reviewed the full data yet. A 2026 analysis of black-market users (not yet peer reviewed) found they lost far less weight than trial patients, and independent tests of sold vials have found wrong, weak or missing ingredients.

safety.summary: Safety outside trials is unknown. In trials the usual GLP-1 stomach effects were common, more people quit for side effects than on placebo, and about 6% reported dysesthesia (odd prickling or burning skin sensations). Black-market products bring their own dangers. In June 2026 Victoria, Australia, reported six cases of acute liver injury since January in people using products labelled retatrutide, possibly from a contaminant. Australia's regulator tested one sample and found semaglutide and no retatrutide at all. US poison centres also report calls about "research" retatrutide.
safety.regulatory: As of November 2026: not approved anywhere; Lilly plans to file in early 2027. FDA sent warning letters to sellers in March and August 2026, saying a "research use only" label does not make human sale legal; a US consumer group counted 14 letters since 2024 and found most sellers kept selling. Lilly sued six US sellers in August 2026. Australia made unapproved peptides an enforcement priority for 2026. Prohibited in sport as an unapproved substance (WADA S0).

entries.cat: Not approved, not tested on you, sold by a guy with a ring light. Bold.
entries.what: An experimental weekly injection aimed at three hormone targets, still unapproved but already sold illegally online.
entries.know: There is no hormone called GLP-3; the label is a sellers' nickname.

entries.name: Rhodiola (golden root)
entries.uses: In Siberia and Scandinavia the root is traditionally taken for stamina, for enduring cold and for low mood. In the Altai mountains a bunch of golden root is said to have been given to newlyweds for fertility. Soviet research on adaptogens (plants thought to raise the body's general resistance to stress) made it famous. EMA lists a traditional use for fatigue and weakness from stress.

history.text: Popular accounts say Vikings took it for strength. In the Soviet era it was studied on soldiers and athletes, and reportedly on cosmonauts.

research.text: Small trials on stress, fatigue and mild depression found modest effects. A 2015 US trial compared it with sertraline, an antidepressant: it did a little less well but caused fewer side effects.

safety.summary: It can make people irritable, and can disturb sleep if taken late in the day. It may change blood sugar and blood pressure. Not for people with bipolar disorder. Avoid in pregnancy.
safety.regulatory: Since 23 February 2023 every Rhodiola species is on CITES Appendix II, so international trade in the roots and extracts needs permits; finished retail products are exempt. Wild Rhodiola rosea is listed as rare in the Red Book of the Russian Federation.
safety.ethics: Wild stands in the Altai have been over-harvested. Cultivated roots take three to four years to grow, so buy cultivated.

entries.what: A hardy plant of Arctic and mountain slopes whose rose-scented root is taken as a tonic for stamina and stress.
entries.know: A Greek herbal from the 1st century CE already describes it, under the name rhodia riza, "rose root".

entries.name: Rhus toxicodendron
entries.uses: In homeopathy, its picture is the "rusty gate": stiffness worst on first moving and better with continued motion, worse in cold, damp weather. Also given for sprains and for itchy, blistering rashes.

research.text: No good trials show a reliable effect beyond placebo.

safety.summary: Low potencies may contain urushiol, the oil in poison ivy that causes an allergic rash.

entries.what: Poison ivy diluted into a homeopathic remedy for stiffness that eases once you keep moving.

sources.title: Australian NHMRC, Information Paper: evidence on the effectiveness of homeopathy (2015)

entries.name: Rooibos
entries.uses: The Khoi and San of the Cederberg mountains drank it first, and it is now drunk worldwide as a caffeine-free tea. In South Africa it is traditionally given to colicky babies and used for allergies and skin.

history.text: It has been sold commercially since the early 1900s. In 2021 it became the first African food with EU protected designation of origin status, so in the EU only rooibos from its home region of South Africa may use the name.

research.text: Mostly lab studies of its antioxidants. One small South African trial (2011) in adults at risk of heart disease found better cholesterol numbers after six weeks of drinking it.

safety.summary: Gentle. There are a few case reports of liver injury.
safety.ethics: Under a 2019 agreement the rooibos industry pays a share of its earnings to Khoi and San communities, for their traditional knowledge of the plant.

entries.what: A caffeine-free red tea made from the needle-like leaves of a South African bush.
entries.know: The leaves are green on the bush. They turn red when they are cut, bruised and left in heaps to oxidise.

sources.title: van Wyk, van Oudtshoorn & Gericke, Medicinal Plants of South Africa (2009)
Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database

entries.name: Rose
entries.latin: Rosa damascena, R. gallica, R. centifolia
entries.uses: From the Middle East to India and Europe the rose is used to cool and calm the heart and mind. Rosewater is splashed on the skin and used to bathe tired eyes. In Ayurveda, India's traditional medicine, gulkand (rose petal jam) is eaten to cool pitta, the hot, fiery energy. In Chinese medicine the buds of a related rose (Rosa rugosa) are used to move stuck qi (the body's flowing life energy) for low mood and period cramps. The EMA accepts rose petal preparations as a traditional use for mild inflammation of the mouth, throat or skin.

history.text: Rosewater distilling was perfected in Persia around the 10th century. Today the Rose Valley around Kazanlak in Bulgaria and the Isparta region of Turkey distil most of the world's attar of roses.

lore.text: The flower of Venus, Aphrodite and the Virgin Mary, and the root of the word rosary. Sufi poets wrote of the rose as divine love. "Sub rosa", under the rose, means in secret: a rose hung over a meeting meant nothing said there would leave the room.

research.text: A few small trials, mostly in Iran, tested breathing rose oil for anxiety and period pain.

safety.summary: Gentle. For eating and drinking, buy food-grade rosewater: cosmetic rosewater may contain alcohol and preservatives.

entries.what: The garden rose's scented petals, made into rosewater, rose oil (attar), jam and tea.
entries.know: It takes about three to four tonnes of rose petals to distil one kilogram of rose oil.

entries.name: Rose geranium oil
entries.uses: Used in aromatherapy for the skin, for calm and for a sense of balance, and as an insect repellent. The plant grows wild in southern Africa.

research.text: A few small studies, for example on anxiety during labour.

safety.summary: It can irritate skin or cause skin allergy.
safety.pets: Toxic to cats and dogs.

entries.what: A rosy-smelling oil distilled from the leaves of a scented pelargonium from South Africa.
entries.know: The red-flowered pot plants most people call geraniums are really pelargoniums, and so is the plant this oil comes from.

sources.title: Tisserand & Young, Essential Oil Safety, 2nd ed. (2014)
ASPCA Animal Poison Control, toxic and non-toxic plants

entries.name: Rosehip
entries.uses: Across northern and eastern Europe rosehips are made into a tart, vitamin-rich tea and syrup for the winter. In Russia shipovnik syrup is a classic for children, and in Sweden people eat rosehip soup (nyponsoppa). Rosehip powder is sold for stiff joints.

history.text: In the Second World War, British children picked wild rosehips for vitamin C syrup when oranges could no longer be shipped in. Soviet pharmacies sold holosas, a rosehip syrup, for the liver and bile.

lore.text: The briar rose is the thorny hedge that grows round Sleeping Beauty's castle. In Balkan and Slavic folk belief, wild rose branches laid in a coffin or on a grave kept the dead from rising.

research.text: A few trials of rosehip powder made with the seeds found a modest drop in osteoarthritis pain.

safety.summary: The hairs inside the hip irritate the skin and gut (children used them as itching powder), so strain the tea well. Much of the vitamin C is lost when the hips are dried or heated.

entries.what: The red, berry-like fruit a wild rose leaves behind when its petals fall.

entries.name: Rosemary
entries.uses: In Europe rosemary is taken "for remembrance" and memory, drunk as a tea for weak digestion, rubbed in as a warming oil for aching muscles, and used as a hair rinse. The EMA accepts its traditional use for indigestion, and in the bath for minor muscle and joint aches.

history.text: Greek students are said to have worn rosemary garlands while studying. Hungary water, a rosemary spirit, is said to have restored a 14th-century queen of Hungary; the written recipes date from the 1600s.

lore.text: In Hamlet, Ophelia says rosemary is "for remembrance". It was burned to clean the air of sickrooms, grown by the door against witches, and carried at weddings and funerals.

research.text: A few small studies linked the smell of rosemary oil with better memory scores. One small trial found rosemary oil on the scalp did about as well as 2% minoxidil for common hair thinning over six months.

safety.summary: Kitchen amounts are fine. The oil contains camphor, which can set off seizures in people with epilepsy, and it is not to be swallowed. Strong extracts may affect blood thinners and blood pressure pills (ACE inhibitors), and in theory lithium.

entries.what: A needle-leaved, piney-smelling Mediterranean shrub, used in cooking and as a tea, hair rinse and oil.
entries.know: In 2017 botanists moved rosemary into the sage genus, so its proper name is now Salvia rosmarinus.

entries.name: Royal jelly
entries.uses: Taken as a rejuvenating tonic in China, Russia and Japan. Every bee larva gets royal jelly for its first days, but only a future queen is fed it for life, which is the root of its reputation.

research.text: Small trials looked at menopause symptoms and cholesterol, with some positive results.

safety.summary: It can cause severe allergic reactions. Asthma attacks and deaths have been reported, mostly in Australia, where products must carry a warning.

entries.what: A milky paste worker bees feed to queen bees, sold fresh or in capsules.

sources.title: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database

entries.name: Rue
entries.uses: Today rue is mostly a protective herb. In Latin American limpias (spiritual cleansings) a healer sweeps a bundle of rue over the body, and many people wear it or hang it by the door against the evil eye. In the past women drank it to bring on a late period, which was dangerous.

history.text: Roman writers said painters and engravers ate rue to keep their eyesight sharp. The Italian cimaruta, "sprig of rue", is a silver charm against the evil eye shaped like a rue branch hung with tiny symbols.

lore.text: It was called the herb of grace, and was used, it is said, to sprinkle holy water. In Lithuania rue (rūta) is the national plant, and brides wore a crown of rue.

research.text: Its furanocoumarins (compounds that make skin burn in sunlight) and alkaloids have been studied in the lab. It is toxic.

safety.summary: Poisonous taken by mouth. Women who drank it to end pregnancies have died. Sap on the skin followed by sunlight causes severe blistering burns, so wear gloves when cutting it.
safety.pets: Toxic to pets.

entries.what: A bitter, blue-grey garden shrub with a strong smell, best known today as a protective herb.

entries.name: Sacred tobacco
entries.uses: In many Indigenous traditions tobacco is the first medicine. A pinch, or a little cloth tie of it, is offered to the earth, the fire and the spirits before anything is asked, and it is smoked in the pipe in ceremony. In the Amazon, healers blow mapacho smoke over people during healing, and rapé (a fine tobacco snuff) is blown into the nose.

history.text: Tobacco was grown in the Americas thousands of years before Columbus. Ceremonial tobacco, often the strong N. rustica, is a different practice from commercial cigarettes.

lore.text: Tobacco carries prayers upward. It is given in thanks when a plant is harvested or a teaching is asked.

research.text: Nicotine is highly addictive. The WHO calls commercial tobacco use the world's leading preventable cause of death.

safety.summary: Nicotine poisoning can come from handling wet green leaves (green tobacco sickness), from strong snuff, or from swallowing tobacco. N. rustica holds far more nicotine than cigarette tobacco. Commercial smoking is deadly.
safety.pets: Nicotine is highly toxic to dogs and cats; a swallowed cigarette end or pouch is an emergency.

entries.what: Tobacco as many Indigenous peoples of the Americas use it: a sacred plant offered in prayer, not cigarettes.
entries.know: Charred wild tobacco seeds in a Utah hearth show people were using tobacco about 12,300 years ago.

entries.name: Saffron
entries.uses: In Persian medicine it is used to lift the spirits and is said to bring on laughter. It is also used for women's cycles and as an aphrodisiac. In India a few threads go into warm milk.

history.text: Wall paintings at Akrotiri on Santorini, from about 1600 BCE, show young women gathering saffron. Iran now grows most of the world's crop. Its colour gave its name to the "saffron" robes of Buddhist monks, which are often dyed with cheaper plants.

lore.text: The spice of the Sun, joy and royalty. Wealthy Romans strewed it in their halls and baths.

research.text: Several small trials, mostly from Iran, found it lifted mild depression and eased premenstrual symptoms compared with placebo.

safety.summary: Food amounts are fine. Large amounts (several grams) are poisonous and were once used to cause abortion. Saffron is often faked or bulked out with other plant parts and dyes.

entries.what: The red threads (stigmas) of a purple crocus, picked by hand; the world's most expensive spice.
entries.know: It takes the stigmas of about 150 flowers to make a single gram of saffron.

sources.title: NIH National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health, Herbs at a Glance
Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database

entries.name: Sage
entries.uses: In Europe people gargle sage tea for sore throats and gums, drink it for night sweats and hot flushes, and take it after heavy meals. The EMA accepts its traditional use for heavy sweating, a sore mouth and throat, and indigestion.

history.text: A medieval Latin verse from the medical school of Salerno asks why a man should die when sage grows in his garden. The name Salvia comes from the Latin salvere, to be well. It is not the same plant as white sage.

lore.text: A herb of wisdom, long life and protection. An English saying holds that sage grows best where the wife rules the house.

research.text: A few small trials tested sage for hot flushes and for memory in older adults, with some positive results.

safety.summary: Sage contains thujone, which can cause seizures in large amounts, so skip high doses and the essential oil. Kitchen amounts are fine. Strong extracts may affect seizure medicines, diabetes medicines and sedatives.

entries.what: The grey-green garden sage of stuffing and roasts, also brewed as a tea and gargle.

entries.name: Salt (sea salt, rock salt, salt rooms)
entries.uses: Salt-water gargles and nasal rinses are traditional everywhere. Underground salt mines, such as Wieliczka in Poland and Soligorsk in Belarus, host speleotherapy (sessions spent breathing the mine air). In folk magic a line of salt across a threshold keeps evil out.

history.text: The Wieliczka mine near Kraków opened brine baths in 1839, and in the 20th century it added an underground health resort more than 100 metres down.

research.text: A Cochrane review found saline nasal rinses ease the symptoms of long-term sinusitis. Evidence for salt rooms and salt caves is weak.

safety.summary: Use sterile, distilled or boiled and cooled water for nasal rinses: rare fatal brain infections from amoebas in tap water have been reported.

entries.what: Sea and rock salt, used in gargles, nasal rinses, salt-mine breathing sessions and protective folk magic.

sources.title: Cochrane Library systematic reviews

entries.name: Salve and ointment
preps: herbs infused in oil (warm or sun), strained, thickened with beeswax
entries.uses: Traditionally made by steeping calendula, comfrey, plantain, St John's wort or arnica in oil and setting it with beeswax. It is rubbed on skin, small wounds and sore muscles.

history.text: Apothecaries kept their ointments in jars labelled unguentum.

lore.text: In witch lore, flying ointments were rubbed on before the night flight to the sabbat. The old recipes call for nightshades such as belladonna, henbane and mandrake.

research.text: Depends on the herb.

safety.summary: Fresh plant matter in oil can spoil or grow bacteria. Salves are not for deep or infected wounds, or for serious burns. The nightshades in flying-ointment recipes are poisonous even through the skin: never make one.

entries.what: A soft ointment made by steeping herbs in oil and setting it with beeswax.

sources.title: Maud Grieve, A Modern Herbal (1931)

entries.name: Sandalwood
entries.latin: Santalum album (Indian); S. spicatum (Australian); S. paniculatum (Hawaiian)
entries.uses: In Ayurveda the cooling paste is traditionally spread on the forehead and skin to calm excess pitta (the fiery, hot energy) and settle the mind, and the oil is taken for burning urination. Sandalwood is burned in temples and used in meditation across Asia and beyond.

history.text: Hawaii's sandalwood trade, from about 1790 to 1840, stripped the islands of their sandalwood. In India the trees long belonged to the state, and Mysore sandalwood was a state monopoly.

lore.text: Wood of the gods. In Indian poetry snakes coil round sandalwood trees for their coolness and scent, and the tree stays sweet. Sandal paste marks the forehead (tilak) in devotion.

research.text: A few small studies on skin and on its scent.

safety.summary: Skin reactions are rare.
safety.regulatory: Indian sandalwood (Santalum album) is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List. India restricts its export, and smuggling is common.
safety.ethics: Buy certified plantation Indian or Australian sandalwood only, and avoid unlabelled oils.

entries.what: The fragrant heartwood of slow-growing tropical trees, ground into paste, burned as incense and distilled into oil.
entries.know: The Indian state of Mysore opened a government soap factory in 1916 to use its sandalwood oil, and Mysore Sandal Soap is still made today.

sources.title: IUCN Red List of Threatened Species

entries.name: Sangre de drago
entries.uses: In the Amazon people dab it on cuts, bites and sores, where it dries into a second skin, and drink a few drops in water for stomach upsets.

history.text: Crofelemer, a drug made from this sap, was approved by the FDA in December 2012 for diarrhoea in people with HIV.

research.text: Crofelemer is an approved medicine for that one use. The crude sap is less studied.

safety.summary: Generally safe on skin. There is little safety data for drinking it.

entries.what: The blood-red sap of an Amazon tree, dabbed on cuts where it dries into a thin protective film.
entries.know: Rubbed into the skin, the red sap turns into a pale, creamy foam.

entries.name: Sarsaparilla
aka: tu fu ling (Chinese, related S. glabra)
entries.uses: In Central America and the Caribbean people boil the root as a "blood purifier" for skin and joints. It reached Europe in the 1500s as a remedy for syphilis.

history.text: Sarsaparilla soda was a popular 19th-century American drink. Its cowboy-saloon image comes mostly from Western films.

research.text: Its saponins (soap-like compounds) have been studied in the lab. There is little clinical work.

safety.summary: It can upset the stomach and may change how other drugs are absorbed.

entries.what: The root of a thorny tropical vine, boiled into "blood purifier" tonics and the first sarsaparilla sodas.

sources.title: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database

entries.name: Sassafras
entries.uses: Cherokee and other nations used the root bark as medicine, and Choctaw people ground the dried leaves into filé, which still thickens Louisiana gumbo. Europeans bought the root as an all-purpose "blood purifier".

history.text: It was one of the first goods shipped from North America to England, with whole cargoes sailing in the early 1600s. It was the original flavour of root beer.

research.text: Safrole, the main oil in the root, causes liver cancer in rats and mice.

safety.summary: Root bark tea and the oil contain safrole. Filé made from the leaf has much less.
safety.regulatory: The FDA banned safrole and sassafras oil as food additives in 1960. Safrole is also a controlled chemical because it can be used to make MDMA.

entries.what: A North American tree with mitten-shaped leaves; its root gave root beer its first flavour.
entries.know: One sassafras tree carries three leaf shapes at once: plain ovals, mittens and three-lobed leaves.

sources.title: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database
US FDA, dietary supplement warnings and safety information

entries.name: Saw palmetto
entries.uses: Seminole people and earlier Florida peoples ate the berries as food. Today men take extracts for the urinary symptoms of an enlarged prostate. The EMA accepts one extract made with hexane (a solvent) as a well-established use for this, and other preparations as traditional use.

history.text: The berries came into American pharmacy around 1880 and entered the US Pharmacopoeia in the early 1900s, then the National Formulary until the 1940s.

research.text: Two large US trials (STEP in 2006, CAMUS in 2011) and a 2023 Cochrane review found it did no better than placebo for urinary symptoms.

safety.summary: Mild stomach upset is the usual complaint. There are a few reports of bleeding, so it is cautioned with blood thinners and before surgery. It may affect hormone therapies.

entries.what: A low fan palm of the US Southeast whose berries are sold for men's prostate and urinary symptoms.

sources.title: NIH National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health, Herbs at a Glance

entries.name: Schisandra
entries.uses: In Chinese medicine wu wei zi is an astringent herb: it "holds in" what leaks out, such as sweat, a long cough or loose bowels. It is also said to calm the shen, the spirit as it shows in sleep and mood. Russian reports tell of Nanai hunters in the Far East chewing a handful of dried berries to keep going on long hunts.

history.text: Soviet scientists studied it as an adaptogen from the 1940s. It is said to have been given to cosmonauts and athletes. In Korea omija-cha is an everyday tea.

lore.text: It holds all five tastes at once: sour, sweet, bitter, salty and pungent. In Chinese thought each taste belongs to one organ, so the berry is said to touch all five.

research.text: Lab studies on the liver. A few small trials on tiredness.

safety.summary: It can cause heartburn. It changes how the liver breaks down some drugs and has raised tacrolimus levels in transplant patients. Traditional texts caution it in epilepsy.

entries.what: A tart red berry from a climbing vine of northeast Asia and the Russian Far East.
entries.know: In Korea omija berries are steeped cold into a pink summer drink.

entries.name: Sea buckthorn
entries.uses: In Russia oblepikha oil is traditionally dabbed on burns, radiation burns and wounds, and swallowed for the stomach lining. In Tibetan medicine the sour berry is an important herb for the lungs, the blood and digestion.

history.text: It is said to have been in Soviet cosmonauts' rations and to have been used for radiation burns after Chernobyl.

lore.text: Hippophae means "shining horse". Old stories say horses fed on its leaves grew glossy coats, and that it was the favourite food of Pegasus.

research.text: Small trials on dry eyes and on skin.

safety.summary: A common food. It may lower blood pressure and slow blood clotting.

entries.what: A thorny shrub with bright orange berries, pressed for juice and a deep orange oil in Russia and Tibet.
entries.know: Its roots fix nitrogen, so China has planted it in huge numbers to hold the eroding soil of the Loess Plateau.

entries.name: Selenium
entries.uses: Taken as an antioxidant and for the thyroid; Finland has added it to farm fertiliser since 1984, and China gave out selenium tablets and selenised salt in selenium-poor regions.

history.text: In 2008 a mislabelled US supplement held about 200 times the stated selenium; over 200 people lost hair and nails.

research.text: The large SELECT trial found selenium didn't prevent prostate cancer, and another trial raised a signal for type 2 diabetes with long-term use.

safety.summary: Too much causes selenosis: garlic breath, brittle hair and nails, skin rash, nerve damage. Brazil nuts vary hugely in selenium.

entries.what: A trace mineral built into the body's own antioxidant enzymes; a couple of Brazil nuts can hold a day's worth.

nutrient.low: Rare outside selenium-poor soils; in parts of China it caused a heart disease (Keshan disease).
nutrient.limit: US 400 mcg a day; EU 255 mcg a day (lowered in 2023).

entries.name: Self-heal
entries.uses: In Europe it was laid on cuts and gargled for sore throats. In Chinese medicine the dried flower spikes are used to cool "liver fire" (heat rising to the head) for red, sore eyes, headaches and swollen glands. In Guangdong people drink it in liang cha, the herbal "cooling teas".

history.text: Called carpenter's herb, for cuts from tools. Herbal tea stalls in Hong Kong and Guangdong still sell cooling teas made with it.

research.text: Studied in the lab only.

safety.summary: Gentle. In Chinese medicine it is used with care by people with a weak, cold digestion.

entries.what: A small purple-flowered lawn plant of the mint family, used in both European and Chinese herbal traditions.
entries.know: Its Chinese name, xia ku cao, means "summer-withered herb", because the flower spikes dry up in midsummer.

entries.name: Semaglutide
entries.uses: Prescribed for type 2 diabetes and long-term weight management, and in people with heart disease and obesity to lower the risk of heart attack and stroke. Also sold illegally online as a "research peptide" and in copied versions, and talked about everywhere for weight loss.

history.text: Built on human GLP-1, a hormone the gut releases after eating. FDA approved it as Ozempic for diabetes in 2017, as Wegovy for weight in 2021, and as a daily Wegovy pill in December 2025.

research.text: Big trials found average weight loss of about 15% over 68 weeks at the weight-loss dose. A large trial reported in 2023, in people with heart disease and overweight, found about 20% fewer heart attacks, strokes and heart deaths. Most of the weight usually comes back after stopping.

safety.summary: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea and constipation are common. Serious risks include pancreatitis, gallstones, kidney injury from dehydration, and muscle lost along with fat. It carries a warning about thyroid C-cell tumours, seen in rodents. With insulin or sulfonylureas it can push blood sugar too low. European regulators list a very rare optic-nerve stroke (NAION) that can cost sight in one eye. The slowed stomach can cause choking on vomit under anaesthesia. It is stopped at least two months before a planned pregnancy. Fake pens and "research" vials have caused overdoses and hospital stays.
contra: personal or family history of medullary thyroid cancer or MEN2
safety.regulatory: As of November 2026: prescription only. FDA declared the semaglutide shortage over in February 2025, which ended the mass copying the shortage had allowed. In 2026 FDA moved to restrict the bulk ingredient used in mass-marketed copies (February), sent warning letters to 30 telehealth firms (March) and to dozens of compounders, and in April 2026 proposed keeping semaglutide off the 503B list (ingredients for large outsourcing pharmacies); that proposal was not final when checked. "Research" semaglutide sold online is illegal. Allowed in sport: WADA keeps it on its monitoring list for 2027.

entries.what: A weekly injection (and now a daily pill) copying the gut hormone GLP-1, licensed for diabetes and weight loss.
entries.know: The whole GLP-1 drug family started with exendin-4, a hormone found in the 1990s in the saliva of the Gila monster, a venomous desert lizard.

entries.name: Semax and Selank
parts: synthetic peptides based on ACTH (Semax) and tuftsin (Selank)
entries.uses: Registered medicines in Russia, where Semax is prescribed for stroke recovery and concentration and Selank for anxiety. Sold abroad as nootropics, taken as nasal drops or sprays.

history.text: Both came from the Institute of Molecular Genetics of the Russian Academy of Sciences in Moscow. Semax was registered in Russia in the 1990s and Selank in 2009.

research.text: Mostly Russian trials, many of them small; little independent replication.

safety.summary: Long-term safety outside Russian use is unknown. Nose irritation is reported. Grey-market quality abroad varies.
safety.regulatory: As of November 2026: approved in Russia and some neighbouring countries; not approved in the US or EU. In the US, FDA's advisory committee voted 8 to 5 in July 2026 to allow Semax in compounding, and the October 2026 HHS policy covers nasal Semax on prescription. Selank was taken off Category 2 in 2024 (its nominator meant a different substance) and is not covered.

entries.what: Two Russian nasal-drop peptides, registered medicines in Russia, sold abroad as "nootropics" (focus drugs).

entries.name: Senna
entries.uses: Traditionally used in Arab and Unani medicine (the Greek-Arabic medicine of South Asia) as a purgative to clear the bowels. In Prophetic medicine, the healing taught in the hadith, a narration in Sunan Ibn Majah praises senna with sanut, saying the two hold healing for every illness except death; scholars read sanut as honey, dill or cumin. Today it is a licensed stimulant laxative, and the EMA lists it as a well-established use for short-term constipation.

research.text: Well proven as a short-term laxative.

safety.summary: Causes cramps. Long use can make the bowel dependent on it and lower potassium, which matters with heart and water pills. Not for children under 12, or with a blocked or inflamed bowel. Used with caution in pregnancy.

entries.what: A desert shrub of Arabia and North Africa whose leaves and pods make a strong laxative tea.

sources.title: European Medicines Agency, Committee on Herbal Medicinal Products (HMPC) monographs

entries.name: Sesame oil (abhyanga oil)
entries.uses: In Ayurveda warm sesame oil is the traditional base for abhyanga (daily self-massage), oil pulling (swishing oil round the mouth), nasya (oil drops in the nose) and most medicated oils. It is used to calm vata, the airy energy behind dryness, cold and restlessness.

history.text: "Open sesame", the magic words in the tale of Ali Baba, name the seed whose ripe pods split open.

research.text: Studies on oil pulling are small.

safety.summary: Sesame allergy can be severe. In oil pulling, oil breathed into the lungs has caused a rare lung inflammation (lipoid pneumonia) in case reports.

entries.what: Oil pressed from sesame seeds; in Ayurveda it is warmed and massaged into the whole body each morning.
entries.know: Sesame is one of the oldest oil crops: charred seeds from the Indus Valley cities are about 4,000 years old.

sources.title: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India

entries.name: Shatavari
aka: tian men dong (Chinese, related A. cochinchinensis)
entries.uses: In Ayurveda it is the chief rasayana (rejuvenating tonic) for women. People take the root powder in milk or ghee around fertility, breastfeeding and menopause. It is also taken as a cooling, soothing herb for an acid stomach.

lore.text: The name is often read as "she who has a hundred husbands", or as "a hundred roots", for its bunch of tuberous roots. Ayurveda calls it cooling, sweet and bitter. It calms pitta (the hot, fiery dosha) and vata (the airy, restless one).

research.text: Small studies on breast-milk supply have mixed results.

safety.summary: People allergic to asparagus can react to it. It makes you pass more urine (a diuretic effect), so it adds to water pills and can affect lithium levels. It is cautioned when there is fluid retention (oedema).

entries.what: The root of a climbing wild asparagus from India, taken in milk as a women's tonic.
entries.know: It is a close cousin of garden asparagus, in the same genus.

sources.title: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India
Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database

entries.name: Shea butter
entries.uses: Made by women across the Sahel, who collect the fallen fruit, boil, dry, roast and pound the nuts, then knead the paste with water until the butter floats. It is traditionally rubbed on babies after their bath, on cracked heels, sore muscles, dry hair and small wounds, and used as a cooking fat.

history.text: Traded across West Africa for well over 1,000 years. It is called women's gold because women make and sell it and keep the income.

research.text: Small cosmetic studies on dry skin and moisture. Little clinical work.

safety.summary: Gentle on skin. Allergic reactions are rare, even in people with nut allergies, because refined shea has almost no nut protein. Raw shea contains traces of latex and is sometimes said to bother people with latex allergy.
safety.ethics: Choose shea from women's cooperatives and fair-trade sources.

entries.what: A creamy fat pressed from the nuts of the shea tree of the African Sahel, used on skin and in cooking.

sources.title: PROTA4U, Plant Resources of Tropical Africa

entries.name: Shepherd's purse
entries.uses: In Europe people drink the tea to slow heavy periods and nosebleeds; the EMA accepts its traditional use for heavy periods in women with regular cycles. In China the young leaves (ji cai) are a spring vegetable in dumplings and wontons.

history.text: In the First World War, when ergot and goldenseal (the usual drugs to stop bleeding) ran short, an extract of it was used instead.

research.text: Very little work in people.

safety.summary: Bleeding that is new, heavy or unexplained can have serious causes. It may affect blood pressure, thyroid hormone and blood thinners.

entries.what: A small roadside weed of the cabbage family, named for its heart-shaped seed pods like little purses.
entries.know: In Japan it is one of the seven spring herbs cooked into rice porridge (nanakusa-gayu) on 7 January.

sources.title: European Medicines Agency, Committee on Herbal Medicinal Products (HMPC) monographs
Maud Grieve, A Modern Herbal (1931)

entries.name: Shiitake
entries.uses: In East Asia people eat it as food and as a tonic for a long life and for the blood. In Japan an injected extract, lentinan, was approved for use alongside chemotherapy for stomach cancer.

history.text: People in China have grown shiitake on cut logs for about a thousand years.

research.text: Japanese trials of lentinan with chemotherapy for stomach cancer reported longer survival in some studies. Studies of eating shiitake are small; one found changes in immune markers in healthy young adults.

safety.summary: Raw or undercooked shiitake can cause shiitake dermatitis: an itchy rash of long red streaks, as if from a whip, a day or two after eating.

entries.what: A brown, meaty mushroom grown on logs, one of the most-eaten mushrooms in the world.

sources.title: National Cancer Institute PDQ: medicinal mushrooms, mistletoe and other complementary topics
Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database

entries.name: Shilajit
preps: purified resin dissolved in milk or water
entries.uses: In Ayurveda it is a great rasayana (rejuvenating tonic), dissolved in milk or water for strength and vitality and for the urinary and reproductive organs. In Russia and Central Asia it is sold as mumijo for broken bones and recovery.

history.text: It oozes from cracks in cliffs in the summer heat. Soviet scientists studied mumijo extensively.

lore.text: It is said to be the sweat of the mountains. Its name is read as "conqueror of mountains and destroyer of weakness". Monkeys are said to have been seen eating it.

research.text: Small trials on testosterone and tiredness. Its fulvic acid has been studied.

safety.summary: Raw or unpurified shilajit can carry heavy metals and fungi, and fakes are common. Buy tested products only. It may raise uric acid.

entries.what: A dark, tar-like substance that seeps from Himalayan rock in summer, purified and sold as a tonic.

sources.title: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India
Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database
Saper et al., Heavy metal content of Ayurvedic herbal medicine products, JAMA 2004

entries.name: Shirodhara
parts: warm oil, buttermilk or milk poured in a steady stream on the forehead
entries.uses: In Ayurveda used for sleeplessness, anxiety and headaches. You lie on your back while warm oil, buttermilk (takradhara) or milk runs from a pot hung above you onto the forehead, over the spot called the third eye, for 30 to 60 minutes.

research.text: Small trials on sleep and anxiety, where people reported feeling calmer and sleeping better.

safety.summary: Oil that is too hot burns. Oil running into the eyes stings.

entries.what: Warm oil poured in a slow, steady stream over the forehead while you lie still; from Ayurveda.

sources.title: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India

entries.name: Sho-saiko-to (Xiao Chai Hu Tang)
parts: bupleurum, scutellaria, pinellia, ginseng, jujube, licorice, ginger
entries.uses: In Chinese and Japanese medicine it is the chief "harmonising" formula. It is given when an illness lingers halfway between the surface and the inside, with chills and fever taking turns, a bitter taste and no appetite. In the 1990s it was widely prescribed in Japan for chronic hepatitis.

history.text: From the Shang Han Lun, a Chinese classic on fevers of around 200 CE.

research.text: In 1990s Japan it caused interstitial pneumonia (lung inflammation), especially in people also on interferon, and some died. Prescribing then fell sharply.

safety.summary: It can inflame the lungs: a cough, breathlessness or fever means stop at once. It must never be combined with interferon. Its scutellaria has also been linked to liver injury.

entries.what: A seven-herb Chinese and Kampo formula for lingering fevers, built around bupleurum root.

sources.title: Japan Ministry of Health, Kampo formulas approved for national health insurance (148 formulas)
NIH LiverTox: herbal and dietary supplements

entries.name: Si Wu Tang (Four Substances Decoction)
parts: dong quai, rehmannia (prepared), white peony, chuanxiong
entries.uses: In Chinese medicine it is the foundation formula to nourish and regulate the blood, which here means both the fluid and its nourishing power. It is traditionally used for a pale, tired look, scanty or irregular periods and recovery after birth. Hundreds of later formulas start from these four herbs.

history.text: It is first recorded in a Tang-dynasty book on injuries and broken bones from around 846 CE. The Song dynasty's imperial pharmacy formulary later made it the standard women's formula.

research.text: Small studies on period pain.

safety.summary: It carries dong quai's cautions: it can raise the effect of warfarin and add to bleeding.

entries.what: A four-herb Chinese formula, the classic base recipe for nourishing the blood and the monthly cycle.

sources.title: Bensky, Clavey & Stöger, Chinese Herbal Medicine: Materia Medica, 3rd ed. (2004)

entries.name: Siberian fir oil
entries.uses: In Russia the oil is traditionally breathed in for coughs, rubbed into aching joints after a hot bath, and dropped onto the hot stones of the banya (the steam bath). In Siberian winters fir and pine needles were steeped in water against scurvy.

lore.text: The breath of the taiga. In the banya, fir branches are said to drive out bad spirits.

research.text: Little clinical study.

safety.summary: Old, oxidised oil irritates skin. Keep it away from babies' faces. Use caution in pregnancy.
safety.pets: Pine and fir oils are toxic to cats.

entries.what: A pine-fresh oil from the needles of Siberian fir, a Russian pharmacy staple and a banya scent.

sources.title: Sokolov & Zamotaev, Handbook of Medicinal Plants (USSR, 1984/1990)
Tisserand & Young, Essential Oil Safety, 2nd ed. (2014)

entries.name: Sichuan pepper
entries.uses: In Chinese medicine it is used to "warm the middle" (the stomach) and ease cold belly pain, and to expel worms. Its numbing effect made it a folk remedy for toothache. In Japan sansho goes into Daikenchuto, a Kampo formula given for a cold, bloated belly.

research.text: A 2013 London study found its compound hydroxy-alpha-sanshool makes the lips feel a vibration of about 50 times a second.

safety.summary: Food amounts are fine.

entries.what: The dried husks of a prickly ash tree, with a lemony taste that makes the lips tingle and buzz.
entries.know: The US banned Sichuan pepper imports from 1968 to 2005, because the trees can carry a citrus disease.

sources.title: Bensky, Clavey & Stöger, Chinese Herbal Medicine: Materia Medica, 3rd ed. (2004)

entries.name: Sidr (Christ's thorn jujube)
preps: leaf powder for washing the dead and hair
entries.uses: Ground leaves are traditionally mixed with water to wash hair and body. In Islamic burial the dead are washed with water and sidr, as the Prophet instructed in hadith. In ruqyah (healing by reciting the Qur'an), green leaves are crushed into water while verses are read, and the water is drunk and bathed in against magic. Sidr honey is eaten as a tonic.

lore.text: The Qur'an speaks of the Sidrat al-Muntaha, the lote tree of the utmost boundary (53:14), which tradition places beyond the seventh heaven, and of thornless lote trees in paradise (56:28). Some Christians believe its branches made Christ's crown of thorns.

research.text: Little.

safety.summary: Gentle.

entries.what: A thorny desert tree whose leaves are ground for washing and whose flowers give a prized honey.
entries.know: Bees feeding on sidr in Yemen's Hadramawt valley make one of the most expensive honeys in the world.

sources.title: Ibn Qayyim al-Jawziyya, Medicine of the Prophet (al-Tibb al-Nabawi, 14th c.)
https://sunnah.com/bukhari:1253
https://quran.com/53/14

entries.name: Slippery elm
entries.uses: Iroquois, Cherokee and many other nations used the inner bark as a soothing food and as a poultice on wounds, boils and sore throats. Settlers made a gruel of the powder for an upset stomach, and lozenges for coughs are still sold.

history.text: It is said to have been used to dress gunshot wounds during the American Revolution.

research.text: There are few trials of it alone. In the US it is sold in sore-throat lozenges, and it is classed as generally recognised as safe (GRAS, a US food-safety category).

safety.summary: The slime (mucilage) can slow the absorption of medicines taken by mouth, so it is taken 1 to 2 hours apart from them. The whole bark was once used to end pregnancies, so it is avoided in pregnancy.
safety.ethics: Stripping a tree's bark kills it, and Dutch elm disease has hit the species hard. United Plant Savers lists it as at-risk.

entries.what: A North American elm whose inner bark turns slimy in water, made into gruels and throat lozenges.

entries.name: Sound bath and singing bowls
parts: bowls, gongs, tuning forks, voice, drums
entries.uses: Bells and metal bowls are struck in Buddhist temples across Asia; in Japan a bowl called a rin marks the start and end of a sitting. Modern sound baths, which grew from the 1970s on, ring bowls and gongs around people lying down, for deep relaxation. In many shamanic traditions a steady drumbeat carries the drummer on a journey.

lore.text: Nada Brahma: in Indian thought, the world is sound. Each chakra has its own tone. In Siberia the drum is the shaman's horse.

research.text: Small studies found people felt less tense and in a better mood after a session.

safety.summary: Loud gongs, and headphones at high volume, can damage hearing. Some people find the sounds unsettling.

entries.cat: Lie down, a stranger hits a bowl, you feel better. Cats invented this. It's called purring.
entries.what: Lying still while bowls, gongs and other instruments ring around you.

sources.title: NCCIH, health topics A-Z (practices: acupuncture, massage, yoga, tai chi, meditation)

entries.name: Sour jujube seed
entries.uses: In Chinese medicine it is the chief seed for sleeplessness, a racing heart and night sweats that come from "deficiency", meaning the body is running low rather than overheated. It is the heart of Suan Zao Ren Tang, a formula from a medical classic of around 200 CE.

research.text: A few small trials of the formula for insomnia.

safety.summary: It can cause drowsiness and may add to sleeping pills and other sedatives.

entries.what: The seed of a wild, sour jujube, the classic Chinese herb for sleepless nights.

sources.title: Bensky, Clavey & Stöger, Chinese Herbal Medicine: Materia Medica, 3rd ed. (2004)

entries.name: Soursop (graviola)
entries.uses: In the Caribbean people drink the leaf as a calming bush tea for sleep and fevers. The fruit is eaten fresh and made into juice.

history.text: Internet claims about cancer drove a large trade in the leaf. In 2014 the FDA sent warning letters to graviola sellers over cancer claims.

research.text: Annonacin, a compound in the leaf and seeds, damages nerve cells in the lab. In Guadeloupe, heavy use of soursop is linked with an unusual form of parkinsonism.

safety.summary: Heavy or long-term use of the leaf and seeds is linked with nerve damage. It is avoided with Parkinson's disease.

entries.what: A spiky green tropical fruit with sweet white flesh; its leaves are brewed into a bush tea.

sources.title: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database
US FDA, dietary supplement warnings and safety information

entries.name: Spagyrics (alchemical herbalism)
parts: whole plant separated into "mercury, sulphur and salt" and rejoined
preps: fermentation, distillation, calcination of the residue to white ash, recombination
entries.uses: An alchemical method, still practised. The plant is separated into its spirit (the alcohol from fermenting it), its soul (the essential oil) and its body (salts from the burned residue). Each part is purified and then they are recombined, with the work timed by planetary hours.

history.text: The word was coined in the 16th century from Greek words meaning "to draw apart" and "to gather". German and Swiss pharmacies revived spagyric remedies in the 20th century.

lore.text: Solve et coagula, "dissolve and bind together". Each herb is worked under its ruling planet.

research.text: Not studied in clinical trials.

safety.summary: Distilling and burning down the residue mean open flame near alcohol vapour, which catches fire easily.

entries.cat: Burning a plant to ash and putting it back together. Finally, a human project with some style.
entries.what: Alchemical plant medicine: a herb is taken apart into spirit, oil and salt, purified and rejoined.

sources.title: Maud Grieve, A Modern Herbal (1931)
research/HEALING-CODEX.md in this repo (fuller prose on many of these items)

entries.name: St John's wort
entries.uses: In Europe it is traditionally taken for melancholy and nervous exhaustion, and the red oil (the flowers steeped in olive oil) goes on wounds, burns and nerve pain. The EMA accepts standardised extracts for mild to moderate depression as a well-established use. In Russia zveroboi was called "the herb against 99 diseases".

history.text: Named for St John's Day (24 June), when it flowers. It is said to have been the wound herb of the crusading Knights of St John.

lore.text: Fuga daemonum, "the devil's flight": hung over doors and burned on Midsummer bonfires to drive evil away. The red sap is the Baptist's blood, and the devil pricked the holes in its leaves in a rage.

research.text: Many trials and a Cochrane review found standardised extracts did better than a dummy pill for mild to moderate depression, and about as well as standard antidepressants with fewer side effects. Results varied a lot between countries and products.

safety.summary: It has some of the most dangerous herb-drug interactions known. It makes many medicines stop working: the contraceptive pill, ciclosporin and tacrolimus, HIV drugs, warfarin, digoxin, methadone, many cancer drugs and anaesthetics. With SSRIs and other antidepressants, or triptans, it can cause serotonin syndrome, a dangerous overload of serotonin. It makes skin burn more easily in the sun. Not for people with bipolar disorder, and stop it well before surgery.
contra: any prescription medicine (check the interaction list)
safety.pets: Grazing animals that eat it get sunburn-like skin damage. Listed as toxic to dogs, cats and horses.
safety.regulatory: Prescription-only in Ireland since 2000. Sold with interaction warnings across the EU.

entries.cat: Lovely Midsummer herb. Also cancels your pill and fights your antidepressants. Read the red box, genius.
entries.what: A yellow-flowered meadow plant, the best-known herbal medicine for low mood, with serious drug interactions.
entries.know: Hold a leaf up to the light and you can see tiny clear oil glands like pinholes. They gave it the name perforatum, "pierced".

entries.name: Star anise
entries.uses: In Chinese medicine it is used to warm the belly and ease cold, cramping pain and wind. It is one of the spices in Chinese five-spice powder, and it simmers in the broth of Vietnamese pho.

lore.text: A star for luck, carried or placed on altars. In Japan its poisonous cousin, shikimi, is planted at Buddhist temples and graves, and its bark is burned as incense.

research.text: Its shikimic acid is a real drug starting material. The teas have not been studied.

safety.summary: Japanese star anise (Illicium anisatum) is a nerve poison that looks almost the same, and it has turned up in star anise teas. Babies given star anise tea for colic have had seizures. No star anise tea for babies.

entries.what: A star-shaped brown seed pod from a Chinese evergreen, tasting of liquorice; a key flavour in pho.
entries.know: Tamiflu, the flu drug, was first made from shikimic acid taken from star anise.

sources.title: US FDA, dietary supplement warnings and safety information
Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database

entries.name: Steam inhalation
parts: hot water with herbs, oils or boiled potatoes
preps: towel over the head above a bowl
entries.uses: Traditionally used for blocked noses and chesty colds: chamomile, eucalyptus or pine over hot water, or the Russian habit of breathing over a pot of boiled potatoes under a blanket.

research.text: A Cochrane review of heated, humid air for colds found no clear benefit.

safety.summary: Scalds are common, especially in children, who should never do it. Essential oils in the steam can set off asthma.

entries.what: Breathing the steam from a bowl of hot water, often with herbs, under a towel over the head.

sources.title: Cochrane Library systematic reviews

entries.name: Stevia
entries.uses: The Guaraní of Paraguay and Brazil used the leaf to sweeten mate and bitter medicines.

history.text: Japan took it up widely as a sweetener in the 1970s.

research.text: Purified steviol glycosides are approved sweeteners: GRAS in the US since 2008, and approved in the EU as E 960 since 2011. The whole leaf is less studied.

safety.summary: Purified forms are generally safe. Whole leaf and crude extracts are not approved as food additives in the US or the EU.

entries.what: A small Paraguayan shrub whose leaves taste far sweeter than sugar, now a sweetener used worldwide.
entries.know: Purified stevia sweeteners are about 200 to 300 times sweeter than sugar.

sources.title: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database

entries.name: Sulphur (homeopathic)
entries.uses: In homeopathy, a deep constitutional remedy (one chosen for a person's lifelong type, not a passing symptom) for hot, itchy, burning skin that is worse for washing and warmth, and for the "ragged philosopher": warm, untidy and full of ideas. It is called the king of polychrests (remedies with a very wide range of use). The sulphur is first triturated, ground for hours with milk sugar, before dilution.

research.text: No good trials show a reliable effect beyond placebo.

safety.summary: At usual potencies the pills contain no measurable sulphur.

entries.what: Plain sulphur, ground and diluted into one of homeopathy's broadest constitutional remedies.
entries.know: Sulphur is the brimstone of "fire and brimstone".

sources.title: Australian NHMRC, Information Paper: evidence on the effectiveness of homeopathy (2015)

entries.name: Sumac
entries.uses: In Middle Eastern medicine its sour, puckering taste is used for upset stomachs and loose stools. Indigenous peoples of North America soak staghorn sumac berries in cold water to make a pink "lemonade".

research.text: A few small trials looked at blood sugar and cholesterol.

safety.summary: Food sumac is safe. Poison sumac (Toxicodendron vernix), with white berries, is a different plant that burns the skin like poison ivy. Food sumac's berries are red.

entries.what: Dried, crushed red berries with a lemony sour taste, sprinkled on Middle Eastern salads and kebabs.

sources.title: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database

entries.name: Sutherlandia (cancer bush)
entries.uses: Khoi, Nama and Zulu healers traditionally give the bitter tea as a tonic for wasting, weakness and a long list of ailments. In the AIDS years it was widely handed out as a tonic in South African clinics.

research.text: A 2015 South African trial in adults with HIV found no change in viral load or CD4 count; two people taking it with the TB drug isoniazid developed tuberculosis. A small study in healthy men found it lowered blood levels of the HIV drug atazanavir by about a fifth.

safety.summary: May lower the levels of some HIV medicines and may clash with TB preventive treatment. Despite the name, it is not a cancer medicine. Not used in pregnancy.

entries.what: A silvery South African shrub with red pea flowers whose bitter leaves are brewed as a tonic tea.

sources.title: van Wyk, van Oudtshoorn & Gericke, Medicinal Plants of South Africa (2009)

entries.name: Sweat lodge (Inipi)
parts: willow-frame lodge, heated stones (grandfathers), water, sage, cedar, sweetgrass
preps: ceremony led by a recognised elder, in rounds
entries.uses: A sacred purification ceremony of many Plains and Woodland nations, led by a recognised elder with prayer and song, in rounds. Water poured on the heated stones fills the lodge with steam. It is a ceremony, not a spa.

history.text: Canada outlawed major Native ceremonies such as the potlatch and Sun Dance until 1951, and the US suppressed Native religion until the American Indian Religious Freedom Act of 1978. In 2009 three people died in an imitation "sweat lodge" at a paid self-help retreat in Sedona, Arizona.

lore.text: The stones are the grandfathers. The lodge is the womb of Mother Earth.

research.text: Not studied.

safety.summary: Heat illness, and deaths when it is run carelessly or for profit. Not with heart disease.
safety.ethics: This ceremony belongs to specific nations. Attend only when invited, and only with a recognised leader.

entries.what: A sacred purification ceremony of many Native nations, held in a small dark lodge over heated stones.

sources.title: Daniel Moerman, Native American Ethnobotany (1998) and the BRIT Native American Ethnobotany database

entries.name: Sweet almond oil
preps: a few drops in warm milk (Unani)
entries.uses: In Unani (the Greek-Arabic medicine of India) and in Ayurveda it is traditionally massaged into the head for the brain and for sleep, and a few drops are taken in warm milk for constipation. It is also used as a gentle skin and baby oil.

research.text: Little clinical study.

safety.summary: Not for people with nut allergy. Bitter almond oil is a different product: unless it has been treated, it contains cyanide compounds and is poisonous.

entries.what: A light, mild oil pressed from sweet almonds, used for massage and on babies' skin.
entries.know: An almond is the seed inside the stone of a fruit, a close cousin of the peach.

sources.title: National Formulary of Unani Medicine (India)

entries.name: Sweet basil
entries.uses: Used as a digestive herb in cooking and tea. In South Asia soaked seeds go into summer drinks like falooda, taken to cool the body.

history.text: Basil came to Europe from India through the Middle East and was grown in Greek and Roman gardens.

lore.text: In Italian folk custom a pot of basil on the balcony told suitors a woman was ready to be courted. In Romanian and Moldovan custom, a young man who accepts a sprig of basil from a girl is promised to her. In hoodoo basil draws money and protects the home.

research.text: Its oil contains estragole. Little clinical work.

safety.summary: Food amounts are fine. The seeds swell a lot in liquid; eaten dry or half-soaked they can choke.

entries.what: The soft, sweet-smelling leaf of pesto and Thai stir-fries; its seeds swell into jelly in drinks.

sources.title: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database
Maud Grieve, A Modern Herbal (1931)

entries.name: Sweet clover
entries.uses: Traditionally used for heavy legs, varicose veins and bruises, and in compresses for aching joints. EMA lists a traditional use for heavy legs from minor vein problems.

history.text: Farmers in North Dakota and Alberta lost cattle to "sweet clover disease" in the 1920s. In 1940 a Wisconsin lab isolated dicoumarol, which forms when the hay spoils. It led to warfarin, sold first as a rat poison (1948) and then as a medicine.

research.text: The plant contains coumarin, the compound behind the sweet-hay smell. Small trials have looked at vein complaints.

safety.summary: Coumarin can damage the liver in high doses. Mouldy plant contains dicoumarol, which thins the blood. Not to be combined with warfarin or other blood thinners. Not for people with liver disease or bleeding disorders. Avoid in pregnancy.

entries.what: A tall yellow-flowered clover that smells of fresh hay; dried, it is used for heavy, tired legs.
entries.know: Mouldy sweet clover hay made cattle bleed to death on the North American prairies in the 1920s, and the culprit led to the blood thinner warfarin.

sources.title: European Medicines Agency, Committee on Herbal Medicinal Products (HMPC) monographs
Sokolov & Zamotaev, Handbook of Medicinal Plants (USSR, 1984/1990)

entries.name: Sweet violet
entries.uses: In Unani medicine (the Greek-Arabic tradition of South Asia and the Middle East) banafsha syrup is taken to cool fevers and soothe coughs, and violet oil is rubbed on the head for headache and to bring sleep.

history.text: Greek poets called Athens "violet-crowned", and the violet was its emblem. Napoleon's followers wore violets and called him Corporal Violet, the one who would come back in spring.

lore.text: Violets stand for modesty and for the faithful dead. In some tellings Persephone was picking violets when the lord of the underworld carried her off.

research.text: A few small trials in Iran tested violet oil drops in the nose for insomnia.

safety.summary: The flowers and leaves are gentle. The roots and seeds make you vomit.

entries.what: A small, sweet-scented purple spring flower, made into syrup and oil in Persian and Unani medicine.
entries.know: Violet scent contains ionones, which briefly switch off the nose's smell receptors, so the perfume seems to come and go.

sources.title: National Formulary of Unani Medicine (India)
Maud Grieve, A Modern Herbal (1931)

entries.name: Sweet wormwood
entries.uses: In Chinese medicine qing hao "clears summer heat" and is used for fevers that come and go. A 4th-century Chinese handbook of emergency recipes told readers to soak a handful in cold water, wring out the juice and drink it.

history.text: That line guided a Chinese research team in the 1970s to artemisinin, which won the 2015 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Artemisinin combination drugs are now the first-line malaria medicines worldwide.

research.text: Artemisinin is an established drug. Tea or powder of the herb does not give a reliable dose, and the WHO advises against using them for malaria.

safety.summary: Malaria is an emergency. The WHO says never to use the tea or leaf powder in place of proper malaria drugs: it can fail, and it may breed resistance to artemisinin.

entries.what: A feathery, sweet-smelling annual from China, the plant behind the malaria drug artemisinin.
entries.know: Most artemisinin still comes from the farmed plant, but since 2013 some has also been made with brewed yeast.

sources.title: WHO monographs on selected medicinal plants (vols 1-4)
NIH National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health, Herbs at a Glance
