entries.name: Sweetgrass
entries.uses: Anishinaabe, Lakota, Cree and many other peoples braid it and burn it in ceremony to bring in good spirits, often after sage has cleansed the space. In Poland and Russia a blade of the grass flavours bison-grass vodka.

history.text: One of the four sacred medicines (tobacco, sage, cedar and sweetgrass) of many Great Lakes and Plains nations.

lore.text: Sweetgrass is the hair of Mother Earth. It is braided in three strands, for mind, body and spirit.

research.text: It contains coumarin, the compound behind its vanilla-like smell. It has not been studied as a medicine.

safety.summary: Coumarin can harm the liver and thin the blood, so it is limited in foods. Heavy smoke indoors irritates the lungs.
safety.ethics: It is a sacred medicine. If you buy it at all, buy from Indigenous growers.

entries.what: A sweet-smelling wild grass that many Indigenous nations of North America braid and burn in prayer.
entries.know: Polish bison-grass vodka, flavoured with the same grass, was kept out of the US for decades over its coumarin.

sources.title: Daniel Moerman, Native American Ethnobotany (1998) and the BRIT Native American Ethnobotany database

entries.name: Syrup and oxymel
parts: herbs with honey, sugar or vinegar
preps: herb decoction thickened with sugar or honey
entries.uses: Traditionally taken for coughs and used to make bitter herbs easier to swallow. The Greek oxymel (honey and vinegar) and Persian sekanjabin are drunk to cool the body in summer.

history.text: The Arabic sharab, "drink", gave English both syrup and sherbet.

research.text: Honey itself has some evidence for children's coughs: a Cochrane review found it probably eases them a little more than no treatment.

safety.summary: Never give honey to babies under one year (botulism). Sugar matters with diabetes.

entries.what: Herbs kept in honey or sugar, or in honey and vinegar (an oxymel), to make a remedy taken by the spoon.
entries.know: Sekanjabin, the Persian mint oxymel, is still drunk in Iran with iced water on hot days, or used as a dip for lettuce leaves.

sources.title: Ibn Sina (Avicenna), The Canon of Medicine (al-Qanun fi al-Tibb, 1025)
Maud Grieve, A Modern Herbal (1931)
Cochrane Library systematic reviews

entries.name: Talbina (barley porridge)
entries.uses: In Prophetic medicine a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari reports that talbina comforts the heart of the sick and lifts some of their sorrow. Aisha had it cooked for the family when someone died, and it is still given to mourners and people getting over illness.

research.text: Barley beta-glucan, a soluble fibre, lowers LDL cholesterol, and regulators accept that claim. A small Malaysian trial in 30 older adults in a care home found lower depression and stress scores after three weeks of talbina.

safety.summary: Contains gluten, so it is avoided with coeliac disease.

entries.what: A soft barley porridge cooked with milk and honey, given to the sick and grieving in Prophetic medicine.
entries.know: The name comes from laban, milk, because the porridge is white and soft like milk.

sources.title: Ibn Qayyim al-Jawziyya, Medicine of the Prophet (al-Tibb al-Nabawi, 14th c.)
https://sunnah.com/bukhari:5417
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3593710/

entries.name: Tamanu
entries.uses: Across Polynesia, Southeast Asia and Madagascar the kernels are dried for weeks until they turn sticky with oil, then pressed. The oil is traditionally rubbed on cuts, burns, rashes and scars.

lore.text: In Tahiti and elsewhere in Polynesia the tree was planted on marae (sacred open-air temples), and its hard wood was carved for canoes and bowls.

research.text: Mostly lab studies, plus small cosmetic tests on skin.

safety.summary: The oil is for skin only and is not to be swallowed. People with nut allergies can react to it.

entries.what: A thick green oil pressed from the nut of a seaside tree that grows from East Africa to Polynesia.

sources.title: Kamakau, Ka Poʻe Kahiko and the Hawaiian lāʻau lapaʻau literature; Bishop Museum ethnobotany

entries.name: Tangerine peel
entries.uses: In Chinese medicine aged peel "regulates qi", keeping energy in the belly moving downward, and "dries damp", the heavy, sticky fluid said to build up with poor digestion. It is traditionally used for bloating, nausea and a cough full of phlegm. Peel from Xinhui in Guangdong, aged for years and sometimes decades, is the most prized and is cooked into duck, beef and red-bean soup.

research.text: Studied mainly as a food.

safety.summary: Thought to be gentle in food amounts.

entries.what: Dried, aged mandarin peel, a Chinese kitchen spice and one of the most common herbs in formulas.

sources.title: Bensky, Clavey & Stöger, Chinese Herbal Medicine: Materia Medica, 3rd ed. (2004)

entries.name: Tansy
entries.uses: In the past people took it against worms and strewed it on floors to keep flies and moths away. Today it is used only outside the body, hung up or rubbed on as an insect repellent.

history.text: In England, tansy cakes and puddings were eaten at Easter. In colonial New England it was packed into coffins and winding sheets to keep the dead fresh.

lore.text: Ganymede, the story goes, was given tansy to make him immortal, and the name may come from the Greek athanasia, "immortality". A herb of eternal life and of the dead.

research.text: Rich in thujone, a known poison.

safety.summary: Poisonous taken by mouth (thujone): it causes seizures and liver and kidney damage, and deaths are recorded. Not for internal use.
safety.pets: Toxic to pets.

entries.what: A tall roadside plant with flat yellow button flowers and a strong camphor smell. Poisonous to eat.

sources.title: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database
Maud Grieve, A Modern Herbal (1931)

entries.name: TB-500 (thymosin beta-4 fragment)
parts: synthetic fragment of thymosin beta-4, a natural repair protein
entries.uses: Sold and discussed for muscle tears, tendon injuries, stiffness and recovery, often injected together with BPC-157 (the "Wolverine stack" on forums). It was used on racehorses before it reached gyms.

history.text: Racing laboratories began finding it in horses in the early 2010s, and it spread from stables to gyms and clinics.

research.text: Animal studies on wound, heart and eye repair. Small human trials used the whole natural protein (as eye drops and a wound gel), not the TB-500 fragment sold online, and none led to an approval. The injected fragment has not been studied in people.

safety.summary: Safety in people is unknown. It carries the same theoretical tumour worry as BPC-157, since thymosin beta-4 drives cell movement and blood-vessel growth. Grey-market vials carry the same risks of wrong dose, contamination and infection.
safety.regulatory: As of November 2026: not approved for people anywhere. FDA listed it in Category 2 in 2023 and took it off in April 2026. In July 2026 the FDA advisory committee voted 8 to 6, with one abstention, to allow it in pharmacy compounding; FDA has not added it to the list, but the October 2026 HHS enforcement policy covers single-ingredient injectable TB-500 on prescription (blends such as BPC-157 with TB-500 are outside it). Prohibited by WADA (S2) and in horse racing.

entries.what: A lab-made piece of thymosin beta-4, a repair protein found in most body cells, sold as an injectable recovery peptide.
entries.know: Thymosin beta-4 was at the centre of Australia's Essendon football doping case; in 2016 the sports court banned 34 past and present players.

entries.name: Tea tree oil
entries.uses: Bundjalung people of northern New South Wales traditionally crushed the leaves and breathed them in for coughs and colds, and laid them on wounds as a poultice. Today the oil is dabbed, diluted, on spots, fungal nails, athlete's foot and dandruff, and is added to gels and shampoos.

history.text: Commercial production took off in the 1920s after a Sydney chemist reported that the oil killed germs. Australian soldiers in World War II are often said to have carried it in their first-aid kits.

research.text: Trials found a 5% gel reduced mild acne spots, and stronger solutions gave some relief in athlete's foot.

safety.summary: Never swallow it: in children it has caused confusion, unsteadiness and coma. It can cause skin allergy, especially once old and oxidised. Never put it in an ear with a perforated eardrum.
safety.pets: Highly toxic to cats and dogs, even on the skin; it has caused weakness, paralysis and deaths.

entries.cat: You put tea tree on me, I put you in the will as "deceased". Highly toxic to cats.
entries.what: A sharp-smelling oil from the leaves of an Australian paperbark tree, put on spots and fungal skin.

sources.title: NIH National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health, Herbs at a Glance
Tisserand & Young, Essential Oil Safety, 2nd ed. (2014)

entries.name: Temazcal
parts: dome of stone or adobe, hot volcanic stones, herbs, water
preps: ceremony led by a temazcalero, with songs and herbs; rounds in darkness
entries.uses: Used by Aztec and Maya peoples, and today across Mexico, for purification, healing and recovery after childbirth. A guide (temazcalero) pours water and herbs onto hot volcanic stones in the dark, with songs and prayers, over several rounds. The dome is the womb of the earth.

history.text: Spanish colonial authorities tried to stamp it out. Ancient sweat baths survive at Maya sites such as Piedras Negras in Guatemala.

lore.text: Coming out of the dome is a rebirth from the earth's womb.

research.text: Little study.

safety.summary: Heat illness, especially with poorly trained "ceremony" operators. Not with heart disease or after alcohol. Cautioned in pregnancy.

entries.what: A Mexican steam-bath ceremony in a low dome of stone or adobe, from Aztec and Maya tradition.
entries.know: The Aztecs honoured the goddess Temazcalteci, "grandmother of the bathhouse", as the temazcal's patron.

sources.title: Schultes & Hofmann, Plants of the Gods (1979/2001)

entries.name: Tesamorelin
entries.uses: Prescribed to reduce excess deep belly fat in people with HIV who have lipodystrophy (fat that builds up in the wrong places, partly from older HIV drugs). Also prescribed off-label in longevity clinics.

history.text: FDA approved it as Egrifta in November 2010.

research.text: Trials found less deep belly fat in this group while on the drug; the fat tends to return after stopping. It has not been tested as an anti-ageing drug.

safety.summary: Joint pain, swelling from fluid, injection-site reactions, raised blood sugar and occasional allergic reactions. Prescription only.
safety.regulatory: As of November 2026: a prescription medicine in the US. Prohibited in sport by WADA (S2).

entries.what: A licensed daily injection that raises growth hormone, prescribed for belly fat in people with HIV.

entries.name: Thai massage (nuad thai)
parts: compression, stretching along sen energy lines, herbal compress (luk pra kob)
entries.uses: Practised in Thailand at temples like Wat Pho and in family lineages. The giver presses along the sen (energy lines) and moves the receiver into yoga-like stretches. Steamed balls of herbs (luk pra kob) are pressed on aching muscles. Nuad Thai joined UNESCO's intangible heritage list in 2019.

research.text: Small trials on back pain and headache.

safety.summary: Forceful stretching can cause injuries. Not with osteoporosis or soon after surgery.

entries.what: A floor massage from Thailand, done fully clothed, mixing pressure with assisted stretches.
entries.know: Wat Pho temple in Bangkok has stone tablets from the 1830s carved with massage diagrams; they are on UNESCO's Memory of the World register.

sources.title: NCCIH, health topics A-Z (practices: acupuncture, massage, yoga, tai chi, meditation)

entries.name: The 12 tissue salts
parts: twelve mineral salts (calc fluor, calc phos, calc sulph, ferrum phos, kali mur, kali phos, kali sulph, mag phos, nat mur, nat phos, nat sulph, silica) at 6X
preps: small lactose tablets dissolved on the tongue
entries.uses: Used in biochemic practice, begun by a German physician in the 1870s. It teaches that illness follows a shortage of one of twelve mineral salts in the body's cells, and that small doses (6X) restore the balance. Mag phos is taken for cramps, kali phos for nervous exhaustion, ferrum phos at the start of a fever.

research.text: No good trials show a reliable effect beyond placebo.

safety.summary: The tablets are lactose (milk sugar), a problem for people with lactose intolerance.

entries.what: Twelve mineral salts in tiny lactose tablets, a German offshoot of homeopathy from the 1870s.
entries.know: Each salt has a number, from No. 1 (calc fluor) to No. 12 (silica), and many shops sell them by number.

sources.title: Australian NHMRC, Information Paper: evidence on the effectiveness of homeopathy (2015)

entries.name: Thyme
entries.uses: In Europe thyme tea and syrup are taken for coughs and colds; the EMA accepts this as a traditional use, and thyme mixed with ivy or primrose root is sold as cough syrup in pharmacies. People also drink it after meals and use it in mouthwashes. Thymol, from thyme oil, is one of the active ingredients in Listerine.

history.text: Thyme is said to have been used in Egyptian embalming, and Roman soldiers are said to have bathed in thyme water for courage. In Russia wild thyme is the Mother of God's herb, laid by the icons on the feast of the Dormition in late August.

lore.text: Fairies live in beds of wild thyme. A sprig under the pillow keeps nightmares away. Ladies stitched a sprig of thyme on knights' scarves for courage.

research.text: A few trials found thyme-ivy and thyme-primrose syrups cut down coughing fits in acute bronchitis.

safety.summary: Kitchen amounts are fine. The oil burns the skin and the lining of the mouth if used undiluted, and is not to be swallowed. Strong extracts may affect blood thinners.

entries.what: The small-leaved kitchen herb and its wild cousin, brewed as a tea and syrup for coughs.

entries.name: Thymosin alpha-1
entries.uses: Prescribed in China and several dozen other countries (not the US) for hepatitis B and C and alongside vaccines and cancer care. Sold in longevity clinics for "immunity".

research.text: Trials in hepatitis and sepsis, of mixed quality. A large trial in China, published in 2025 with about 1,100 sepsis patients, found no drop in deaths at 28 days.

safety.summary: Generally tolerated in trials, with some injection-site irritation. Because it stirs the immune system, it works against immunosuppressant drugs.
safety.regulatory: As of November 2026: approved in China and other countries; not FDA-approved. FDA took it off Category 2 in September 2024 when the nomination was withdrawn, and FDA staff advised against adding it to the compounding list at a December 2024 meeting. It is not on that list.

entries.what: A peptide first found in the thymus gland, licensed in China and elsewhere to rouse the immune system.
entries.know: It was first isolated from calf thymus in the 1970s.

entries.name: Ti leaf
preps: leaves on the forehead for fever
entries.uses: In Hawaii a cool leaf is traditionally laid on the forehead for fever and headache. The leaves are worn as lei and hula skirts, wrapped around food for the imu (earth oven), and planted around houses for protection and good luck. Kahuna (priests and expert healers) used ti in blessing and cleansing ceremonies.

lore.text: Ti is sacred to Lono, god of rain and harvest, and to Laka, goddess of hula. A leaf worn or carried in a pocket is said to keep harm away, and a ti hedge marks a protected home.

research.text: Not studied.

safety.summary: Laying the leaves on skin and wrapping food in them is gentle. There is little safety data for eating other parts of the plant.
safety.pets: Toxic to cats and dogs: vomiting, drooling and loss of appetite, and dilated pupils in cats.

entries.what: A tall tropical shrub with long glossy leaves, sacred in Hawaii and used for wrapping food, skirts and protection.
entries.know: Hawaiians baked the sweet root in earth ovens, and after European contact it was distilled into a liquor called ʻōkolehao.

sources.title: Kamakau, Ka Poʻe Kahiko and the Hawaiian lāʻau lapaʻau literature; Bishop Museum ethnobotany
ASPCA Animal Poison Control, toxic and non-toxic plants

entries.name: Tincture
preps: plant macerated in alcohol (often 25–70%) for weeks, pressed and strained
entries.uses: Herbs are traditionally soaked in spirit for weeks; the tincture keeps for years and is quick to take. Russian pharmacies sell valerian, motherwort, hawthorn and calendula tinctures. In Ayurveda, arishtas and asavas are herbal wines made by fermenting herbs with sugar or jaggery.

history.text: Medieval distillers steeped herbs in aqua vitae ("water of life", early distilled spirit). Tinctures filled the 19th-century pharmacopoeias, the official lists of medicines.

research.text: Alcohol draws out different compounds from water.

safety.summary: It contains alcohol. Take care with children, in pregnancy, with liver disease and in recovery from drinking. Avoid it with metronidazole and disulfiram, and take care with sedatives.

entries.what: Herbs soaked in alcohol for weeks and then strained, making a strong extract that keeps for years.
entries.know: Polish families make nalewki, sweet fruit and herb liqueurs, and age them for years like wine.

sources.title: Maud Grieve, A Modern Herbal (1931)
Sokolov & Zamotaev, Handbook of Medicinal Plants (USSR, 1984/1990)

entries.name: Tirzepatide
parts: synthetic dual GIP and GLP-1 hormone analogue
entries.uses: Prescribed for type 2 diabetes, long-term weight management and obstructive sleep apnoea (breathing that stops in sleep) with obesity. Also sold illegally online as "tirz" vials.

history.text: FDA approved it as Mounjaro for diabetes in May 2022, as Zepbound for weight in November 2023, and for sleep apnoea in December 2024.

research.text: Large trials found average weight loss of about 20% at the top dose over 72 weeks. A head-to-head trial published in 2025 found more weight loss than with semaglutide, about 20% against 14%.

safety.summary: Much like semaglutide: stomach upset, pancreatitis, gallbladder disease, dehydration and the thyroid C-cell tumour warning. Blood sugar can drop too low with insulin or sulfonylureas. It can make the contraceptive pill less reliable for four weeks after starting and after each dose rise, so a non-oral or barrier method is advised for those weeks. Counterfeit pens and vials circulate.
safety.regulatory: As of November 2026: prescription only. FDA declared the tirzepatide shortage over in October 2024 (confirmed that December), and pharmacies' grace period for making copies ended in February and March 2025. The 2026 crackdown on mass-marketed copies and the proposed 503B exclusion cover it as they cover semaglutide. Allowed in sport (on WADA's monitoring list for 2027).

entries.what: A weekly injection copying two gut hormones (GIP and GLP-1), licensed for diabetes, weight and sleep apnoea.

sources.title: FDA, concerns with unapproved GLP-1 drugs used for weight loss
https://www.orrick.com/en/Insights/2026/05/FDA-Moves-to-Shut-the-Door-on-Large-Scale-Compounding-of-GLP1-Drugs
https://www.world.rugby/keep-rugby-clean/news/1048285/wada-publishes-2027-prohibited-list

entries.name: Tremella (snow fungus)
preps: sweet soup with pear and goji
entries.uses: In Chinese medicine it is simmered into sweet soups with pear, jujube and goji to moisten the lungs and skin. It is said to have been the beauty secret of Yang Guifei, a famous Tang dynasty consort. Skincare brands now add it to creams.

research.text: Lab and cosmetic studies show its sugars (polysaccharides) hold water well on skin. There are no real health trials.

safety.summary: An everyday food.

entries.what: A clear, frilly white jelly mushroom, cooked into sweet dessert soups in China.

sources.title: Bensky, Clavey & Stöger, Chinese Herbal Medicine: Materia Medica, 3rd ed. (2004)

entries.name: Trikatu
parts: black pepper, long pepper, dry ginger
entries.uses: In Ayurveda it is taken with honey before meals to kindle agni (the digestive fire) and to burn ama (undigested residue, thought to clog the body). It is also used to clear kapha, the heavy, damp energy behind phlegm and slow digestion. Practitioners add a pinch to other formulas so the body takes them up.

research.text: A few studies, mostly in animals, found it raised the absorption of other drugs and herbs.

safety.summary: Too heating for people with reflux or stomach ulcers. Through piperine it can raise blood levels of many drugs.

entries.what: An Ayurvedic powder of three hot spices: black pepper, long pepper and dry ginger.

sources.title: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India

entries.name: Triphala
entries.latin: Phyllanthus emblica + Terminalia chebula + T. bellirica
preps: powder in warm water at night
entries.uses: One of the most-used Ayurvedic formulas. People stir the powder into warm water at night as a gentle bowel tonic and a rasayana (a rejuvenating tonic). It is said to balance all three doshas (Ayurveda's energies of air, fire and water). It was also used as an eyewash, which is not advised now.

history.text: It is named in the classical Sanskrit medical texts, including the old surgical compendium, from about 2,000 years ago.

research.text: Small trials have looked at constipation, and at triphala mouthwash for gum health.

safety.summary: It loosens stools. The amla in it may slow blood clotting and lower blood sugar. Imported products have been found with heavy metals, so buy tested ones.

entries.what: A powder of three dried Indian fruits, the best-known Ayurvedic formula, usually taken in warm water at bedtime.

sources.title: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India
Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database

entries.name: True lilies (Easter, tiger, stargazer)
preps: bai he bulb in Chinese soups (L. brownii)
entries.uses: In Chinese medicine the cooked bulb (bai he) is traditionally used to moisten the lungs in a dry cough and to calm the shen (the spirit, the mind's settled presence). It is also cooked into sweet soups with lotus seeds. In Europe the lily is the flower of purity, of Mary and of funerals.

lore.text: The white Madonna lily is the flower of the Annunciation, and the Easter lily stands for the resurrection.

research.text: Eaten as a food in China; little modern research.

safety.summary: For people the cooked bulb is a food. For cats every part of a true lily or a daylily, even pollen licked off the fur or water from the vase, causes sudden kidney failure and death. Keep lilies out of homes with cats.
safety.pets: Deadly to cats (kidney failure). A cat that has touched a lily is an emergency, even before it looks ill.

entries.cat: Lilies. In this house? Over my dead body. Literally.
entries.what: Garden and bouquet lilies, harmless-looking flowers that are deadly to cats, though their bulbs are eaten in China.

sources.title: ASPCA Animal Poison Control, toxic and non-toxic plants
Bensky, Clavey & Stöger, Chinese Herbal Medicine: Materia Medica, 3rd ed. (2004)

entries.name: Turkey tail
entries.uses: In Chinese medicine yun zhi is used for damp (a heavy, sticky state in the body) and for immunity. In Japan a purified extract, PSK, is given alongside chemotherapy.

research.text: Japanese trials of PSK given with chemotherapy for stomach and bowel cancer found a modest gain in survival in some studies, according to the US National Cancer Institute's review.

safety.summary: Usually well tolerated. PSK has caused nausea, dark stools and darkened fingernails. It may interact with chemotherapy.

entries.what: A thin bracket fungus on dead wood, striped in browns like a turkey's fanned tail.
entries.know: An extract of it, PSK (sold as Krestin), was approved in Japan in 1977 and became one of the country's best-selling cancer medicines.

sources.title: National Cancer Institute PDQ: medicinal mushrooms, mistletoe and other complementary topics
Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database

entries.name: Turmeric
entries.uses: In Ayurveda (India's classical medicine) it is used for the skin, joints, digestion and wounds, and as a blood purifier. Before an Indian wedding, family rub turmeric paste on the bride and groom at the haldi ceremony. In Indonesia women drink jamu kunyit asam, turmeric with tamarind, around their periods. In Hawaii ʻōlena juice is dropped in sore ears and sniffed for blocked sinuses.

history.text: People in India have cooked with it for about 4,000 years, and the classical Ayurvedic texts describe it. Polynesian voyagers carried it across the Pacific as a canoe plant, one of the few plants they took to new islands.

lore.text: In Hindu homes it is the gold of good fortune, offered to Ganesha and Lakshmi. A thread dyed in turmeric is tied at weddings in South India as the sign of marriage.

research.text: Curcumin, the main yellow compound, is poorly absorbed by the body. Many small trials on joint pain and inflammation markers gave mixed results. In lab tests curcumin often shows up as active when it isn't, which muddies a lot of the early work.

safety.summary: Food amounts are fine. Strong curcumin supplements, especially ones with piperine (black pepper extract) added, have been linked to liver injury. Supplements may raise bleeding risk with blood thinners and can make gallstones worse. Some imported turmeric, notably in Bangladesh, has been coloured with lead chromate, a lead poison.

entries.cat: Golden milk. Golden everything. Your liver didn't order the extract with pepper.
entries.what: A bright orange root in the ginger family, dried and ground into the yellow powder in curries.
entries.know: Pots from the Indus Valley city of Farmana, more than 4,000 years old, still held traces of turmeric and ginger.

sources.title: NIH National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health, Herbs at a Glance
NIH LiverTox: herbal and dietary supplements
Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database

entries.name: Uva ursi (bearberry)
entries.uses: In Europe the leaf is taken in short courses for the burning and urgency of a bladder infection; the EMA accepts its traditional use for mild, recurring lower urinary tract infections in women once anything serious has been ruled out. Many Native nations of North America smoke the leaves in kinnikinnick, a smoking blend.

history.text: It appears in the Physicians of Myddfai, medieval Welsh medical texts from the 13th century. It is still sold in German pharmacies.

research.text: Its arbutin breaks down into hydroquinone, which kills bacteria, in the urine. One small trial in 57 women found fewer repeat infections over a year.

safety.summary: Short courses only, because hydroquinone may harm the liver over time. Not for people with kidney disease, or for children. It can turn urine greenish-brown.

entries.what: A low evergreen shrub of northern heaths whose leathery leaves are taken in short courses for bladder trouble.
entries.know: Uva ursi is Latin for "bear's grape", and bears really do eat the red berries.

sources.title: European Medicines Agency, Committee on Herbal Medicinal Products (HMPC) monographs
Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database
Daniel Moerman, Native American Ethnobotany (1998) and the BRIT Native American Ethnobotany database

entries.name: Vacha (calamus)
entries.uses: In Ayurveda tiny amounts of the root are given for speech, memory and clarity, once even to small children, a practice now discouraged. It is also used in nasya (medicine taken through the nose). Cree and other nations chew it for sore throats and stamina, and Slavic folk medicine uses it as a bitter.

lore.text: The name means "that which speaks". It is said to open the channels of the mind.

research.text: Beta-asarone, a compound in most types of calamus, causes cancer in lab animals.

safety.summary: Indian and other Asian types carry the most beta-asarone, European types less, and the North American type little or none. Beta-asarone causes cancer in animals, and calamus is banned as a food additive in the US.
safety.regulatory: The US FDA banned calamus in food in 1968.

entries.what: A reed-like marsh plant with a spicy, scented root, used in Ayurveda for speech and memory.
entries.know: Cree people call it wîhkês; in English it is often called rat root there, because muskrats eat it.

sources.title: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database
Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India
Daniel Moerman, Native American Ethnobotany (1998) and the BRIT Native American Ethnobotany database

entries.name: Valerian
entries.uses: In Europe valerian is taken for sleeplessness and nervous tension; the EMA accepts some extracts as a well-established use for mild nervous tension and trouble sleeping, and other forms as a traditional use. In Russia valerian drops are the classic thing to reach for when someone is upset.

history.text: The Greeks called it phu, for its smell. In Britain it was given for shell shock in the First World War and for air-raid nerves in the Second.

lore.text: Cats go wild for the smell of the root, so in Russian it is "cat root". Rat-catchers are said to have baited traps with it, and some say the Pied Piper carried it. A herb of love and of making up after quarrels.

research.text: Sleep trials disagree. Some reviews find a possible small effect, others none.

safety.summary: It can cause drowsiness, a groggy morning and headache, and rarely liver injury. Don't drive after taking it. It adds to sedatives, benzodiazepines, alcohol and anaesthetics.

entries.cat: Smells like old socks and makes me roll on the floor. You're welcome to it after.
entries.what: A tall meadow plant with pale pink flowers whose strong-smelling root is taken for sleep.

entries.name: Vanilla
entries.uses: The Totonac and Aztecs used it to flavour their cacao drinks, as a perfume and as a love charm. Today people wear the scent to feel calm and attractive.

history.text: In 1841 a 12-year-old enslaved boy on Réunion island worked out how to pollinate the flowers by hand, which made vanilla farming possible outside Mexico. Madagascar now grows most of the world's vanilla.

lore.text: In Totonac legend, a princess and her lover were killed for running away together. Where they fell, a vanilla orchid grew, climbing the tree that sprang from his blood.

research.text: Studied only as a scent and flavour.

safety.summary: Food amounts are fine.

entries.what: The dried, fermented seed pod of a climbing Mexican orchid, the source of real vanilla flavour.
entries.know: Each vanilla flower opens for only one day, so growers pollinate every one by hand.

sources.title: James A. Duke, Handbook of Medicinal Herbs (2nd ed., 2002) and Dr. Duke's Phytochemical and Ethnobotanical Databases

entries.name: Varuna
entries.uses: In Ayurveda the bark is boiled into a decoction (Varunadi kwath) for urinary stones and bladder complaints.

lore.text: It shares its name with Varuna, the Vedic god of the waters.

research.text: Animal studies on stone formation.

safety.summary: There is little safety data. It is cautioned in kidney disease.

entries.what: A small riverside tree of India with three-part leaves; its bark is boiled for the bladder and kidneys.

sources.title: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India

entries.name: Vervain
entries.uses: In European folk practice vervain tea is drunk to relax tense, overdriven nerves, and as a bitter to wake up a slow digestion.

history.text: The Romans swept their altars with sacred plants they called verbenae. Roman envoys carried vervain as a sign of peace when they went to talk with an enemy.

lore.text: The herb of enchantment. Roman writers say the magi gathered it at the rising of the Dog Star, "when neither sun nor moon is seen", and that the Gauls used it to cast lots and tell the future. Later it was worn against witchcraft and evil spirits, and put into love charms.

research.text: Very little work in people.

safety.summary: It is said to stir the womb, so it is avoided in pregnancy. Its tannins may lower iron absorption.

entries.what: A wiry plant with tiny lilac flowers, sacred in Roman religion and a classic herb of European magic.
entries.know: An old English charm was said over vervain while picking it: "Hallowed be thou, vervain, as thou growest on the ground."

sources.title: Maud Grieve, A Modern Herbal (1931)
Bensky, Clavey & Stöger, Chinese Herbal Medicine: Materia Medica, 3rd ed. (2004)

entries.name: Vetiver
entries.uses: In India the roots are traditionally woven into screens (khus tatti) that hang in doorways and are kept wet, so the hot summer wind blows through cool and scented. Khus syrup is stirred into summer drinks. In aromatherapy the oil is used as a grounding, calming scent.

history.text: Haiti produces about half of the world's vetiver oil.

research.text: Only animal studies so far, on anxiety.

safety.summary: Mild.

entries.what: The root of a tall Indian grass, with a deep, smoky, earthy scent.
entries.know: Vetiver roots grow 3 to 4 metres straight down, so the grass is planted around the world to hold soil on slopes.

sources.title: Tisserand & Young, Essential Oil Safety, 2nd ed. (2014)
Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India

entries.name: Vitamin A
entries.uses: Taken as a supplement, in cod liver oil and in multivitamins; given in high doses by public health programmes to young children in countries where deficiency is common.

history.text: Night blindness was treated with liver in ancient Egypt. Vitamin A was the first vitamin given a letter, in the 1910s.

research.text: Deficiency is a leading cause of preventable childhood blindness worldwide, and WHO-backed dosing programmes lower child deaths where it is common. In two large trials, beta-carotene supplements raised lung cancer rates in smokers.

safety.summary: Too much preformed vitamin A builds up in the liver: headaches, liver damage and weaker bones. High doses in early pregnancy cause birth defects, so pregnancy supplements use beta-carotene or low doses. Smokers: beta-carotene supplements raised lung cancer risk in trials. Acne medicines like isotretinoin are vitamin A relatives and must not be stacked with it.

entries.what: A vitamin your eyes, skin and immune system run on, found ready-made in liver and as beta-carotene in orange vegetables.
entries.know: Polar bear liver holds so much vitamin A that Arctic explorers who ate it fell seriously ill.

nutrient.low: Poor vision in dim light first, then dry eyes; dry, rough skin; more infections.
nutrient.limit: Preformed vitamin A (retinol, not beta-carotene): US 3,000 mcg a day; EU 3,000 mcg a day.

sources.title: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements, vitamin and mineral fact sheets (health professional versions)
National Academies (IOM), Dietary Reference Intakes: tolerable upper intake levels
EFSA, overview of tolerable upper intake levels (2024 update)

entries.name: Vitamin B1 (thiamin)
entries.uses: Taken in B-complex tablets; given routinely to people who drink heavily, because alcohol drains it.

history.text: Beriberi swept through Asian navies and prisons when polished white rice became the staple. A Japanese navy surgeon cut it sharply in the 1880s by adding barley and meat to rations.

research.text: Deficiency diseases (beriberi, and Wernicke's brain damage in heavy drinkers) are well understood. Extra thiamin for people who aren't low shows little effect.

safety.summary: Very safe by mouth. Heavy drinking, some diuretics, raw fish (it holds an enzyme that breaks thiamin down) and large amounts of tea or coffee lower thiamin.

entries.what: The B vitamin that turns food into energy for nerves and muscles; whole grains and pork are rich in it.

nutrient.low: Tiredness, irritability, numb or burning feet, poor memory; in heavy drinkers, confusion and unsteady walking.
nutrient.limit: No upper limit set (US or EU): excess leaves in urine.

sources.title: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements, vitamin and mineral fact sheets (health professional versions)
National Academies (IOM), Dietary Reference Intakes: tolerable upper intake levels

entries.name: Vitamin B12
entries.uses: Taken by vegans, older people and people on certain medicines; B12 shots are a fixture of "energy" clinics.

history.text: Pernicious anaemia was fatal until 1926, when patients were fed huge amounts of raw liver; the discovery won a Nobel Prize in 1934.

research.text: Supplements reliably fix deficiency; for people with normal levels, extra B12 shows no energy benefit.

safety.summary: Very safe. Absorption falls with age and with metformin, stomach-acid medicines (PPIs) and long-term nitrous oxide use, which inactivates B12 and has caused nerve damage in young recreational users.
interactions: proton pump inhibitors and H2 blockers

entries.what: A cobalt-containing vitamin from animal foods that keeps nerves and blood cells healthy; vegans need it from supplements or fortified foods.
entries.know: B12 is made only by microbes, never by plants or animals themselves.

nutrient.low: Tiredness, pale skin, tingling or numb hands and feet, poor memory, a smooth sore tongue, low mood.
nutrient.limit: No upper limit set (US or EU).

sources.title: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements, vitamin and mineral fact sheets (health professional versions)
National Academies (IOM), Dietary Reference Intakes: tolerable upper intake levels

entries.name: Vitamin B2 (riboflavin)
entries.uses: Taken in B-complex tablets; high-dose riboflavin is also sold for migraine prevention.

history.text: Isolated in the 1930s from milk, where it gives whey its greenish-yellow glow.

research.text: A few small trials found high-dose riboflavin cut migraine frequency; quality is limited.

safety.summary: Very safe; bright yellow urine is harmless.

entries.what: A yellow B vitamin used to burn food for energy; it is why high-dose vitamins turn urine bright yellow.
entries.know: Riboflavin glows yellow-green under ultraviolet light.

nutrient.low: Cracks at the corners of the mouth, a sore red tongue, scaly skin by the nose.
nutrient.limit: No upper limit set (US or EU).

sources.title: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements, vitamin and mineral fact sheets (health professional versions)
National Academies (IOM), Dietary Reference Intakes: tolerable upper intake levels

entries.name: Vitamin B3 (niacin)
entries.uses: Taken in B-complex tablets; high-dose nicotinic acid was once prescribed for cholesterol; niacinamide is common in skin creams; NAD-boosting forms are sold for ageing.

history.text: Pellagra killed thousands in the American South in the early 1900s, where people lived on untreated corn. In Mexico, corn was soaked in lime (nixtamalisation), which frees its niacin, and pellagra was rare.

research.text: High-dose niacin raised "good" cholesterol, but large trials found no fewer heart attacks, and it fell out of use. Nicotinamide lowered new skin cancers in people with a history of them in one Australian trial.

safety.summary: Doses above the limit cause flushing, itching and stomach upset; slow-release high doses have caused serious liver damage. Can raise blood sugar and uric acid (gout).

entries.what: A B vitamin the body uses in hundreds of energy reactions; in big doses it makes your skin flush hot and red.

nutrient.low: Pellagra, in its full form: rough dark skin where the sun hits, diarrhoea, confusion.
nutrient.limit: From supplements: US 35 mg a day; EU 10 mg nicotinic acid, 900 mg nicotinamide.

sources.title: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements, vitamin and mineral fact sheets (health professional versions)
National Academies (IOM), Dietary Reference Intakes: tolerable upper intake levels
EFSA, overview of tolerable upper intake levels (2024 update)

entries.name: Vitamin B5 (pantothenic acid)
entries.uses: Taken in B-complex tablets; panthenol is in skin creams, nappy-rash ointments and shampoos.

history.text: Its name comes from the Greek "pantothen", from everywhere, because it is in nearly every food.

research.text: Panthenol creams soothe minor skin irritation in small studies; oral supplements show little for people who eat normally.

safety.summary: Very safe; very large doses can cause diarrhoea.

entries.what: A B vitamin found in almost every food, used to build coenzyme A, the body's fuel-handling molecule.

nutrient.low: Almost never seen; in starvation, "burning feet" and numbness.
nutrient.limit: No upper limit set (US or EU).

sources.title: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements, vitamin and mineral fact sheets (health professional versions)
National Academies (IOM), Dietary Reference Intakes: tolerable upper intake levels

entries.name: Vitamin B6
entries.uses: Taken in B-complex tablets and magnesium-B6 blends; prescribed with doxylamine for pregnancy sickness in several countries; sold for PMS.

history.text: Australia's medicines regulator logged about 250 nerve-damage reports from 2023 to late 2025, many from people who didn't know their products held B6. From June 2027, stronger B6 products there will be sold only in pharmacies.

research.text: Good evidence for pregnancy nausea (with doxylamine); mixed for PMS.

safety.summary: Long-term high doses damage nerves: numbness, tingling and burning in hands and feet, clumsy walking. It has happened at doses well under the US limit, from several products stacked together (multivitamins, magnesium blends, energy drinks). Check every label you take.

entries.what: A B vitamin used for over a hundred enzyme jobs, from making brain messengers to building red blood cells.

nutrient.low: Sore cracked lips, a sore tongue, low mood, confusion, anaemia.
nutrient.limit: US 100 mg a day; EU 12 mg a day (EFSA lowered it in 2023 because of nerve damage reports).

sources.title: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements, vitamin and mineral fact sheets (health professional versions)
National Academies (IOM), Dietary Reference Intakes: tolerable upper intake levels
EFSA scientific opinion on the tolerable upper intake level for vitamin B6 (2023)
https://www.tga.gov.au/news/safety-updates/medicines-containing-vitamin-b6-pyridoxine-pyridoxal-or-pyridoxamine

entries.name: Vitamin B7 (biotin)
entries.uses: Sold in "hair, skin and nails" supplements, often at doses hundreds of times the daily need.

history.text: Raw egg whites hold a protein (avidin) that locks biotin away; "egg-white injury" in rats led to its discovery in the 1930s.

research.text: Biotin helps people who are truly deficient; there's little evidence it improves hair or nails in people who aren't.

safety.summary: High-dose biotin throws off many blood tests, including thyroid and heart (troponin) tests, giving falsely high or low results; the FDA has warned about missed heart attacks. Stop it a few days before blood tests and tell the lab.

entries.what: A B vitamin used to process fats and sugars, heavily marketed for hair and nails.

nutrient.low: Rare: thinning hair, a red scaly rash around eyes, nose and mouth, brittle nails.
nutrient.limit: No upper limit set (US or EU).

sources.title: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements, vitamin and mineral fact sheets (health professional versions)
US FDA, dietary supplement warnings and safety information

entries.name: Vitamin C
entries.uses: Taken by the gram at the first sneeze around the world; added to foods as an antioxidant (E300).

history.text: Scurvy killed more sailors than battles in the age of sail. A 1747 trial by a British naval surgeon found citrus fixed it; the navy issued lemon (later lime) juice from 1795, giving British sailors the nickname "limeys".

research.text: Cochrane: regular vitamin C slightly shortens colds (about 8% in adults) but doesn't prevent them for most people; taking it only once a cold starts showed no clear effect.

safety.summary: Large doses cause diarrhoea and wind. Long-term high doses raise kidney-stone risk, especially in men. It increases iron absorption, a problem in iron-overload disease (haemochromatosis).

entries.what: The vitamin that holds collagen together; without it gums bleed and old wounds reopen, as sailors found out.
entries.know: Humans and other apes and monkeys, guinea pigs and many fruit bats can't make vitamin C; most animals can.

nutrient.low: Tiredness, bleeding gums, easy bruising, slow-healing wounds; full scurvy after weeks with none.
nutrient.limit: US 2,000 mg a day; the EU set no upper limit.

sources.title: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements, vitamin and mineral fact sheets (health professional versions)
National Academies (IOM), Dietary Reference Intakes: tolerable upper intake levels
Cochrane Library systematic reviews

entries.name: Vitamin D
entries.uses: Taken through dark northern winters, and given to babies and older people in many countries; cod liver oil by the spoonful was a Scandinavian and British childhood ritual.

history.text: Rickets bent the legs of children in smoky industrial cities. In the 1920s, cod liver oil and sunlight were shown to fix it.

research.text: Clearly stops and reverses rickets and bone softening. The large VITAL trial (25,000 people) found vitamin D didn't lower cancer or heart disease overall; fracture benefits are small and show up mainly when calcium is given too, in older people who are low or live in care homes.

safety.summary: Too much over months raises blood calcium: thirst, nausea, confusion, kidney damage. Most cases come from high-dose products, mislabelled ones or misread units. Sarcoidosis and some lymphomas make people very sensitive to it.
interactions: steroids and some anticonvulsants lower levels

entries.what: The "sunshine vitamin": your skin makes it in sunlight, and you need it to absorb calcium for bones.

nutrient.low: Bone pain, aching muscles, weakness; in children, soft bent bones (rickets).
nutrient.limit: US 100 mcg (4,000 IU) a day; EU 100 mcg (4,000 IU) a day.

sources.title: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements, vitamin and mineral fact sheets (health professional versions)
National Academies (IOM), Dietary Reference Intakes: tolerable upper intake levels
EFSA, overview of tolerable upper intake levels (2024 update)

entries.name: Vitamin E
entries.uses: Taken as an antioxidant capsule and rubbed on scars and skin; part of the AREDS eye formula.

history.text: Found in 1922 as a factor rats needed to bear young; "tocopherol" is Greek for "bearing offspring".

research.text: Big trials found no protection against heart disease or cancer, and the SELECT trial found more prostate cancer in men taking it. Its skin and scar reputation isn't borne out by trials.

safety.summary: High doses raise bleeding risk, especially with blood thinners and before surgery. Creams can cause skin allergy.

entries.what: A family of fat-soluble antioxidants found in nuts, seeds and plant oils.

nutrient.low: Very rare: nerve and muscle problems, mostly in people who can't absorb fat.
nutrient.limit: US 1,000 mg a day (supplements); EU 300 mg a day.

sources.title: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements, vitamin and mineral fact sheets (health professional versions)
National Academies (IOM), Dietary Reference Intakes: tolerable upper intake levels
EFSA, overview of tolerable upper intake levels (2024 update)

entries.name: Vitamin K
entries.uses: Given as a shot to newborns in most countries to stop a rare bleeding disorder; K2 is sold with vitamin D for bones and arteries.

history.text: Named K for "Koagulation", from its 1930s Danish discoverer's paper.

research.text: The newborn shot almost wipes out vitamin K deficiency bleeding (established). K2 for bones and arteries: small, mixed studies.

safety.summary: Vitamin K directly undoes warfarin. People on warfarin need a steady vitamin K intake, without sudden changes from supplements, green smoothies or natto. Newer blood thinners (apixaban, rivaroxaban) don't work this way.
interactions: warfarin and other vitamin K antagonists

entries.what: The clotting vitamin: your blood needs it to seal a cut. Leafy greens are full of it.
entries.know: Natto, Japan's sticky fermented soybean breakfast, is the richest food source of K2.

nutrient.low: Easy bruising and bleeding; in newborns, sudden bleeding in the gut or brain.
nutrient.limit: No upper limit set (US or EU).

sources.title: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements, vitamin and mineral fact sheets (health professional versions)
National Academies (IOM), Dietary Reference Intakes: tolerable upper intake levels

entries.name: White horehound
entries.uses: Traditionally boiled into syrups and hard candy for coughs, and taken as a bitter before meals to wake up the appetite. The EMA lists traditional use for coughs with colds, mild indigestion and loss of appetite.

history.text: Horehound candy was a staple of 19th-century American general stores. Older herbals say Egyptian priests called it the "seed of Horus".

research.text: Its bitter compound, marrubiin, has been studied in the lab and in animals. There are hardly any human trials.

safety.summary: Large amounts are said to upset heart rhythm and lower blood sugar, so take care with heart rhythm drugs and diabetes medicines. Avoid in pregnancy; it was once used to bring on periods.

entries.what: A woolly, grey-green mint-family herb with a very bitter taste, boiled into old-fashioned cough sweets.
entries.know: The name comes from Old English hāre hūne, "hoary herb", for the white down on its leaves.

sources.title: European Medicines Agency, Committee on Herbal Medicinal Products (HMPC) monographs
Maud Grieve, A Modern Herbal (1931)

entries.name: White peony root
entries.uses: In Chinese medicine bai shao nourishes the blood and "softens the liver", the system said to keep muscles and tendons supple and moods even. In Kampo (Japan's own form of Chinese herbal medicine) it is paired with licorice as Shakuyaku-kanzo-to, traditionally given for sudden muscle cramps such as night leg cramps.

lore.text: In China the peony is the king of flowers. In Greece it was named for Paeon, the healer of the gods.

research.text: Shakuyaku-kanzo-to has been studied for leg cramps in Japan, including in liver disease and dialysis.

safety.summary: It can loosen the stools. The licorice in Shakuyaku-kanzo-to can raise blood pressure and drop potassium, sometimes badly, with long use.

entries.what: The peeled, boiled root of the garden peony, a staple of Chinese and Japanese herbal formulas.
entries.know: The city of Luoyang in China has held a peony festival every spring since 1983.

sources.title: Bensky, Clavey & Stöger, Chinese Herbal Medicine: Materia Medica, 3rd ed. (2004)
Japan Ministry of Health, Kampo formulas approved for national health insurance (148 formulas)

entries.name: White sage
entries.uses: Several California Native nations, including the Chumash, Tongva and Cahuilla, burn white sage in ceremony for purification and prayer. Some also drink it as a tea for colds and use it in sweat lodges.

history.text: For about a century US rules banned many Native ceremonies, smudging among them. The American Indian Religious Freedom Act of 1978 finally protected the right to practise them.

lore.text: In ceremony the smoke carries prayers up and clears what lingers. It belongs to living cultures, not to a decor trend.

research.text: Only lab work on its scented oils.

safety.summary: The smoke irritates the lungs, especially for people with asthma, babies, birds and cats.
safety.pets: Smoke harms birds and cats.
safety.ethics: Wild hillsides in Southern California are being stripped by commercial poachers. Tribal groups ask non-Natives not to buy wild-harvested white sage, and to burn garden herbs (rosemary, garden sage, juniper) for their own cleansing. Many consider calling it "smudging" outside Native ceremony to be appropriation.

entries.cat: Not yours. Buy rosemary, light that, and keep your hands off the hillside.
entries.what: A silvery sage from the hills of Southern California, burned in ceremony by the Native nations there.
entries.know: Bees love it: white sage honey is one of California's prized honeys.

sources.title: United Plant Savers, Species At-Risk list
Daniel Moerman, Native American Ethnobotany (1998) and the BRIT Native American Ethnobotany database
research/HEALING-CODEX.md in this repo (fuller prose on many of these items)

entries.name: Wild cherry bark
entries.uses: Cherokee, Iroquois and many other nations used the bark for coughs and colds. It went into American pharmacy syrups for dry, tickly coughs.

history.text: Wild cherry syrup was a standard American cough syrup from the 1800s. The "cherry" taste of cough medicine today echoes it.

research.text: The bark contains prunasin, which releases cyanide in the body. There are almost no clinical studies.

safety.summary: Bark, leaves and pits can all release cyanide. Only properly dried and prepared bark is used, for short spells. The leaves and pits are toxic.
safety.pets: The leaves (wilting ones most of all), bark and pits are toxic to dogs, cats, horses and cattle.

entries.what: The inner bark of the American black cherry tree, long cooked into syrups for dry coughs.

sources.title: Daniel Moerman, Native American Ethnobotany (1998) and the BRIT Native American Ethnobotany database
Maud Grieve, A Modern Herbal (1931)
ASPCA Animal Poison Control, toxic and non-toxic plants

entries.name: Wild lettuce
entries.uses: In the 1800s the dried sap, called lactucarium, was sold as a gentle sleep and cough remedy and listed in official drug books (pharmacopoeias).

history.text: The Egyptian fertility god Min's sacred lettuce was a tall cultivated cousin, prized for its milky white sap.

research.text: No good trials in people.

safety.summary: Large amounts cause poisoning: sweating, a racing heart, dizziness and hallucinations. It is sold online with exaggerated claims. It adds to sedatives and alcohol.

entries.what: A tall, bitter wild cousin of garden lettuce whose milky sap was dried as a mild sleep remedy.
entries.know: Its old nickname is "lettuce opium", but the dried sap contains no opium.

sources.title: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database
Maud Grieve, A Modern Herbal (1931)

entries.name: Wild yam
entries.uses: Native and settler healers used the root for colic and menstrual cramps. Today creams are sold as "natural progesterone".

history.text: Diosgenin from Mexican yams was the raw material for the first contraceptive pills in the 1950s.

research.text: The body cannot turn diosgenin into progesterone, and creams contain none unless it has been added.

safety.summary: Generally mild, with possible hormone effects.
safety.ethics: United Plant Savers lists wild yam as at-risk.

entries.what: A twining North American yam whose root is used for cramps; creams of it are sold as "natural progesterone".

sources.title: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database
NIH National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health, Herbs at a Glance
United Plant Savers, Species At-Risk list

entries.name: Willow bark
entries.uses: For thousands of years people chewed or boiled willow bark for pain, fevers and aching joints. The EMA accepts it as a well-established use for short spells of low back pain.

history.text: Ancient Sumerian and Egyptian texts mention willow for pain. In 1763 an English vicar wrote to the Royal Society that willow bark brought down fevers. Its salicin led chemists to aspirin, first made by Bayer in 1897.

lore.text: Willow is the weeping tree of grief and of moon goddesses. In Russia Palm Sunday is Willow Sunday: pussy-willow branches are blessed in church and children are tapped with them for health.

research.text: Trials and a Cochrane review found modest relief of low back pain. It acts more slowly and gently than aspirin.

safety.summary: It contains salicylates, aspirin's relatives. Avoid it with an aspirin allergy, aspirin-sensitive asthma, stomach ulcers or blood thinners, and before surgery. Never give it to children or teenagers with a fever or viral illness (risk of Reye's syndrome, a rare brain and liver illness). It adds to aspirin, NSAIDs (ibuprofen-type painkillers) and methotrexate.
safety.pets: Toxic to cats, which cannot clear salicylates.

entries.what: The bark of white willow and its cousins, the plant source behind aspirin.
entries.know: Salix, the Latin name for willow, gave us salicin, salicylic acid and acetylsalicylic acid, which is aspirin.

entries.name: Wintergreen oil
entries.uses: Indigenous peoples of eastern North America traditionally drank a mild tea of the leaves for aches. The oil is the active ingredient in many sports rubs and liniments.

research.text: Methyl salicylate is a well-known painkilling rub, sold over the counter.

safety.summary: One teaspoon of the oil holds about as much salicylate as 20 adult aspirin tablets. Swallowed, it has killed toddlers and adults, and overuse of rubs on the skin has caused fatal poisoning. Not for people allergic to aspirin or taking blood thinners. Like aspirin it is not for children and teenagers, because salicylates are linked to Reye's syndrome, a rare and serious illness of the brain and liver. Avoid in pregnancy.
safety.pets: Toxic to cats, which are very sensitive to salicylates, and to dogs.

entries.what: A minty oil from a small American woodland plant; it is almost pure methyl salicylate, the active part of many muscle rubs.
entries.know: Wintergreen mints give off blue sparks when you crunch them in the dark, and the wintergreen oil makes the glow brighter.

sources.title: Tisserand & Young, Essential Oil Safety, 2nd ed. (2014)

entries.name: Witch hazel
entries.uses: Haudenosaunee, Cherokee, Menominee and other nations used the bark for swellings, bruises and sores. Today people dab witch hazel water on spots, piles (haemorrhoids) and minor skin irritation, and the EMA accepts these as traditional uses.

history.text: Forked branches were used as water-dowsing rods. "Witch" here comes from Old English wice, meaning pliant or bendy.

research.text: Small trials on skin irritation and haemorrhoids found modest effects.

safety.summary: It is gentle on skin. It is not for drinking.
safety.regulatory: In the US witch hazel is an approved over-the-counter astringent.

entries.what: A small North American shrub whose bark and twigs make the clear witch hazel water sold in drugstores.
entries.know: The ripe seed pods snap open and shoot their seeds up to about 10 metres, hence the name snapping hazel.

entries.name: Wood betony
entries.uses: In European folk practice the tea was drunk for headaches, nervous tension and digestion. Anglo-Saxon healers used it for many complaints.

history.text: A Roman treatise credited to the emperor Augustus's physician lists 47 uses for it. An Italian proverb says "sell your coat and buy betony".

lore.text: Planted in churchyards against ghosts, and carried against "elf-sickness" and bad dreams.

research.text: Hardly studied.

safety.summary: Gentle. It is avoided in pregnancy, as it was said to stir the womb.

entries.what: A purple-flowered meadow plant of the mint family, once one of Europe's most trusted herbs.

sources.title: Maud Grieve, A Modern Herbal (1931)

entries.name: Wormwood
entries.uses: In Europe it is one of the bitterest herbs there is, taken for poor appetite, indigestion and worms. The EMA accepts its traditional use for appetite and indigestion. It flavours vermouth (from the German Wermut) and absinthe.

history.text: It is said to appear in the Ebers Papyrus, an Egyptian medical scroll from about 1550 BCE. Absinthe, the Green Fairy, was the drink of 19th-century Paris. Switzerland, the US and France banned it between 1910 and 1915; it came back under thujone limits in the EU from 1988, in Switzerland in 2005 and in the US in 2007.

lore.text: In Russia polyn is the bitter herb of Rusalka week in early summer, carried against the rusalki, the water spirits. A rusalka asks "wormwood or parsley?": answer "wormwood!" and she flees. Chornobyl is the Ukrainian name of mugwort, a close cousin, and some read the disaster as the star Wormwood of the Book of Revelation.

research.text: Two small trials in Crohn's disease reported promising results. Its thujone content is limited by law.

safety.summary: Thujone can cause seizures and kidney damage with the oil or high doses. Short use only, and never the essential oil. People allergic to daisy-family plants may react. Not for people with epilepsy or kidney disease. It may affect seizure medicines.
safety.regulatory: The EU and US limit thujone in food and drink.

entries.what: A silvery, fiercely bitter shrub that flavours absinthe and gave vermouth its name.
entries.know: Absinthe was blamed for madness, but 2008 tests on bottles from before the bans found thujone well within today's limits.

entries.name: Xiao Yao San (Free and Easy Wanderer)
parts: bupleurum, dong quai, white peony, atractylodes, poria, licorice, ginger, mint
entries.uses: In Chinese medicine it is one of the most prescribed formulas. It is traditionally used when "liver qi" is constrained, meaning stress has knotted the smooth flow of energy and mood, and the "spleen" (digestion) is weak as well. That picture shows up as irritability, low mood, premenstrual tension, tiredness and a poor appetite.

history.text: From the Song dynasty's imperial pharmacy formulary, compiled in the early 1100s.

lore.text: Named after the first chapter of the Zhuangzi, the Daoist classic, about wandering free and easy.

research.text: Trials in China for depression and indigestion. Their quality varies.

safety.summary: It carries the cautions of its licorice (blood pressure, potassium) and dong quai (warfarin). Product quality varies between makers.

entries.what: A classic Chinese herbal formula of eight herbs for stress, low mood and tension before a period.

sources.title: Bensky, Clavey & Stöger, Chinese Herbal Medicine: Materia Medica, 3rd ed. (2004)

entries.name: Yarrow
entries.uses: In Europe people press the leaves on cuts and nosebleeds, drink the tea hot to sweat out a fever, and take it for crampy periods and poor digestion. The EMA accepts its traditional use for poor appetite, stomach and period cramps, and small wounds.

history.text: Its Latin name, Achillea, comes from Achilles. In 1960 yarrow pollen was found with a Neanderthal burial in Shanidar Cave, Iraq, and read as a flower burial; a 2023 study argues burrowing bees probably carried the pollen in.

lore.text: The centaur Chiron taught Achilles to stop his soldiers' wounds bleeding with yarrow. Fifty dried yarrow stalks are the traditional way to cast the I Ching, the Chinese Book of Changes. Sleep with yarrow under the pillow and you will dream of a future love.

research.text: Very little work in people.

safety.summary: It can cause allergy in people sensitive to daisy-family plants, and may make skin more sensitive to the sun. It is said to stir the womb, so it is avoided in pregnancy. It may add to blood thinners and sedatives.

entries.what: A feathery-leaved meadow plant with flat white flower heads, the classic European wound herb.
entries.know: In Sweden yarrow was once brewed into beer in place of hops.

entries.name: Yaupon holly
entries.uses: The Muscogee (Creek), Timucua and other Southeastern nations brewed the roasted leaves very strong as the ceremonial "black drink", taken for purification before councils and rites. It is usually called North America's only native caffeinated plant.

history.text: The Latin name vomitoria came from European observers, who saw ritual vomiting at black drink ceremonies and blamed it on the plant. The vomiting belonged to the rite, not to the leaf.

research.text: It contains caffeine and theobromine.

safety.summary: Caffeine. The red berries are toxic and cause vomiting.

entries.what: A holly of the American South whose leaves hold caffeine, brewed by Native nations as the ceremonial "black drink".
entries.know: Pottery beakers from Cahokia, the great city near today's St Louis, still hold traces of yaupon drink from about 1050 to 1250 CE.

sources.title: Daniel Moerman, Native American Ethnobotany (1998) and the BRIT Native American Ethnobotany database

entries.name: Yellow dock
entries.uses: In European and North American folk practice the root is taken as a gentle laxative, as a "blood cleanser" for skin troubles, and in iron tonics.

history.text: Children rub dock leaves on nettle stings, chanting "dock in, nettle out".

research.text: The root contains anthraquinones (natural laxative compounds). There is little work in people.

safety.summary: It is rich in oxalates, which can feed kidney stones, and a man died of oxalate poisoning after eating a large amount of the leaves. Like other anthraquinone laxatives it is not for a blocked bowel or for long-term use.
safety.pets: Grazing animals that eat a lot of dock can be poisoned by the oxalates.

entries.what: A tall weed with wavy-edged leaves and rusty seed heads, whose yellow root is used as a bitter tonic.

sources.title: Maud Grieve, A Modern Herbal (1931)
Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database

entries.name: Yerba mate
entries.uses: First drunk by the Guaraní people, and now drunk all over Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay and southern Brazil. One gourd is refilled with hot water and passed around the circle, for energy and to take the edge off hunger.

history.text: In the 1600s Jesuit missions in Paraguay grew it on plantations, so it was called "Jesuits' tea".

lore.text: In a Guaraní legend Yasí, the moon, came down to earth and was saved from a jaguar by an old man. She gave him the mate plant in thanks.

research.text: Studied mostly for its caffeine. Drinking mate very hot is linked to cancer of the oesophagus, as with any very hot drink.

safety.summary: Caffeine. Drink it warm, not scalding. Smoke-dried mate can contain PAHs, smoke compounds linked to cancer. It adds to other stimulants and can clash with MAOI antidepressants.

entries.what: The caffeine-rich leaf of a South American holly, sipped through a metal straw from a shared gourd.
entries.know: Argentina made mate its national drink by law in 2013.

sources.title: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, About Herbs database

entries.name: Yew
parts: all parts poisonous except the red aril flesh
entries.uses: Historically planted in churchyards as a tree of death and eternity, and cut for longbows. The cancer drug paclitaxel (Taxol) was found in Pacific yew bark, collected for testing in 1962 and identified in 1971.

lore.text: Churchyard yews are often older than the church beside them. The yew belongs to the dead and to rebirth, because old trees hollow out and grow new trunks from inside.

research.text: Taxanes from yew (paclitaxel, docetaxel) are established cancer drugs.

safety.summary: Deadly. A handful of leaves can stop the heart, sometimes with no warning signs first. The seed inside the red cup is poisonous; only the red flesh is not. Poisoning is an emergency. History and lore only.
safety.pets: Deadly to pets and livestock, horses and cattle above all.

entries.what: A dark evergreen tree with red berry-like cups, planted in churchyards and poisonous except for the red flesh.
entries.know: The Fortingall Yew in Scotland is thought to be 2,000 to 3,000 years old, one of the oldest trees in Europe.

entries.name: Ylang-ylang
entries.uses: In Indonesia the flowers are said to be scattered on the bed of newlyweds. In the Pacific they are worn in garlands and steeped in coconut oil. In aromatherapy the oil is used to calm and as a love scent.

history.text: In the 1800s Macassar hair oil, often scented with ylang-ylang, stained so many chair backs that people covered them with cloths called antimacassars.

research.text: Small trials found lower blood pressure and heart rate after people breathed it in or had it rubbed on the skin.

safety.summary: Too much can cause headache and nausea. It can cause skin allergy.
safety.pets: Pet poison services list it among oils toxic to cats and dogs.

entries.what: A heady, sweet oil from the yellow flowers of a tropical Asian tree, used in perfume and as a love scent.

sources.title: Tisserand & Young, Essential Oil Safety, 2nd ed. (2014)

entries.name: Yoga
entries.uses: In India yoga is a spiritual discipline. Its "eight limbs" run from ethics and posture to breath, meditation and union with the divine. Around the world, postural yoga is practised for flexibility, strength, calm and back pain.

history.text: The Yoga Sutras are usually dated to around 400 CE. Modern postural yoga took shape in early 20th-century India, especially in Mysore in the 1930s, and then spread around the world.

lore.text: Prana (life breath) flows through 72,000 nadis, or channels. Kundalini, a coiled energy, sleeps at the base of the spine and rises through the chakras, the wheels of energy along it.

research.text: Good evidence for chronic low back pain. Moderate evidence for easing symptoms of anxiety and depression.

safety.summary: Injuries come from forcing poses. Headstands and other upside-down poses are cautioned with glaucoma and with uncontrolled high blood pressure. Hot yoga adds heat stress.

entries.what: An Indian practice of postures, breathing and meditation, now done worldwide mostly for fitness and calm.
entries.know: In 2014 the UN declared 21 June the International Day of Yoga; the first was held in 2015.

sources.title: NCCIH, health topics A-Z (practices: acupuncture, massage, yoga, tai chi, meditation)
Cochrane Library systematic reviews

entries.name: Yohimbe
entries.uses: Traditionally the bark is boiled in Cameroon, Gabon and Nigeria as an aphrodisiac and stimulant. Abroad it is sold in sexual performance and fat-burner supplements.

research.text: Yohimbine, the purified prescription drug, had a modest effect on erectile dysfunction in older trials. Tests of yohimbe supplements found many with wrong or missing labelling of how much yohimbine they hold.

safety.summary: Raises heart rate and blood pressure and can cause anxiety and panic. Heart attacks and seizures have been reported. Dangerous with antidepressants, especially MAOIs, and with other stimulants. Not used in pregnancy or with heart disease, anxiety or kidney disease.
safety.regulatory: Banned in foods and food supplements across the EU since 2019 (Regulation 2019/650). Yohimbine is prescription-only in Canada and Australia.

entries.what: The bark of a Central African tree, sold in sex and fat-burning supplements for its stimulant yohimbine.

entries.name: Yokukansan (Yi Gan San)
parts: atractylodes, poria, chuanxiong, uncaria (gou teng), dong quai, bupleurum, licorice
entries.uses: In Kampo (Japan's own form of Chinese herbal medicine) it is traditionally used to calm an overactive "liver", the system said to rule temper and tension. It was first given to children for irritability, crying at night and teeth grinding, with the mother taking it too. In Japan today it is widely given for agitation in dementia.

history.text: A Ming-dynasty Chinese children's formula from 1555 that became a Japanese favourite.

research.text: Several small Japanese trials reported calmer behaviour in dementia. The first full placebo-controlled trial, in Alzheimer's disease (2017), found no overall difference, with some signs of benefit in subgroups.

safety.summary: The licorice in it can drop potassium, which has been reported in older people. It may add to diuretics and heart drugs.

entries.what: A seven-herb Kampo formula for irritability and restlessness, widely given in Japan to people with dementia.

entries.name: Yu Ping Feng San (Jade Windscreen)
entries.uses: In Chinese medicine it is traditionally used to firm up the "protective qi" (wei qi), the energy said to guard the skin like a screen. It is given to people who catch every cold, sweat easily or react to "wind", meaning outside influences such as cold air, colds and allergies. The name pictures a precious screen of jade keeping the wind out.

history.text: Usually traced to 14th-century teaching from the Yuan dynasty, first printed in a collection of 1481.

research.text: Small trials in repeated chest infections and hay fever.

safety.summary: By the tradition's own rule it is not taken during an active fever.

entries.what: A three-herb Chinese formula for people who catch every cold going.

sources.title: Bensky, Clavey & Stöger, Chinese Herbal Medicine: Materia Medica, 3rd ed. (2004)

entries.name: Za'atar
entries.latin: Origanum syriacum (and blends with thyme, sumac, sesame)
entries.uses: In the Levant children eat bread dipped in olive oil and za'atar before school exams "to sharpen the mind". The herb is also brewed as a tea after meals.

history.text: Families have picked wild za'atar on the hills for generations.

lore.text: Most scholars think the hyssop of the Bible, used to sprinkle water in purification rites, was this plant.

research.text: Rich in thymol and carvacrol, its scented oils; studied only in the lab.

safety.summary: Food amounts are fine. The blend usually holds sesame, a common allergy.
safety.regulatory: Israel declared wild za'atar a protected plant in 1977, so picking it in the wild can bring a fine. Many Palestinians see the rule as cutting them off from a family tradition, and Israeli authorities have said they are reconsidering how it is enforced (status checked November 2026).

entries.what: A wild Levantine herb like oregano, and the blend made from it with sumac and sesame.

entries.name: Zagovor (charm healing)
parts: whispered words, water, salt, bread, egg, wax
preps: whispered over water or the patient
entries.uses: Traditionally practised by village healers: znakharki and babki (wise women) and sheptuny ("whisperers"). They whisper charms over water, salt, bread or the sick person. People come to them for fright (ispug), the evil eye (sglaz), hernias, warts, bleeding and babies who cry through the night.

history.text: Charm texts survive among the medieval birch-bark letters of Novgorod. The practice is still common in Ukraine, Belarus and rural Russia.

lore.text: Many charms open with the words "on the sea-ocean, on the island of Buyan, lies the stone Alatyr", the holy stone at the centre of the world. In wax pouring (vylivanie voska) the healer pours melted wax into water held over the patient's head, and the shape it sets in shows what frightened them. In egg rolling, a raw egg is rolled over the body to draw the trouble out.

research.text: Not studied.

safety.summary: Heavy bleeding is an emergency.

entries.cat: Whispering over water. Respect. Still call the ambulance if it's spurting.
entries.what: Slavic charm healing: a village healer whispers old spoken charms over water, salt or the sick person.
entries.know: Buyan, the magic island named in so many charms, is also where Russia's best-loved fairy tale in verse, the Tale of Tsar Saltan (1831), takes place.

entries.name: Zinc
entries.uses: Sucked as lozenges at the start of colds; zinc oxide is the white paste in nappy creams and sunscreens.

history.text: Zinc deficiency was first described in the 1960s in young men in Iran and Egypt who were short and slow to mature on unleavened-bread diets.

research.text: Zinc acetate lozenges may shorten colds slightly in some trials; results are mixed. Zinc with antioxidants (AREDS) slowed one type of macular degeneration.

safety.summary: Long-term doses above the limit cause copper deficiency: anaemia and nerve damage. Lozenges cause nausea and a metal taste. Zinc nasal sprays have caused permanent loss of smell, and the FDA warned against them in 2009.

entries.what: A trace mineral the immune system, skin and sense of taste depend on; oysters hold more than any other food.

nutrient.low: Slow-healing wounds, more infections, hair loss, loss of taste or smell, diarrhoea.
nutrient.limit: US 40 mg a day; EU 25 mg a day.
